title: High-tech Manufacturing Execs Confident of Robust Growth
content: The survey, conducted for UPS by IDC Manufacturing Insights, found that while high-tech companies still favor the strategy of off-shoring as a means to cut labor costs, a large number also have begun "right-shoring." This strategy optimizes the supply chain to take advantage of cost benefits and local resources to achieve the best customer service and overall profit margins. CITC also shows high-tech companies increasingly are entering emerging markets and exploring 3D printing for new product designs and prototypes. IDC polled 516 high-tech executives in North America, Europe, Asia Pacific and Latin America. Respondents were senior high-tech supply chain professionals. The results reveal an ongoing evolution in their supply chains that affects the placement of companies' owned facilities and the selection of their suppliers. "High-tech companies are building more flexibility into their shoring strategies and supply chains so they can respond better to demanding market dynamics," said Dave Roegge, high-tech marketing director at UPS. They're thinking more holistically about their strategies to evaluate their transportation costs and the time it takes companies to deliver goods. “Customer requirements change rapidly, especially considering the steady stream of high-tech innovations and the fact that there is little to no downtime between product generations,” Roegge said. Many of these companies see right-shoring as the solution. Right-shoring balances a number of factors to determine the proximity of sourced materials to production, warehousing and distribution. These metrics could include cost, quality and the time it takes to recover from any operational failures. Forty-five percent of survey respondents said they use right-shoring strategies. Offshoring, which moves manufacturing or assembly to countries with low labor costs, remains the most common strategy. Forty-seven percent of survey respondents said they offshore. Near-shoring, which moves manufacturing or assembly closer to the location of demand, continues to gain in popularity as companies improve service levels, reduce inventory in transit and seek greater control over product quality and intellectual property. Thirty-five percent of respondents said they near-shore. That’s a gain of 25 percentage points since 2010. “It’s about having a nimble supply chain,” Roegge said. Industry export growth continues; new opportunities emerge The growth outlook for high-tech exports is strong, the CITC survey showed. Forty-six percent of the respondents said they expect industry export growth globally to increase at the current pace over the next two years, while 28 percent of them expect faster growth. North American and Latin American respondents were the most optimistic about the future of high-tech exports. High-tech companies have successfully penetrated many emerging markets. Among survey respondents, 71 percent said they are already selling products in China, 45 percent in India and 42 percent in Brazil. Some high-tech markets once considered “emerging” have now emerged, but growth opportunities remain. The top three markets that high-tech companies are planning to enter this year are Brazil, Russia and India. Although new-market penetration is high, barriers to expansion continue to evolve. In 2013, the top barrier to expanding in emerging markets was difficulty assessing the likely appeal of products. In the most recent survey, 35 percent of survey respondents said navigating the regulatory environment was the new highest hurdle to expansion.

title: DB Schenker Launches Weekly Air Cargo Service
content: Designed to serve the oil and gas, automotive and industrial sectors, the new service offers guaranteed capacity with Boeing 747-8 freighters. According to DB Schenker, the service will benefit its U.S. Midwest customers with freight moving from southeast China to the U.S. Southwest, Gulf of Mexico and northern Mexico. Service options provided by the jet cargo division include one to two days (First Class), three to four days (Business Class) and within six days (Economy). Other features include direct main-deck capacity from China, time-definite transit options, consolidation services and land-transport connections. Schenker possesses a national permit covering all Remote Location Filing (RLF) ports nationwide, with trained and licensed brokers across the country. title: Lower Shipping Cost Trumps Desire for Quick Delivery, Study Says
content: According to a survey of Canadian and U.S. shoppers conducted by Purolator International, the cost of shipping was identified most often as the single most important concern in terms of the delivery of their purchases. The survey found that 76 percent of Canadian consumers who made an online purchase from a U.S.-based retailer within the last six months, as well as 63 percent of U.S. online shoppers, identified shipping costs as very important; while 44 percent and 32 percent, respectively, said it was the single most important factor. Most shoppers chose extended delivery times for their online purchases; a majority of Canadians (78 percent) and Americans (58 percent) typically opted for shipping that took four days or longer. A majority of online shoppers in both countries (65 percent Canadian, 55 percent American) demonstrated this willingness to wait, responding that they have “very often” or “always” adjusted their delivery date to a longer period to obtain a reduced cost; and 37 percent and 28 percent, respectively, said the availability of an economical delivery option with a longer delivery time was very important to them. Two-thirds of shoppers in both nations identified a free shipping option as very important in their purchase decision making. “Even in this day and age of ‘I want it now,’ when consumers balance cost versus convenience, they most often fall on the side of cost,” said John Costanzo, president of Purolator International, the United States-based subsidiary of Purolator Inc., a provider of cross-border logistics between the U.S. and Canada. “These findings represent an opportunity for U.S. retailers looking to expand their reach across the northern border, by identifying what helps to drive – or hinder – final purchase decision making,” he added. An estimated $300bn of goods are imported into Canada from the United States annually, Costanzo noted. Shipping cost and time for delivery become especially of issue during the holiday shopping season, as 63 percent Canadians and 49 percent of Americans said they decided against purchasing a holiday item last year because of high shipping costs; 53 percent and 43 percent, respectively, decided against a holiday purchase because it would not be delivered in time. Postal Delivery Option and Cross-Border Concerns Regarding the delivery of their purchases, more than half (58 percent Canada, 57 percent U.S.) of the online shoppers ranked the reputation and reliability of the carrier as a very important consideration. In Canada, 80 percent of consumers surveyed said they would choose postal service delivery in order to obtain a lower shipping cost. A majority of Canadians (62 percent) and Americans (60 percent) said they see postal delivery as an acceptable alternative to other types of carrier delivery services. “Our postal hybrid solution, PuroPost, addresses this consumer preference, giving Canadians making online purchases from U.S. e-tailers a courier-like experience at a cost they are willing to pay,” Costanzo said. “With PuroPost, we can deliver to virtually all of the Canadian population with transit times that match industry standard ground trans-border services,” Costanzo added. Canadians purchasing from across the border are concerned about additional fees as well, with nearly half of those surveyed identifying taxes and tariffs as a very important concern – 15 percent of Canadians surveyed said it was the single most important factor in the decision for their purchase.

title: Pasha Hawaii service boosts links with mainland America
content: Signifying the next stage in the revitalization and development of the Jones Act U.S. fleet, a combined container/ro-ro (con-ro) carrier has been phased into the Hawaii-U.S. mainland trade. Built in Mississippi to a proven European design, the Marjorie C can handle up to 1,400 20-foot-equivalent unit containers, as well as 1,100 vehicles, in trades linking California with the Hawaiian Islands. Commissioned from VT Halter Marine’s Pascagoula yard, the ship made its service debut in early May, loading in San Diego for Honolulu. Owner Pasha Hawaii, a wholly owned subsidiary of family-owned logistics and transport group Pasha, said Marjorie C represented a $200 million commitment to the trade. The number of major competitors in that trade lane dropped from three to just two earlier this year, with Pasha’s acquisition of Horizon Lines’ Hawaiian business and its fleet of four U.S.-flag box ships. Now Pasha competes one-on-one with dominant Hawaiian carrier Matson for business in the lane. The design of Pasha’s new Marjorie C is based on that used by Croatia’s Uljanik Shipyard for a series of multipurpose ro-ros of the Grande Angola class, which were delivered to Grimaldi, the Naples group, between 2008 and 2011. Marjorie C is the second vessel built using an established design from Uljanik. Pasha Hawaii had made its debut in the Hawaiian market in 2005 with its pure car and truck carrier newbuilding Jean Anne. With two versatile ships now dedicated to the traffic, the company has raised its ro-ro sailing frequency from fortnightly to weekly and created a wider offering in scheduled shipping and logistics services for all sizes and types of containers, automotive and rolling cargo and oversize items of freight. “With the addition of Marjorie C, we can now offer customers increased service and capacity between the U.S. West Coast and Hawaii… on vessels providing superior reliability and cargo protection,” said Pasha Hawaii president and chief executive George Pasha IV. © 2026 S&P Global. title:
Think Tank
 RSS
content: West Coast dockside labor and management are certainly giving lip service to a renewed spirit of cooperation, following ratification of a new five-year contract, retroactive to July 1, 2014. Speaking for terminal operators, Pacific Maritime Association president and chief executive officer Jim McKenna said the pact "provides an important framework for the hard work ahead to overcome new competitive challenges and to continue to position the West Coast ports as destinations of choice for shippers worldwide." He insisted that "our interests are aligned" toward ensuring that the region's ports continue to operate efficiently, in order to handle future growth in container volumes. A statement by the International Longshore and Warehouse Union, whose members approved the contract by a margin of 82 percent, said it will “maintain excellent health benefits, improve wages, pensions and job safety protections; limit outsourcing of jobs and provide an improved system for resolving job disputes.” Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti expressed gratitude over conclusion of the talks, thanking, among others, PMA and ILWU leadership “for their partnership in resolving their differences and putting this critical economic engine back on track.” Following tentative approval of the contract by ILWU and PMA negotiators in February of this year, longshore workers began clearing out the massive logjam of ships that were waiting to be unloaded at every major West Coast port. The backup was the direct result of a months-long slowdown by ILWU members, who, in protest of the drawn-out negotiations, and shielded by a lack of arbitration requirements, suddenly began withholding the labor that was needed to work the ships. Now the shipping channels are clear, and manning levels have returned to normal. But the pain that the union wrought hasn’t been forgotten. Importers and exporters had to incur huge expenses to get their products to market, or simply failed to do so. The Agriculture Transportation Coalition (AgTC) has estimated that losses in agricultural sales alone reached $1.75bn per month. Many of the hardest-hit companies were small or medium-sized businesses that operate in highly competitive markets, and can’t afford the slightest disruption to their supply chains. West Coast ports, so dominant in the age of trans-Pacific trade, lost a good deal of market share. Just in the month of April, East and Gulf Coast ports saw volume increases of 12 percent and 20 percent, respectively, while activity at West Coast ports dropped 4 percent, according to the Journal of Commerce. Much of that business will now return to the West Coast, of course, but shippers are paying serious attention to locating permanent alternative gateways. Retailers aren’t climbing aboard the Good Ship Harmony. The National Retail Federation issued a statement declaring itself “happy” to see the contract ratified. At the same time, NRF warned that “it’s not going to be long before we go through this process all over again.” The retailers’ group was even more blunt than that. “The past year was fraught with disruptions, slowdowns and partial shutdowns,” it said. “This is something we will no longer tolerate.” NRF called on negotiators to begin their talks early enough to have a new contract in place before the old one expires, “without active or passive threats to the economy and the millions of jobs dependent on our nation’s ports and supply chain. “The current process is impractical and unsustainable and fails to meet even the most basic requirements of a modern, global supply chain,” NRF said. Industry ought to go even further, to ask a basic question: should a highly compensated group of longshore workers be permitted to hold an entire nation’s economy hostage, when they don’t get their way? Congress just is beginning to tiptoe into the issue. Four Republican senators have introduced S. 1298, a bill that would monitor the impact of port disruptions on the economy, and set the stage for faster government intervention when they occur. The bill’s provisions sound fairly innocuous, calling for the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Bureau of Transportation Statistics to set up a port performance statistics program, and for the Secretary of Transportation to report to Congress on the state of port operations before and after the expiration of a longshore labor contract. The last thing we need is another statistics-stuffed government report that gathers dust on the shelf. But S. 1298, or a similar measure, is just the opening salvo in an effort to prevent a replay of the inexcusable events of the past year. Last time, all ILWU had to do was refuse to extend the arbitration provisions of the previous contract. Then its members could act with impunity, daring management to lock them out and take the blame for the shutdown. Employers didn’t bite, but the impact on the nation’s commerce was no less severe. AgTC has fired off a letter of support to the sponsors of S. 1298, calling it “a strong first step to demonstrating that Congress will not stand by idly and allow U.S. agriculture exports to lose our hard-earned foreign customers, due to port congestion and dysfunction relating to longshore labor negotiations (or any other factors).” Still to come is a means of measuring port productivity and determining the severity of a disruption – all the while preserving the union’s right to a fair wage and collective bargaining. For many whose livelihood depends on a smoothly functioning network of ports, however, the time for change is now.

title: Transportation Industry Drives Toward Non-Petroleum Energy
content: In total, 8.5 percent of fuel used by the transportation sector came from non-petroleum sources in 2014. Biomass from corn-based ethanol - still supported by generous government subsidies - represented the largest non-petroleum energy source and was used primarily to fuel cars and other light vehicles. Use of natural gas to operate pipelines followed close behind. The report also shows smaller but still significant increases in the use of electricity, biodiesel and natural gas in vehicles. Climate change and fluctuating oil prices has made moving away from petroleum when possible a priority for governments and corporations alike. But it’s still uncertain which fuel will be the best and greenest replacement, according to Christopher R. Knittel, an MIT professor of energy economics. Ethanol, natural gas, hydrogen and electricity are all possibilities. "We don’t know where we’ll be 50 years from now," said Knittel. "There are four potential replacement for petroleum, and, ultimately, we don’t what's going to win out."

title: Allcargo Logistics joins Alibaba in e-commerce logistics
content: India’s Allcargo Logistics, through its wholly owned non-vessel-owning common carrier arm Ecu Line, made its first foray into the e-commerce logistics market by entering into a cargo consolidation contract with China online shopping giant Alibaba. “Players in e-commerce business have never been customers of the company and with an intention to leverage the benefits of e-commerce into our business, the company has tied up with Alibaba in logistics space,” Mumbai-based Allcargo said in a written statement. “As per the agreement, the company will provide its logistics services to Alibaba for transporting less-than-container-load consignments from China region to the rest of the world.” The shipping and logistics group’s entry comes as e-commerce volumes in India are set for phenomenal growth and will be worth $100 billion over the next five years. E-commerce spending in the country is projected to have grown by 34 percent (compound annual growth rate) since 2009 to reach $16.4 billion in 2014, according to a recent PwC India report. “The sector is expected to be in the range of $22 billion in 2015. “A significantly low (19 percent) but fast-growing internet population of 243 million in 2014 is an indicator of the sector’s huge growth potential in India,” PwC India said. “It is evident that in absolute terms India’s Internet users are short by only 36 million, compared with 279 million in the U.S. and higher than that in Japan, Brazil and Russia.” Allcargo, which has significantly consolidated its international cargo business via two recent acquisitions such as Miami-based Econocaribe Consolidators in September 2013 and Netherlands-based FCL Marine Agencies in December same year, offers a diversified portfolio of logistics and transportation services that include container freight station and inland depot operation, project cargo handling and trucking. Ecu Line, which became part of the Allcargo group in 2006, operates a worldwide shipping network in about 90 countries across owned offices and third-party agent partnerships, covering more than 4,000 port pairs. The NVOCC operator handled 422,000 20-foot-equivalent units in the fiscal year ended March 31, a year-over-year increase of 26 percent. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: XPO Logistics raising $3.6 billion to finance acquisitions
content: XPO Logistics is raising $1.26 billion from institutional investors and plans to sell $2 billion in bonds to cover the costs of its latest acquisitions and lay the foundation for more. The infusion of funding shows the strength of investor confidence in XPO’s strategy for rapid growth, based largely on acquisition. "We're delighted to deepen our relationships with several of our largest shareholders and also welcome new blue chip investors to XPO,” Bradley S. Jacobs, chairman and CEO of the Greenwich, Connecticut-based international logistics operator, said in a statement. The $3.26 billion will help finance the $3.5 billion purchase in April of Norbert Dentressangle, the Lyon, France-based third-party logistics company, as well as the $100 million acquisition of U.S. drayage carrier Bridge Terminal Transport Services. The Norbert Dentressangle acquisition made XPO a truly global supply chain solutions provider. Norbert Dentressangle is a $5.5 billion company, with offices in 25 countries and 42,600 employees. In 2014, XPO reported $2.4 billion in revenue. When completed, the $3.5 billion acquisition will boost XPO Logistics’ 12-month revenue run to $8.5 billion and give the U.S.-based company access to customers, lanes and markets worldwide. XPO is expected to make more acquisitions in Europe. “I want to stress we’re still in the early innings of growth at XPO Logistics,” Jacobs said in an interview last month. “We believe scale is imperative in this business to serve customers effectively.” The continued support of global institutional investors and shareholders is critical to building that scale. The group providing the $1.6 billion includes the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan, Canada’s Public Sector Pension Investment Board and GIC, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund. These institutions, which made a $700 million investment in XPO last September, increased their holdings and were joined by 12 institutional investors. The separate $2 billion bond offering will consist of senior notes issued in up to four tranches. In addition to covering acquisition-related expenses, some of the funds will be used to pay down Norbert Dentressangle debt, XPO said in a statement. Contact William B. title: CMA CGM Launching New Container Service Between North America, North Europe
content: The group said it will expand its existing trans-Atlantic services with creation of the New Vespucci service, and the addition of a port of call in Baltimore to its Liberty Solo service. The additions will bring to 15 the number of ports covered by the group's combined North America and North Europe services. The New Vespucci service will deploy fifteen 4,500 twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU) vessels with a rotation of Antwerp, Rotterdam, Bremerhaven, Le Havre, Southampton, New York, Norfolk, Charleston, Savannah, Charleston, Norfolk, New York and Antwerp. The service will be operated in cooperation with Hamburg Sud and UASC. The Liberty Solo service includes four of CMA CGM's 1,800 to 2,000-TEU vessels, with a new rotation of Rotterdam, Bremerhaven, Le Havre, New York, Baltimore, Charleston and Rotterdam. title: Maersk Goal to Cut CO2 Emissions 60 Percent Per Container Within Five Years
content: The company has stated that the five year-emission reduction plan will save the climate around 200 million tons of CO2, roughly the amount of emissions of all passenger cars in France over the period of a year. The announcement comes after Chief Commercial Officer Stephen Schueler recently launched the company's 2014 Sustainability Update at a session dedicated to sustainable supply chains. Singe Bruun Jensen, Global Head of Sustainability at Maersk Line, said: “We lead the way in ‘doing more with less. We constantly seek out innovative and commercially viable ways to reduce our environmental impacts, be it CO2 and other air emissions, ballast water, or the materials we use to build our vessels. Therefore, we have set a bold target.”

title: Transport technology firms merge as shippers demand 'mobility'
content: Increased demand for mobile, end-to-end networked computing systems in freight distribution is spurring acquisitions among transportation technology companies. For shippers, that increased merger activity should lead to greater innovation, hopefully driving even greater gains in supply chain efficiency. PeopleNet, a trucking technology company owned by $2.4 billion Trimble, last week purchased Cadec Global, a pioneer in fleet management technology and creator, in 1985, of the first automated truck driver’s log. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Cadec joins a growing family of trucking and distribution technology companies owned by Trimble, including ALK Technologies, TMW Systems and GeoTrac. Trimble, which specializes in asset-locating or positioning technologies, acquired PeopleNet in 2011, TMW in 2012 and ALK in 2013. Since 1978, Trimble has acquired dozens of companies that offer, in some manner, navigation and positioning technology, from marine navigation to rail equipment management and construction and forestry logistics businesses. The technology needs of these disparate industries are converging as asset-tracking and management systems evolve to enable an interconnected “Internet of Things.” The fleet management technology industry will consolidate and become increasingly global, with the total number of onboard telematics units in vehicles in North and South America reaching 12 million by 2018, European technology research firm Berg Insight predicts. That will mean more data flowing from trucks and onboard devices back to motor carriers and fleet operators, with more data on freight being directed to shipper customers, as well. Increased use of onboard technology will also enable more vehicle-to-vehicle communications and interconnected supply chains. The Cadec acquisition gives PeopleNet, which offers Internet-based mobile computing and communications systems for trucking operators, new routes into the foodservice and shipper private fleet markets, Cadec’s target markets since its launch in 1976. Cadec customers include grocery chains such as Publix, Giant and Harris Teeter, food suppliers such as Land O’Lakes and Martin’s, restaurant chains such as Wendy’s and Braum’s and food distributors such as Saldino’s and Kuna Foodservice. The Manchester, New Hampshire-based company also has many fuel distribution customers. The merger comes at a critical point for shippers managing their own distribution fleets. As for-hire truck capacity gets tight and rates rise, shippers with private fleets are wringing as much efficiency and costs as they can from them. Foodservice companies are preparing for tough new regulatory requirements from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Combined, PeopleNet and Cadec Global can offer shippers a broader, integrated mobile computing network, Brian McLaughlin, PeopleNet president, said. “Cadec brings its expertise in world-class web enterprise, business intelligence and back-end analytics tools to the company, while PeopleNet brings its industry-leading mobile platforms, complementary M2M (machine-to-machine) and cloud-based technologies and infrastructure,” McLaughlin said in a statement. Under PeopleNet, Cadec Chief Customer Officer Angela Shue will become general manager of Cadec, working with the combined organization to develop new and innovative products for foodservice and private fleet customers. Other transportation technology companies offering mobility and asset-management services are growing by acquisition. Orbcomm, an asset-tracking company with its own network of low-earth-orbiting satellites, acquired competitor SkyWave in January. Omnitracs, a pioneer in trucking mobile communications, last year acquired XRS, and prior to that, Roadnet Technologies. Acquisition activity is likely to increase in the transportation technology market, as companies look to expand product portfolios they offer and build the scale they need to keep pace with growing customers. title: SEKO takes on Greenbriar as equity investor to speed growth
content: With its management flexibility constrained by a fractured ownership structure, SEKO Logistics has brought in a private equity partner to recapitalize its balance sheet, transform its many local joint venture owners around the globe into shareholders and provide the resources to grow through acquisitions. Greenbriar Equity Group, which specializes in negotiated investments within the global transportation industry, took a substantial, but undisclosed stake in the Chicago-based logistics provider in May in a deal that allows SEKO to buy out local partners in many of its overseas affiliates, which are getting shares in the recapitalized company in place of their ownership in the local companies. “We can accelerate our growth by bringing in a partner like Greenbriar that has the expertise to analyze deals,” said SEKO CEO Bill Wascher. “In the next 24 months, you’re going to see SEKO making strategic acquisitions.” With Greenbriar as an equity partner, SEKO plans to acquire more logistics companies in overseas markets and also to buy trucking assets that will enable it to provide transport services for its customers. “As an asset-light organization, we may acquire last-mile providers in certain markets, mainly in the U.S.” Wascher said in an interview with JOC.com. “The (Greenbriar) private equity investment should help them become more recognizable and maybe more of a market force,” said Dick Armstrong, chairman of Armstrong & Associates, a logistics consultancy. “They have been around for some time now, but have never become a household word.” As a non-vessel-operating common carrier, SEKO saw its business increase sharply in 2014 when port congestion on the West Coast led many small and medium-sized beneficial cargo owners to seek alternate routing for their shipments, especially to the East Coast. “A lot of the BCOs don’t trust the steamship lines as much as they used to with regard to service and visibility, so more and more they are moving to NVOs,” Wascher said. “We are small time in relation to the whole ocean market, but our percentage growth is significantly higher than the market as a whole, because we are grabbing market share.” SEKO invested heavily to centralize its NVOCC business in 2013 after it saw its U.S. market share decline in 2012. In 2014 its global ocean freight volume jumped by more than 40 percent and by 38 percent in the U.S. “The recapitalization will give us added resources to grow even faster over the next five years,” said Jose Quesada, SEKO’s vice president of ocean services. “Our strong growth is due in part from centralization of the product, along with strategically moving away from being part of associations and not moving full container loads via co-loaders,” said Jose Quesada, SEKO’s vice president of ocean services. “Now we’re doing everything direct under our own NVOCC.” As an NVOCC SEKO ships about 100,000 twenty-foot-equivalent units annually. Imports through West Coast ports increased by 9 percent last year, and exports by 6 percent. East Coast shipments grew faster, with imports up 15 percent and export by 8 percent. Despite the settlement of the contract with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union this year, SEKO saw its volume of ocean freight imports moving through the East Coast through April 15 increase by 10 percent year-over-year, while West Coast imports increased by 6 percent. “More cargo is shifting to the East Coast because shippers are nervous about the West Coast,” Wascher said. “This year everybody thinks the West Coast is going to be a debacle again, because a number of owner operators went out of business and they are afraid the hours of service rules will affect the availability of trucks.” With its global ownership structure realigned through the Greenbriar investment, SEKO is already starting to replicate some of the supply-chain management services developed in the U.S. in overseas markets. For example, it is setting up a control tower in Ireland for its Medtech demo program, which manages the inventory of high-tech diagnostic equipment for medical-device manufacturers. “It will replicate in Europe that whole vertical market that we’ve had great success with in the U.S.,” Wascher said. SEKO is planning to replicate other supply chain management products and services in other global markets. Wascher was the leader of a team of executives who performed a management buyout of SEKO from U.S. Freightways in 2002. Since then, SEKO has increased its logistics business and revenues at double-digit rates, mainly in the U.S., the UK, Hong Kong and China. Those executives retain a “significant” stake in SEKO, but no longer have a controlling stake. One of the fastest areas of growth has come from selling technology it has developed for managing supply chains. The technology, called My SEKO Harmony, is an interface across a user’s supply chain that enables it to manage its purchase orders, its freight operating systems, warehouse systems and customs. “It gives them visibility from the front end of the supply chain all the way to the back end,” Wascher said. Looking ahead, Wascher is focusing its plans for growth on emerging markets. “Our trade in Europe and Asia is pretty well developed. We are expanding and developing our markets in Central and South America and the Caribbean. We intend to become a player in those markets, so we are starting with boots on the ground there and then start to market some of our vertical product there.” Contact Peter Leach at peter.leach@ihs.com and follow him on Twitter: @petertleach © 2026 S&P Global. title: SeaLand Adds North Atlantic Express to Latin America Service
content: The enhancement, which is subject to regulatory approval, is being provided under a vessel-sharing agreement between SeaLand and APL. According to the carrier, the service was designed to create more connections across the SeaLand network, calling the west coast of South America, Central America, the Caribbean and U.S. East Coast. Under the NAE service, three vessels, two operated by SeaLand and one by APL, will offer a weekly frequency and capacity of 1,700 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs). The port rotation will be Cartagena, Manzanillo, South Florida, New York, Philadelphia, Savannah and back to South Florida. The service, which is scheduled to launch in late June or early July, will also offer connections between Colombia, Panama (through the hub in Manzanillo) and the U.S. East Coast ports of South Florida, New York, Philadelphia and Savannah, Ga. The service, which is scheduled to launch in late June or early July, will also offer connections between Colombia, Panama (through the hub in Manzanillo) and the U.S. East Coast ports of South Florida, New York, Philadelphia and Savannah, Ga.

title: DCs Are Best Line of Defense for Driving Omnichannel Profits, Satisfying Customers
content: But most retail stores are not set up to function as mini distribution centers (DCs). In fact, retailers will admit that while they are pulling off omnichannel processes in stores, they are not doing it profitably. The good news is that while many retailers feel that they are being slowly squeezed by Amazon, smart practices at their distribution centers can drive efficiencies, revenue and, more importantly, profits. The need to secure the sale at any cost has led to some extreme measures, with single items being expensively air-freighted from stores thousands of miles apart. For example, a colleague in Boston was looking for a new pair of winter hiking boots. After a record-breaking snowfall, he was unable to find a pair in his size within a 300-mile radius. Keen to satisfy the customer, the retailer sourced a pair – from Anchorage, Alaska – with free expedited shipping thrown in. That is a costly exercise to keep a customer happy, and cannot become the standard way of handling omnichannel fulfillment. It is equally costly to have out-of-stocks in the store or, worse, to be unclear what stock is being held. The latter can lead to problems such as "frozen inventory," where the retailer might think the store is holding the minimum acceptable level of stock for an item but due to theft, misplacement or poor stock-keeping practices the shelf is actually empty. It can take a long time, if ever, to spot and fix this kind of anomaly, and the out-of-stock could be fueling customer negativity over a long period. However, retailers do have strengths to draw on to help maintain stock visibility as well as their competitiveness. In particular, a well-run DC that correctly uses technology to accurately monitor inventory data can really make a difference. Retailers that have invested in RFID process automation at the DC and are source-tagging merchandise are ahead of the game. With an RFID solution integrated into warehouse management and inventory management systems of record, the creation of one hundred percent accurate advance shipping notices for retailers is possible. Every item ordered has its own unique identifier encoded into its label. The physical inventory contained in crates, pallets and individual boxes can be checked against the shipping manifest. In this manner, errors can be addressed before they are dispatched to the retailer, saving time for hard-pressed store staff to sort it out at their end. Automating shipment confirmation is key to making sure the truck loads are fully optimized in the right way. Real-time data means DC operations can be smarter with how they allocate, pick, pack and ship inventory to stores. Shipments based solely on historical retail data are not going to allow for flexibility or meet "real world" demand – the end result can be those high airfreight charges for single-item dispatch. Instead of sending a set number of shipments to stores at regular intervals based on last year's sales data, it is more profitable to supply what is actually selling today to outlets in different regions. RFID delivers a quick and accurate snapshot of specific local demand that the DC can go on to fulfill. This eliminates waste, reduces overall transportation costs and ensures that the right products are in the right place. To reduce transportation and handling costs, retailers want full trucks heading to stores – and full of things people are actually going to buy. Finally, the best practices found at the most optimized DCs can be migrated along the supply chain to flagship stores. Insightful retailers are beginning to look at RFID inventory management and RFID-enabled omnichannel fulfillment to turn flagship stores into mini-DCs to service smaller stores and the large surrounding populations. If such operations properly invest in their mini-DC status and do not just overload the existing staff with online fulfillment duties on top of regular store functions, then this can be a win-win strategy for retailers and customers. While online retailers may initially appear all-dominating, the use of innovative tools and strategies from source to shopper, combined with unmatched in-store personal service, gives aggressive brick-and-mortar retailers a competitive edge. And that ultimately results in increased customer satisfaction and profitability.

title: UK to sell remainder of Royal Mail
content: LONDON – The U.K.’s newly elected Conservative government today announced it will sell the state’s remaining 30 percent stake in Royal Mail to help reduce the country’s bulging deficit. The sale of the postal and delivery company, which is expected to raise up to 1.5 billion pounds ($2.3 billion), will start later this year, the Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne told Parliament. “There is no reason why we should hold a minority stake,” he said. The government sold an initial 60 percent stake in the 498 year old company via an initial public offering in October, 2013, that raised 3.3 billion pounds. The privatization drew criticism from opposition lawmakers and labour unions for selling the company too cheaply as the share price surged almost 90 percent following the IPO. The shares which were floated at 330 pence ($5) each closed at 526 pence on Wednesday. Royal Mail boosted operating profit in the year through March 29 by six percent to 740 million pounds on a one percent increase in revenue to 9.4 billion pounds. The company’s core domestic parcels business is facing stiff competition from Amazon, which launched its first same-day delivery service in the U.K. in October. GLS, the pan-European parcels unit, grew its operating profit to 115 million pounds from 108 million pounds on a six percent increase in delivery that boosted revenue by seven percent to 1.65 billion pounds. title: CaroTrans launches new US-Japan export service
content: CaroTrans is launching a new weekly less-than-container-load service between Southeastern U.S. and Japanese markets, cutting out transshipment and avoiding congestion at ports in Los Angeles and Busan. The New Jersey-based non-vessel operating common carrier said Wednesday the new service will take cargo from Atlanta, Georgia to a slew of major Japanese destinations including Tokyo, Yokohama, Kobe, Nagoya and Osaka. According to CaroTrans CEO Greg Howard, the new service is part of the carrier’s ongoing effort to employ new options for shippers, especially in the trans-Pacific lane. “Recent market challenges revealed the need for transportation alternatives for global supply chains,” Howard said in a statement. Congestion continues to haunt U.S. Pacific Coast ports, now months after the labor dispute between the International Longshore and Warehouse Union and port operators came to an end. “Today’s trans-Pacific supply chains require service flexibility and increased transportation choices to ensure reliable, timely freight delivery,” Howard said. “We’re committed to dependable, secure U.S.-Japan consolidation and deconsolidation and transportation services to ensure our clients are effectively serving their customers’ transpacific shipping needs.” CaroTrans will now offer 29-day freight service between Atlanta and Tokyo. Service between Atlanta and Yokohama will take 30 days. Service to Osaka, Nagoya and Kobe will each take 33 days. The new service will completely eliminate the need for transshipment and double handling at ports in Los Angeles and Busan. CaroTrans has promised that will translate fewer costs, speedier delivery, less risk and greater reliability and stability for cargo and cargo owner alike. To date, CaroTrans has added six new weekly, direct LCL and full-container-load services in the past six months. Last month, the NVOCC launched a weekly direct LCL service from Montreal to Le Havre, France, also pitched as an effort to cut costs and provide more options and flexibility to customers. © 2026 S&P Global. title: On The Cutting Edge of Consumer Delivery
content: The disruption of the retail segment by electronic commerce has forced merchandisers to focus on "last-mile" delivery. Traditional fulfillment systems were designed around the movement of large pallets from warehouses to supermarkets or big-box stores. With e-commerce, by contrast, customers shop online to purchase a single item that's shipped separately to the door. "It's never going to be profitable for a logistics company to deliver one parcel at a time for people who are not at home," says Moos. There's a big discussion going on about the need for same-day or even hour-specific delivery. But what customers really want, in Moos's view, is transparency. Certainty turns out to be more important than speed, even though so many e-commerce websites are pushing ever-faster delivery times. Another important element of a successful e-commerce offering is the presence of multiple delivery options. They've been shown to result in more finalizations of the shopping cart, says Moos. "You need to provide the options to people that suit their everyday lives the best," he adds. That might entail the ability to pick up parcels when they go to the supermarket. The idea is to place deliveries "in the normal, everyday life of the consumer." The locker box offers an alternative to expensive home delivery. It's currently enjoying popularity in Europe, especially in Denmark, Moos says. Unlike in a parcel shop, customers don't have to wait in line to pick up their packages. They go to a station, which can be in an existing store, type in a code and retrieve their items immediately. This so-called "click-and-collect" option offers merchandisers a big advantage, Moos says. And it helps traditional retailers to meld their operations with the growing world of e-commerce. title: Tanker Operators Tie Their Prosperity to Decreased Shale Oil Production, Boost in Oil Imports
content: Tanker operators are pinning their hopes on a rise in U.S. crude oil imports as domestic shale oil extraction becomes increasingly unprofitable. Low oil prices have made crude extraction unprofitable for many U.S. producers, leading to a fall in U.S. rig counts and shrinking exploration and production investment. "Continued expansion of refinery capacity in Asia is likely to maintain growth in the global oil trade over the next five years," said Rajesh Verma, Drewry's tanker shipping lead analyst. "But demand from Asia alone will not be sufficient to sustain the improvement in tonnage utilisation. The only alternative source of growth is a recovery in U.S. oil imports, especially when declining European refinery capacity will mean lower import volumes to EU countries." Following two years of slow growth, the global trade in oil has accelerated over the past nine months due to increased stocking. And Drewry expects this trend to continue through to the end of 2016. However, thereafter we expect the influence of stocking activity to wane and hence continued development in trade will depend on rising Asian demand and a recovery in U.S. imports. On the supply side, tanker fleet growth is expected to remain muted in 2015, growing at just 1.3 percent year-on-year, before gathering momentum in 2016, when vessel deliveries are expected to rise over 60 percent compared to this year. Buoyant fleet growth will also be supported by a slowdown in scrapping activity. "Large vessels dominate the order book and this is a reflection of the expected increase in long voyage trades," said Verma. "And next year's opening of the widened Panama Canal will further support demand for the bigger classes of ships." Tanker vessel earnings are expected to remain strong on ample oil supply and the resultant softness in bunker prices.

title: Matson Wraps Up Acquisition of Horizon Lines
content: Total value of the transaction is $469m, based on Matson's acquisition of Horizon stock at 72 cents per fully diluted common share, or $69m, and repayment of Horizon's outstanding debt. The deal includes Horizon's Alaska operations as well as all of its non-Hawaii business liabilities. Just before completion of the transaction, Horizon sold its Hawaii trade-lane assets and liabilities to The Pasha Group for $141.5m. Matson said it will continue Horizon's presence in Alaska with a three-vessel deployment of diesel-powered containerships in twice-weekly service from Tacoma to Anchorage and Kodiak, and weekly service to Dutch Harbor. In addition, Matson will operate port terminals in Anchorage, Kodiak and Dutch Harbor, and acquire several reserve steam-powered containerships, authorized for domestic service under the Jones Act, that can be used for drydock relief. title: The Changing Face of E-commerce Home Delivery
content: Customers today "have very high expectations in terms of getting product to homes in a very short time," says Escobar. They expect free returns and pinpoint tracking information on their orders. Contrary to the predictions of some that free shipping will eventually go away, Escobar says customers have been trained to expect it, or at the very least nominal charges for delivery. The challenge for retailers is offering the best possible service while preserving the bottom line. "Ultimately," says Escobar, "I think free shipping is here to stay." As a clothing rental service, Gwynnie Bee must deal with a 100-percent returns rate. To cope with that bidirectional flow, it is examining how to create consolidation centers that would return product back to the distribution center within two to three days. "I've had lot of consultants come through our D.C., scratching their heads when they see the returns process in the middle of it," says Escobar. "It's part of the cost of the model." Gwynnie Bee is also looking at alternative methods of delivery, including locker services and an Uber-like option for getting orders to the customer. "That's something that's very exciting for us," says Escobar. Other service features in demand by customers today include the regular updating of shipping capabilities and order tracking on social media. "We're continuing to drive streamlined information about packages," Escobar says. To view the video in its entirety, click here

title: The Industrial Internet of Things Grows in Importance - Not Least in Transportation, Logistics
content: "If you look at from supply chain perceptive, IoT is going to be transformative in connecting the physical world to digital world in a new way," Mark Wheeler, director of supply chain solutions at Zebra Technologies, said. "This technology allows intelligent assets to be visible in the cloud and accessible in a new way." Although consumers may be most enamored by the Apple Watch or other technological toys, the really exciting uses will be in the realm of industrial IoT and machine-to-machine (M2M) applications. By every measure, the understanding is nearly unanimous - and supply chain organizations are already getting hopping on the bandwagon. "There are very strong expectations that this will be transformative across industries and organizational functions," said Wheeler. "In transportation and logistics, better visibility translates into better utilization."

title: Empowered Consumers Change the Future of Retail, Survey Says
content: Earlier this year 5,000 U.S. consumers were surveyed. The results indicate consumers plan to research and purchase more frequently using their mobile devices, they are influenced by social media, and free shipping continues to drive purchasing decisions. New in this year’s study, most consumers (93%) shop at small retailers: • 61 percent shopped at these locations because they offer unique products • 49 percent couldn't find what they needed from traditional stores • 40 percent wanted to support the small business community In addition, 40 percent of consumers have purchased from retailers based outside the U.S., with nearly half (49 percent) reporting they did so to find better prices, and 35 percent said they wanted items that couldn’t be found in U.S. stores. Online shoppers frequently change retail channels during their shopping experience. Better prices (57 percent) and selection (49 percent) are the top reasons for purchasing online after researching an item in-store. Nearly half (48 percent) of online shoppers have used ship-to-store in the past year, and 45 percent of those consumers made an additional purchase when picking up their online purchase. When a purchase is made online from a retailer that has an online and physical store, 39 percent of consumers who make returns prefer to ship the product back while 61 percent prefer to return the item to the store. When making an in-store return, 70 percent purchase an additional item compared to only 42 percent who make a new purchase while processing an online return. Respondents said they continue to use personal computers to shop and compare prices, and complement their use as they become more comfortable using mobile technology: 41 percent use their smartphone for research, while 30 percent make purchases. Online shoppers appreciate the convenience of smartphones on-the-go and in-store. Smartphone users project making more purchases on their device in the next year. Retailers need to continue to advance their mobile platforms, as 38 percent who have a mobile device but do not use it to make purchases said product images are not large or clear enough, and 30 percent said it's hard to compare products. Many consumers connect to shopping activities through social media with 43 percent reporting they discover new products on social media sites. Facebook is the most influential channel but shoppers also embrace visually-oriented sites such as Pinterest. Retail continues to evolve as some online shoppers consider using mobile technologies in store: 33 percent find electronic shelf labels appealing, 29 percent said they will consider mobile checkout, and 27 percent said they are open to using touch screens to receive information, make purchases or arrange deliveries. Free shipping remains the most important option during checkout according to 77 percent of online shoppers. More than half (60 percent) have added items to their cart to qualify for free shipping. The study provides insight to help retailers increase sales – 48 percent of online shoppers said they ship items to the store, with 45 percent of those saying they made additional purchases when picking up their orders. According to the report, only 62 percent of consumers are satisfied with the online returns process: 67 percent review a retailer's return policy before making a purchase, 66 percent want free return shipping, 58 percent want a hassle-free "no questions asked" return policy, and 47 percent want an easy-to-print return label. Compared to last year's study, more consumers are open to alternate delivery options. In 2014, 26 percent said they prefer to have packages delivered to locations other than their home, this year it rose to 33 percent. When not at home to sign for a package, 32 percent want it shipped to another convenient retail location. "The future of retail is driven by ever increasingly sophisticated and savvy shoppers who research at home and in a store, but more are turning to mobile as capabilities improve for online product display and promotion," said Alan Gershenhorn, UPS executive vice president and chief commercial officer. "They also want more flexibility and alternate delivery options."

title: Euro’s slide breathes new life into European 3PL sector
content: Europe’s normally low-key logistics sector is suddenly hitting a high note, as a flurry of billion-dollar acquisitions kick-starts the long-stalled consolidation of a fragmented industry. U.S. companies are playing a key role in the makeover as they capitalize on the euro’s steep, yearlong slide against the dollar to snap up European logistics firms at attractive prices to expand their global networks. The U.S. presence will become more visible on European highways in the coming months, when Greenwich, Connecticut-based XPO Logistics paints its logo on the 7,700 trucks operated by France’s Norbert Dentressangle, its $3.5 billion acquisition. FedEx’s pending 4.4 billion-euro ($4.8 billion) acquisition of Dutch delivery company TNT Express will boost the Memphis-based giant’s share of the cross-border European express and parcels business from about 5 percent now to 17 percent, second only to Germany’s Deutsche Post DHL and ahead of U.S. rival UPS. XPO and FedEx cited the euro’s weakness against the greenback as a major impetus to their takeovers. Dentressangle, for example, would have been 20 percent more expensive a year ago. The slow but steady economic recovery in the troubled 19-nation eurozone also is playing a role in whetting U.S. companies’ appetite for trans-Atlantic expansion. “Europe has had a tough last few years,” XPO Logistics CEO Brad Jacobs said after tying up the Dentressangle deal. “My sense of the situation is that you’re seeing the beginnings of a rebound in the euro area.” Europe is the world’s largest contract logistics market, with more than a third of global revenue, although it’s likely to be overtaken by the Asia-Pacific region by 2017, according to logistics research and consulting firm Transport Intelligence. Europe, along with the U.S. and China, also will drive a 6.8 percent compound annual growth of global contract logistics through 2018, U.K.-based TI forecasts. “We believe that contract logistics growth will steadily accelerate in the coming years, although this relies heavily on European and U.S. economic performance improving and merely a gradual slowdown of the Chinese economy,” said David Buckby, a TI analyst. UPS’s decision to invest 1 billion euros to expand its European package delivery network underscores the region’s potential. “We will strongly expand our network in Germany and the rest of Europe,” said Frank Sportolari, UPS’s Germany chief. The Atlanta-based company “has lost time” since European regulators in 2013 shot down its own 5.2 billion-euro bid for TNT Express because of competition concerns, he told German business magazine Wirtschaftswoche. Asian companies seeking to expand their networks also could target European logistics interests, according to TI. Japanese companies, for example, are looking beyond their domestic market, pulling off a couple big-ticket deals this year — Japan Post’s $5.1 billion acquisition of Australia’s Toll Group and Kintetsu’s $1.2 billion takeover of APL Logistics — that could pave the way for others to flood into Europe to keep pace with the industry’s global consolidation. Additional moves in Europe by XPO can’t be ruled out either, with Jacobs saying the Dentressangle transaction that has catapulted it into the top 10 among global logistics providers is just the beginning. European companies themselves also have been active. Dentressangle paid $750 million for Jacobson, a Des Moines, Iowa-based contract logistics company last September, sparking XPO’s interest in the privately held French company. Denmark’s DSV was involved in discussions in December about the acquisition of California-based UTi Worldwide in what would have been its biggest takeover since it paid 750 million euros for Belgium’s ABX Logistics in 2008. That the deal collapsed hasn’t dulled DSV’s growth ambitions. “We have a clear intention of further expanding our network through additional acquisitions, provided we can find the right candidates,” CEO Jens Bjorn Andersen said. “We are keeping an eye out for companies that can strengthen DSV’s network outside Europe, in particular.” Panalpina CEO Peter Ulber said the Swiss forwarding and logistics giant would be ready to participate in the consolidation process by the end of 2016, after it rolls out a new IT and management system across its global network. Denmark’s DFDS, northern Europe’s largest short-sea and logistics company, is also on the prowl after a 56 percent jump in pretax profit in 2014. “Based on our solid performance, we are well-positioned to expand our activities through both organic growth and acquisitions, should the right opportunities materi-alize,” CEO Niels Smedegaard said. DFDS hasn’t pulled off a big-ticket deal since its $425 million acquisition of Maersk’s Norfolkline subsidiary in 2011, and, having pulled out of bids for European roll-on, roll-off shipping operator Scandlines, Turkey’s UN RO-RO and Sea France, it might opt to beef up its logistics business. Dascher, the $5.3 billion-a-year German logistics provider, also is on the takeover trail, eyeing acquisitions across the Atlantic to expand its relatively small share of the U.S. ocean and air freight markets. Despite the recent run of deals, the transportation and logistics sector trails other industries in M&A activity and consolidation. There were 195 transactions worth a combined $13.8 billion in 2014, down from 248 deals worth $29.9 billion in 2013, according to financial services firm Dealogic. Even as their domestic markets rally, European logistics companies are bracing for tough times beyond their shores. The global transportation and logistics markets are under extreme pressure, according to Rudiger Grube, CEO of Deutsche Bahn, Germany’s giant state railway and a major logistics player through DB Schenker, its 15 billion euro-a-year subsidiary. These pressures are taking their toll on some of Europe’s largest companies, none more so than Damco, Maersk’s Group’s troubled logistics business that continues to lose market share as it struggles to climb out of the red. Although Damco managed to trim its first- quarter 2015 loss to $9 million from $10 million a year earlier, revenue declined by $66 million to $749 million, ocean traffic dipped 2 percent and air freight crashed by 19 percent. The company is Maersk’s worst-performing business, with the rate of return on invested capital deteriorating to a negative-11.2 percent in the first quarter from 9.3 percent a year earlier, while the group’s overall figure improved to 13.8 percent from 10 percent. Analysts see Damco as a potential disposal when it emerges from intensive care. Deutsche Post DHL, the world’s biggest logistics company, also is struggling to turn around its floundering forwarding unit, whose botched transformation program it blamed for the group’s reduced first-quarter profit and abandoning its original 2015 earnings forecast last year. The company suspended a pilot program to implement new IT systems before they were rolled out across its global network because it was hurting day-to-day operations. “We will take time out to see if we can reduce the complexities before we decide on a new rollout,” Chief Financial Officer Larry Rosen said. Industry analysts also are charting the progress of another major operator, CEVA Logistics, two years after the Netherlands-based company won support from bondholders for a debt-for-equity swap that slashed net debt by 1.2 billion euros. The company, owned by U.S. private equity group Apollo Global Management, launched a new business model in 2015 that eliminated the previous region-based structure in favor of 17 local geographic clusters of countries with uniform governance standards and business rules. “We are seeing the visible impact of the operational improvements, ongoing streamlining of processes and greater responsiveness to our customers’ needs enabled by the new operating model,” CEO Xavier Urbain said when he unveiled an 18.6 percent increase in adjusted first-quarter earnings to $51 million as ocean freight volume rose 5 percent, air cargo traffic increased 5.2 percent and freight management revenue grew 6.1 percent. While small and medium-sized companies struggle to survive amid fierce competition, bulging overcapacity and rising investment demands — the number of insolvencies in the U.K. logistics sector soared 20 percent year-over-year in 2014 to 221, double the 2010 figure — the largest companies are boosting their markets at home and abroad. Deutsche Post’s DHL Express unit again dominated the group’s early 2015 performance, with first-quarter operating profit surging 20 percent to 332 million euros, outpacing a 12.5 percent growth in revenue to 3.2 billion euros. The company plans to create as many as 10,000 jobs by 2020 in Germany alone as it races to keep up with the explosive growth in e-commerce. “We want to be the global market leader in logistics for e-commerce,” CEO Frank Appel told shareholders at the annual general meeting at the end of May. To achieve this, the group plans to expand DHL’s domestic parcel business model across its global network. Swiss giants Kuehne + Nagel and Panalpina are leveraging their market-leading ocean and air freight market shares to expand their contract logistics operations against the backdrop of a surging Swiss franc that undermines their bottom lines while strengthening their ability to expand their networks and mount acquisitions. Kuehne + Nagel’s net earnings stalled in the first quarter following a record 1 billion-franc ($1 billion) profit in 2014 as the currency soared following the Swiss central bank’s January decision to stop intervening to cap its value against the euro. Panalpina more than doubled its operating profit to 116.7 million francs in 2014, with contract logistics losses tumbling to 8.2 million francs from 49.9 million in 2013, helped by the disposal of money-losing facilities and unprofitable trucking operations. The logistics business swung to a 1.2 million-franc profit in the first quarter of 2015 from a year-earlier loss of 5.5 million francs as it exited from underperforming sites. Europe’s state-owned logistics giants are finding it tougher to increase profits as nimbler private companies eat into their markets. DB Schenker’s adjusted earnings stalled at 332 million euros in 2014, but contract logistics stood out as a star performer, with revenue surging more than 10 percent to 2 billion euros, while air and ocean volumes posted modest growth and rail freight declined. France’s SNCF Logistics boosted its profit to 431 million euros in 2014 from 337 million in 2013 on revenue that was flat at 8.8 billion euros. The parent of Geodis relied on its operations beyond Europe, which grew 5.8 percent and offset a 0.2 percent decline in its domestic market. Leaner medium-sized private companies that have built up a solid customer base in key markets are outperforming the state-owned behemoths. Dascher boosted 2014 revenue by 5.2 percent to 5.3 billion euros as it capitalized on the trend toward outsourcing internationally complex logistics to drive organic growth. Dascher also expects integrated supply chain solutions for multinational customers to be a major source of growth in the future. “Our global network, enhanced by our customized contract logistics solutions in Europe, Asia and the U.S., as well as our own air and sea freight network, allow us to create complete supply chains,” said Bernhard Simon, CEO of the family owned company. This optimistic outlook is gaining traction across Europe’s logistics sector as a cheap euro boosts exports of increasingly competitive European products worldwide and a recovering continental economy improves prospects in domestic markets. title: Forwarder Lynden International acquires US-based Haas Industries
content: Freight forwarder Lynden International acquired Haas Industries, strengthening Lynden’s home delivery, trade show and specialized delivery services in the U.S. and Canada. The combined organizations, which merged June 1, have 26 company-owned service centers throughout the U.S. and Canada, including locations in Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico. The merger of Haas into Seattle-based Lynden International “will allow us to provide a wider array of services with greater reach,” the companies said in a statement. "The combination of our two companies will allow us to continue building our domestic service portfolio,” John Kaloper, vice president of Lynden’s America Division, said. The rise of e-commerce is spurring interest in home delivery and specialized delivery capabilities, such as delivering and installing appliances or equipment at homes or businesses. Transportation providers of various types, from less-than-truckload carriers to third-party logistics companies, are either adding or acquiring home delivery operations. Lynden International is the freight forwarding arm of the multimodal Lynden family of companies, which offer global air and ocean forwarding, logistics, trucking and Alaska shipping services. Lynden pioneered freight delivery to Alaska via the Alaska Highway in the 1950s. In addition to trucking, the company is involved in barge, air cargo and intermodal rail shipping. The forwarding operation recently expanded in Eastern Canada, opening a service center in St. John’s, Newfoundland, in part to support the province’s growing oil and gas industry. Haas, based in Haymarket, California, was founded in 1989. The company now operates as Lynden International. The companies did not disclose financial terms of the acquisition. Contact William B. title: Solution Rolled Out to Address 'Complexities' in Omnichannel Inventory, Order Routing, Fulfillment
content: The Enspire Commerce Enterprise Commerce Management (ECM) platform is designed to enable companies to readily leverage and rapidly integrate any or all of Enspire Commerce's solutions, including: Retail Engagement/Point of Sale, Trading Partner Management, Order Management and e-Commerce. "Many mid-market companies face the same omnichannel complexities as larger retailers," says enVista CEO Jim Barnes. "We founded Enspire Commerce to address gaps in the marketplace for price-competitive solutions that solve the complexities of omnichannel inventory visibility, order routing and fulfillment execution between retailers and their stores, logistics partners and vendors. At the heart of our ECM platform is an integration framework that allows trading partners to connect and create trading partner communities. This is a very different, customer-centric approach to retail that drives revenue and profitability by capturing sales, fulfilling from multiple inventory sources and delivering a unified cross-channel brand experience to consumers."

title: The Age of 'Click-and-Collect' Lockers for Home Delivery
content: The notion of "click and collect" allows customers to order product in any way they wish, then pick up the goods at the location of their choice – whether the store, their homes or a locker. It can apply to a broad variety of products, from fast food to home-improvement items. The idea of the locker is the latest addition to the growing menu of e-commerce delivery options. It can be located outside of a store, within a retail outlet, at a railway station, in a parking lot or even within a multi-tenant apartment building. Or it can be placed at the location of a special event. Traditional store pickup often entails waiting in long lines at a service counter. Lockers placed up front, by contrast, allow for instant access to goods by the buyer. In such instances, lockers “automate the process, and make it quick and convenient,” Savage says. He views the locker option as an idea whose time has come. The reason, he says, is the arrival of technology that enables real-time communication with back-end systems. At the same time, consumer expectations of service are developing rapidly, to the point where ease of delivery becomes a key selling point for the retailer. Lockers can benefit the retailer as well, in that they can draw on merchandise that’s already on hand. In effect, the store becomes a distribution center for the fulfillment of online orders. Still, “the retailer must be able to make a promise to the customer, and keep that promise,” Savage says. “That takes a holistic approach.” At the moment, the concept of lockers is more popular in Europe. But Savage believes it will quickly migrate to the U.S. “Interest level is at an all-time high,” he says. “In the next 12 to 18 months, this explodes.” To view the video in its entirety, click here

title: Post-acquisition, XPO looking beyond Norbert Dentressangle
content: Now that he’s closed his biggest acquisition yet — European logistics operator Norbert Dentressangle SA — Bradley S. Jacobs is already looking for new prospective purchases as he transforms U.S.-based XPO Logistics into a “global supply chain solutions provider.” XPO Logistics on June 8 finalized the purchase of all shares of Norbert Dentressangle held by the Dentressangle family, representing 67 percent of the Lyons, France-based company’s stock. Norbert Dentressangle iconic red trucks — the company is one of the largest truck operators in Europe — are already being refitted with XPO signage. XPO’s first European trucks will be rolled out during the Tour de France bicycle race, debutting at the Grand Départ of the race July 4. XPO’s odyssey from a $150 million company in 2011 to one with an $8.5 billion 12-month revenue run rate today has more twists and turns than the Tour de France course. Jacobs and his team have built XPO rapidly through more than a dozen acquisitions, from freight brokerage firms to last-mile logistics and intermodal drayage companies. “We believe scale is imperative in this business to serve customers effectively.” Jacobs said in an interview in April. Norbert Dentressangle gives XPO significant global reach and scale beyond North America and beyond Europe as well, with access to Asia-Europe trade lanes. The acquisition is expected to increase XPO's global freight forwarding revenue to approximately $425 million a year. In 2014, Norbert Dentressangle was a $5.5 billion company, with offices in 25 countries and 42,600 employees. In 2014, XPO reported $2.4 billion in revenue. XPO now claims to be the second-largest freight brokerage, after C.H. Robinson Worldwide, the largest provider of last-mile logistics for heavy goods and the largest manager of expedited shipments. Combined, XPO and Norbert Dentressangle would have ranked 12th on the JOC.com/SJ Consulting Group list of Top 50 Global 3PLs ranked by revenue in 2014. XPO is looking at more European acquisitions, as well as North American companies. “We are actively looking at other great companies to buy in Europe that would fit in well with the footprint that we just established,” Jacobs told JOC.com in May. “Europe has had a tough last few years. My sense of the situation is that you’re seeing the beginnings of a rebound in the euro area.” The company is actively seeking to expand its operations in last-mile, intermodal, global forwarding, supply chain, expedite and freight brokerage services. Now that XPO has evolved into global company, Jacobs said he feels less limited by geography. Norbert Dentressangle was looking at several acquisitions in Europe, “and they look pretty good to us too.” Contact William B. title: The 'Uberfication' of Home Delivery
content: "People are tired of not knowing when something is coming to them," says Sion. Yet he believes the problem will disappear within two to three years. The reason is the extension of the personal-transportation option, pioneered by Uber for passengers, to packages. An Uber-like model will give customers transparency as to when their packages will arrive. Sion believes the market is dictating its development. "People are more and more expecting same-day and one-hour service," he says. "And they expect to be part of the experience." An urban setting, because of its high concentration of population, is likely the best place to develop the service. But even in less-crowded areas, it could provide customers with complete driver visibility and delivery within a matter of hours, Sion says. He believes this service-intensive approach will become essential to the survival of retailers, much as the creation of the internet eventually dictated that every company would have a website. "The concept is changing the experience for the customer," he says. Sion isn't sure whether an enhanced delivery offering like that of Bringg would compete with Amazon, Google and other established players, or work with them. "Amazon is a possible customer," he says, "but it’s not our target." Regardless of who is offering it, an on-demand service platform "equates with customer retention," Sion says. "It's quite an amazing change, when you think about it." To view the video in its entirety, click here

title: L.A., Long Beach Struggle Against Ports That Can Handle Bigger Ships
content: "The dominance of Southern California as the Asia gateway is facing a lot more competition," said maritime consultant John Martin, who analyzed the trade data. The loss in market share represented an estimated 12,300 direct and indirect California jobs in 2013, and more than $112m in state and local tax revenue, according to Martin's research. The sudden growth of ship size has ports across the world scrambling to update infrastructure. Many are moving faster than L.A. and Long Beach, which are in the throes of multibillion-dollar expansions. Ports along the East Coast and in Houston have invested billions of dollars to deepen harbors, expand terminals and upgrade rail systems that connect to lucrative markets in the Midwest. The port of Savannah, Ga., has more than doubled the volume of imported container goods over the last decade, while the Canadian government and railways expanded British Columbia's Port of Prince Rupert to become a direct competitor to U.S. ports farther south.

title: Increase in Airfreight Volume Is Good News for Freight Forwarders
content: Europe to Asia had the largest increase, climbing 7 points to 58.2, while Europe to the U.S. increased 3 points to 62.7. U.S. to Europe was up 0.7 points to 48.1 and the Asia-to-Europe lane slid 2 points to 52.6. The report is based on responses from a monthly survey, completed by several logistics professionals. Questions regarding volumes they are currently experiencing, relative to the time of the year, and what they see coming up in the next six months are raised in the survey. The four trade lanes covered are Europe to Asia, Asia to Europe, Europe to the U.S. and the U.S. to Europe. Based on respondent's answers, airfreight is improving while sea freight demand is falling. Airfreight volumes were strong in all trade lanes except Asia to Europe. In fact, current airfreight volumes are accelerating with May airfreight volume at 55.5, which reflects expansion for 11 consecutive months. Europe-Asia and Europe-U.S. were particularly strong, bolstered (in their view) by favorable currency swings.

title: 3PL Sunset Transportation expands geographical reach
content: Sunset Transportation has opened a Bend, Oregon office and expanded operations at its Grand Haven, Michigan location, allowing the third-party logistics provider to expand its geographical reach. Bend, Oregon is one of the country’s fastest growing cities, and has been the site of an expansion by trucking company Old Dominion Freight Lines. “As the city continues to expand and flourish, Sunset’s Bend team is ready to provide the needed local and national logistics expertise to support the Pacific Northwest, a key transportation region,” Lindsey Graves, vice president of operations said in a statement. The St. Louis-based company has posted triple digit growth in the Midwest to necessitate the relocation of its Michigan headquarters to a larger facility. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: U.S. Manufacturing Fuels Shipping on St. Lawrence Seaway
content: According to the St. Lawrence Seaway, shipments of steel, aluminum, wind turbines and other heavy machinery were up by 5 percent to 629,000 metric tons from April 2 to May 31. Steel and Canadian aluminum headed to U.S. Great Lakes ports such as Oswego, Detroit and Toledo to be used in the thriving automotive industry. Local manufacturers also exported mining equipment via the Port of Milwaukee to Europe. Looking ahead, U.S. energy projects are expected to boost wind turbine shipments in the Great Lakes this season. The Port of Duluth-Superior has already booked 20 ships for its general cargo dock this year, including multiple loads of wind turbine components. The Port Authority recently broke ground on its $17.7m Port of Duluth Intermodal Project to enhance its heavy-lift and project cargo capacity. While it was another late start to the season due to icebreaking constraints, grain from Canada and the U.S. continued to flow out of the St. Lawrence Seaway to export markets, totaling 1.9 million metric tons so far this season, up 7 percent over 2014. And dry bulk shipments, including road salt, coke for steel production, and construction materials totaled 1.7 million metric tons, up four percent. Despite these star performers, year-to-date total cargo shipments via the St. Lawrence Seaway were 6.4 million metric tons, down by 7 percent compared to 2014 due to low global prices for North American iron ore and coal exports. Iron ore shipments via the Seaway were down 30 percent, while coal shipments dipped 27.5 percent compared to the same period the year before.
