title: Cargo's Crystal Ball: The Power of Machine Learning
content: Shippers opened their contingency playbooks and began the costly process of rebooking shipments on other container lines; in some cases, shippers had to resort to alternative modes of transportation to mitigate shipment delays. But what if shippers had known well in advance that Hanjin was on the brink of collapse? With the diffusion of so-called “machine learning” technologies, such foresight into looming supply-chain disruptions may no longer be the undertaking of a soothsayer with a crystal ball. Although early warning systems have long been around to help cargo avoid weather hazards, such as an oncoming blizzard or hurricane, utilizing available data to detect the deteriorating financial state of a supply chain partner requires a different barometer. DHL Resilience 360’s Supply Watch, for instance, utilizes a machine-learning algorithm to recognize indicators for more than 140 different types of risk. Supply Watch was created out of a desire to pick up the “more nuanced risks, like supply failure, financial issues and compliance issues that may be very specific to companies and suppliers that our customers work with,” said Shehrina Kamal, senior product manager at DHL Resilience 360. Machine learning represents the next iteration of data analytics, and finds applications in situations where rules-based programs cannot be developed to determine a solution, or when the volume of data is too large to handle manually. The algorithm “gives us an automated way of dealing with vast amounts of data in a proactive way,” said Kamal.

title: Opinion: Using Automation to Combat the Impending Labor Shortage
content: As a result of many shippers outsourcing their logistics operations or utilizing third-party staffing agencies, they have become a layer removed from the labor market and might be unaware of the impending challenges on the horizon. The silver lining is that the labor shortage could push the logistics industry to evolve at an unprecedented rate - and present an opportunity for firms to gain a competitive advantage if they are willing to innovate and adapt quickly. As the economy in North America continues to rebound, we expect the labor pool for drivers and material handlers to tighten as workers transfer back into higher-paying positions in competing industries. The current political environment in the U.S. is pointing toward a crackdown on undocumented workers, which will have a negative impact on the contract labor force. Also, an increased minimum wage could tighten the pool of available laborers as people transition into less physically demanding positions with comparable pay. In addition to the economic and political pressures that make it difficult for 3PLs to find and keep labor, so too will evolving customer expectations. Customers of logistics services expect higher levels of service for lower costs. As a result, 3PLs are providing more and more value-added services such as assembly. Kitting and converting of subassemblies into finished goods remains strong due to the pressure to quickly convert and ship an item the same day. For example, the custom sports apparel business does extensive embroidery and screen printing as an outbound service prior to shipping.

title: Amazon Is Seeking a Home for Its $5Bn Second Headquarters
content: The Seattle-based company says it plans to invest $5bn in construction and operation of the new location, which it is calling Amazon HQ2. “We expect HQ2 to be a full equal to our Seattle headquarters,” Jeffrey P. Bezos, founder and chief executive of Amazon, said in a statement. “Amazon HQ2 will bring billions of dollars in up-front and ongoing investments, and tens of thousands of high-paying jobs. We’re excited to find a second home.” (Bezos also owns The Washington Post.) Amazon is seeking proposals from local, state and provincial government leaders, and says it is focusing on metropolitan areas with more than 1 million people. It is also looking for areas that can attract and retain technical workers and “a stable and business-friendly environment.” Among the criteria it will consider, Amazon says, are tax exemptions and other incentives, including relocation grants and fee reductions. “The initial cost and ongoing cost of doing business are critical decision drivers,” the company said in its request for proposals.

title: Drones Play Increasing Role in Hurricane Recovery Efforts
content: In the first six days after the storm hit, the Federal Aviation Administration issued more than 40 separate authorizations for emergency drone activities above flood-ravaged Houston and surrounding areas. They ranged from inspecting roadways to checking railroad tracks to assessing the condition of water plants, oil refineries and power lines. The total climbed above 70 that Friday and topped 100 by Sunday, including some flights prohibited under routine circumstances, according to people familiar with the details. Industry officials said all of the operations — except for a handful flown by media outlets — were conducted in conjunction with, or on behalf of, local, state or federal agencies. One person familiar with the details said certain applications were processed within hours, an unusually fast turnaround for federal safety regulators accustomed to days or weeks of analysis for such decisions. title: CargoSphere’s global reach expands via new parent company
content: CargoSphere is one of the more than 95 companies in JOC's Container Shipping Technology Matrix. An Australian logistics software company has acquired CargoSphere, giving the container rate management provider more global reach, boosting its research, and enhancing product development. In addition to the $9.2 million acquisition of the North Carolina-based company WiseTech Global Limited has acquired air cargo rate management company Cargoguide for $5.5 million, according to Reuters. WiseTech, a publicly traded company in Australia, did not disclose the price of each acquisition. Cargosphere will also benefit from access to WiseTech’s 7,000 customers, which should also encourage more carriers to partner with the company, said Neil Barni, president, and a founder, of CargoSphere. “We will benefit from the global strength and powerful innovation capability of WiseTech and we remain committed to integrating with ocean carriers and with our customers, and to delivering on our vision for fully automated digital rate distribution,” Barni said. The acquisitions follow a slew of other purchases by WiseTech in recent months, including: Australian land transport solution provider, CMS Transport systems; Taiwanese forwarding and customs solutions provider, Prolink; Australia-based tariff compliance software provider, Digerati; and Brazilian customs solution provider, Bysof. WiseTech’s flagship product, CargoWise One, helps customers manage freight forwarding, customs clearance, warehousing, shipping, and other tasks. Established in 1999, CargoSphere provides a cloud-based rate “mesh” that enables customers to manage contracts and allows for more simple rate quoting, rate distribution and agent rate collaboration, with confidential information provided by other parties. Barni has argued that its customers are best served by being able to exchange rates and other information in private, rather than publicly — as is the case in a number of booking marketplaces that operate somewhat like a marine cargo version of Expedia, with rates available for all to see. Despite its extensive history, CargoSphere is often lumped in with a wave of start-ups — including marketplaces, digital freight forwarders, and transportation management systems — that have emerged in recent years, seeking to harness technology to transform the cargo shipping industry. Critics say the industry has been slow to adapt to new technology and take advantage of the efficiencies and cost cutting that it offers. WiseTech Global CEO, Richard White, said the acquisitions of CargoSphere and Cargoguide would complement the rate management capabilities of CargoWise and improve efficiency and accuracy for customers. Eventually that will enable the companies to more fully automate the process, increasing productivity for freight forwarders, he said. Contact Hugh R. title: 'Ware-bnb': The Rise of On-Demand Distribution
content: After shopping around at warehouse operators, the owners were disappointed to find that most were too expensive or wanted a minimum year-long lease and an upfront fee, or required them to give up control of their goods to a 3PL. But soon they stumbled upon a new startup called Flexe, which offered not part of a single warehouse but a network of warehouse spaces all around the region, and allowed them the flexibility to change the amount of space they leased as they needed it. The terms of the lease also enabled them to use the space for as little as six weeks or indefinitely, if they so chose. True Fabrications ended up working with Flexe and saved about $170,000 during the busy fourth quarter, paying about 67 percent less than their next-best estimate: a nine-month lease at a conventional warehouse operator. And the company was never charged extra fees or up-front costs. True Fabrications decided to stay on with Flexe to continue using the “virtual warehouse” network and changing the amount of space they need, whenever they need it. The wine retailer discovered what a lot of North American shippers and 3PLs are finding out — it is now possible to enjoy the benefits of a warehouse and complete fulfillment services without ever having to commit to a long-term lease or deal with the hassle of maintaining a distribution center. Much like the way Airbnb revolutionized the way consumers sought hotel accommodations, companies such as Flexe are quietly but steadily disrupting the warehousing market. Call it a “Ware-bnb” for the logistics community — pay for only what you need, when and where you need it, and then walk away.

title: XPO Logistics doubling last-mile footprint
content: E-commerce demand has risen at XPO Logistics has risen by double digits this year. XPO Logistics is putting the last mile first, doubling its North American last-mile presence to 85 service hubs to capture more of the fast-growing heavy-goods segment of e-commerce. The expansion, which will be completed in 2018, follows the global logistics operator’s doubling of last-mile capacity around Chicago earlier this year. The next eight hubs will open in Birmingham, Alabama; Buffalo, New York; Jacksonville, Florida; Long Island, New York; Los Angeles, California; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Tulsa, Oklahoma; and Washington, DC. “We’re seeing significant growth in our last-mile business, in the high teens overall, and what’s driving that growth in a single word is e-commerce,” Will O’Shea, last-mile senior vice president, sales solutions, told JOC.com on Wednesday. “We’re seeing big demand for large-format items requiring services at delivery really exploding.” XPO already claims to be the largest US last-mile home delivery company for large goods such as appliances and furniture, and this expansion highlights the importance of last-mile logistics to the $14.6 billion company. XPO handles nearly 13 million home and commercial deliveries each year, and large, bulky shipments that require assembly and installation make up the majority. “Our customers are seeing e-commerce business surge .… The heavy goods sector is what we notice the most,” Charles Hitt, president of XPO’s last-mile business unit, told JOC.com in May. Last-mile revenue has been growing by double digits, rising 14.8 percent year over year in the second quarter to $230.4 million. In 2016 the last-mile division’s sales totalled $838.2 million, a nearly 20 percent gain in a year. Despite that double-digit growth, XPO’s last mile business represented only about 5.7 percent of the diversified logistics operator’s total revenue. That leaves plenty of room to grow and XPO hopes to lengthen its last-mile reach by combining elements of its contract logistics, trucking, and last-mile businesses to give large online shippers end-to-end control over fulfillment. “We can serve an e-tailer by handling the supply chain from the manufacturer, or e-tail facility, to our warehouse, to our LTL crossdock, to the last-mile delivery, to installation inside the home,” CEO Bradley S. Jacobs said in August. “Consumers are more comfortable with ordering items online, and large format. Our last-mile is an integral part between our LTL unit and our supply chain unit,” O'Shea said. “Our supply chain team has the ability to hold inventory and do curbside delivery, but if customers want a more enhanced service, full-white glove, installation, or removal services, that goes through last-mile hubs.” Last-mile delivery of large and bulky items such as refrigerators takes unique skills and training, and XPO said the new hubs will be staffed by teams able to perform inspections, repairs, pre-assemblies, and other value-added services in preparation for delivery. Not to confuse these last-mile hubs with a traditional distribution center, as the hubs are more of a “hybrid cross dock” where XPO performs value added services for everything from furniture to fitness equipment, O’Shea told JOC.com. The demands of e-commerce players such as Amazon are rewriting the basic operational DNA of transportation and logistics. Amazon Prime and Prime Now, which promises same-day delivery, are spurring the spread of smaller fulfillment centers embedded in urban areas, close to end customers ordering everything from refrigerators and gun safes to light bulbs online. Second-quarter US retail e-commerce sales rose 16.2 percent to $111.5 billion, a 4.8 percent gain over the first quarter, according to US Census Bureau data. Total retail sales increased 4.1 percent in the same period, and e-commerce accounted for 8.9 percent of total sales. That growth has led truckload, less-than-truckload, logistics, and parcel operators to jump into the last or final-mile market. Those that have entered the space or expanded their presence recently include Werner Enterprises, Schneider National, YRC Worldwide, Estes Express, and ABF Freight. In addition to growing consumer demand for large and bulky shipments, these companies have been reporting an uptick in business-to-business e-commerce. XPO, which became one of the world’s largest third-party logistics companies in less than a decade via an aggressive strategy of mergers and acquisitions, said it is once again considering acquisition targets following a brief hiatus. The company reported a 2.2 percent year-over-year rise in revenue in the second quarter to $3.76 billion, while net profit rose 11.7 percent to $47.6 million. title: Irma freight recovery hinges on fuel availability
content: The Florida Highway Patrol has been escorting fuel trucks to ensure they reach their destination as quickly as possible. Refined petroleum products — gasoline, diesel and jet fuel — are starting to pour back into Florida, both from the sea and over land, as the state struggles to recover from Hurricane Irma. Fuel and power outages are the most immediate obstacle to recovery efforts across the state, but getting gasoline to pumps may be a bigger issue than the availability of diesel. IHS Markit estimates about half of the state’s filling stations have fuel now, though widespread shortages were still being reported Tuesday, as the first evacuees began to return home. For many motorists, the best source of information on where gasoline is available has been crowd-sourced online filling station tracker from mobile app GasBuddy. The damage to US refining capacity from Hurricane Harvey in August makes getting fuel into Florida more difficult. IHS Markit estimates about 9 percent of US distillation capacity, 1.7 million barrels per day, was still offline Tuesday, down from 27 percent of the US total at the peak of the Houston-area flooding. “At this point, it is difficult to predict how quickly the remaining offline capacity returns to service,” IHS Markit, the parent company of JOC.com, said Tuesday. Diesel, more than gasoline, is needed to fuel tractor-trailers and other vehicles delivering immediate relief supplies and other aid throughout the state, as well as to power emergency generators. The good news is diesel stocks in Florida may not have been drawn down as much as gasoline before the storm, according to IHS Markit analysts and other sources. “There’s a strain on the gasoline supply before a storm hits, almost always,” Daniel Cullen, vice president of advisory services at Breakthrough Fuels, said. “We saw this in Texas (before Hurricane Harvey in late August) and in Florida.” Irma’s impact on diesel was smaller, he said. Breakthrough Fuels helps shippers craft fuel spending and management programs. “Diesel didn’t have the shortage ahead of time, or the price impact ahead of time,” that was seen with gasoline in Florida and Texas, Cullen said. “We’ve been working with clients to secure supply, especially if they’re have a dedicated fleet or private fleet of trucks,” he said. Many trucking operators also rely on private fueling facilities, rather than commercial filling stations. UPS, the largest US transportation company, has fueling stations at all its facilities, which helps the company get back on the road quickly, spokesman Matt O’Connor said. UPS is working to get package and freight pickup and delivery operations rolling again “as quickly as possible,” O’Connor said. “The question is, really, once we can restore operations, what are our customers able to do?” he said. “There were a lot of people evacuating Florida.” That’s another reason it will be some time yet before supply chains that deliver goods in Florida’s major metropolitan markets or move them through the state really get rolling. In Florida, the availability of fuel, whether for personal use or commercial or emergency services, depends on the ports. Most fuel arrives in Florida by ship and is transferred from port facilities to wholesale terminals by local pipeline before being trucked to retail pumps. Florida’s Port Miami, Port Everglades, and Port Tampa Bay reopened Tuesday morning. Port Everglades and Port Tampa Bay are critical for the state’s fuel supplies and Gov. Rick Scott said he prioritized opening those ports as soon as possible after the storm cleared. Three petroleum tank ships arrived Tuesday at Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale to offload 18 million gallons of gasoline, 3.5 million gallons of diesel and 14.7 million gallons of jet fuel, the port said. Two more tank ships are scheduled to arrive Wednesday and Thursday. Ten of the 12 petroleum companies that operate at Port Everglades have reopened. Trucks began hauling reserve supplies of fuel, about four days’ worth, from the port Monday. At Port Canaveral, further north on Florida’s East Coast, the US Coast Guard began allowing restricted commercial shipping Tuesday to support the arrival of critical fuel supplies. Seaport Canaveral “is moving gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel throughout the state. The steady stream of trucks that were in queue for loading fuels beginning last night, have been loading and moving out to make their deliveries,” CEO John Murray said in a statement Tuesday. On Wednesday, four petroleum vessels were unloading gas at Port Tampa Bay. At least seven more were expected within 24 hours, spokesperson Samara Sodos said. “Tanker trucks are still loading up at all facilities both inside and outside the port,” she said in an e-mail. “There have been hundreds of tanker trucks at Port Tampa Bay over the past few days, tripling the normal amount of activity. Florida Highway Patrol continues to escort tanker trucks.” She stressed there had been no shortage of fuel at the port; tanker trucks began loading up with gas shortly after Tampa Bay opened its ground facilities Monday. The new arrivals will keep gasoline and diesel flowing out to service stations in the Tampa Bay area and beyond. Contact William B. title: As Amazon Pushes Forward With Robots, Workers Find New Roles
content: Now Scott, 21, watches her replacement — a giant, bright yellow mechanical arm — do the stacking. Her new job at Amazon is to babysit several robots at a time, troubleshooting them when necessary and making sure they have bins to load. On a recent afternoon, a claw at end of the arm grabbed a bin off a conveyor belt and stacked it on another bin, forming neat columns on wooden pallets surrounding the robot. It was the first time Amazon had shown the arm, the latest generation of robots in use at its warehouses, to a reporter. “For me, it’s the most mentally challenging thing we have here,” Scott said of her new job. “It’s not repetitive.” Perhaps no company embodies the anxieties and hopes around automation better than Amazon. Many people, including President Trump, blame the company for destroying traditional retail jobs by enticing people to shop online. At the same time, the company’s eye-popping growth has turned it into a hiring machine, with an unquenchable need for entry-level warehouse workers to satisfy customer orders. Amazon’s global work force is three times larger than Microsoft’s and 18 times larger than Facebook’s, and last week, Amazon said it would open a second headquarters in North America with up to 50,000 new jobs.

title: Trimble buys shipper-focused visibility technology firm
content: Trimble's acquisition is another sign of the intense demand for shipment level visibility throughout supply chains. Software and technology company Trimble is moving deeper into shipping and transportation markets by acquiring 10-4 Systems, a technology firm that helps businesses track freight across several modes at the shipment level, both in US and international supply chains. Trimble already has several subsidiaries that provide technology to motor carriers and freight brokers, including transportation management software company TMW Systems, telematics provider PeopleNet and routing and navigation software developer ALK Technologies. The freight visibility solutions offered by 10-4 Systems will give Trimble’s transportation business a bigger presence among shippers, the purchasers of transportation services, and push it beyond its trucking roots into more a multimodal and international environment. “We are really keen on getting deeper into transportation and supply chain, being able to bring together both demand and capacity,” David W. Wangler, president of Trimble Transportation Enterprise, or TTE, said Thursday. “We think there’s a great opportunity to capture information on freight and capacity to do a better job solving this visibility problem for the shipper.” With 10-4 now part of Trimble’s family, Wangler sees greater opportunity to develop products that provide visibility across Trimble’s diverse customer base, which in addition to truck operators and shippers includes construction, rail and many types of field service businesses. “More than likely, there are visibility opportunities across Trimble,” he said. “When you think of all the equipment that gets moved by our customers, the opportunities are really exciting.” Trimble is getting into the visibility game at the right time: Shippers are seeking greater control over international and domestic freight movements, which are often interlinked. Three quarters of the truck freight brokers polled at the Transportation Intermediaries Association annual conference in April said shippers consider real-time visibility a prerequisite to doing business. In August, Descartes, a global logistics and trade software firm, acquired MacroPoint, another provider of shipment-level supply chain visibility. Visibility provider FourKites in August announced a partnership with 3GTMS, a transportation management software company, to create a “unified, powerful offering” to shippers and third-party logistics companies. Visibility and freight tracking “is table stakes” in shipper-3PL negotiations, Bob Biesterfield, president of North American surface transportation at C.H. Robinson Worldwide, said. “It’s the expectation rather than the exception, and that’s really changed rapidly,” he said. What’s also changing rapidly is the level of visibility shippers demand, the speed at which data are delivered and the technology itself. “Just knowing where a truck is is no longer a differentiator,” Biesterfield said during a panel discussion on shipper-3PL relations. That’s exactly the point behind the acquisition of 10-4 Systems, which tracks shipments, not vehicles, and follows freight as it moves from container ship to intermodal rail to truck. “We’ve made the shipper our core customer and worked with the largest carriers in America as a byproduct of that,” Travis Rhyan, president and CEO of 10-4 said Thursday. 10-4’s visibility solution combines order and shipping data from shipper TMS and warehouse software with real-time asset-tracking and location from carriers and third-parties to provide a SKU-level view of freight movement in supply chain. The system is customizable, so shippers can configure their own delivery windows, geofence facilities and create dashboards. Shippers aren’t just looking for visibility to reduce their transportation costs. Like trendsetter Amazon, they want to offer shipment visibility to the end customer, Rhyan said. “Once a shipper’s customer service group and support teams understand the data they’re receiving, then they begin to roll out that information directly to their customer,” he said. 10-4 customer Anheuser-Busch, for instance, provides visibility data to its wholesaler network, he said. “They’re getting that core information to the people on the docks receiving the trucks. Now not only do they know where that truck is, but they know what’s on it. And they know whether there are other orders tied to the incoming orders on that truck.” Shippers also use that data in price negotiations with carriers, he said. “They now have The ability to create best-in-class scorecards themselves. Our early shippers wanted to take this data and when they bid business show carriers how they’re improving — which loading sites cause detention and what they’re doing to reduce that. That makes a massive difference.” That real-time data may also unlock capacity and help restore flexibility to supply chains that are getting increasingly brittle as demands for faster order fulfillment clash with tighter regulatory restrictions on truck driver work hours. “There’s a tremendous amount of empty miles on the road,” Rhyan said. He puts the estimated value of those empty miles at $90 billion. Gaining inbound and outbound visibility across modes is key to solving “the freight problem” by tapping those empty miles, Wangler said. “Shippers have always desired this complete visibility. Technologies have finally come to bear to enable that.” Contact William B. Cassidy at bill.cassidy@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @wbcassidy_joc © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: Hovering on the Edge: Will Airships Go Mainstream?
content: In the fields adjacent to the U.K.'s Cardington Airfield, aviation enthusiasts lurked, cameras at the ready, while the test pilots and engineers readied the unusual craft for flight. At 08:12 a.m., the massive airship un-masted and, for 98 minutes, flew over Bedfordshire before approaching the mooring mast for landing. That's when things started heading south. A diesel engine that powered the hydraulic pumps driving the winch conked out, delaying the landing and forcing the pilot to go airborne again. As the aircraft ascended, the mooring line was retracted through a panel in the cabin door but, as the aircraft rose, the mooring line fell out under its own weight, and dangled dangerously close to the ground. That faulty winch would come back to haunt Chris Daniels, head of communications and partnerships at Hybrid Air Vehicles, who explained that its broken handle “prevented us from attaching the mooring line to the mooring mast.” Under pressure, human error became a factor. The aircraft nosed down steeply, began to descend, and struck the ground, causing damage to the cabin flight deck area. That slow-motion crash pushed airships into the public consciousness for the first time in decades, and quickly became the biggest airship story of the year — one video of the incident has almost 10 million views.

title: At Long Last, A.I. Comes to the Logistics Industry
content: We're finally seeing the concepts of expert systems and A.I. brought to bear on the countless decisions that go into running a complex logistics operation. But what form is A.I. taking in that area? Does it promise to replace human experts, or supplement them? And just how "smart" is present-day A.I., anyway? On this episode, we discuss the coming of A.I. to logistics with Spencer Askew, founder and chief executive officer of Teknowlogi, creator of an expert system for that industry. He assesses the current state of A.I., with a particular emphasis on how the technology can provide an answer to the problem of an aging workforce. We’ll learn where humans fit into the equation, and the types of new skills they’ll need in the age of A.I. We’ll see how A.I. can aid companies in making everyday business decisions, as well as predicting future trends. And we’ll answer a key question: Does A.I. advise on necessary actions, or does it dictate them? Hosted by Bob Bowman, Managing Editor of SupplyChainBrain. Look for a new episode of the podcast, which can be downloaded or streamed, every Friday on the SupplyChainBrain website and iTunes. A blog post by Spencer Askew on logistics expert systems.

title: Indian ports pursue integrated container-tracking network
content: The Indian government wants to expand to the benefits of RFID tracking at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust to smaller gateways. A key driver of productivity for larger container ports on India’s west coast, radio-frequency identification (RFID) company DMICDC Logistics Data Services (DLDS) is expanding its container tracking technology to smaller ports as the government works to smooth cargo flows and reduce costs through the supply chain. “Ongoing discussions with the container handling port terminals in southern India to extend the [logistics data bank] LDB services would help to create a ‘single container tracking system’ for the users on a pan-India basis,” DLDS said in a trade update. The RFID program has significantly improved container dwell times throughout the supply chain at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT), from terminals to off-dock warehousing sites and hinterland points, DLDS said. The system helped APM Terminals-operated Gateway Terminals India bounce back from the June 27 cyber attack on Maersk Group’s global system, reflected by the 12.3 percent increase in throughput year over year, according to DLDS. The RFID services provider also said discussions are under way with shipping lines "to enable them to leverage the LDB system effectively." The RFID tagging and tracing procedure, which is also operational at the private ports of Mundra and Hazira, allows exporters and importers to track goods in transit through the port to inland container depots, container freight stations and to end-users, thus bringing down logistics costs by optimizing and improving the predictability of cargo flows. DLDS plans to add APM Terminals’ Pipavav port as well as the southern ports of Chennai, Tuticorin, Krishnapatnam, and Kattupalli to its logistics data network in the next stage, and the eastern port of Kolkata on the last leg. Some challenges still persist on the rail front at JNPT, as mixed train operations, instead of dedicated trains for each terminal, typically result in longer dwell times, reaching 102 hours in August against normal average dwell time of 34 hours for railed cargo during the month. Still, JNPT had a clear edge over Mundra on dwell times for imports via rail in August, averaging 79 hours compared with 214 hours at the private rival. “Mixed container stacking at [the] yard of different terminal leads to challenges in retrieving the same and at times, leads to the possibility of containers missing the vessel,” the report said. To tackle those issues, the port in coordination with rail authorities is setting up a “common rail yard” for all terminals, and current indications are that the Rs. 100-crore ($15.6 million) integrated facility would be ready toward the end of next year. While JNPT performed better than Mundra for railed imports, dwell times for imports by truck were the same as the prior month, at 27 hours, the DLDS analysis shows. Those dwell times should shorten in the coming months as JNPT last week cleared another legal hurdle to its long-contemplated common trucker pooling arrangements for direct port delivery (DPD) shipments when the Indian Supreme Court turned down a request from a challenge of a lower court mandate that allowed the pool, port sources told JOC.com. Technology-backed ease-of-doing-business measures at Indian ports are expected to gather further pace with an RFID-based “electronic self-sealing” scheme for factory-stuffed export shipments, which is scheduled to go into effect Oct. 1. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Consolidation among logistics companies looms
content: Industry consolidation that has defined container carriers in recent years could be creeping into logistics companies. The logistics business could be about to go down the consolidation route that has significantly reshaped container shipping over the past year with more merger and acquisition (M&A) deals on the horizon. The persistent rumors of takeover and mergers among leading logistics firms in recent months could be about to translate into reality with Geodis, a unit of SNCF, France’s state-owned railway, reportedly on the verge of snapping up CEVA Logistics. The Netherlands-based freight forwarding and logistics operator has been mentioned as a potential takeover target for several months. Geodis, the acquisition-hungry US group XPO Logistics, and Swiss logistics and forwarding giant Kuehne + Nagel are the most likely bidders. The French company is the hot favorite as SNCF has been steadily building up its logistics business and has sought government approval to boost its debt by around 1 billion euros ($1.2 billion) in order to finance the 2.5- to 3-billion-euro CEVA takeover that would meet its target of catapulting Geodis into the top five world rankings from its eighth position currently. Geodis highlighted its global ambitions a little over two years ago when it acquired Brentwood, Tennessee-based OHL from private equity fund Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe in a deal worth some $800 million that quadrupled its US revenues. CEVA’s owner, Apollo, the US private equity company, will be a willing seller now that its long-troubled logistics unit has turned the corner and is forecasting “robust” 2017 results following a strong second quarter. A takeover of CEVA would make Geodis a major global player with an expanded client portfolio and annual revenue of around 15 billion euros. The freight forwarding market has space for more M&A activity, with the Top 10 firms accounting for 43.5 percent of the $141 billion global revenue in 2016, according to Ti, a UK-based consultancy. Germany’s DHL Global Forwarding topped the rankings with a 7.9 percent share, just ahead of Kuehne + Nagel at 7 percent, while CEVA was 10th with a 2.3 percent take. Although CEVA is courting the most attention right now, other companies remain under the M&A spotlight as the logistics and freight forwarding industry prepares for a possible outbreak of deals. The two companies that have dominated takeover talk in the past — the Maersk Group’s Damco and Deutsche Post DHL’s global forwarding unit — are attracting less attention right now, but they could be back in the rumor mill at any time. Damco remains a major headache for Maersk, so much so that taking out its costs is one of the group’s priorities in 2017 alongside closing on the 3.7-billion-euro acquisition of German carrier Hamburg Süd, according to CEO Soren Skou. The fact that Damco broke even in the second quarter compared with a year-earlier profit of $10 million for a first half loss of $8 million against a $12 million profit during the same time last year does not look good in a recovering global logistics/forwarding market. The persistent challenges at Damco come despite Maersk's stated strategy of shedding its oil and gas businesses to become an integrated transportation and logsitics player, which presumably it could not accomplish without a logistics capability. Deutsche Post DHL was seen as potentially offloading its global forwarding and freight business following a 345-million-euro write-off and the resignation of the unit’s CEO in 2015 when its troubled information technology system was ditched. The business has slowly recovered, but an operating profit of just 67 million euros on revenue of 3.6 billion euros in the second quarter makes it a possible spin-off candidate as the group’s growth is mainly driven by its surging global express, international parcels, and e-commerce operations. One of the most mentioned companies to hit the takeover headlines any time soon is DSV, the Danish trucker and forwarder that is posting record results quarter by quarter as it cashes in on the $1.35 billion acquisition of California-based UTi Worldwide in early 2016. DSV, which was set up by nine Danish trucking companies in 1976, has become one of the world’s leading logistics players with annual revenues of more than nine billion euros, largely due to a string of acquisitions, including Dutch trucker Frans Maas and Belgium’s ABX Logistics. And there are likely more to come. For now most attention is fixed on Kuehne + Nagel, which is expected to go on the takeover trail to accelerate its growing ocean and air cargo markets shares. Although there has been some speculation it might pounce on its smaller Swiss rival Panalpina, it is more likely to opt for smaller niche deals with CEO Detlef Trefzger eyeing “selected acquisitions” to grow profits that hit an all-time high in 2016 but stalled in the first half of this year. The company acquired the U.S. transportation broker Retrans in 2015. The logistics/forwarding industry is also awaiting the next move by XPO, whose CEO Bradley Jacobs said recently that the US company is ready to return to M&A, with $8 billion to spend on takeovers on either side of the Atlantic after a two year break since buying France’s Norbert Dentressangle for $3.5 billion and Con-Way Inc. for $3 billion. And then there is China, which has jumped onto the consolidation bandwagon in container shipping and port terminals, and could soon make waves in the logistics markets as Best Inc., a Chinese logistics company backed by Alibaba Group, prepares to make its debut on the New York Stock Exchange Wednesday. title: Shippers losing out from reluctance to share data
content: A lack of trust in the supply chain is a major obstacle to realizing the gains of shipping technology. LONG BEACH — The potential to use reasonably-priced technology to cut transportation costs is often squandered because of reluctance among beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), terminal operators, container lines, and truckers to share information. “Today the challenge is not the technology,” Brian Moran, vice president of product management at Savi Technology, which provides asset-tracking products, told the Intermodal Association of North America (IANA) Intermodal Expo Monday. “The resistance comes in getting everyone to share data,” Moran said. Dozens of technology providers exhibited their wares or addressed dialogue sessions at the annual IANA event in Long Beach, California. They showed products and services designed to promote information sharing and improve efficiency in every sector of the supply chain, from the marine terminal to the distribution center or rail ramp. BCOs and carriers do not shy away from these technological tools because of cost. “I don’t hear customers talking about cost,” said Adam Compain, chief executive of ClearMetal, which utilizes predictive analytics to improve cargo booking. “They ask about reliability and service to customers,” he said. However, even if a technology is proven to reduce costs and provide information on intermodal shipments that would be of value to service providers, the data too often remains locked up in small silos within the carriers, BCOs, or service providers because of security concerns with cloud-based technology, said James Pope, director of strategy and innovation at AT&T. In reality, the cloud can be made quite secure, he said. The Port of Los Angeles and GE Transportation are attempting to address these fears in a pilot project through which carriers, terminal operators, BCOs, freight forwarders, truckers, and railroads have access to information on shipments as much as two weeks before the vessel arrives in port. Jennifer Schopfer, vice president, transport logistics, at GE Transportation, said the port portal is working. “We anticipate eight to 12 product improvements,” she said. Nevertheless, despite the deliverables, the port and GE Transportation continue to encounter a resistance among supply chain partners as they attempt to extend the pilot portwide. The main challenge continues to be to convince business partners that “it’s OK to collaborate around shared data,” she said. Data sharing can be a challenge even within the same corporate family until deliverables are recorded and trust is rewarded. title: Global Port Throughput Maintains Upward Trend
content: According to the report, the World Bank forecast a global GDP growth rate of 2.7 percent in the second quarter, the growth rate remaining stable on the whole. International trade activities boomed, the foreign trade environment improved and staple commodity prices stood high, thanks to the overall positive world economy. The cargo throughput at major ports around the world saw a year-on-year increase of 6.8 percent, significantly picking up compared to the growth in the second quarter of 2016. Container throughput at major ports was up by 7.2 percent year on year, and up by 9.8 percent quarter on quarter, with the growth rate rising again compared to that in the previous quarter. Dry bulk throughputs at major ports around the world presented divergent trends of growth. The dry bulk throughput at Qinhuangdao, China, grew substantially in the second quarter, doubling that in the same quarter of 2016 with an amount of 78.633 million tons. The growth of dry bulk throughput at major ports in Australia slipped as a result of the throughput of the coal terminal at the Port of Hay Point declining by 82 percent in April. The crude oil market had brisk supply and demand thanks to the continuous decline in global oil prices, and the liquid bulk throughput at major ports around the world sustained the trend of growth of the previous quarter.

title: Direct ChassisLink, GT Nexus founder fund ClearMetal
content: ClearMetal uses advanced technology to help predict when and where assets will be needed. ClearMetal, the San Francisco-based start-up company seeking to put predictive logistics to work in the container shipping industry, has gained an additional $9 million in venture capital funds, some of it from chassis provider Direct ChassisLink Inc., and the founder of GT Nexus. ClearMetal is one of a passel of newcomers armed with venture capital funding that are seeking to radically rearrange the cargo movement industry by harnessing digitization, artificial intelligence (AI), or other technologies. Some analysts say the industry is well behind others in technological uptake, and is ripe for new tech-fueled processes and systems to take hold. The Series A, or first round of venture capital, came from seven investors and took its total financial support to $12 million, ClearMetal said in a statement released Wednesday. The funding round was led by Prelude Ventures, a venture capital fund focused on start-ups that help mitigate climate change, and Innovation Endeavors, the fund backed by Eric Schmidt, executive chairman of Alphabet, Inc., the parent company of Google. Also investing is PSA unboXed, the venture capital arm of port operator PSA International. “PSA and ClearMetal share a vision for the future of a truly data intelligent supply chain and ClearMetal’s platform has the potential to revolutionize how we look at logistics flow,” said Elton Fong from PSA unboXed, one of the investors. “Our common aim is to enable supply chain players to offer better service to their customers, which will ultimately benefit the end consumers.” ClearMetal provides software to its customers that enables them to better organize data held internally and to forecast the progress of cargo — right down to an individual box — through the supply chain. That knowledge enables the user to better make decisions about resource allocation, preparation for the arrival of cargo, and how to use carrier space more efficiently. ClearMetal’s tally of $12 million puts it in the top dozen startups ranked by amount of venture funding received for work on the container industry, which was created by JOC.com based on data compiled by Crunchbase. Better funded start-ups include: Flexport, a digital freight forwarding company whose funding of $94 million is the largest haul among the start-ups; Freightos, a digital marketplace that has received $54 million; and Macropoint, which provides freight tracking technology and has received $44 million. The company is aiming its software at four industry sectors: carriers, shippers, terminals, and freight forwarders. The software uses AI, mathematical algorithms, and machine learning — in which a computer can accumulate information without specifically being programmed — to analyze a wide range of data provided by the user and prescriptive analysis. ClearMetal CEO Adam Compain founded the company in 2014 with two fellow students from Stanford University, where he studied for his MBA. The company’s Data Intelligence Platform was developed by top AI engineers from Stanford University, Silicon Valley, and executives from Google, GT Nexus, VF Corporation, Navis, and the broader logistics industry. The company received its first round of funding, of $3 million, 18 months ago. “ClearMetal has rapidly established itself as the category leader for predictive logistics by tackling the industry’s core data challenges and operational complexity,” said Gabriel Kra, managing director at Prelude Ventures. “Their granular approach to data mining, modeling, and simulating presents vast new opportunities for supply chain players to operate smarter, more efficiently, and with greater sustainability based on data intelligence.” Contact Hugh R. title: Truckers Are in No Hurry to Have Their Hours Tracked
content: Federal and state officials have given truckers until December to install electronic monitors that track their time on the road. The new devices are meant to make highways safer by keeping drivers from overshooting the hours they are supposed to drive. But some truckers who get paid by the mile could see their incomes drop with a more accurate accounting of the time it took them to make a delivery. And lower pay could exacerbate a driver shortage in an industry with a reputation for high turnover. “You’ll see smaller carriers leave the business,” said Rod Nofziger, chief operating officer for the Missouri-based Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association, which has 158,000 members. Since 2003, truckers have been limited to 11 hours of driving during a 14-hour on-duty stretch. Waiting at a loading dock or getting stuck in traffic counts against that time. That tempts truckers to say in their logs that deliveries happened faster than they did. Driving-log violations are the largest share of citations that police issue during truck inspections, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration says.

title: In the Future, Warehouse Robots Will Learn on Their Own
content: "It figures out the best way to grab each object, right from the middle of the clutter," said Jeff Mahler, one of the researchers developing the robot inside a lab at the University of California, Berkeley. For the typical human, that is an easy task. For a robot, it is a remarkable talent - something that could drive significant changes inside some of the world's biggest businesses and further shift the market for human labor. Today, robots play important roles inside retail giants like Amazon and manufacturing companies like Foxconn. But these machines are programmed for very specific tasks, like moving a particular type of container across a warehouse or placing a particular chip on a circuit board. They can’t sort through a big pile of stuff, or accomplish more complex tasks. Inside Amazon’s massive distribution centers — where sorting through stuff is the primary task — armies of humans still do most of the work. The Berkeley robot was all the more remarkable because it could grab stuff it had never seen before. Mahler and the rest of the Berkeley team trained the machine by showing it hundreds of purely digital objects, and after that training, it could pick up items that weren’t represented in its digital data set. “We’re learning from simulated models and then applying that to real work,” said Ken Goldberg, the Berkeley professor who oversees the university’s automation lab.

title: What to Expect From Nafta 2.0
content: Nafta, the free-trade pact among the U.S., Canada and Mexico, came under constant, withering fire during the last presidential campaign, for being unfair to American companies and workers. Now, President Trump has initiated a renegotiation of the 23-year-old pact. Talks are underway, but it’s unclear in the early days of talks what a new Nafta will look like. On this episode, we’ll get some ideas from Eugene Laney, head of international trade affairs with DHL Express U.S. He talks about the need for negotiators to focus on trade harmonization and the removal of cross-border barriers. He also discusses how the parties might address the issue of digital trade flows, which wasn’t part of the original agreement. Can the digital trade provisions of the proposed Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement, from which the U.S. has withdrawn, serve as a guide for Nafta negotiators? And what’s at stake if the talks don’t reach a conclusion that’s satisfactory to all parties? It could damage efforts to reach free-trade agreements with other countries in future. Hosted by Bob Bowman, Managing Editor of SupplyChainBrain. Look for a new episode of the podcast, which can be downloaded or streamed, every Friday on the SupplyChainBrain website and iTunes. A Nafta summary from U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

title: Six Next-Gen Technologies That Are Reshaping the Energy Industry
content: "There are hundreds of technologies out there that could impact BP, either positively or negatively, and we're constantly scanning to identify and track these," says Dan Walker, BP's emerging technology team leader. "We have to evaluate these technologies, analyze their strategic fit to BP and then prioritize them for potential action. Back in 2015, we saw the emergence of battery and fuel cells technologies, while just a couple of years later in 2017 we've seen blockchain and next generation wind technology come into focus." The next significant technologies on BP's radar are: Blockchain is a digital ledger that creates and stores records, called blocks, and then links those blocks to one another in a chain. The data in a blockchain is time stamped and the information recorded cannot be altered retrospectively — thus making records verifiable and permanent. The records are then stored in a transparent, shared database where users can see the data, but it is protected from tampering and deletion. The technology enables the direct exchange of assets or tools, such as money, contracts or intellectual property rights, in a secure way without the involvement of intermediaries to manage the exchange, like banks, utility companies or governments. The digital currency Bitcoin is the best-known example of blockchain technology, with $7bn worth in circulation today according to estimates. Blockchain could disrupt whole industries, by changing how trading is carried out and how transactions are processed and cleared. It could transform a sector such as banking, for example, where the banks currently act as intermediaries in the supply chain.

title: Growth Drivers in Place for Strong Finish This Year, Air Cargo Group Says
content: According to the organization, freight traffic in all major international markets is growing at around 10 to 15 percent, year-over-year, and "airline heads of cargo remain positive about the outlook over the year ahead." World trade finally began to improve during the first half, with volumes growing 4.1 percent, y-o-y, with support from emerging markets for the strongest first half since 2011. Meanwhile, overall confidence in the economy has also tracked upward, with consumer confidence driving strong consumer spending and increased demand for airfreight. Globally, higher demand led to FTK growth of 11.8 percent for the second quarter, which accelerated, compared with the first quarter. North America was the primary contributor to growth during Q2 of 2017, as airlines across the continent saw their share of global FTKs rise sharply, y-o-y. Asia-Pacific and European airlines also made sizeable contributions to growth in 2017, but those regions’ contributions to global growth were largely stable between the first and second quarters. In terms of cargo throughput, Asia-Pacific airports saw the strongest growth numbers early in the third quarter, particularly the Shanghai, Singapore and Hong Kong airports. Los Angeles International Airport also reported strong growth, while the Middle East — particularly Abu Dhabi, which declined 5.9 percent y-o-y in June — lost out in terms of growth as other regions compete for market share.

title: Robots Endangering Workers Drives German Startup to Airbags
content: Now, in a development that's drawn interest from car makers including Volkswagen, entrepreneurs Roman Weitschat and Hannes Hoeppner, working at the German Aerospace Center outside of Munich, say they have designed a way to better safeguard interactions between humans and robots with the aim of allowing them to work more closely. Their newly-created company, Cobotect GmbH, is using the decades-old concept of airbags to cushion potentially dangerous automated parts and prevent workers from getting hurt. Increased safety would mean robots could work more efficiently and at a faster pace when near humans, according to the researchers. “A lot of people were complaining about unsafe robots and robot tools,” Weitschat said in an interview in his laboratory. Sharp edges on parts handled by robotic arms can pose risks to workers if they are accidentally hit, making it hard to gain approval for the machines to be positioned close to humans, he said. The death in Germany, and a clutch in the U.S., are evidence of the potential dangers posed by industrial automation. While global statistics aren’t readily available, a search through the U.S. Department of Labor’s website under accidents involving robots is grim reading. The 38 incidents between 1987 and 2016 include employees amputated, asphyxiated, struck or crushed by robots, including the most recently documented: a fatal accident at a Nissan plant four years ago.

title:
Think Tank
 RSS
content: That, at least, was the chief takeaway from this year's Supply Chain Predictions Panel, an annual event presented by the San Francisco Roundtable of the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals. Each year, the S.F. Roundtable offers up a select group of industry leaders, who venture guesses about the next wave of innovations to roil supply-chain executives. Each prediction is then subjected to critical feedback from other panel members, as well as from the audience. The affair is moderated by Carl Guardino, president and chief executive officer of the Silicon Valley Leadership Group. Here, there, are the panel’s visions for 2018 and beyond: Prediction: Driverless technology for interstate trucking will be approved for prototyping in 2018, according to T.S. Khurana, vice president of global sourcing and operations engineering with Facebook. He believes automation “will disrupt the way we move freight around this country by 2025.” Last year, Khurana noted, there were 120,000 deaths related to big rigs on the nation’s highways, and 95 percent of them were ascribable to human error. The continuing death toll will motivate regulators to move more quickly than one might expect, he suggested. Response: Panelist Mike Thomas, vice president of logistics with Grocery Outlet, disagreed — but mostly about the timing. “Seven years to make that happen is a little bit too quick,” he said. The major stumbling block will be the nature of urban transportation, in particular the “final mile” of delivery within cities. That piece of the puzzle will still be subject to human control beyond 2025, Thomas said, and most members of the audience agreed. Panelist Kerry McCracken, a former senior vice president with Flex Connect, thought Khurana might be on the right track after all. She noted the rapid transformation of society wrought by the iPhone in its 10 short years of existence. “I don’t think this is insurmountable,” she said. Prediction: Rumors of the death of brick-and-mortar retailing are entirely premature, said Thomas. “Even in 2030, people will still be going to the grocery store.” Those who believe otherwise are likely to reside in the Bay Area, he suggested, which has a blinkered view of technology. “There’s a huge chunk of the country to the East that’s a little bit different from what we experience out here,” he said. Response: Thomas received no opposition from the panel, but some audience members noted the growing dominance of the Amazon.com model, whereby even the most basic commodities can be ordered online and delivered to homes almost instantly. Millennials are especially fond of the practice, they said. Prediction: Within two to three years, a large original equipment manufacturer or supply-chain company will be “completely upended” by a startup entity, said McCracken. The reason: the blockchain. The ability to create a secure, reliable system of record within the public sphere will obviate the need for transactions within traditional enterprise resource planning (ERP) applications, she said. “Companies that take advantage of this technology are going to leapfrog, just like Uber did to the taxi industry.” Response: The panel was split. Again, the disagreement was over timing. “Two to three years is too soon to see that level of destruction,” Thomas said. “Maybe five years from now.” Audience members agreed that blockchain will have a disruptive impact on industry, but said it will take time to happen. A significant portion of the audience admitted to not knowing exactly what blockchain was. McCracken reiterated the iPhone and Uber analogies, while noting that the latter is taking over passenger transportation one city at a time. “But we’re going to see some exciting things happen in the next two to three years,” she said. McCracken also predicted that blockchain will come to play a major role in consumer commerce, especially in areas such as prescription drugs. Prediction: Oil prices “will not change appreciably” over the next six to seven years, said Khurana. He pointed to the huge reserves of oil discovered in Australia, which will pose a challenge to Mideast producers. As a result, Khurana said, “there will be no big change to the China or Mexico mass-manufacturing model.” Response: Again, a split panel and audience. Thomas said many companies will be switching to greener technologies in spite of high oil reserves. Governments, meanwhile, will push for alternative fuels as a hedge against the impact of extreme weather events that disrupt petroleum flows. But Khurana stressed that low oil prices will keep current manufacturing models in place for some time to come. “Cheap energy is here to stay,” he said. Prediction: Addressing the issue of driverless passenger vehicles, Thomas predicted that many grocery shoppers will still be driving to the store in their own cars — driven by themselves — in 2030. Response: “The grocery store will come to people. People will not go the grocery stores,” countered Khurana. McCracken said the cost of cars will make ownership unattractive. But Thomas insisted that Americans will cling to the “tremendous freedom” of car ownership, as least for the next 13 years or so. While ownership and human driving “may eventually go the way of the dinosaurs,” he said, “it’s not going to be in 2030, for the vast majority of people.” Prediction: Artificial intelligence and machine learning will have a profound effect on the supply chain, in areas such as customer service and education, said Khurana. “It will prompt us to rethink how we educate our population,” he said. Lower-impact jobs of relatively less value will be automated, with robots performing them “more efficiently than humans can possibly imagine.” Response: McCracken disagreed that people will need to be extensively retrained to adjust to the new technology, which will feature an intuitive interface. “Smart shelves” will make purchase suggestions, she said. “It’s going to feel more natural to people.” Prediction: Within the next 12 months, corporate tax rates will dip below 30 percent, international tax loopholes will remain in place, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average will break 23,000, said Khurana. Thomas said a 30-percent corporate tax rate won’t make that much of a difference anyway. Others thought Khurana’s predictions were either off base or too optimistic on all three fronts. title: Makers of Fuel-Guzzling Big Rigs Try to Go Green
content: Spurred by new pollution regulations and sluggish demand, truck makers including Navistar International Corp., Daimler AG, Paccar Inc. and Volvo AB, along with engine manufacturer Cummins Inc., are rethinking everything from engine design to the shape of the trailer to bump up fuel efficiency. Even small gains can have a big environmental impact. Each year in the U.S., roughly 1.7 million tractor-trailer trucks consume about 26 billion gallons of diesel. Getting an extra mile a gallon would equal removing more than 200,000 trucks from the road. It also could save trucking companies billions of dollars. Some truck makers want to ditch the combustion engine entirely. Cummins introduced the industry’s first fully-electric heavy-duty demonstration truck in August while Tesla Inc. plans to announce its own prototype next month. But it may be years before they hit the road in big numbers. Meanwhile, the industry is betting on squeezing fuel savings from diesel trucks. “The race is on,” said Steve Gilligan, vice president of marketing for Navistar’s North America business. “Every truck manufacturer is looking for a technology advantage versus their competition.”

title: DP-DHL Launches Tool to Identify Supply Chain Disruption Risk
content: Even after the season ends, complete recovery will be a long process - with impacts that many haven't yet considered. Deutsche Post DHL Group is encouraging logistics providers to consider and prepare for impacts caused by events like hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria, and has introduced a risk-management tool called DHL Resilience360 - with the goal of allowing its customers "to detect future obstacles along the supply chain and take early actions to mitigate business risks," says Tobias Larsson, head of Resilience360 and DHL customer solutions. Resiliance360 is a cloud-based platform that combines DHL’s risk exposure index, which is weighted across about 30 risk categories, with supply chain and business impact data from its customers to predict future obstacles. In an example of the type of notice Resiliance360 provides, DHL said that analytics from the platform predicted shortages of chemicals surrounding widespread U.S. Gulf Coast production outages during Hurricane Harvey, and the likely impact of those shortages on the automotive, life sciences and healthcare and electronics industries. A company that needs those chemicals, and receives the prediction that production in and supply from the area could be cut off by the storm, could pre-order the necessary supplies ahead of time.

title: Wal-Mart Is Testing Grocery Delivery Straight Into Your Fridge
content: Wal-Mart said on Friday it is testing a service with tech company August Home in which workers can bring deliveries all the way into your kitchen and even unload the items into your refrigerator and freezer in your absence. The retailer, looking to get any new advantage it can in grocery delivery over Amazon.com now that its biggest rival has bought Whole Foods, is testing the idea in Silicon Valley only for now and restricting it to August Home customers who opt in. Customers will need an August Home smart lock that lets a delivery person from Deliv, the service Wal-Mart's sister chain Sam's Club already works with, into the house. The system grants the driver a one time permission for entry and a customer can monitor the proceedings remotely via security camera after being alerted to the driver's arrival via a text. Once the delivery is done, the homeowner gets a notification that the August lock has been closed. While this is only a test for now, Wal-Mart suggested it is likely to roll this out further if it takes with customers. The company also seemed to anticipate misgivings, or even feelings that the service is creepy and invasive, in the blog post, but made clear that Wal-Mart's first priority right now is to experiment and find services customers want. "What might seem novel today could be the standard tomorrow. This may not be for everyone — and certainly not right away — but we want to offer customers the opportunity to participate in tests today and help us shape what commerce will look like in the future," Sloan Eddleston, vice president of Wal-Mart eCommerce Strategy & Business Operations said in a blog post.

title: Shipper demand pushes limits of supply chain visibility
content: ATLANTA — The top priority of shippers in the Amazon era is increasingly clear: visibility. The need to know where inventory is in the supply chain, not once or twice a day but in near real-time, has never been greater, driven by fulfillment cycles as tight as two hours, let alone two days. The definition of visibility, however, is changing as quickly as the speed with which goods are ordered and delivered online. Supply chain visibility is not limited to tracking trucks, or freight, and gaining a clearer view of the supply chain is just a first step, not an end in itself. “Five years ago, visibility meant where’s my stuff and when’s it going to be there. Today, we’re down to the SKU level,” Bob Biesterfeld of C.H. Robinson Worldwide said at the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals (CSCMP) annual conference, held here this week. “As we capture data in 15 minute increments, we’re getting a better understanding of what are the supply chain risks,” and the further steps needed to protect customers, said Biesterfeld, president of North American surface transportation for the $13 billion logistics company. “This becomes critical when you think of the Food Safety Modernization Act, the need for temperature controls and monitoring of freight in transit,” he said. “The ability to provide real-time temperature data while in transit will help us create a more efficient supply chain.” The demand for visibility does not stop at the shipment level or the increasingly regulated food supply chain. Shippers, brokers, and carriers need greater visibility when it comes to their logistics partners and customers to more clearly and accurately assess and mitigate risk. “It’s really about having the visibility into your supply chain you need to identify choke points that could shut you down,” such as a flooded supplier in Houston, Henry Canitz, product marketing director for supply chain software provider Logility, said at the CSCMP conference. The biggest choke point en route to that goal is determining how to use the massive amount of data on shipments, vehicles, and assets streaming toward transportation management systems, he said. “And you need master data sets to complement transactional data,” he said. That master data includes data, valid and verifiable data, on transportation and logistics partners, right down to the street address of carriers and consignees. That data form the digital infrastructure that visibility programs and other supply chain software tools need to function. With many businesses reducing inventories but selling more products, and turning products from shelf to customer faster, visibility needs to encompass supplier networks, not just shipments, Aaron Parrott, a specialist leader in Deloitte Consulting's supply chain and manufacturing practice, said in an interview. “There's a growing need to really understand the tiers of your supply network, who is actively involved, and what is the risk exposure," Parrott said. "Visibility not just mapping the network, but understanding how it is working at all times, so you can [be] managing through crises as well as on a day-to-day basis.” “What customers are striving for is not so much visibility to track the truck, though we can do that, but to achieve long-range inventory optimization and supply chain planning,” Canitz said. “There’s still a lot of ‘firefighting’ in the supply chain, but we’re seeing more long-term planning.” There are more visibility tools for shippers to fight supply chain fires and optimize operations than ever. The rapid growth of mobile technology, propelled by the ubiquitous smartphone, has made the SKU-level tracking mentioned by Biesterfeld a reality in less than a decade. Investment money is flowing toward firms offering visibility products. Descartes’ $107 million acquisition of $12.5 million MacroPoint sent a clear signal validating tracking technology, expectations for growing visibility demand, and the underlying need that technology meets. That validation is underscored by the large number of new visibility products and alliances announced at the CSCMP conference. “We believe visibility is now table stakes for shippers negotiating with brokers and carriers,” said Brent Hutto, chief relations officer at Truckstop.com. The online freight marketplace and load board operator this week said it would offer GPS-based load tracking free with its premium service offerings to third-party brokers and shippers, including its Truckstop Pro, LoadPay and Rate Analysis services, and Rate API subscriptions. More and more shippers are demanding real-time location data from their third-party logistics providers and brokers, making visibility the “number one pain point” for non-asset and asset companies alike, said Bill Vitti, chief commercial officer for Truckstop.com. FourKites, which signed a major deal with Schneider National last week, announced an alliance with less-than-truckload data and software provider SMC3 at the CSCMP meeting. That agreement follows a partnership with 3GTMS, a transportation management software provider. In many ways, truck tracking began with Schneider National, which installed satellite-based Qualcomm truck tracking equipment in its fleet in 1988. The company’s partnership with FourKites focuses on tracking shipments moved by its non-asset supply chain division. Trimble recently acquired 10-4 Systems, a company that helps shippers track freight across modes at the shipment level, both in US and international supply chains. Trimble adds 10-4 to a portfolio of transportation offerings that includes TMW Systems, PeopleNet, and ALK Technologies. Visibility has evolved quickly from tracking trucks to trailers and containers to individual shipments. Research firm Gartner expects that level of visibility to be ubiquitous within two to five years. The next step will be analytics that make supply chains, not just shipments, clearer. title: Container Ships Need Better Fire-Fighting Systems, Insurance Group Says
content: Recent examples of fires include those on NNCI Arauco (9,000 TEU) in September 2016 during welding operations whilst alongside in Hamburg, Hanjin Pennsylvania (4,000 TEU) in November 2002 claiming the lives of two crew members and resulting in a constructive total loss; and MSC Flaminia (6,732TEU) in July 2012, resulting in three fatalities and also a constructive total loss. In remote locations and on the open sea, it can often be hours or even days after a fire has broken out before external assistance arrives. As a rule, only seagoing tugs carry the necessary equipment for effective firefighting. Until they arrive, the crew has to rely on its own resources, and the fire can spread extensively. As a result, as with the MSC Flaminia, it can take weeks to bring the fire under control. Whilst IUMI expressly welcomes the 2014 amendment to the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) to increase the effectiveness of firefighting, the association believes more should be done. "Recent amendments to SOLAS are a move in the right direction but they do not go far enough,” said Helle Hammer, IUMI political forum chair. The legal requirements prescribed by SOLAS were originally developed for fires on board general cargo vessels, and these ships are structurally very different to a container vessel, and cargo is stored differently. We believe the mode of fire-fighting set out in SOLAS is not suitable for a modern container ship."

title: How Consumer Brands Can Surf 'The Black Wave'
content: Ad executive, author and business strategist Daniel Brian Cobb calls it "the black wave" - a world in which old advertising methods are no longer effective means for communicating with consumers. Instead, he says, brands must embrace digital marketing. He joins us on this episode to explain the term, and tells why it's essential to the survival of brands. He discusses how advertisers can cope with consumers' increasingly short attention spans, how they can become compelling “story makers,” and how they can transform themselves into “purpose-driven” brands. That can be a risky move, if consumers detect inauthenticity in the message. But when done properly, it can elevate a brand above the noise that permeates all media today. The key, Cobb says, lies in building customer-relationship networks, which can reach millions of people with individualized messaging. Look for a new episode of the podcast, which can be downloaded or streamed, every Friday on the SupplyChainBrain website and iTunes. Cobb’s book, Surfing the Black Wave: Brand Leadership in a Digital Age.

title: Opinion: Four Tips to Renewing Your Freight Broker Bond
content: Every year, freight broker bond renewal deadlines for many brokers fall in early October, and a number of others follow in November and December. This typically means a lot of work for sureties and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) - which can create delays. In order to make the deadline brokers are advised to renew as early as possible. 1. Remember the deadline. If you tend to forget deadlines, make sure to be reminded of this one because missing it can create difficulties for your status as a licensed freight broker. Typically sureties will remind their clients well in advance of a bond renewal deadline — often once within 90, and then within 60 and 30 days of the deadline. If you haven't received notice of your surety, play it safe by double-checking your bond expiration date. If you operated as a freight broker in or before 2013, it is highly likely you will need to renew your bond in October or latest by December 1. 2. Renew early to avoid delays. While you should renew your bond no later than 30 days before its expiration date, it's much better to renew earlier. With so many brokers having to renew their bonds around the same time, delays can and often do occur. Due to the FMCSA's requirement that sureties notify it 30 days prior to a bond's expiration, things can sometimes get complicated for brokers who renew in the last minute. To avoid delays and complications, strive to renew your bond as soon as you get notified by your surety or, roughly, between 60 and 30 days prior to its expiration date. 3. Improve your credit score to improve your rate. Generally, if you want to get a better rate on your bond, you need to make improvements in one or more of the various factors that influence bond cost. The most important such factor is your personal credit score. By regularly making improvements there, you can expect a year-over-year improvement in your bond premium as well. This year in particular, your credit score is likely to improve on its own. As of July 1, tax liens, civil judgments and other civil debts have been excluded from credit reports. As a result you are also likely to see a lower premium on your bond. To be sure that any negative items have been removed from your credit report, contact a credit report to get your free yearly report. 4. Check your bond premium before you renew. Bond cost can vary from one year to the next. Typically, the cost of your freight broker bond is determined by your surety when you apply. Your surety considers your credit score, your financial statements as well as other personal financials in determining your premium. If you've improved your credit score but haven't seen much of an improvement in your rate or are generally unhappy with your bond cost, you could request a quote at another surety agency for comparison. When requesting a quote at another surety, make sure you choose an agency that performs soft pulls of your credit. Each hard pull negatively affects your credit. Apart from renewing your freight broker bond, you may also need to update your information with the FMCSA. While the Administration's intent was to launch the Unified Registration System (URS) this year, this has been executed only in part.
