title: Warehouse Conversions Aren't Just for Cities Anymore - Or Just for Warehouses
content: And in the ensuing years, the trend seemed to play out mostly in dense urban areas, where tight quarters necessitated that residents be creative. Now, however, in an era when homes and offices seem to embrace industrial décor, such “adaptive-reuse” projects are turning up in more suburban areas, in a slew of building types, like power plants, churches, schools, prisons, railroad stations, hospitals and factories. Despite their growing popularity, the conversions can be complex, time-consuming and expensive, scaring off some developers. And projects can also risk a backlash: Plans for luxury housing in buildings that once employed entire neighborhoods may not sit well with every community. But as the market for conversions expands, developers are becoming inventive, as with two current New York-area projects.

title: 3M Report: Where Buyer-Supplier Collaboration Is Falling Short
content: A new report by The 3M Company reveals some surprising conclusions about the state of buyer-supplier collaboration. Or, to be more precise, the lack of it. Turns out that many suppliers are far from embracing true collaboration. The 3M research finds fewer than half of surveyed suppliers feeling "fully empowered" to collaborate with their nominal partners. Half are holding back from making strategic recommendations, due to a lack of incentives or customer openness. And 70 percent of suppliers say that at least half of their customers lack a strong system to support collaboration. So why this disconnect between dream and reality? Jose Varela, vice president of sourcing and packaging engineering with 3M, joins us on this episode to explain where things have gone wrong. But he also delivers some good news, in the form of new efforts by both sides to strengthen ties. He explains how 3M manages an army of suppliers the world round, inviting them to offer creative input and creating a culture of transparency that promises to elevate “collaboration” above the status of everyone’s favorite buzzword. Hosted by Bob Bowman, Managing Editor of SupplyChainBrain. Look for a new episode of the podcast, which can be downloaded or streamed, every Friday on the SupplyChainBrain website and iTunes. 3M’s survey, “Driving Growth and Innovation Through Supplier Partnerships.”

title: Japanese logistics companies pile into Myanmar SEZ
content: The Thilawa special economic zone has been growing steadily since its 2015 opening. Japan’s logistics industry continues to pour money into Myanmar’s Thilawa special economic zone (SEZ), with four companies opening warehouses there in the past six months. That interest is expected to continue to grow as the SEZ embarks on an 100-hectare (247 acres) expansion with financial support from the Japan International Cooperation Agency that is scheduled for completion in mid-2018. Fujitrans Corp. is the most recent to open facilities in the SEZ, with a 34,980-square-meter (376,521-square-foot) site that hosts a 5,120-square-meter warehouse and 6,000-square-meter container yard. Fujitrans joins Konoike Transport, Yusen Logistics, and Nippon Express in establishing new operations in the SEZ since the start of fiscal year 2017, which began in April. As of the end of July, there were a total of 79 companies from 17 foreign countries and regions, including 39 Japanese companies, that had set up operations in the Thilawa SEZ. Most of the 79 companies are manufacturers of various products who want to take advantage of Myanmar’s cheap and abundant labor force to make products for sale in local and neighboring markets. As the SEZ expands, the government of Myanmar is working to add capacity to its port system with a new container terminal at Thilawa to meet the growing demand. The current port, at Yangon, is too small to handle the larger ships now in service across the globe because of its draft. Japan’s Toyo Construction Co. and JFE Engineering Corp. said in January 2016 they had won a contract from the Myanmar Port Authority to build the new Thilawa port. The duo will remove 208,000 cubic meters of sediment and construct an 18-hectare container yard with two hac-type berths with drafts of 10 meters, lengths of 400 meters, and widths of 40 meters. In June this year, Japan’s Mitsui Engineering & Shipbuilding Co. (MES) said it had won a contract to supply eight cranes for the new container terminal, which is scheduled to be completed in the autumn of 2018.Contact Tomoo Yatsuhashi at yiu45535@nifty.com. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Quality control specialist highlights speed-to-market dangers
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] The humble fidget spinner sheds light on an important issue for retail supply chains. Photo credit: Shutterstock Under increasing pressure to meet the newest fad, such as fidget spinners, retail shippers risk shipment delays and even seizures when they prioritize speed over product quality control. With an increasing number of products powered by lithium-ion batteries, including the jazzed-up fidget spinner, the push for rapid delivery in a fast-paced retail market is compromising safety, according to quality control company Asia Inspection. The specialist wrote in a white paper that it was common for new and popular products to hit the stores without sufficient testing or assessment of proper use, with the pressures of speed to market the underlying reason. Asia Inspection highlighted the fidget spinner as an example. Originally marketed as a tool to assist concentration in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism, the fidget spinner quickly became the toy of choice around the world in 2017 and the gadget was soon banned in classrooms. Its distracting nature was not the most dangerous side of the fidget spinner. Asia Inspection said health and safety risks to users have resulted in the spinners becoming banned, recalled, and investigated. A variety of designs appeared on the market, including spinners that have LED lights and can play music from mobile devices through Bluetooth speakers. These high-tech fidget spinners run on lithium-ion batteries and suffer from the same problems as all other devices with that power source. As of July 2017, there have been at least three cases of spinners overheating, catching fire, or melting — sometimes while charging, sometimes during play. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission and the UK Chartered Trading Standards Institute have begun investigating the incidents, looking for an effective way to protect consumers. Lithium-ion batteries are causing mounting concern to transport providers, especially airlines. The batteries are used in a staggering amount of devices, from mobile phones and laptops to hoverboards and vaping pens. The frequency of incidents involving products powered by these batteries has spiked in recent years. “The numbers recently released by the US Federal Aviation Administration [FAA] are a good indication of the scale of the problem,” the Asia Inspection white paper noted. Between March 1991 and May 2017, the FAA recorded a total of 160 incidents involving lithium-ion batteries in cargo and baggage. As many as 48 of them — or 30 percent — took place during 2016 and the first four months of 2017. Most of these incidents were caused by batteries overheating or exploding. “It was none other than lithium-ion battery problems that resulted in the largest smartphone recall in history: the two-part recall of Samsung Galaxy Note 7 in 2016 that cost the company at least $5 billion,” Asia Inspection said. The original recall was caused by a design flaw in Note 7 phone batteries, which made their internal structure vulnerable. Soon after the manufacturer had replaced the recalled phones, it turned out that the second batch of batteries was no better. The rush to get the replacement phones to users exacerbated quality control issues, and as a result, many batteries suffered from subpar welding quality and some lacked the crucial element that separates the volatile chemicals inside them. “Ultimately, the entire Note 7 production run was recalled. Months later, this story received an epilogue when a fire broke out at one of the Tianjin factories supplying batteries to Samsung. The cause: discarded faulty batteries that were not properly disposed of.” The counterfeit battery business and misdeclaration of the cargo are the greatest threats to aviation safety and airlines and rechargeable battery makers have been waging a joint campaign to get governments to clamp down. The International Air Transport Association has teamed up with the Portable Rechargeable Battery Association (PRBA) to promote greater government oversight in the production of lithium batteries. It is an uphill battle, however, and Asia Inspection said the pace of modern-day retail kept increasing, with the first companies to get products to market being the ones that would reap the most benefits. “In this environment, it can be tempting to try and compete on speed before quality. This approach may work when chasing profitability in the short term. In the medium to long term, however, it leads to an influx of unsafe, low-quality products that risk consumer well-being and damage brand reputations. Plus, a recall on a large enough scale can cut into a company’s revenues, easily offsetting the initial gain of products rushed to the market. For an example of that, look no further than the Samsung recall of 2016.” Asia Inspection said regulatory compliance was the minimum requirement, while ensuring real product safety required a proactive approach at every stage of design and manufacturing. title: Multiple ship schedule changes undermine visibility
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] Shipping lines so frequently change schedules that it is exceedingly difficult for shippers to plan adequately and track shipments. Photo credit: Shutterstock The lack of visibility over cargo shipments regularly tops the list of pain points expressed by shippers, and data just released by CargoSmart reveal the extent of changing carrier schedules that make managing supply chains so difficult. Not only are schedules changing regularly, but many of the changes involve a time difference of more than 24 hours.According to the Hong Kong-based CargoSmart, the average number of schedule changes by carriers calling at Europe ports between July and September was 6.1 changes made per schedule, and almost half of those schedule changes were greater than 24 hours.Of the top three Europe container ports, Antwerp had the highest average number of changes at 7.4 per shipping schedule, and Rotterdam had the highest percentage of schedule changes that were over 24 hours at 49 percent.Although the schedule changes do not always result in delays, shippers told JOC.com that the many changes make it difficult to plan their supply chains and achieve real visibility of cargo along the ocean leg.A shipper on the Asia-Europe trade said, “Multiple vessel schedule changes per year and the summer versus winter deployment make the planning of consistent lead times difficult.”The logistics director for a major European importer was more blunt. “Even when we have visibility we do not have control over our shipments,” he said. “Containers will be rolled and we only know when the vessel arrives and our containers are not on board. So all in all, visibility is hopeless.”The head of supply chain at a global retailer said his main frustration was the lack of any credible container visibility platform or solution he could use to confirm loading (or not) and which he could trust. “For instance, vessels and ports are unable to deal with low visibility in northern and eastern China, and there is no solution to sweep up and catch containers left behind due to unplanned omissions,” he said.Significant investment is being made toward solving the issue of supply chain transparency, which is increasingly cited as crucial to improving logistical efficiency.CargoSmart believes the greater transparency shippers are seeking can be achieved by applying Internet of Things technology throughout a product's transportation life cycle. Using sensors, shippers or forwarders can track goods from the raw materials warehouse to the retail store and beyond with vastly improved supply chain visibility.Jeremy Nixon, CEO of Ocean Network Express, said earlier this year when he was still international head of NYK that placing a sensor inside a container or chassis would have tremendous value to players in the supply chain.“The problem today is the technology is accelerating, but we’re not quite there at a low enough cost to be able to deploy sensors in 1 million containers,” he said. “We’re not that far away in terms of being able to do that. When we do that, it will be a revolution in our industry.”Advances in tracking and data technology have seen several startups rushing to meet the need. They include Traxens, a French company developing a container data monitoring system that has attracted investment from Mediterranean Shipping Co. and CMA CGM, and SkyBitz, which helps track containers by monitoring the trailer underneath. DHL's Ocean View platform gives real-time visibility to the location of freight and can help forecast when it will arrive, as well as alerting shipper customers of possible disruption that may require a change of route. title: Rhenus opens double-hubs to handle growing Europe volume
content: Jörn Schmersahl, CEO of Rhenus air and ocean Europe, addresses a supply chain conference in Berlin. Credit: Rhenus Rhenus has opened two separate air and ocean gateways to consolidate growing shipment volumes flowing through Europe and to address increasing capacity bottlenecks. The German logistics group has opened an air cargo gateway at Frankfurt airport and an ocean freight center established at Hilden in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia.“By consolidating air and sea consignments at the new hubs, the logistics specialist aims to make its transport operations more efficient and dovetail them more closely with its overland network,” said Jörn Schmersahl, CEO of Rhenus air and ocean Europe.Schmersahl said at the International Supply Chain Conference in Berlin that import and export tonnage for both air and sea freight at Rhenus has reached high growth rates during the past few years. The sea freight gateway at Hilden has been pooling consignments since July 2017, which are then imported and exported via the nearby North Europe ports of Rotterdam and Antwerp.The less-than-containerload services between Hilden and the ports operate in line with a set timetable. “As a result, our customers can make reliable plans,” said Schmersahl.The air freight gateway is located at the CargoCity-Süd logistics hub at Frankfurt International Airport. All consignments, including temperature-controlled items and hazardous goods, can be handled during the 24/7 operations and X-rayed for security purposes. Freight is mainly shipped to Asia, North and South America, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates.“There are currently capacity bottlenecks in the market place, particularly on the air freight routes from Europe to the United States, from Europe to China, and from China to Europe,” Schmersahl said. “Using our gateway at Frankfurt Airport, we want to strengthen our market position by pooling goods and offering our customers attractive rates.” The catchment area for consignments is due to be expanded in the near future with Rhenus focusing on Austria, Poland, Slovakia, Switzerland, the Czech Republic, and Hungary.Many of the other global forwarders are also benefiting from strong air and ocean volume flowing through Europe. DSV has just released its third quarter results and the Danish forwarder reported a 50 percent increase in net profit year over year, with earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) up 31 percent.Kuehne + Nagel reported a 20 percent increase in air freight volume in the third quarter, with net income up 4 percent and EBIT rising 4.5 percent compared with the same quarter last year. Swiss compatriot Panalpina, however, went the other way. Despite handling 9.3 percent more air freight volume in the third quarter, its gross profit declined by 1.1 percent, net income fell 25 percent, and EBIT dropped by 8.5 percent.The fourth quarter should prove to be the best of the year and with the air cargo peak season still to come, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) expects to significantly upgrade its demand forecast for 2017. title: Growing air and ocean business leads DSV to solid third quarter
content: A resurgent air freight market has been good news for DSV this year. Credit: DSV DSV continues to reap the benefits of its UTi acquisition by reporting a 50 percent increase in third-quarter net profit and earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) up 31 percent, driven mainly by strong air and ocean business but also cost synergies gained from absorbing UTi into its operations.The Danish forwarding, trucking, and logistics group’s third-quarter net revenue increased by 9 percent to 18.7 billion krone ($ 2.97 billion), pushing up operating margins by 7 percent compared with the same quarter last year.Net profit for the first nine months of the year was double that of the same period in 2016, and the EBIT for the three quarters of 2017 was 46 percent higher year over year at 3.7 billion krone."A strong commercial and operational performance in the third quarter has driven earnings growth of more than 30% and a volume performance in line with or above the market,” said CEO Jens Bjørn Andersen. “We are pleased to see our business continuously improving, and based on this we upgraded our expectations for 2017 and launched a five-month share buyback programme of 1.25 million krone."Andersen said the revised expectation was partly driven by higher than expected activity levels, mainly in the air and sea division. Volumes were up especially in the air freight segment that recorded an almost 12 percent more volume year over year.European airlines have been reporting air cargo growth in excess of 10 percent and DSV managed to capture a greater business in this segment as a result, although even with greater volume the yields fell as a result of foreign exchange movements.The Danish forwarder handled 355,291 TEU in the third quarter, an increase of around 4 percent. Its January through September volume is just more than 1 million TEU, also a 4 percent increase compared with the first nine months of last year.In the road segment, DSV said tight capacity has driven up haulier rates with revenue, but the forwarder carried 4 percent more shipments and reported an EBIT increase of almost 8 percent on top of stable gross margins.Andersen said cost synergies from the UTi integration were achieved faster than expected in 2017, and the remaining full-year impact from cost synergies in 2018 was now anticipated to be 200 million krone. The savings were previously expected to be around 300 million krone. DSV acquired loss-making UTi Worldwide for $1.35 billion in a surprise announcement that represented a 50 percent premium on UTi’s closing price at the time. Since UTi was running at a significant loss, the takeover initially diluted DSV’s conversion ratio and operating margin. The company said based on its integration plan, it expected operating margins of the combined entity to be lifted back to pre-acquisition level by 2018.DSV has aggressively expanded by acquisition in the past few years, taking over Ontime Logistics, SBS Worldwide, Airmar Cargo, and Seatainers Group. The freight-forwarding market has space for more merger and acquisition activity, with the Top 10 companies accounting for 43.5 percent of the $141 billion global revenue in 2016, according to Ti, a UK-based consultancy. Germany’s DHL Global Forwarding topped the rankings with a 7.9 percent share, just ahead of Kuehne + Nagel at 7 percent, while CEVA was 10th with a 2.3 percent take. CEVA Logistics has most recently been the subject of rumors that France’s Geodis had lined it up as a takeover target, with XPO Logistics and Kuehne + Nagel also tipped as potential suitors. title: Parcel carriers fare best in top 50 revenue growth
content: Small package carriers were a bright spot in an otherwise lackluster 2016 for the global transportation industry. Photo credit: Shutterstock Continued slow growth in the global economy suppressed revenue at the world’s top 50 transportation service providers, according to an annual analysis conducted for JOC.com by SJ Consulting Group. The latest analysis found the top 50 providers of transportation services generated aggregate revenue of $669.9 billion in 2016, down 1.5 percent from 2015. Of the 50 companies listed, only about a dozen — including UPS, FedEx, CMA CGM, Nippon Express, Yamato Holdings, SNCP Geodis, XPO Logistics, DSV, DPD/GeoPost, Hitachi Transport, J.B. Hunt, and Schneider — registered increased revenue. As usual, the new list covers international and domestic traffic, but numbers relating to ocean traffic are entirely international. In the past, currency fluctuations have had an impact on the top 50 rankings, but for the latest list, foreign exchange fluctuations were not a factor, said Mark D’Amico, senior analyst at SJ Consulting Group. The yen was up, the euro was flat, but collectively, foreign exchange rates were not a factor. For the United States, 2016 was a slow growth year. GDP grew 1.5 percent, which affected every sector of transportation in the country, D’Amico said. The truckload market, the less-than-truckload sector, and rail revenue were all down, though the decline in LTL and truckload revenue was primarily attributed to lower fuel surcharge revenue, as diesel prices continued their decline. Ocean freight carriers had another down year in 2016, with revenue declining 8.2 percent collectively. That compares with a decline of only 1.5 percent for the total revenue of the top 50 service providers. By and large, the only success stories from a revenue perspective on the top 50 list were the parcel carriers, in the United States and global markets. Continued growth in the parcel sector benefitted from a broad-based expansion in e-commerce and the online retailers who deploy continuing improvements in related technologies. Overall, those companies for which parcel transportation was the dominant revenue source grew at an aggregate rate of 9.5 percent in 2016. As in the past year, this included the same familiar names: UPS, FedEx, and DHL (which is also a 3PL). FedEx’s acquisition of TNT in the May 2016 contributed to Memphis-based FedEx’s 13.7 percent increase in revenue during 2016. Even excluding the impact of the company’s May 2016 acquisition of TNT Express, revenue still grew at 6.1 percent for the year. That is especially strong in comparison to the rest of the list, which was down 1.5 percent for the year. Hit by weak freight rates, many ocean carriers produced negative revenue numbers. Collectively, freight rates on eight of the major trans-Pacific and trans-Atlantic shipping lanes were down 12 percent in 2016 compared with 2015, D’Amico said. Major carriers such as MOL (minus 8.5 percent), Cosco Shipping (minus 2.6 percent), Hapag-Lloyd (minus 12.7 percent), Hamburg Sud (minus 7.3 percent), Orient Overseas International (minus 10.6 percent), Hyundai Merchant Marine (minus 22.9 percent), Evergreen Group (minus 10.9 percent), and Yang Ming Marine Transport (minus 10.0 percent) suffered significant declines in 2016, compared with the previous year. One exception was CMA CGM, whose revenue grew 1.9 percent, a modest figure considering that CMA CGM acquired Neptune Orient Lines in December 2015, thus enabling the firm to include an entire year in its revenue figures for 2016. Elsewhere in East Asia, China Cosco merged with China Shipping Container Lines, but their revenue was nevertheless down for 2016. Neither of Taiwan’s major shipping companies, Evergreen and Yang Ming, made any acquisitions, contributing to the weakness of their overall revenue. Acquisition activity in the ocean market continued into 2017, with Maersk acquiring Hamburg Sud in March 2017 and CMA CGM acquiring the Brazilian cabotage line Mercosul in June 2017. In addition to M&A activity in the ocean market, the 91 percent growth figure enjoyed by XPO Logistics during 2016 was, “strongly driven by acquisitions” made in earlier years, when XPO’s management made a concerted effort to acquire a long list of companies to broaden its portfolio of complementary logistics services. XPO has not made any major acquisition since its October 2015 acquisition of Con-way, the second largest LTL transportation provider in North America. Rather than acquire additional companies in 2016, XPO Logistics has been focusing on successfully integrating the various companies it has acquired. “They are improving operations and profitability of the companies that they bought earlier, rather than stay on that buying spree they were on,” D’Amico said. “They have been successful especially with their acquisition of Con-way, which was their biggest one. They have driven tremendous profitability in that company,” increasing their profit margins by 4 or 5 percent. During the four quarters of 2016 — which were the first four full quarters following Con-way’s acquisition by XPO, Con-way’s LTL operating margin improved by an average of 4.4 percent. Denmark-based DSV is the company on the top 50 list that has grown at the second-highest rate. Acquiring UTI Worldwide in January 2016, DSV added about $4 billion in revenue to its financial results. DSV is active in air, ocean, and truck brokerage in Europe; as well as air and ocean forwarding, and warehousing. D’Amico explained that UTI was in all of those activities as well, so that its acquisition by DSV was “driven by opportunity to gain from a larger scale in the different divisions." According to DSV, this acquisition made it the fourth-largest global freight forwarder, adding 50 percent to its existing revenue, coupled with a more diversified geography and business mix, including more than 40,000 employees, operations in more than 80 countries, more than 1,000 offices and logistics facilities, and 4.7 square meters of warehousing space. It also noted that with UTi in the fold, DSV is now the sixth-largest ocean and seventh-largest air freight operator. Meanwhile, each of the nine railroads on this year’s top 50 list of global transportation providers registered declining revenue, including those near the top of the list, such as China Railways (ranked fourth) and Russia Railways (ranked sixth), and Canadian Pacific (ranked 44th). This was due in part to lower fuel surcharges — linked to declining oil prices. In the United States, as well as abroad, freight volumes were also down because lower truck rates weakened the value proposition of using rail, rather than truck. The growth of parcel companies was not limited to the major US- and Europe-based companies near the top of the list. Outside North America, smaller parcel companies also enjoyed growing revenue, with Japan’s Yamato Holdings up 14 percent, Japan’s Sagawa up 6 percent, China’s SF Express up 18 percent, and France’s DPD/GeoPost up 8.4 percent. A major reason was the rapid growth of deliveries to people’s homes by parcel carriers, and a reduction in shipments that are transported from distribution centers to retail outlets for pick up by consumers. Naturally, that trend continues to negatively impact some of that trucking activity, D’Amico said. What lies ahead for 2017? During the first half of 2017, container freight rates and stagnant economic growth started to reverse, D’Amico said, already sparking an improvement in the results for the top 10 carriers on the list, excluding China Railways. For those top 10 carriers, revenue is up 9.6 percent year over year during the first half of 2017. Even excluding the acquired revenue from TNT for FedEx, the revenue for the top 10 carriers was up 6.8 percent year over year through the first half of 2017. In another encouraging sign for global transportation providers, global container volumes grew an average of 6.7 percent during the first half of 2017, according to analyst Alphaliner. Moreover, during the second quarter, global container volume accelerated to 7.4 percent, compared with 5.9 percent during the first quarter. Container volumes at South Asia ports are driving the growth, up 9.3 percent during the first half. At the country level, ports in China (up 8.4 percent) and the United States (up 8.2 percent) grew at the fastest rate, thus providing greater opportunities for transportation service providers that are active in those countries. Ranking is based on 2016 revenue, in millions of US dollars. title: Dallas packaging center to seek West Coast resin exports
content: Ports around the United States are competing for a projected surge in plastics exports. Warehouse operator Katoen Natie has started construction on a Dallas packaging center that will package and containerize bulk shipments of synthetic resins produced at Gulf Coast plants for rail movement via West Coast ports to Asia. The new facility is scheduled to open in the third quarter of 2018 in the Prime Pointe industrial park adjacent to Union Pacific Railroad, which is promoting a “Dallas-to-Dock” intermodal rail service for movement of resins to West Coast ports. BNSF Railway also is working with packagers to develop bulk-to-container transloading centers in the area. The efforts are aimed at winning a share of resin exports that are forecast to more than double to approximately 1 million TEU annually during the next few years. IHS Markit chemical analysts expect more than a half-dozen large new plants along the Gulf Coast to begin production by late 2018. Several already have begun production. The surge in resin manufacturing is driven by low-cost US natural gas feedstocks. The Port of Houston through the first eight months of the year handled 39 percent of US containerized resin exports, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com. Other ports, including Los Angeles, Long Beach, New Orleans, Charleston, and Savannah also are gunning for a share of the increased volume. US containerized exports of synthetic plastic resins through August are down 10.5 percent from last year to 406,517 TEU, according to PIERS. Hurricane Harvey forced more than 50 percent of polyolefin and olefin production in the region offline, according to IHS Markit chemical analysis. These closures delayed shipments, and ports including Houston were shut down for nearly one week, which contributed to the decline. Houston’s stiffest competition for resin exports is expected to be intermodal rail shipments via Dallas-Fort Worth, an import hub that has a large supply of empty containers, to the West Coast, which has ample vessel capacity by carriers eager for westbound backhauls to Asia. Kenny Rocker, Union Pacific vice president and general manager, industrial, said the new Katoen Natie facility at Dallas “aligns with container availability, a core need of our customer base,” and that intermodal connections to West Coast ports will enable producers to reach overseas destinations. "The Dallas facility will assist our customers in diversifying their export channels to global markets," said Frank Vingerhoets, president of Katoen Natie, who spoke along with Rocker at a groundbreaking ceremony for the packaging center, which will be the company’s 20th North American location. Katoen Natie’s Dallas facility will start with at least 250,000 square feet of warehouse space that could be expanded to as much as 2.5 million square feet. title: 'Logistics insourcing' leverages tech to cut shipper costs
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] Some companies want to retain as much control over their supply chain as possible. Photo credit: Shutterstock Relying on cloud-based technology and two new partnerships, a start-up logistics company hopes to help US shippers build and retain in-house supply chain expertise rather than outsource. Haversack Logistics claims to be not a third-party logistics provider (3PL) but a “first-party” logistics provider, a term and concept that will be new to many shippers. “We are the anti-3PL,” says Chris Nadeau, president of Haversack Logistics. He is not talking about managed transportation either. “We want our clients to manage their logistics to gain competitive advantage. We don’t garner control.” Nadeau sees an underserved market: shippers that want to either keep logistics functions in-house, rather than outsourcing them, or to bring those functions back under their roof. Many shippers outsource responsibility for transportation and logistics execution to 3PLs and lose control over those functions and talent. Nadeau wants to offer them a different choice. “With us, the shipper controls all aspects of their business, and we go with their decisions,” the former US Army officer and trucking executive said. “They’re going to make the best decision for their organization every time, as long as they have the ability to do that.” Haversack identifies potential supply chain savings, and is only paid if those savings are realized, he said. The company, which launched services March 1, claims to have saved its initial clients 22 to 52 percent, lowering less-than-truckload (LTL), parcel, and truckload costs through proactive analysis and “micro audits.” Haversack starts with an assessment of transportation and warehousing volumes and costs and looks for opportunities to improve sourcing, route, and load optimization. Once a shipper client approves Haversack’s suggested plan, a specific instance of Haversack's "in-the-cloud" software platform is configured for that shipper. Pricing and routing data is confirmed, carrier integrations are verified, key production indicators are set, and the shipper’s transportation team is trained and coached on operating features and business analytics. Haversack makes money solely through the savings generated for the customer. “We are an invested partner in improving their profit and loss statement, so if the operational execution of our plan doesn't generate projected savings, we don't earn our fees,” Nadeau said. “Our clients see every day how cost per mile or hundredweight goes down. They have complete visibility.” Haversack is not an “Uber for Trucking” company, but it is one of the new crop of startups that are building new business models on the back of the latest cloud-based technology and real-time data communications via application programming interfaces. Those technologies, closely tied to the expansion of mobile computing, are creating opportunities for innovation. “The whole concept of how customers interact is fundamentally changing, and it’s all being driven by the iPhone and Amazon,” Michael Seneski, director of corporate strategy at Ford Motor Company, said at a recent conference on supply chain automation organized by project44. Nadeau believes similar change is possible in how shippers interact with their partners. He launched Haversack after five years in the LTL industry with Con-way Freight and XPO Logistics and a career as a combat engineer with the US Army, most recently serving as brigade command sergeant major, responsible for operations at the 2nd Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division. Logistics was key to that job. “I went from moving tanks to moving brown boxes,” Nadeau said. He said the latest technology makes it possible for shippers, large and small, that formerly had to outsource logistics to gain greater efficiency and savings to bring those functions back in-house. For many shippers, exercising direct control over execution-level functions is likely to become more important as supply chain fulfillment becomes faster and more demanding. “Yesterday’s solution will become today’s problem, if you don’t constantly look at it and audit yourself,” Nadeau said in an interview. The need for more experienced transportation and logistics managers will lead to “insourcing,” he said. In many cases, “If you gave a shipper the best technology and expert advice, they can run the supply chain themselves.” Haversack may be the “anti-3PL,” but it is not against working with other logistics service providers on behalf of its clients. The goal is not necessarily the “disintermediation” often associated with “digitalization” but an expanded set of options for shippers. “Transparency is key,” Nadeau said. “Shippers have to see where they’re spending, what’s trending.” To provide that transparency, the Davidson, North Carolina-based company partnered with transportation management software developer MercuryGate and logistics application programming interface provider project44. Haversack is one of the first companies to resell MercuryGate’s TMS software, he said, offering a “private label” version of the TMS. Partnering with project44 gives Haversack access to a network of application programming interfaces (APIs) for the real-time exchange of pricing information, shipment status, electronic documents, and other data. The APIs connect to the MercuryGate TMS system. The result, Nadeau said, will be “immediate connection” to a broad array of multimodal transportation providers. There is plenty of room for 3PLs and “1PLs” to grow, with large and small shippers. “We come across a lot of shippers that have no technology at all in-house, but rely on carrier websites,” Nadeau said. “Then there are big companies that aren’t taking full advantage of the technology they have. And there are a lot of legacy systems out there that haven’t been updated.” Convincing business with long-established practices to look at logistics in a new way is not easy. “There’s a learning curve you’ve got to start with,” he acknowledged. But as truck and intermodal pricing pressure intensifies and capacity tightens, more shippers will be looking for new options and routes to supply chain savings. “If you’ve got the right tools and position yourself correctly you’re going to be successful,” Nadeau said. title: Bangladesh starts work on single window
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] The single window is part of a wider program of infrastructure investment to make logistics in Bangladesh easier. Photo credit: Shutterstock Bangladesh will spend 5.85 billion taka ($69.46 million) to establish a single window for customs with the goal of easing pressure on regularly congested infrastructure. The single window will bring all of the government departments involved in importing and exporting under an integrated information technology network and eliminate the use of paper for numerous customs declarations such as certificates of origin. “If we can submit documents electronically and those are checked immediately online, we will be able to get our goods exported and delivered quickly,” said Alamgir Hossain, an electronic goods importer. The single window will also cut down on tax and duty evasion by making it more difficult to carry out fraud. Bangladesh’s National Board of Revenue will implement the project, which will connect the customs department, the central bank, Bangladesh Investment Development Authority, the Office of the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms, all the banks, and service-providing agencies. The World Bank will provide 5.29 billion taka of the funding, with Bangladesh providing the remainder 561 million taka. Bangladesh’s exports doubled their world market share between 1995 and 2012 as the value of those exports also doubled as a result of rapid growth in the ready-made garments industry. That industry makes up 80 percent of Bangladesh’s exports, according to IHS Markit data. Bangladesh’s infrastructure is in dire need of improvement, particularly the Chittagong port, which is crippled by congestion more often than not. "The inability of the transport and logistics network to keep up with the pace of demand is hampering trade performance,” the World Bank said in the single window project document. The country ranks 87 out of 160 countries on the World Bank’s 2016 Logistics Performance Index, compared with 35 for India. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: Logistics reforms power Indian jump in World Bank ranking
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] From ports to highways, India's supply chains are flowing faster. Photo credit: Shutterstock Indian efforts to make it easier to do business in the country paid off on Tuesday as the country jumped up 30 spots to 100 in the World Bank’s 2018 'Doing Business' report. Among those reforms are a shift to paperless customs, a number of operational changes at ports throughout the country, a monetary policy adjustment, and tax reforms credited with improving trucking productivity. “With eight reforms making it easier to do business in 2016 to 2017, India was the only economy in South Asia to join the list of the 10 top improvers,” the global lender stated in its latest report. The report particularly highlighted the rapid progress Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) made in reducing “border compliance times” with infrastructure and process improvements. With direct port delivery services for the clearance of import cargo and a similar fast-track scheme for gate-in of factory-stuffed exports, cargo dwell times have shortened dramatically at JNPT, lowering logistics costs and cutting congestion. Other steps included automated gate procedures and a radio-frequency identification (RFID) technology-enabled container tracking system. In a recent report, the RFID service provider said JNPT terminals are able to process ships between two and two-and-a-half days and that overall dwell times there average 48 hours. “Thanks to the increased use of electronic and mobile platforms, since July 2016, importers under the authorized economic operator [AEO] program have been able to clear cargo faster through simplified customs procedures,” the World Bank stated. The government said the big leap resulted from widespread stakeholder consultations on addressing user needs, redesigning rules and procedures in sync with trade requirements, and streamlining all of these to a “more conducive business environment.” Cargo clearance at all other gateways in India has also become much faster as well, with most of those processes going online and the infrastructure upgrades. Digitization should gain further pace at Indian ports with an electronic self-sealing program for factory-stuffed export cargo in the works. Authorities are also working toward a "port community system" to integrate all trade processes tied to delivery orders, transport orders, gate open-cut off times, delivery gate schedules, gate-in bookings, and pre-gate schedules under a single digital tool. Additionally, new legislation to transform all major state ports into independent companies will give them a freer hand to improve their infrastructure and compete better with privately-operated minor rivals. India could make further gains thanks to its Sagar Mala port-led program to reduce import and export costs that undermine the country’s trade competitiveness and make logistics cost 14 percent to 18 percent of GDP. Last week the government also unveiled an immense Rs. 6.92-trillion (approximately $106.63 billion) road-building program for over the next five years. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: GE-LA port pilot targets predictive capabilities
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] The full benefits of GE's information portal will be realized when it goes port-wide in 2018. Photo credit: Port of Los Angeles The Port of Los Angeles' information portal that is under development now seeks to provide more predictive capability that will enable beneficial cargo owners (BCOs) to plan for when their shipments will be available for delivery at the marine terminal, port managers said Tuesday. “Anticipated delivery is absolutely critical information for BCOs,” Eric Caris, director of cargo marketing, told a Propeller Club of Southern California meeting Tuesday. The port in late 2016 teamed up with GE Transportation to develop a single window through which port users can access the information they need to carry out their roles in the supply chain. The pilot project involving APM Terminals, Maersk Line, and Mediterranean Shipping Co. has been gradually increasing its functionality. The port and GE Transportation are now expanding the portal to include all terminal operators and shipping lines, with the goal being to go live with a port-wide portal in mid-2018, said Chris Chase, cargo marketing manager. BCOs, truckers, railroads, third-party logistics providers, customs brokers, and intermodal equipment providers (IEPs) each require specific information on shipments, as far in advance of vessel arrival as possible, in order to plan their schedules for cargo pickup or delivery. The vessel manifest is the triggering document for this information, Chase said. Chase said Los Angeles executive director and former president of the Americas at APL, Gene Seroka, noted that the manifest information is known to the shipping line as much as two weeks before the vessel reaches a US port. “Cargo is on the water for two weeks, so he said, ‘Why don’t we do something with the information?’” Chase said. If the information is shared in advance of vessel arrival so the discharge of each container can be forecasted, terminals can plan their labor and equipment needs, IEPs will ensure they have the right number of chassis available at each terminal, truckers can plan their dispatch schedules, railroads will plan their intermodal trains, and BCOs and third-party vendors will prepare the logistics details for delivery to their facilities. Initial experience with the pilot has shown that all of this information is available, but it is scattered throughout the transportation supply chain. GE Transportation is developing the platform into one that allows all port users to plug in their particular information technology systems for the purpose of sharing data with their customers and vendors. The way the industry has operated so far, each member of the supply chain gathers its internal information digitally, but then shares the information via email, fax, or phone with its customers and vendors, Chase said. The key to providing the information through a secure single portal is to make sure that each supply chain participant has access only to the information needed to fulfill its role in the transportation move. Since US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) information is involved in the process, the port had to choose a system developer that is approved to hold Customs data, and GE Transportation has that authority, Chase said. The Port of Los Angeles does not have access to the information, except at a high level that is available to all participants. “The port is not even allowed to see the data — by design,” Chase said. Participants must register to be granted access to the portal. Each participant must be authorized by its supply chain vendor or customer in order to access data provided by that company, he said. BCOs will be able to access information on the availability of their individual containers through “vessel unload progress updates,” Chase said. The vessel operator knows how many containers are on the ship, the location of each container on the vessel, and which shipments have been pre-cleared by CBP. This information will be shared with the marine terminal operator (MTO) so the MTO can predict when each container will be available for delivery, he added. The information portal is designed as a visibility tool, not as an instrument for making trucker appointments or carrying out other functions that are already assisted through products offered by private-sector technology providers, Chase said. However, those providers will be encouraged to plug their systems into the information portal so users do not have to search through dozens of websites to get the data they need, he said. A half-dozen port authorities, both landlord and operating ports, have inquired about the Los Angeles information portal, Chase said. GE Transportation will work with other ports that seek to develop their own portals, he said. Mark Hirzel, district manager at A.N. Deringer, who participates on a Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) supply chain optimization advisory panel, said the FMC is exploring the feasibility of a model that could potentially be implemented by all ports. Although Los Angeles and GE Transportation feel their portal provides significant opportunities for additional functionality, the true potential will be realized only when the portal goes port-wide next year with participation by all terminals and shipping lines, Chase said. “This is a work in progress,” he said. cleaned_content: The full benefits of GE's information portal will be realized when it goes port-wide in 2018. “Anticipated delivery is absolutely critical information for BCOs,” Eric Caris, director of cargo marketing, told a Propeller Club of Southern California meeting Tuesday. The port in late 2016 teamed up with GE Transportation to develop a single window through which port users can access the information they need to carry out their roles in the supply chain. The pilot project involving APM Terminals, Maersk Line, and Mediterranean Shipping Co. has been gradually increasing its functionality. The port and GE Transportation are now expanding the portal to include all terminal operators and shipping lines, with the goal being to go live with a port-wide portal in mid-2018, said Chris Chase, cargo marketing manager. BCOs, truckers, railroads, third-party logistics providers, customs brokers, and intermodal equipment providers (IEPs) each require specific information on shipments, as far in advance of vessel arrival as possible, in order to plan their schedules for cargo pickup or delivery. The vessel manifest is the triggering document for this information, Chase said. Chase said Los Angeles executive director and former president of the Americas at APL, Gene Seroka, noted that the manifest information is known to the shipping line as much as two weeks before the vessel reaches a US port. “Cargo is on the water for two weeks, so he said, ‘Why don’t we do something with the information?’” Chase said. If the information is shared in advance of vessel arrival so the discharge of each container can be forecasted, terminals can plan their labor and equipment needs, IEPs will ensure they have the right number of chassis available at each terminal, truckers can plan their dispatch schedules, railroads will plan their intermodal trains, and BCOs and third-party vendors will prepare the logistics details for delivery to their facilities. Initial experience with the pilot has shown that all of this information is available, but it is scattered throughout the transportation supply chain. GE Transportation is developing the platform into one that allows all port users to plug in their particular information technology systems for the purpose of sharing data with their customers and vendors. The way the industry has operated so far, each member of the supply chain gathers its internal information digitally, but then shares the information via email, fax, or phone with its customers and vendors, Chase said. The key to providing the information through a secure single portal is to make sure that each supply chain participant has access only to the information needed to fulfill its role in the transportation move. Since US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) information is involved in the process, the port had to choose a system developer that is approved to hold Customs data, and GE Transportation has that authority, Chase said. The Port of Los Angeles does not have access to the information, except at a high level that is available to all participants. “The port is not even allowed to see the data — by design,” Chase said. BCOs will be able to access information on the availability of their individual containers through “vessel unload progress updates,” Chase said. The vessel operator knows how many containers are on the ship, the location of each container on the vessel, and which shipments have been pre-cleared by CBP. This information will be shared with the marine terminal operator (MTO) so the MTO can predict when each container will be available for delivery, he added. title: Ryder rolls out electronic logging platform for truck renters
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] The provision of ELDs in Ryder vehicles will remove a host of complications that renters would have faced in order to comply with federal law. Photo credit: Shutterstock Ryder System is rolling out an electronic logging device (ELD) and software platform that will help businesses renting trucks on a short-term basis comply with the ELD mandate. The truck rental and leasing company, which reported $6.8 billion in revenue in 2016, will install its portable ELDs in all of its trucks in the fourth quarter. The ELD mandate takes effect on Dec. 18. Ryder expects the mandate, which will require commercial truck drivers to switch from paper logbooks to ELDs to record their work and rest hours, to drive more business its way. “When you look at the complexity that ELDs are bringing, that could bring even more momentum to the outsourcing trends that we're seeing,” Dennis Cooke, president of global fleet management solutions at Ryder, said during an Oct. 24 earnings call with Wall Street analysts. “As we get into next year, our rental fleet will be prepared with ELDs for any of our customers,” Robert Sanchez, Ryder chairman and CEO, said during the call, transcribed by Seeking Alpha. That is plenty of ELDs. In the United States, Ryder last year had a rental fleet of about 31,000 vehicles, and more than 32,000 rental customers. The impact of ELDs on small business shippers and truck renters is another example of the sweeping effect the mandate will have on US businesses and domestic and international supply chains. Truckload carriers and owner-operators may feel the brunt of the impact, but the ELD mandate could affect supply-chain strategies that extend well beyond trucking. The introduction of Ryder’s ELD platform also follows a victory for the company in Washington. In October, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) granted a Truck Rental and Leasing Association petition asking for a limited exemption to the ELD mandate. Businesses or drivers renting a truck for 8 days or less will not have to use ELDs to record hours of service. The exemption will benefit not only shippers renting trucks to meet short-term demand, but truckers that must rent a vehicle when a truck breaks down. “An exemption period of up to 8 days … would give most carriers sufficient time to repair or replace their usual vehicles while minimizing any temptation to extend non-ELD operations,” the FMCSA said in its decision. The goal of Ryder’s ELD platform is to simplify compliance for thousands of US businesses that rent trucks for days, weeks, or months. Those businesses range from farms and bakeries to beverage and fireworks distributors. They may use straight trucks and tractor-trailers, and even operate small private fleets of vehicles, but for-hire trucking is not their primary business. The electronic logging mandate poses a special challenge to those companies, adding a new layer of logistics complexity and cost to their business, according to Ryder. First, many businesses would have to purchase and install ELDs in rental trucks. They could be stuck with an annual contract and bill for an ELD in a truck they might use less than 30 days. If a rental truck comes with an ELD pre-installed, that device might not integrate with an ELD system already used by the renter, or with their transportation software. Ryder is trying to solve those problems by introducing a portable device for electronic logging and cloud-based software to create and manage driver profiles and logs as well as tracking and managing vehicles. The ELD platform was developed in partnership with Geotab, a fleet telematics and compliance management provider. To capture hours of service or duty status records, drivers will simply need to download and log into the Geotab Drive app on a cellular data-connected mobile device. All current Ryder rental customers are pre-registered in the company’s system. Customers can use their own portable device or Ryder’s ELD. Ryder plans to notify customers once its enrollment period has begun and provide details on logging into the new platform. The importance of an ELD solution for rental trucks became clear in the third quarter, when Ryder saw stronger than seasonal growth in rental demand, in addition to rental demand generated by hurricane relief efforts in Florida and along the US Gulf Coast. Ryder’s total truck lease and rental revenue improved 2.5 percent year over year to $823.2 million in the quarter. Total Fleet Management Solutions revenue rose 4 percent on an annualized basis to $1.2 billion in the quarter. Ryder’s total revenue for the quarter rose 7.2 percent to $1.8 billion. Approximately 40 percent of its growth in leased fleets came from customers new to outsourcing. “We continue to tap into non-outsourced markets,” Sanchez said. Contact William B. title: XPO's Jacobs on 4Q: 'Fasten your seatbelts'
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] Revenue growth at XPO Logistics has accelerated steadily throughout the year. Photo credit: XPO Logistics XPO Logistics is bracing for what chairman and CEO Bradley S. Jacobs expects will be a very busy peak holiday shipping season, with a steady increase in online shopping driving freight volumes and pricing higher across the logistics landscape from North America to Europe. “All of our customers are saying fasten your seatbelts,” Jacobs said in an interview Wednesday. XPO has been preparing for a bull rush in last-mile deliveries, opening eight new last-mile hubs this fall to bring its total number to 53. Jacobs said XPO will open at least two more this year and 85 by the end of 2018. “We will have a bigger footprint this year going into the busy season,” he said. “We not only have more hubs, we’ve got larger docks in large metropolitan markets.” XPO also will hire 6,000 temporary workers, 20 percent more than last year, based on the strength of the holiday forecast. E-commerce, however, is no longer just a holiday story. It is increasingly becoming just “commerce,” as expectations set by online fulfillment spill over from the consumer to commercial and industrial distribution markets. That has ramifications for all types of logistics and transport operators. “There’s no doubt our e-commerce customers are our fastest growing customers, with some growing 20 percent or more a year,” Jacobs said. E-commerce directly affects four of XPO’s diversified lines of business, Jacobs said, but, indirectly, online sales affect all of them. All of XPO’s operations saw significant growth in the third quarter, when XPO revenue rose 4.9 percent year over year to $3.89 billion. E-commerce not only pushed more business to e-fulfillment, reverse logistics, and last-mile logistics divisions, it filled truck trailers, too. Less-than-truckload (LTL) shipments per day in North America were up 1.8 percent from the same quarter last year and average weight per shipment increased 3.7 percent. That generated a 5.6 percent increase in LTL tonnage at the second-largest stand-alone US LTL trucking operator. “In LTL, our revenue per load was up 6 percent, where it was down 1 percent in the second quarter,” Jacobs said, another indicator that LTL pricing is moving upward. Pricing on contract renewals on average is up 5.1 percent year over year, he said. E-commerce is helping, but so is higher US industrial output and a tightening of truckload and LTL capacity, said Jacobs. The same trends fueled a 15.5 percent jump in freight brokerage revenue in North America to $628.6 million. “Our truck brokerage business was off the charts in the quarter,” Jacobs said. “That continued in October. The aftermath of the storms created strong truck demand.” By Nov. 1 that demand had lessened somewhat, but remained strong in many regions. “The West Coast is extremely tight,” he said. “In many California metro markets, rates have soared up to 20 percent.” Shipper priorities are changing, thanks to the flip in the marketplace. “As much as shippers were focused on price in the last few years, they’re now very focused on actual access to capacity and service and reliability,” Jacobs said. They’re also turning to the spot market more for capacity. “We’re now 50 percent spot market. We used to be 20 percent.” XPO’s revenue growth accelerated from 0.2 percent in the first quarter to 2.2 percent in the second quarter and now 4.9 percent, fueled by e-commerce, but also a “more positive” US economy and an uptick in global trade that benefited an increasingly global company. Despite a 4.4 percent increase in operating costs, the company more than doubled its profits, increasing net profit 230 percent to $71 million. “We had the highest revenue, net income and highest cash flow of any quarter in our history and beat expectations for EBITDA [earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization], cash for operations, and free cash flow,” Jacobs said. “Our diversification is yielding results.” The rise of global trade helped XPO close $2.1 billion in new business this year through September, a 49 percent year-over-year gain and up from $1.43 billion in new sales in the first six months. “Our global sales pipeline continues to exceed $3 billion,” Jacobs said. That number is likely to move higher as transportation and logistics costs climb. Tight capacity is pushing transportation pricing northward, and not just in the US trucking and intermodal markets. Tight capacity is “a common theme in North America and Europe,” Jacobs said. “You’ve got 2 to 3 percent economic growth in most countries and yet [transportation] capacity is going down. The see-saw has moved toward an imbalance, with tight capacity and upward demand.” It is a good time to own assets and to be a non-asset broker, he said. The four business lines most affected by e-commerce at XPO are its e-fulfillment operation in Europe, last-mile logistics in North America and Europe, omnichannel distribution, and reverse logistics. “Everything e-commerce-related in Europe is going gangbusters,” Jacobs said. “We signed new e-commerce and cold chain contracts in Europe, in the United Kingdom and Spain" in the quarter, he said. European trucking revenue rose 6.2 percent to $629.8 million, with. European truckload revenue moving up 4.2 percent, and LTL revenue 10.1 percent. Jacobs does not see indication that current trends will reverse themselves anytime soon. The US economy GDP is moving “in a positive direction and feels buoyant,” he said. “On the capacity side, carriers have not added a lot of trucks. I don’t see that turning around soon.” Contact William B. Cassidy at bill.cassidy@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @wbcassidy_joc © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: Cyber-attack impact hangs over Maersk’s Q3 earnings
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] Maersk is expected to report strong volume and revenue on the key east-west trades. Photo credit: Shutterstock Maersk Line will first have to factor in an up to $300 million loss from its July cyber attack before joining peers in celebrating the strong growth in peak season volume and revenue when the Danish carrier reports its third-quarter results tomorrow.The results will reflect the financial damage inflicted by the late-July cyber breach, and it remains to be seen whether the impact will be enough to offset the profitability earned from strong volume on key east-west trades.The NotPetya virus forced Maersk Group to shut down all its communications with customers and within the company, affecting the carrier, APM Terminals, and forwarding arm Damco. It was several weeks before business was back to normal, and the loss of business was estimated to have been as high as USD300 million.But encouraging for the carrier, which reported a second-quarter profit of $339 million, is the solid results of its peers such as OOCL, which posted a 26.5 percent year-over-year increase in revenue to $1.45 billion, with total volumes growing by 5 percent to 1.6 million TEU. Unsurprisingly, out of the major east-west trades, the one that stood out was Asia-Europe, and by some measure. Compared with the third quarter of last year, OOCL volume carried on the trade increased by almost 25 percent to 297,897 TEU. According to Container Trades Statistics, total European imported volume grew by 4 percent in the first eight months of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. More than half of all containers imported into Europe were from Asia, with volume growing by 5.4 percent from January to August.The strong demand on Asia-Europe has not been seen since the frantic restocking in 2010 after retailers ran down inventory following the global financial crisis. Maersk Line is a solid performer on this trade and its scale will certainly be reflected in the third-quarter volume figures.The trans-Pacific trade, another area where Maersk Line has a solid presence, also saw volume increases that have driven up container throughput at US ports to record levels in some cases. Container trade at the Port of Savannah grew by 32 percent in October, with Garden City Terminal moving 410,000 TEU, an increase of nearly 100,000 TEU year on year. It was the first time in the port's history that it topped 400,000 TEU in a single month. For the fiscal year to date (July 1 to Oct. 31), Savannah handled 1.42 million TEU, up by 12.3 percent.The Port of Charleston handled 7 percent more containers from January to August at 1.1 million TEU, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com. Asian container volume through the Port of Jacksonville jumped 19 percent in the last 12 months ending in September to more than 1 million TEU.Container shipping analyst Alphaliner said global container throughput growth was on track to exceed 6 percent in 2017, and which is expected to lift the TEU-to-GDP multiplier to 1.7 times global GDP growth, reversing the recent downward trend that has seen the multiplier drop to below 1 in the previous two years. Following Maersk Line’s good second quarter, the joint Maersk Group and Line chief executive, Soren Skou, said that after using the price war in 2016 to build up his carrier’s market share, the strategy employed in the second quarter was to maintain a profitable business rather than trying to capture more of the market.The approach saw the carrier’s second-quarter container volumes rising just 1.6 percent while average revenue per FEU shot up 21 percent to $2,086 per FEU, so it appears to have been successful.But the third-quarter peak season period was characterised by rising volume and falling freight rates on Asia-Europe and the trans-Pacific, a curious phenomenon that suggests the chase for market share is still going on and that Maersk Line will have no option but to participate.However, other explanations for the high volume-low rate phenomenon have been put forward. One is that when volume began to pick up the carriers brought in extra loaders that quickly added to the structural overcapacity and eroded rates. A series of rate increases on the key trades were ignored by the market and rates declined instead.Another explanation, this one suggested by BIMCO chief economist Peter Sand, is that to test the strength of the market, the container lines kept putting capacity into the trades until the prices began to drop. “Only by doing that can they reveal the true strength of the market,” he said.Maersk Line maintained its expectation that the transport and logistics division would see underlying profit above $1.0 billion, even after absorbing the estimated $200 million to $300 million cost of the cyber attack. In a note to customers, HSBC was positive on Maersk Group and gave three reasons: strong container industry fundamentals will support a recovery in Maersk Line’s profitability, the $600 million of targeted synergies within the transport and logistics division to be achieved by 2019, and the expected value to be created from the separation of the Energy division. Maersk agreed to sell its oil division to Total with effect from 30 June 2017. The enterprise value was $7.45 billion, consisting of 97.5 million Total shares worth $4.95 billion at the time of the announcement and the assumption of $2.5 billion of debt. Asian container volume through the Port of Jacksonville jumped 19 percent in the last 12 months ending in September to more than 1 million TEU.Container shipping analyst Alphaliner said global container throughput growth was on track to exceed 6 percent in 2017, and which is expected to lift the TEU-to-GDP multiplier to 1.7 times global GDP growth, reversing the recent downward trend that has seen the multiplier drop to below 1 in the previous two years. Following Maersk Line’s good second quarter, the joint Maersk Group and Line chief executive, Soren Skou, said that after using the price war in 2016 to build up his carrier’s market share, the strategy employed in the second quarter was to maintain a profitable business rather than trying to capture more of the market.The approach saw the carrier’s second-quarter container volumes rising just 1.6 percent while average revenue per FEU shot up 21 percent to $2,086 per FEU, so it appears to have been successful.But the third-quarter peak season period was characterised by rising volume and falling freight rates on Asia-Europe and the trans-Pacific, a curious phenomenon that suggests the chase for market share is still going on and that Maersk Line will have no option but to participate.However, other explanations for the high volume-low rate phenomenon have been put forward. One is that when volume began to pick up the carriers brought in extra loaders that quickly added to the structural overcapacity and eroded rates. A series of rate increases on the key trades were ignored by the market and rates declined instead.Another explanation, this one suggested by BIMCO chief economist Peter Sand, is that to test the strength of the market, the container lines kept putting capacity into the trades until the prices began to drop. “Only by doing that can they reveal the true strength of the market,” he said.Maersk Line maintained its expectation that the transport and logistics division would see underlying profit above $1.0 billion, even after absorbing the estimated $200 million to $300 million cost of the cyber attack. In a note to customers, HSBC was positive on Maersk Group and gave three reasons: strong container industry fundamentals will support a recovery in Maersk Line’s profitability, the $600 million of targeted synergies within the transport and logistics division to be achieved by 2019, and the expected value to be created from the separation of the Energy division. Maersk agreed to sell its oil division to Total with effect from 30 June 2017. The enterprise value was $7.45 billion, consisting of 97.5 million Total shares worth $4.95 billion at the time of the announcement and the assumption of $2.5 billion of debt.

title: Carriers' pursuit of co-loaders adds to rate volatility
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] Large co-loaders ship hundreds of thousands of TEU annually. Photo credit: Shutterstock The willingness of container carriers to sell capacity to resellers who openly distribute rates to the market is fueling the rate volatility that threatens direct contracting relationships between the carriers and shippers. So-called co-loaders, a niche category of large-volume non-vessel-operating common carriers (NVOCCs), are able to buy wholesale capacity in bulk directly from ocean carriers. Instead of reselling the space privately to their own beneficial cargo owner (BCO) customers, as other NVOCCs do, they resell it to hundreds of forwarders, largely Asia-based. Those forwarders openly market the co-loaders’ rates with ubiquitous daily emails blasted out to virtually the entire industry. The growth of co-loading stems from overcapacity and the chronic intense rate competition among carriers who frequently prioritize volume and market share over profits. The emails containing specific rates go beyond weekly rate indices published by Drewry, Freightos, or the Shanghai Shipping Exchange in showing actual rates on offer between specific port pairs, which allow for direct comparisons with contract rates. Of course, contract rates between BCOs and carriers are usually annualized rates that come with capacity assurances; depending on negotiated terms, they can be adjusted downward if spot rates decline. However, the volatility in rates can still be vexing to BCOs who seek stability in their sourcing of ocean container services, and in recent weeks, some BCOs have openly stated that the volatility is undermining their direct relationships. Co-loaders — sometimes called master loaders or neutral NVOCCs — have become significant players in the trans-Pacific in recent years, based on carrier willingness to sell their space in bulk with the knowledge that it will be openly re-marketed. Local, often Asia-based, forwarders sell space largely into the market of Asia-controlled cargo to Western buyers on a CNF basis. CNF refers to cost and freight, meaning the seller is responsible for paying the ocean freight to the buyer’s location. Estimates are that about 10 percent to 15 percent of the roughly 15 million TEU in annualized eastbound trans-Pacific volumes (to the United States), according to IHS Markit data, is sold on a CNF or “pre-paid” basis, with the ocean freight arranged by local Asia-based forwarders. Since a neutral NVOCC is only a wholesaler and not generally interested in building direct customer relationships, forwarders are willing to buy from them without exposing their customer to the risk of back-selling. Co-loading players such as Honour Lane Shipping, OEC, and Seamaster were among the largest NVOCCs in the eastbound trans-Pacific in the first half of 2017, each shipping well more than 100,000 TEU during the first six months of the year, according to IHS Markit. The public marketing of rates creates pricing transparency, which can be positive, but also can exert downward pressure on the market; newly published rates, especially if they are lower than existing rates, get rapidly shopped across the market and can set a new and lower benchmark. In a fully commoditized market where service is irrelevant, such pressure would be positive for buyers, but in ocean freight, low rates have served to undermine the service quality demanded by large shippers who depend on ocean freight to operate their supply chains. As Ken O’Brien, chief operating officer of Gemini Shippers Group, said recently: “Supply chain managers have to be able to defend decisions to make long-term commitments to carriers in contracts when at certain points in the year NVOCCs and carriers collectively drive spot rates to levels well below their contracted rates.” The phenomenon of rates marketed through co-loaders affects not just carriers in their attempts to create stability around their BCO relationships, but also other NVOCCs who themselves sell to BCOs. “The frustration that Apex and other similarly situated forwarder/NVOCCs experience, where we have the proprietary relationship with the end-customer in North America, is the disruption often caused by the volatile and often extremely low rates proliferating from the co-load market. Our contract rate relationship with our carriers is confidential, as is our rate relationship with our customers,” said Kurt McElroy, executive vice president at Apex. “But carriers that increasingly solicit volumes from master co-loading forwarders can’t control the transparency of those rates in the market, as forwarders generally will shotgun out rates to other forwarders/BCOs to generate business. This becomes a significant factor in how carriers can’t keep a floor on rates when utilizations soften.” The co-load market is the focus of a New York-based startup, called CoLoadX, which aims to open up the co-load market to traditional NVOCCs that normally do not resell capacity to other intermediaries. Its recipe is to make the transaction anonymous to both sides, which it said it is able to do and still keep the transaction legal, so that a forwarder would not fear exposing its own customer to a traditional NVOCC, perhaps a Kuehne + Nagel, Panalpina, or Expeditors, that seeks to develop direct customer relationships and sell them a range of logistics services as part of its core business. Fauad Shariff, the CoLoadX CEO, said: “We enable NVOCCs of all sizes to offer the best service and price options to other NVOCCs and freight forwarders. We are uniquely set up to do this in a neutral manner that protects vital data such as shipper and consignee details for freight forwarders.” Contact Peter Tirschwell at peter.tirschwell@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @petertirschwell. © 2026 S&P Global.
