The average time it took to book a Niagara Bottling load that Friday, from the time it appeared on the Uber Freight app until it was accepted by a driver, was 34 minutes, said Uber Freight product manager Kyle Olney. “That’s pretty paradigm changing,” he said. “It proves the concept of the on-demand freight network that can scale elastically” to meet fluctuating demand, he said. Some of the 127 Niagara truckloads were booked in under as a minute, Olney said. “Even without the hurricane it still would have been difficult to get these loads moved,” he said. “We moved them Friday after 5 o’clock, which would have been challenging anyway.” That speed was important to Niagara, but just as critical was access to a pool of trucking capacity the shipper couldn’t reach otherwise. Uber Freight “is going after a different segment of capacity in the market that is very hard to tap into, especially for large organizations," said Reed. Niagara, shipping 700,000 truckloads a year, certainly is a large organization. It’s also fast-growing. Five years ago, Niagara had nine plants throughout the United States, Reed said. Today, the company has 27 manufacturing facilities. All distribution is handled from those plants. Large businesses shipping high volumes gravitate to large carriers that can provide high levels of capacity. Through third-party logistics providers and brokers, they can access smaller carriers. Uber Freight, however, aims to bring a high level of granularity to capacity, capturing companies with five or fewer trucks. “They are accessing this kind of really small mom-and-pop single-truck-and-trailer market that a lot of the brokers just can’t get access to,” Reed said. Those mom-and-pop operators represent the majority of US truckers, and as a segment they’ve been growing. From January through July, the number of US carriers with up-to-date insurance and operating authority increased 6 percent, according to QualifiedCarriers.com. Among those new for-hire trucking companies were 7,593 newly active businesses with 1 to 6 trucks, a 4.4 percent gain during the first six months of 2017, and 62 percent of the total increase. Competitors may argue Uber Freight isn’t bringing new capacity to the industry (and other brokers also are connecting to very small carriers), but if it helps shippers uncover capacity they wouldn’t find otherwise, those carriers will certainly seem like “new capacity.” “Uber Freight had a unique capability of accessing idle capacity in the hurricane stricken markets that seemed to be a different supply stream than the traditional broker (where we were seeing massive premiums to move freight),” said Ashley Dorna, Niagara’s executive vice president of supply chain. “They were able to aggregate single trucks and very small companies to provide supply at less captive pricing.” That pricing transparency was key to Niagara as well. “I believe Uber Freight is focused on cracking the code and unlocking the market to provide more efficiency in supply, as well as enable the trucker to make more money,” Dorna said. “Ultimately we’re bringing shippers access to capacity they wouldn’t have access to, and for drivers, we’re giving them freight,” said Driegert, who before joining Uber Freight in 2016 spent two years as Amazon.com’s director of planning and innovation and eight years with Coyote Logistics, most recently as the Chicago-based 3PL’s chief innovation officer. Amazon is famously customer-obsessed. Uber Freight, Driegert said, wants to be driver-obsessed. He didn’t say how many drivers have joined Uber Freight since April, but said that number is growing rapidly. “We’re helping these people be better entrepreneurs,” he said. Uber Freight offers what it claims is a driver-centric system, with a free app, one-touch load booking, and payment — through Uber — within seven days. Drivers and shippers see the price of a load up front, just as Uber passengers do in the ride-share app. Truckers using the Uber Freight app are able to choose shipments much as rideshare customers pick and choose cars. “By and large, these are experienced, professional drivers who decided they want to go out on their own and do their own thing. They don’t have the same level of capital investment a larger company would.” What they do have, he said, are smartphones with mobile apps. Reed noted the trucking companies and drivers that delivered Niagara’s water to Houston were “a different bunch.” “They were willing to take a higher level of risk and get out on the road faster,” he said. “If they’re not driving, they’re not making money.” It’s not that the drivers Niagara booked were unsafe, Reed stressed, but they were willing to quickly move relief goods into a disaster zone where flooded roads were still a hazard and deliver the loads. Many of those truck drivers “were coming to the area looking for ways to help, they were having a hard time finding direct access to freight,” Driegert said. “Niagara had a lot of loads they had to get into Houston. We were just one provider they reached out to, but we were able to clear those loads much faster than expected,” because those drivers could book freight directly. “We find drivers check their app first thing in the morning,” he said. “They’re drawn to the simplicity of the one-touch option. The traditional way they would access shipments would be through multiple freight brokers, but now those drivers have direct access to that freight. We had a driver use a turn of phrase I love, we ‘liberate the freight’ for the smaller carriers. “This is a good market change not only for drivers but also on the shipper side,” Driegert said. “If you are a shipper today in today’s dynamic marketplace, especially competing against companies like Amazon, you need an on-demand or spot-market solution that can provide you a strong competitive advantage compared to what was available in the past.” Shippers approach Uber Freight much as they would a traditional broker, he said. “What we provide them ultimately is fast execution from a price and service perspective. We have real time visibility to all the drivers on the platform. Shippers value that access and visibility.” At Niagara, Uber Freight is one of several third party intermediaries and core carriers vying for the bottler’s freight, and not just exception freight like the relief shipments to Houston. “We have three primary types of freight,” Reed told The Journal of Commerce, “first, freight headed to the distribution center of a big box retailer or grocery chain. Then we have direct-to-store shipments. The third type is what we call transfer freight between our plants.” Uber “has worked on a little bit of everything,” Reed said in early November. “We’re doing our yearly bid as we speak, and they’re participating in that. We’re showing them lanes and volumes and demand curves and they’re coming back with answers.” Niagara first began using Uber Freight in June, “and they’ve grown organically within our network, with a scavenger mentality,” said Reed. “Our business is very dynamic. We’re constantly getting new customers and locations, so new lanes pop up continually, and they’ve jumped on those.” The high-tech transport operator plans to expand organically into supply chains at businesses like Niagara, slowly changing how companies book and ship freight. That’s not going to happen overnight, Driegert admits, but he believes shippers as shippers develop confidence in dynamic pricing they eventually will move away from long-term contracts with static price lists. “I no longer plan my rides to the airport,” Driegert said. “I know an Uber rideshare will be available. I expect much the same shift will happen in (freight) transportation. We’re able to build a marketplace where you can find capacity and find loads in a much more liquid way. How shippers plan will change over time as the system becomes as reliable as running water.”

title: Bolloré pact with e-commerce portal highlights B2B growth
content: E-commerce is transforming expectations for business-to-business transportation. Photo credit: Shutterstock A partnership announced Tuesday giving Bolloré Logistics’ customers easy access to a business-to-business (B2B) e-commerce website underscores how logistics providers are deepening links to B2B sites to tap the growing online sector. The partnership will enable Bolloré’s 5,000 customers to buy goods on the OroCommerce site, created by Oro, Inc. of West Hollywood, California, and ship them through Bolloré’s digital LINK platform, which integrates different parts of the supply chain to smooth the movement of freight around the world. The deal, announced by Oro today, follows a variety of partnerships forged by Chinese B2B site Alibaba, to help customers ship goods they have bought through the site, including with Kuehne + Nagel, WCA Ltd, and carriers Evergreen Line, Maersk Line, and CMA CGM. Zvi Schrieber, CEO of online booking and rate quoting platform Freightos, which has partnered with GlobalSources, the China-based B2B site, said agreements such as the Oro-Bolloré deal are significant because they reflect efforts by the growing B2B industry to bring order to the often confusing, complicated business of dealing with the freight industry. “It’s not commonplace,” for an e-commerce site to link up with a logistics company, he said. “But it’s a hot issue right now, especially if its cross-border” trade, which is the “pain-point” for such business, he said. “It’s definitely on the agenda of all B2B sites,” he said. “How do we automate the shipping? How do we reduce the pain of shipping?” Forrester, the market research company, valued B2B e-commerce in the United States in 2015 at about $780 billion, and predicts that it will grow about 7.7 percent per year through the end of the decade. By 2020, the market will be worth $1.1 trillion, or about 12 percent of the B2B market, the researcher predicted. Although e-commerce sales are relatively simple, involving one decision-making consumer, B2B purchases are more complex, and that has to be reflected in the e-commerce and delivery process. A decision to make a B2B purchase, for example, may involve a variety of different decision makers located throughout a company who are governed by internal processes — and all of them may need to be involved in the purchase, to see how it is progressing and approve it. Motti Danino, chief operating officer at Oro, said the company expects that the deal with Bolloré will not only enable the third-party logistics provider to provide e-commerce services to its customers, but will enable both companies to bring in new customers. “Our goal is to market this and to acquire customers that today are not Oro customers, or Bolloré customers,” he said. “We can go out to the market and offer big companies a complete solution from commerce to logistics to warehouse to distribution of goods — all in one package.” This provides for a two-way revenue system. When a company buys the Bolloré Logistics' suite of services that includes e-commerce, then Oro would be paid for the e-commerce portion of the package, the e-commerce site said. If Oro brings one of their clients to Bolloré, for the extra logistics services, then that client would pay Bolloré for its offering, the site said. “When a global e-commerce solution like OroCommerce is brought online by a major international manufacturer or distributor and there is a logistics partner that can be set up and integrated right out of the gate, the benefits and time savings are very powerful,” Danino said. Bolloré’s LINK initiative is a collaborative platform that integrates all parts of the supply chain via web, mobile, electronic data interchange, and application program interfaces. Its scope includes order management, inventory, distribution, and international transportation for major multichannel companies. Contact Hugh R. title: Visibility tools key to combating supply chain disruption
content: [Editorial note: image removed/no longer available] The low quality of available data makes end-to-end visibility difficult. Photo credit: DNV GL End-to-end visibility remains one of the most sought after services by shippers in a never-ending battle to limit disruption to supply chains and avoid the damaging knock-on effects generated by delays and uncertainty.The express integrators have the technology, but the internal company-wide visibility used by DHL, FedEx, and UPS in the express business has been hard to replicate in the wider container supply chain where cargo value is often lower and the focus on managing cost is more intense.Many visibility products are on the market with varying levels of data provision as software companies try to address the demand, but complicating the uptake of these solutions is the diverging needs of shippers and forwarders, said Frank Knoors, managing director of Belgium-based Logit One.Logit One delivers an end-to-end visibility service and counts one of the world’s largest forwarders as one of its customers. It offers the service based on “a competitive price” per container, and Knoors believes the cost justifies itself for most shippers.“However, we have found that the shipper sometimes takes the view that he is paying his forwarder for logistics services and the forwarder should provide the visibility,” he told JOC.com. “But a lot of forwarders are asking why they should invest in the visibility service when the costs they are trying to avoid are much less than those the shipper is avoiding. It is an asymmetric situation that often leads to paralysis.”Nevertheless, Knoors said reliability remained the most important issue being faced by shippers today, and visibility was key to addressing it. He explained how the visibility needs of shippers and forwarders differed.For shippers, more visibility was important to maintain the smooth running of a production process where if the supplier of the inbound logistics was not on time, that process was disturbed and the associated costs were much higher than the logistics cost of the goods being transported to the shipper factory.Similarly, he said, when the inbound logistics was for the positioning of new products for a launch, the whole retail chain structure was planned out, and if the goods do not arrive as planned it leads to tremendous commercial costs.Knoors said visibility was of secondary importance to forwarders organising the goods flow for the shipper as they did not suffer from the consequences of delays. Forwarders have a commercial interest towards their customers and want to position themselves to be in control of the work they are executing for those shippers, and having more visibility means they can be more proactive in organising their logistics process in case something goes wrong.“Visibility is important for forwarders, but visibility is much more important for shippers than forwarders,” Knoors said.Claudio Scandella, CEO of ECU Worldwide, the market leader in less-than-containerload shipments, said intense margin pressure on service providers meant forwarders and non-vessel opearting common carriers had to become more tech enabled and to improve the operational side of the business.“The digital age provides ample opportunity to enhance services and operate in a different way, how to develop new revenue streams, how to make sure you are not just a commodity in the face of global B2C [business-to-consumer] companies,” he said.“We are developing a new customer portal that will allow customers to have much greater visibility and to extend it further, adding more and more value to our customers’ supply chains. Visibility will enable us to also provide better cost and service, be it through the online presence or through talking to the customers.”But even as software companies with new digital solutions target the supply chain, there are still many forwarders and shippers around the world that transmit their data in a non-digital form, Scandella said.“We first need to get rid of all the manual processes. We really need to automate products to get rid of all the non value-adding things done by people entering data, and use people to do the brainwork and to develop solutions because they understand the customer side,” he said.Nicolette van der Jagt, director general of CLECAT, the European association for forwarding, transport, logistics, and customs services, agreed that forwarders needed to change and keep pace with innovation. But she also highlighted the manual processes that in many cases could not be avoided.“The reality is that many people still need to pick up the phone to find out what is happening and to find solutions. If cargo is being delayed you still need some human intervention to sort out the service issues,” she said.Knoors said Logit One recently completed an analysis of the savings a shipper could realise from improving visibly over his cargo. The reduction of safety stock that could be implemented as a result of less uncertainty in the goods flow was a major cost factor for cargo owners.“If you start calculating the kind of cost to be saved, it is not 100 percent because it is difficult to make explicit statements on the amount of uncertainty that can be avoided because it is not that obvious,” he said. “We made some assumptions and it told us that for the average container from China to Europe, a shipper using the visibility service should be a able to make a cost saving of up to 100-150 euros per container. It cannot be achieved immediately but is part of a continuous improvement of the logistics processes that will come over time rather than overnight simply because a shipper is using a new visibility service.”However, achieving the kind of visibility required was difficult in that the data that are available to ensure shippers where their containers are is of a very low quality, Knoors said. For a container travelling from China to Europe by ocean, there are multiple data sources, but each is inconsistent with the other and some areas, such as transshipment, were just a black box. “The low quality of the available data is one of the biggest issues that is on the table at the moment,” he said.Much of the approach to improving visibility has been focused on using mountable real-time tracking devices on containers where electro-mechanical devices use GPS to track where the box is. But in Knoors’ view, this approach has limitations; it comes at a cost, not just for the cost of attaching the device to a container, but also because there is a logistics process behind the handling of that device. Their batteries need to be charged, the device must be customs cleared, and it needs to be taken from the point where it is detached to where it can be re-mounted on another container.Logit One has a different strategy. “We collect multiple data sources from carriers, terminals, and inland movements, but to be useful there needs to be a proper interpretation of that data,” Knoors said. “We subject that continuous data stream to a business intelligence engine that interprets the data and generates logistics facts that are sufficiently reliable. Based on those logistics facts, we call them conclusions, we are continuously updating — not focusing on where the container is but on where the logistics process has been disrupted and is deviating from what was planned.“We continuously take on board the knock-on effects from that part of the logistics chain that has not yet been executed, and that allows the forwarder to know beforehand that something is going wrong and he does that with a higher degree of reliability than he currently has today,” Knoors said. title: Shippers turn to technology to improve payment visibility
content: Shippers use data they collect to mine a wealth of business information. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com Although the fundamental goals of the freight audit and payment sector remain the same, the sector is expanding its reach, aiming to play a more strategic role for savvy shippers anxious to compete nimbly against competitors worldwide. The basics remain the same, said Tom Zygmunt, marketing manager at St. Louis-based Cass Information Systems, one of the largest players in the sector. Shippers want “to make sure they are paying the right rate, and that they make timely payments” and get all the accurate information they need for their financial reporting. “People use services like ours because we can do a better audit. We have expertise they may not have internally.” As freight payment and audit technologies progress, shippers also use the data they collect to mine a broader wealth of business information, Zygmunt said. “Once you start getting some information, you want more. Technology really helps.” Instead of just looking at a report or stronger streams of raw data, companies look at dashboard analytics that help make sense of that data. “You can look very quickly, and try to spot any trends that are going on,” Zygmunt said. Business information and analytics can be used effectively to manage transportation expenses, and may indicate where expenses are out of control. Allan Miner, president of CT Logistics, said CT’s clients talk about the Cloud, analytics, business information, and transportation management systems. His company has invested in the technologies, incorporating them as features and functionalities into CT’s web suite. That way, “people don’t have to invest hundreds of thousands of dollars in software and hardware” of their own, he said. Software tools built into a web-based “software as a service” platform enable shippers to use convenient dashboards and graphical analysis to achieve least-cost routing and rating, tendering, and tracking, Miner said. For his part, Mike Regan, chief of relationship development at TranzAct Technologies, explained that three major changes are occurring in this sector. The first major change is in how data are communicated and exchanged. “The speed of that has changed, and as we transition from EDI [electronic data interchange] to API [application program interface] platforms, we are getting much closer to a ‘real time’ environment where data is available much sooner than it has been in the past,” Regan said. The second major change is the extent to which data from the freight payment process are integrated into other enterprise-wide data platforms. For example, by integrating data from the freight payment process into a company’s enterprise resource planning (ERP), companies can get a much more comprehensive understanding of the correlation between freight and sales activity, as well as freight and procurement/purchasing activity. Because freight data can be shared with multiple departments within an organization, he said, “we see representatives from these departments involved in the decision-making process. Five years ago, the decision to select a freight payment provider was primarily made by transportation and accounting personnel. Today, it is not uncommon to have representatives from these departments plus personnel from procurement, sales, IT [information technology], and finance involved in the decision-making process.” A good freight payment and auditing system can help bridge the gap between what is happening at a company’s “front” door (i.e., how and when customers are buying things) and what is happening at its “back” door (i.e., the freight dock, which is where, when, and how the sales orders are being delivered to customers), according to Regan. If a shipper does not bridge this gap between the front and back door, he is “missing some really important things,” he said. Take, for example, a scenario in which the shipper maintains a “free freight” policy, which goes into effect for all orders valued at $2,500 or more. If a customer understands how this process works, he may order something for $3,000, and get the free freight factor applied on his internal systems, but then come back days later and cancel a portion of that order. If the ERP system does not flag the fact that this is now a $2,000 order, the shipper will still apply the free freight label to the order, thinking it is a $3,000 order. Once they integrate their shipment history/activity data with their sales data, they can make better decisions. “Five years ago, shippers had a tactical orientation toward freight payment applications,” Regan said. The emphasis was on providing solid audit and payment controls and producing data and reports on spending. “That’s changed in a big way. Today, shippers want great controls and analytic capabilities that can be used to help them understand how they can run their business better. That is why today, an effective freight payment and audit system can be a valuable strategic asset that can reduce costs and improve bottom line profitability,” he said. In addition to helping shippers meet the traditional goal of reducing transportation costs, Zygmunt said “our payment process is really meeting different departments’ requirements, such as [those of] companies’ general ledger systems within the shipper’s organizational structure.” In some cases, Cass also uses information collected via freight audit technology to help companies engaged in supply chain financing. “Some shippers are negotiating 60-, 90-, 120-day terms with their carriers, so the carriers have trouble with longer terms.” He said Cass has programs that enable carriers to be paid more quickly. “That allows [shippers] to hold onto their money longer, but still allows the carriers to get paid in a timelier fashion.” Zygmunt noted that a growing number of companies want to use freight audit and reporting services to manage global transportation expenses. “This entire sector started in the United States, and now as you have global organizations — especially the companies we deal with — they want to do the same concept on a global basis." title: Poland becoming critical link in European supply chains
content: The Port of Gdansk is an example of the highly developed transportation infrastructure that has made Poland an alluring option for shippers. Photo credit: DCT Gdansk LONDON — The 21,413 TEU mega-ships, the world’s largest, that call at the DCT Gdansk terminal on their Asia-Europe voyages highlight Poland’s rapid climb up Europe’s logistics ladder over the past decade and underscore its ambition to become a continental logistics hub. DCT Gdansk, whose traffic has skyrocketed from 4,423 TEU in its first year of operation in 2007 to just short of 1.3 million TEU in 2016 and is heading for 1.5 million TEU this year, can count on significant annual increases going forward as it handles the Asia-North Europe hubs of two of the three global container alliances — the 2M plus Hyundai Merchant Marine partnership of Maersk Line, Mediterranean Shipping Co., and HMM, and the recently established Ocean Alliance of CMA CGM, Cosco Shipping Lines, Evergreen Line, and OOCL — the operator of the 21,413 TEU ships. Gdansk’s bid to become a European hub was sealed when the leading ocean carriers opened it up to direct calls from Asia, replacing feeder shipments from Rotterdam, Hamburg, and Bremerhaven. And DCT Gdansk, majority owned and managed by Australia’s Macquarie Global Investment Fund, is well prepared to capitalize on this breakthrough with the opening of a second deepwater berth late last year, doubling its annual capacity to 3 million TEU. Traffic is continuing to grow — China’s Cosco is launching an additional weekly feeder service this week between its Polish hub and Helsinki, Riga, Latvia, and Klaipeda, Lithuania, alongside its current service linking Rotterdam and Gdansk with St. Petersburg and Kotka, Finland. Having secured its position as a Baltic hub — helped by the fact that it is the last port in the region that does not freeze up in the winter — DCT Gdansk, along with the other Polish transport and logistics sectors, is aiming to become the hub of choice for importers and exporters in Central and Eastern Europe and Russia. Poland also wants to link up with Beijing’s Belt and Road project in a bid to become an import hub for Chinese exports. Nearby Finland made its Silk Road debut earlier this month with a train leaving Kouvola, a town between Helsinki and the Russian border, with 41 containers bound for Xi’an in northwest China. Meanwhile, the targeted Central and Eastern Europe market is on a roll, posting its fastest expansion in nine years in the third quarter, with Latvia growing 6.2 percent year over year and the Czech Republic and Poland up 5 percent, outpacing Germany’s 2.8 percent and the 28-nation EU average of 2.5 percent. The Polish economy is projected to grow more than 4 percent for the full year, according to IHS Markit forecasts. Poland’s economic growth has been paralleled by its rapidly expanding transport sector, with rising ocean container traffic propelling investment in rail freight beyond its borders coupled with the invasion of its trucks on the highways of its significantly wealthier EU partners. Poland’s truckers have grabbed the European road transport market by the throat, hauling more than one-quarter of the EU’s cross-border freight traffic and accounting for about 30 percent of its ballooning cabotage market. The importance of trucking to the Polish economy was demonstrated by Warsaw’s success in excluding the industry from a recent EU directive against so-called “social dumping” that would have required lower paid east European drivers travelling across the bloc to be paid the same rate as local truckers. The EU’s attempt to rein in east European truckers was “because Polish transport companies, Czech logistics companies, and Romanian IT [information technology] companies are starting to become more competitive and are succeeding in the European Union,” Polish Deputy Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki said. Poland’s transport transformation is being matched — even overtaken — by its rapid climb up the rankings of Europe’s most favored logistics locations. Poland is among the fastest-growing logistics markets in Europe due to its strong value proposition, proximity to Western Europe and extensive transportation infrastructure, according to ProLogis, a logistics real estate investment trust. “In fact, Central Poland-Lodz was the first market outside Western Europe to win a spot in the top five locations,” according to a report by the San Francisco-based group based on responses from sectors ranging from retail to automotives and electronics. The country’s logistics pull was highlighted by the decision of Zalando, a Berlin-based online fashion group, to invest 150 million euros ($178 million) in a 1.4 million square foot warehouse in Gryfino, a Polish town just more than a mile from the German border, that will export clothes and shoes to Poland, Germany, the Nordic/Baltic region, and beyond. And transport investment is gathering pace, with the European Investment Bank earlier this month agreeing to 650 million euro financing to improve Poland’s rail links to its ports, building on some 2.7 billion euros of EU structural funds to improve its port infrastructure. The Gdansk Port Authority is talking with potential private investors for the construction of a new universal port costing between $1.7 billion and $2.5 billion, the state rail infrastructure company is improving cross-border freight connections with Ukraine, and the Belarus and the Polish governments plan to spend up to 8 billion euros on a new airport between Warsaw and Lodz linked to the national rail network with the aim of establishing a multi-modal Central European logistics gateway. But for now the focus is fixed on DCT Gdansk, which is pushing Poland’s top sea port closer to its peers in Europe’s dominant Le Havre-Hamburg range. And the bullish container terminal operator is pitching for a much wider market. “DCT Gdansk has proven itself a game-changer for the Baltic, opening the market to direct calls from Asia and providing access for Polish importers and exporters as well as enhanced transhipment access across the Baltic for the shipping lines. Our challenge now is to attract new services and to push further into Central Europe, whilst retaining and consolidating our position with our existing customers,” said Cameron Thorpe when he took over as the company’s CEO at the beginning of the year. title: Shipping’s data needs grow, but digitization lags
content: The ITS terminal at the Port of Long Beach is in the middle of a pilot program for data sharing and predictive analytics. Photo credit: Port of Long Beach LONG BEACH — Big data is increasingly driving the delivery of freight to beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), so ports, carriers, and intermediaries must digitize the supply chain in order to process the unprecedented volume of information they are handling, according to transportation industry experts. “The data requirements of yesterday are minor compared to the data requirements of today, which will be miniscule compared to the needs of tomorrow,” Don Leyn, director of business development at KNS Communications, told the PortCon conference Wednesday in Long Beach. Digitization of shipment information is essential to supply chain efficiency because the manual processing of paperwork involved in international transportation is simply not practical anymore. The Port of Long Beach is promoting digitization and information sharing as part of a supply chain optimization program to expedite cargo flow. The port is spending more than $4 billion this decade on infrastructure projects designed to accommodate mega-ships, but modern terminals and expanded road and rail connectors alone will not improve cargo velocity, said Noel Hacegaba, the port’s managing director of commercial operations and chief commercial officer. Long Beach is evolving from a traditional landlord port concerned only about the movement of containers from the dock to the gate, to a port that partners with its stakeholders in developing an end-to-end supply chain built on greater visibility of cargo and predictive analytics. “Knowing when the container is going to arrive is the key,” Hacegaba said. The International Transportation Service (ITS) terminal in Long Beach is piloting a system of information sharing and predictive analytics, he said. Next door in Los Angeles, the port has teamed up with GE Transportation to pilot a port information portal built on data sharing among two carriers, a terminal operator, truckers, and BCOs. Los Angeles is now opening up the portal to all port users. Allen Thomas, chief strategy officer at Advent Intermodal Solutions, which is managing the ITS project in Long Beach, said digitization of the information flow from the manufacturer to the carrier, terminal operator, freight intermediary, trucker, railroad, and distribution warehouse will eliminate the wasteful and redundant transfer of paper documents from one member of the supply chain to another. “The better this works, the faster cargo moves,” Thomas said. The pace of change is occurring much more rapidly than the freight transportation industry is used to, and the first adopters to get it right will win, Thomas said. Variables that must be managed in the international supply chain include identifying the time of vessel arrival and when the container will be available for pickup, making an appointment for the trucker, arranging an intermodal handoff and designating the destination. Considering how advanced some industries are in digitizing their processes, the maritime industry is still far behind, with 52 percent of truck transactions still being handled via faxes, Thomas said. In order to be effective, the digitization of information must be accompanied by process improvements. Hacegaba noted that terminals are working with selective BCOs and truckers to free flow containers through their facilities. Rather than a particular trucker driving into a marine terminal to take delivery of a specific container, the pre-selected truckers proceed directly to a peel off pile and take delivery of the next available container, Hacegaba said. Los Angeles and Long Beach are also encouraging trucker appointment systems that allow terminal operators to manage truck flow into their facilities and ensure truckers quick access to their containers. Nine of the 12 terminals in Los Angeles-Long Beach have trucker appointment systems, Hacegaba said. In order to build what some are calling the smart port, reliable and secure connectivity of port users through a port-wide communications network is necessary, Leyn said. The communications network can be wireless, wired, or most likely a combination of both, he said. Elements of the smart port include Wi-Fi access to the mobile fleet, security cameras, optical character readers, and radio frequency identification tracking of equipment. Long Beach, the second-largest US container port after Los Angeles, has handled 6.2 million TEU through October and is on track for a near-record year and close to a 10 percent increase in volume over 2016, Hacegaba said. The average size of vessels calling at the port is 7,788 TEU and will increase further, with almost 50 percent of the vessels on order globally now of 18,000 TEU capacity or greater. Handling the cargo surges from those mega-ships will be a challenge. “That is one reason why we went into supply chain optimization,” he said. title: Nippon Express expands Africa push with Morocco office
content: Nippon Express has opened two offices in Africa so far this year. Photo credit: Shutterstock Nippon Express, Japan’s top international freight forwarder, has established its second African branch office in Casablanca, Morocco, to cash in on the continent’s increasingly promising logistics market. Morocco is aggressively attracting foreign companies through its special economic zone system, and many Japanese auto parts manufacturers and related companies have already set up operations there. The country seeks to become a logistics hub for North and West Africa with its Tangier-Med container port, according to Nippon Express. Morocco’s international trade with the world has grown 5.5 percent in dollar terms through the first three quarters of the year to $50.1 billion, according to the IHS Markit Global Trade Atlas. The country’s imports have risen 4.5 percent to $32.1 billion as exports rose 7 percent to $18 billion. Traffic at the Tangier-Med port was flat in 2016, growing just 0.1 percent year over year to 3 million TEU, according to industry analyst Alphaliner. The Casablanca branch office in the North African country formally opened for business on Friday, four months after the company made an initial foray into the African market by setting up a branch office in Nairobi, the capital city of Kenya in East Africa. Morocco’s agreement to return to the African Union in January is expected to further deepen Morocco’s economic links to other African countries as well as European countries, Nippon Express said. Nippon Express, which boasts one of the world’s largest global logistics networks, is understood to have previously undertaken Africa-related transportation and logistics services through its German subsidiary supervising its European operations. Nippon Express’s move comes amid a growing interest in the African market among Japanese manufacturing and other companies, including logistics service providers. Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe attended an international conference on the development of Africa in Nairobi in August 2016 and pledged that the Japanese public and private sectors will invest a total of $30 billion in Africa over three years. MOL Logistics (Japan) Co., a subsidiary of major Japanese shipping firm MOL, became the first Japanese logistics company to establish a business foothold in Nairobi in May this year. The Nairobi branch office formally opened for business in July. Contact Tomoo Yatsuhashi at yiu45535@nifty.com. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: Uber shows potential in unlocking small truck fleet capacity
content: The focus of the Uber user experience is on the driver, enabling him or her to quickly find and confirm a load and get paid. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com Transportation markets often tighten with little warning, leaving shippers unprepared and forced to scramble for short-term solutions. Such was the case as US trucking capacity tightened significantly in recent months. “Trucks are harder to find and more expensive than ever before,” Jeff Tucker, CEO of the 3PL Tucker Company Worldwide, said in September. Capacity is just as difficult to find now as the year winds down. On the demand side, the surge is real, driven by US economic strength, illustrated by heightened inventory levels and continuing growth in consumption and factory output. The American Trucking Associations’ (ATA's) advanced seasonally adjusted For-Hire Truck Tonnage Index, reflecting the change in tonnage actually hauled by the fleets before seasonal adjustments, was 10 percent higher in October versus a year earlier, reflecting “a much stronger freight market,” ATA chief economist Bob Costello said. But the trucking capacity crunch is not simply a story of existing capacity unable to cope with demand. Nor is it just related to the looming electronic logging device mandate that could eliminate 2 to 5 percent of truck capacity or more, depending on who is asked. Instead, it is revealing the extent to which available capacity is out of reach for many shippers who need it. Most large shippers responsible for millions of shipments annually rely overwhelmingly on relatively few large trucking companies as their main suppliers. Only infrequently do they reach into the ranks of smaller truckers in search of capacity. Some large companies have successfully built networks of small companies, but they are the exception. And although larger shippers do not normally tap into small fleet capacity, the ranks of the smallest truckers continue to grow. At the JOC Inland Distribution Conference last month, Tucker called their growth “astronomical.” “In the last four years, we’ve seen 93 percent growth in companies with one to six trucks,” said Tucker, who is also CEO of risk management company QualifiedCarriers.com. “How many big carriers would like to get their hands on those drivers?” Technology is giving owner-operators the ability to not just get a backhaul, “but the next haul and the next haul after that,” he said. “Drivers are more knowledgeable and [are equipped] with better tools than at any time in history.” This is precisely why the arrival of Uber into the trucking market this year seems well-timed and possibly transformative. Its strategy, unveiled in May, is focused on bringing small and independent truckers into its ecosystem by making it as easy for a trucker to find a load as it is for a passenger to hail a rideshare using the Uber app. Unlike the ride-hailing app, where the buy side is consumers tapping on smartphones and finding a ride, the buy side is shippers sourcing capacity the way they normally do today, i.e., through tools such as transportation management systems. The vision is not the logistics director booking loads while on vacation with the kids. Instead, the focus of the famous Uber user experience is on the driver, enabling him or her to quickly find and confirm a load and get paid. As the company describes it, “We take the guesswork out of finding and booking freight, which is often the most stressful part of a driver’s day. What used to take several hours and multiple phone calls can now be achieved with the touch of a button.” The idea would seem to have potential. Many one- to six-truck fleets get freight from load boards operated by DAT Solutions and Truckstop.com, but aren’t directly connected to individual brokers, JOC senior editor Bill Cassidy says, which is why, despite the rapid growth of truck freight brokerage firms such as Echo Global Logistics and Coyote Logistics into multibillion-dollar enterprises over the past decade, there is still an opening for additional companies to tap those small companies for large shippers. “In many cases, the only technology the small truckers have is a smartphone,” Cassidy said. “I expect other brokers and logistics companies to up their game in response, providing more tech support to smaller and smaller carriers.” Stories are coming to light of large shippers tapping Uber to access small fleet capacity. After Hurricane Harvey hit the Houston area in late August, Niagara Bottling, a shipper of 700,000 truckloads annually, turned to Uber. Late in the day on Friday, Sept. 1, two days after the hurricane struck the Houston area and a time of the day and week when capacity typically dries up, Niagara was able to book and dispatch 127 truckloads of bottled water into areas devastated by the storm. The average time it took Niagara to book a load that Friday, from the time it appeared on the Uber Freight app until it was accepted by a driver, was 34 minutes, Cassidy reported. And Niagara is not just using Uber for exception loads like those emergency bottled water shipments. The company said Uber is bidding on its freight in all lanes and all types of situations. Although there are differences in how Uber’s ride hailing and trucking businesses function, one aspect is identical: changing perceptions about finding transportation. Before Uber, no one would have thought of flagging down an independent, part-time driver using an app. But for millions of customers, it is completely normal. Similarly for larger shippers, Uber Freight is challenging long-held assumptions about finding capacity. At a time when capacity is harder to come by, that is potentially revolutionary in the United States and beyond, given Uber’s well-known global ambitions. title: FMC green lights carrier positions on NYSHEX board
content: The NYSHEX marketplace aims to reduce the volume of containers that are rolled, or are not delivered as agreed by shippers. Photo credit: Shutterstock. The Federal Maritime Commission on Friday approved four shipping carriers — CMA CGM, Hapag-Lloyd, MOL, and COSCO — as potential candidates to join investors, shippers and company executives on the steering board of the New York Shipping Exchange digital marketplace. The commission approved two agreements that would enable the carriers to take two rotating seats set aside for carrier representatives on the nine-member governing board. The agreements allow the carriers to participate in board meetings and other discussions relevant to the management of NYSHEX. The board voted three to one to take no action, or to allow the agreements to go into place. Commissioners Michael A. Khouri, Rebecca F. Dye, and William P. Doyle voted for it, and Daniel B. Maffei voted against it. Maffei said he was not opposed to the agreement, but would like the commission to have spent more time investigating the implications, especially whether NYSHEX booking contracts could be bought and sold by speculators trying to manipulate the market. NYSHEX dismissed the suggestion, saying they closely monitor all such sales. Two other seats on the board will be filled by shippers - either beneficial cargo owners (BCO) or non-vessel-operating common carrier (NVOCC) - and the remaining five will go to company executives and investors, said CEO Gordon Downes. Those appointments don’t need FMC approval because they are not regulated by the agency, he said. Downes declined to identify the shippers expected to join the board, but said both would be BCOs and called them “very large, respected shippers” that move a large volume of cargo. He said the board nominations would be announced next year. Downes said the FMC vote enables the company to implement its “governance model,” but added that the agreements prohibit any discussion of rates or surcharges. “This gives all our members the assurance that NYSHEX operates in a compliant, fair and transparent way, and that we act in the interests of the shipping industry,” Downs said. NYSHEX is one of a slew of technology-fueled startups that in recent years have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars in venture capital for products that proponents hope will transform the shipping and logistics industry, which critics say has been slow to adapt to new technology. The startups include marketplaces, digital freight forwarding operations, equipment tracking devices, and big data decision-making aides. The NYSHEX platform aims not only help shippers make reservations, but to reduce the uncertainty that stems from shippers that fail to deliver the amount of cargo that they have committed to send, and carriers that don’t ship cargo as agreed and instead leave it on the dock. Shippers can book cargo space through the portal, which also monitors whether the booking is fulfilled by shipper and carrier. Shippers and carriers sign a contract, and if either party fails to fulfill its obligation, it forfeits between 30 to 40 percent of the agreed shipping cost, depending on the route. Carriers pay a $5 per TEU transaction fee and shippers and non-vessel-operating common carriers use NYSHEX at no cost although they must be pre-accredited with NYSHEX to get started. Maffei said he would have liked commission staff to more thoroughly investigate the “forward contracts” used in the NYSHEX system that have some similarities to a futures contracts and “provide a platform for parties to sell space to be used at a future time.” As a result, they have the potential for market “speculation,” he said, adding that NYSHEX appeared to have significant protections in place to prevent that. “It’s novel and there is nothing wrong with that,” he said of the system. “But I just want to make sure we proceed very cautiously in terms of protecting the shipping public.” Doyle said the FMC will monitor the NYSHEX agreement in the future, especially the “forward exit” contracts, in which a “shipper obtains a profit on the resale of space.” “The reason for this concern is that the shipper could perhaps manipulate the market by increasing freight rates,” he said, adding that the commission will also be monitoring other issues such as NYSHEX’s rules and regulations, and its membership requirements. Downes said fewer than 2 percent of contracts result in an exit in which the shipper cannot move the cargo it has committed to move, and transfers the use of the space on the vessel to another shipper. In that scenario, the shipper “can put it back on the exchange and another shipper can take over the contract obligation,” he said. “It’s not buying and selling the contract.” Because NYSHEX contracts are “bilateral,” or involve two specific parties, they can’t be bought and sold — rather the shipper has to find someone to take up responsibility for filling the contract, he said. “We monitor every single exit that takes place to understand the root cause,” Downes said. We provide quarterly reports on exits, and if there appears to be evidence of speculation, we have the ability to impose position limits as per our governance process.” Anyone suspected of speculation would not be allowed to join the market, he said. The appointment of two carriers and two shippers to the board is designed to give balance to the steering body, NYSHEX said. That is in line with the core principals of NYSHEX that are based on the idea that it is “an exchange for the industry governed by the shipping industry,” according to the company. Aside from the nine-member board of directors, the company also has a “member council” of nine seats filled by company customers that is responsible for providing industry feedback to NYSHEX management and providing best practices and suggestions, the company said, “NYSHEX operates with free market principles, so fair and competitive prices are an essential component of what our members expect,” Downes said. “This also allows us to agree on fair standards for digital freight contracting, which helps to simplify the contracting process for all our members, helping them to capture the benefit of digital contracting.” Contact Hugh R. title: Chittagong port to introduce electronic lock system
content: Shippers say congestion at Chittagong Port will increase with a new container lock technology. Photo credit: Shutterstock. Bangladesh’s customs authority will introduce an electronic seal and lock services system (ESEL) on containers transported between Chittagong Port and off-docks to prevent pilferage and tax evasion. Finance Minister AMA Muhith will inaugurate the new lock system for containers in the country’s prime seaport on December 11 — a move that is opposed by port users because it increases their costs by 600 taka ($7) per container or box. The use of an ESEL to ensure cargo security, prevent theft, smuggling, and dumping of unwanted goods is required by international maritime law. After arrival at the Chittagong area, an ESEL will be added to a container immediately after it has been offloaded from a vessel. The device will be removed after the container enters the off-docks or inland container depots (ICD). The same process occurs for outbound containers: the electronic device will be attached to the container before it leaves an ICD and the device will removed after it arrives at the port area. Currently, 17 private ICDs, situated near Chittagong Port, store selected low-risk import items and empty containers, conduct customs clearance formalities, and allow unstuffing/delivery of selected categories of import consignments. The nation’s top export item — the readymade garment — is transported via truck to the ICDs, then packed in containers before being transported to port jetties. Customs officials say some unscrupulous businessmen are breaking the locks of imported containers on their way to ICDs from Chittagong Port and removing a portion of the goods, in order to evade taxes and duties. Further, because traditional locks are used in outbound containers, thieves sometimes break these locks and remove goods from the containers — causing financial loss for importers and exporters. Shippers will be charged 600 taka per box or vehicle for the first 48 hours to use the new lock system. A 50 taka fee will also be charrged for each hour after 48 hours, according to a notification of revenue board. However, shippers have strongly protested the new system. They say that it will further increase their cost of doing business, due to current congestion at the Chittagong Port, which has become a common phenomenon and results in extra charges. In a letter to the revenue authority, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association president said various types of seals and locks systems are being used with export containers that conform with the requirements of foreign buyers. “The locks we use costs us only $0.50 to $0.75, but the new lock system will cost us manifold,” he said. Further, the Chittagong Chamber of Commerce and Industry president, who also heads the Port Users’ Forum at a meeting Monday said the introduction of the new lock system will increase congestion at the Chittagong Port and also in the container depots. “We don’t want the new lock system as it will raise both cost and congestion,” he said. Shipping Agents Association president Ahsanul Huq Chowdhury said currently a bullet seal is being used for containers globally. “The electronic seal and lock services has no use anywhere in the world now. We don’t want it,” Chowdhury said. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. Reproduction in whole or in part without permission is prohibited. title: LA-LB big data drive to wring productivity from existing assets
content: Port officials say data sharing and analytics will increase port productivity with the same physical assets. Photo credit: Port of Los Angeles. The executive directors of Los Angeles and Long Beach are looking to technology and data sharing to unleash the latent physical capacity, cargo-handling productivity, and environmental potential of the largest US port complex. Pilot projects now under way to foster data sharing among beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), carriers, terminals operators, truckers, and railroads are beginning to deliver the efficiencies needed to assure BCOs they should make Southern California their gateway of choice, Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, told the Harbor Transportation Club Tuesday. “We’ve cut through these silos,” Seroka said in reference to the barriers that have prevented port users from data sharing. The port, in collaboration with GE Transportation, has developed a port information portal through which APM Terminals, Maersk Line, Mediterranean Shipping Co. and dozens of BCOs and truckers share shipment information. The portal is already saving truck dispatchers an average of two to three hours per day by feeding shipment information into a cloud-based system that uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to leverage the data, he said. The ports and their stakeholders are utilizing big data to drive process improvements for trucker appointments, chassis management, and extended gate hours, said Mario Cordero, executive director of the Port of Long Beach. Cordero, who until recently oversaw Federal Maritime Commission efforts to study and promote port efficiency, said major gateways across the United States are looking to technology and supply chain collaboration to handle mega-ships and the demands they are placing on port operations. However, both directors said their ports have much work ahead to reach the service levels that BCOs and truckers say are necessary to handle today’s cargo volumes. Seroka on Tuesday recounted how earlier in the day he was driving to the port and witnessed a long line of trucks waiting to get into a terminal. “Turn times of 80 to 120 minutes are completely unacceptable,” he said. “What if we could have zero turn times?” Cordero asked. Although perfection may not be attainable, the ports can use big data in collaboration with their stakeholders to improve the current trucker appointment regime, manage chassis through the pool of pools, and improve cargo flow through processes such as container peel-offs, he said. The ports are promoting and facilitating productivity measures with a sense of urgency. The port complex through October handled 9.98 million laden TEU, up 3.3 percent from the pace that was set in the record year of 2007, according to numbers published on the website of the Pacific Maritime Association. The record volume comes despite the fact that the West Coast as a whole has lost 12 percent market share of US imports from Asia since 2005 to East and Gulf coast ports, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com. The trend appears to be accelerating since completion of the Panama Canal expansion project in 2016 and the project to raise the elevation of the Bayonne Bridge in New York-New Jersey this summer. Vessels with capacities up to 14,000 TEU can now access East Coast ports on all-water services through the Panama Canal. While acknowledging the loss of market share, the port directors noted that their biggest challenge is not handling the competition from East Coast and Gulf Coast ports, but rather efficiently processing the delivery of containers from the even larger vessels that call in Southern California. Seroka noted that in 2016 two vessels, one of 18,000 TEU capacity and another of 15,000 TEU capacity, called at the APM Terminal in Los Angeles simultaneously. This autumn, a Maersk vessel discharged and reloaded 24,000 TEU during one call. The average vessel size today in Los Angeles-Long Beach is almost 8,000 TEU. The ports at present have the physical capacity to handle these mega-ships and their record container exchanges because their leadership over the past 20 years invested in the marine terminals and supporting infrastructure needed to accommodate the large vessels, the port directors said. Los Angeles and Long Beach have also been the leading edge in developing the largest interoperable chassis pool at a US port, trucker appointment systems at nine of the 12 container terminals in the port complex, and process improvements such as container dray-offs and peel-offs. Therefore, the ports seamlessly handled the April 1 shotgun start of the new global vessel sharing alliances. “Not all ports can say that,” Seroka said. Nevertheless, the port community in Southern California and elsewhere still operates in an environment in which basic shipping documentation involving carriers, terminals, BCOs, intermediaries, truckers, and railroads that could be shared to improve cargo flow, mitigate equipment dislocations, shorten truck turn times, and streamline the hand-off of containers among the transportation modes remains siloed in each sector of the industry. The Port of Los Angeles and GE Transportation this past year have piloted a port information portal in which shipment data are shared among BCOs and transportation providers. It is taking place on a cloud-based platform based on the program that GE Transportation put together for its parent corporation to handle $2 billion per year of transportation transactions, Seroka said. This system of systems is designed to enable each port user to plug its system into the platform to promote the sharing of data in a secure environment. According to the port, that means visibility to shipment data from 2,000 vessel calls each year is now available up to two weeks before vessel arrival, compared with two days in the past. The pilot project, which will be expanded to all terminals next year, has already produced overall efficiency gains of 8 to 12 percent, the port stated in a video on the information portal. The information portal is expected to improve the efficiency of existing processes. For example, nine of the 12 terminals have their own trucker appointment systems, and the goal is the establishment of a universal appointment system for all terminals through the portal. In that way appointments can become dynamic, where a trucker who is delivering an export load or empty container can upon completion schedule a visit at the same terminal or another to pick up an inbound load. Although the port complex has sufficient terminal capacity to handle the anticipated growth until about 2030 under current cargo-handling practices, if volumes reach 40 million TEU by 2040 as projected in the best-case port planning scenario, additional capacity will be needed. cleaned_content: Port officials say data sharing and analytics will increase port productivity with the same physical assets. The executive directors of Los Angeles and Long Beach are looking to technology and data sharing to unleash the latent physical capacity, cargo-handling productivity, and environmental potential of the largest US port complex. Pilot projects now under way to foster data sharing among beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), carriers, terminals operators, truckers, and railroads are beginning to deliver the efficiencies needed to assure BCOs they should make Southern California their gateway of choice, Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, told the Harbor Transportation Club Tuesday. “We’ve cut through these silos,” Seroka said in reference to the barriers that have prevented port users from data sharing. The port, in collaboration with GE Transportation, has developed a port information portal through which APM Terminals, Maersk Line, Mediterranean Shipping Co. and dozens of BCOs and truckers share shipment information. The portal is already saving truck dispatchers an average of two to three hours per day by feeding shipment information into a cloud-based system that uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to leverage the data, he said. The ports and their stakeholders are utilizing big data to drive process improvements for trucker appointments, chassis management, and extended gate hours, said Mario Cordero, executive director of the Port of Long Beach. Cordero, who until recently oversaw Federal Maritime Commission efforts to study and promote port efficiency, said major gateways across the United States are looking to technology and supply chain collaboration to handle mega-ships and the demands they are placing on port operations. However, both directors said their ports have much work ahead to reach the service levels that BCOs and truckers say are necessary to handle today’s cargo volumes. Seroka on Tuesday recounted how earlier in the day he was driving to the port and witnessed a long line of trucks waiting to get into a terminal. “Turn times of 80 to 120 minutes are completely unacceptable,” he said. “What if we could have zero turn times?” Cordero asked. Although perfection may not be attainable, the ports can use big data in collaboration with their stakeholders to improve the current trucker appointment regime, manage chassis through the pool of pools, and improve cargo flow through processes such as container peel-offs, he said. The ports are promoting and facilitating productivity measures with a sense of urgency. The port complex through October handled 9.98 million laden TEU, up 3.3 percent from the pace that was set in the record year of 2007, according to numbers published on the website of the Pacific Maritime Association. The record volume comes despite the fact that the West Coast as a whole has lost 12 percent market share of US imports from Asia since 2005 to East and Gulf coast ports, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com. The trend appears to be accelerating since completion of the Panama Canal expansion project in 2016 and the project to raise the elevation of the Bayonne Bridge in New York-New Jersey this summer. Vessels with capacities up to 14,000 TEU can now access East Coast ports on all-water services through the Panama Canal. While acknowledging the loss of market share, the port directors noted that their biggest challenge is not handling the competition from East Coast and Gulf Coast ports, but rather efficiently processing the delivery of containers from the even larger vessels that call in Southern California. Seroka noted that in 2016 two vessels, one of 18,000 TEU capacity and another of 15,000 TEU capacity, called at the APM Terminal in Los Angeles simultaneously. This autumn, a Maersk vessel discharged and reloaded 24,000 TEU during one call. The average vessel size today in Los Angeles-Long Beach is almost 8,000 TEU. The ports at present have the physical capacity to handle these mega-ships and their record container exchanges because their leadership over the past 20 years invested in the marine terminals and supporting infrastructure needed to accommodate the large vessels, the port directors said. Los Angeles and Long Beach have also been the leading edge in developing the largest interoperable chassis pool at a US port, trucker appointment systems at nine of the 12 container terminals in the port complex, and process improvements such as container dray-offs and peel-offs. Therefore, the ports seamlessly handled the April 1 shotgun start of the new global vessel sharing alliances. “Not all ports can say that,” Seroka said. Nevertheless, the port community in Southern California and elsewhere still operates in an environment in which basic shipping documentation involving carriers, terminals, BCOs, intermediaries, truckers, and railroads that could be shared to improve cargo flow, mitigate equipment dislocations, shorten truck turn times, and streamline the hand-off of containers among the transportation modes remains siloed in each sector of the industry. This system of systems is designed to enable each port user to plug its system into the platform to promote the sharing of data in a secure environment. According to the port, that means visibility to shipment data from 2,000 vessel calls each year is now available up to two weeks before vessel arrival, compared with two days in the past. The pilot project, which will be expanded to all terminals next year, has already produced overall efficiency gains of 8 to 12 percent, the port stated in a video on the information portal. For example, nine of the 12 terminals have their own trucker appointment systems, and the goal is the establishment of a universal appointment system for all terminals through the portal. title: ILA-USMX contract talks break off over automation
content: The ILA is refusing to back down in its strong opposition to automation. Photo credit: Kalmar. HOLLYWOOD, Florida — Negotiations on a new International Longshoremen’s Association (ILA) contract broke off abruptly Wednesday as ILA president Harold Daggett accused employers of seeking to use automation to eliminate dockworker jobs. Daggett said the ILA and United States Maritime Alliance (USMX) disagreed on the distinction between fully automated terminals, which he has pledged to fight, and semi-automated terminals that have automated features but are operated by dockworkers. “When they’re talking about fully automated, they mean two or three people on the whole terminal,” he told JOC.com. “We’re not going to accept that. If they install a computer on any equipment, they need to provide a seat for a longshoreman next to it.” Daggett said the union is prepared to avoid bargaining until the current coastwide contract expires on Sept. 30, 2018. However, he has instructed local officials to continue negotiations on supplemental local issues covering pensions, work rules, and other port-specific issues. USMX issued a brief statement suggesting the halt in bargaining was only a temporary detour on the path to a strike-free agreement. “Discussions on a range of issues were open and frank, and USMX expects the talks to continue at some point in the future and looks forward to a successful resolution,” USMX said. Several management and union officials said they were not unduly alarmed by the breakoff in talks, and noted that nearly 10 months remain before the contract expires. USMX and ILA representatives opened talks this week on a note of optimism that they could make substantial headway toward a long-term contract extension. The two sides have been eyeing an extension stretching to 2024, six years after the current agreement expires. Such a deal would leapfrog the five-year extension to mid-2022 that the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) ratified this year for West Coast ports. Daggett said he was “disappointed” that the ILWU contract allowed continued development of fully automated terminals. Daggett said USMX proposed to define fully automated terminals as one in which unmanned vehicles transport containers between dockside gantry cranes and yard stacks. The two most highly automated ILA-staffed terminals, at the Port of Virginia and at GCT Bayonne in the Port of New York and New Jersey, use manned vehicles to shuttle boxes between dockside and remote-controlled yard stacking cranes. The ILA president said USMX’s proposed definition would blur the distinction between semi-automated terminals, which the ILA has accepted, and fully automated terminals. He said it would allow terminals to sharply increase the level of automation but still call themselves semi-automated as long as they use manned transporters between dockside and the container stack. Daggett had said previously that he viewed automation as the main issue in the current negotiations. During a pre-negotiating session last February, delegates also raised issues including jurisdiction over chassis repair and other work, and support of some ports’ underfunded local pensions. The recent ILWU-PMA extension was focused on wages and benefits and avoided more contentious issues such as automation and work jurisdiction. The East and Gulf coast contract talks also are expected to be limited in scope. The ILA has not had a coastwide strike since 1977 but came to the brink of one during the last round of negotiations, in 2012 to 2013. Those talks were settled with a federal mediator’s help after bitter public exchanges, repeated strike threats, and two temporary extensions. An early agreement on a new contract for East and Gulf coast ports would help them retain market share they gained after West Coast labor disruptions including a 10-day lockout in 2002 and months of delays during contract negotiations in 2014 to 2015. East and Gulf coast ports’ share of US containerized imports from Asia rose to 34.6 percent during the first 10 months of this year, compared with 26.3 percent in 2010, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com. ILA and USMX officials began exploring a long-term extension more than two years ago, but the effort lost momentum amid questions about health care and other issues, and eventually opted to await the outcome of the ILWU-PMA negotiations on the West Coast.
