title: LA-LB terminals weigh options to PierPass program
content: The Port of Long Beach with the PierPass facility in the foreground. Photo credit: PierPass. Cargo interests and US truckers should know by early April if the PierPass extended-gates program in Los Angeles-Long Beach, now in its 13th year, will be restructured to incorporate a flat fee coupled with trucker appointments. PierPass has its supporters and detractors, but port users agree that the largest US gateway could not handle 17 million TEU per year without a regular schedule of night and weekend gates. Because many ports also struggle to handle record cargo volumes carried by 10,000 to 14,000 TEU mega-ships, a successful program in Southern California could serve as a template for other ports seeking to establish a cost-effective program of extended gates. The 12 container terminal operators in Los Angeles-Long Beach are assessing the options contained in a study released in early March by Tioga/WCL Consulting. The report followed months of meetings with terminal operators, truckers, beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), and cargo intermediaries that analyzed the pros and cons of the PierPass off-peak program. Truckers bear the brunt of delays at marine terminals, and they generally agree that the report — which leans toward a lower, flat fee, a portwide trucker appointment regime, and greater BCO participation in container peel-off programs at individual terminals — addresses most of their goals. “It’s much of what we’ve been asking for the past three years,” said Weston LaBar, CEO of the Harbor Trucking Association. Container terminal operators who are members of the West Coast Marine Terminal Operators Association must make the final decision on how the off-peak program will be restructured because the association’s agreement with the Federal Maritime Commission specifies that the terminal operators can only discuss matters involving rate setting among themselves and not with outside parties such as BCOs and truckers, PierPass president John Cushing said. Cushing noted that since 2005 the off-peak program has accomplished its major goal of helping the ports handle growing cargo volumes and larger vessels while mitigating congestion on local freeways through a regular schedule of four weeknight gates and one weekend gate. A traffic-mitigation fee of $144.14 per FEU covers about 81 percent of the additional costs terminals face for running five off-peak gates each week, according to the study. Despite mitigating traffic impacts and allowing the ports to grow without having to build costly new terminals, periods of congestion are common daily. The study found long truck lines at the beginning of the first shift and especially in late afternoon when the first shift ends at 5 p.m. until the second shift begins at 6 p.m. The traffic-mitigation fee that BCOs pay runs through 6 p.m. on weekdays, and it contributes to congestion and trucker delays in two ways, LaBar said. Some truckers enter the terminal as early as 4 p.m. and remain inside until the fee is no longer charged at 6 p.m. Many truckers simply line up at the terminal gates in the late afternoon and park there for an hour or two until 6 p.m. The study lists a proposal to replace the traffic-mitigation fee that BCOs pay only for peak-period moves with a lower, flat fee that would be charged on all truck moves, day and night. The study did not recommend what the lower flat fee should be. When Oakland International Container Terminal in 2016 established its extended-gates program, it assessed a flat fee of $30 per container whether the containers move during the day or at night. Mandatory trucker appointments would accompany the flat fee proposal to ensure truck traffic spreads out over 16 hours each day. Under the current arrangement, which disincentivizes peak calls, 42 percent of truck traffic moves during the day shift, when the fee is charged, and 58 percent at night, when the fee is waived, according to the study. Because terminals can only handle a certain number of moves each hour, appointments would be made on a first-come, first-served basis, thereby spreading the available slots throughout the day. The study floated the concept of a portwide peel-off program in which containers consigned to particular BCOs, normally larger ones capable of aggregating a critical mass, are segregated into their own piles. When truckers serving a particular BCO arrive at the terminal, they proceed immediately to the designated pile and containers are peeled off from the top. This eliminates the need for each trucker to proceed deep into the terminal in search of a specific container. Although BCOs and truckers said a portwide peel-off program could be cumbersome to manage, they encouraged individual terminals to have their own programs. Cargo interests and US truckers should know by early April if the PierPass extended-gates program in Los Angeles-Long Beach, now in its 13th year, will be restructured to incorporate a flat fee coupled with trucker appointments. PierPass has its supporters and detractors, but port users agree that the largest US gateway could not handle 17 million TEU per year without a regular schedule of night and weekend gates. The 12 container terminal operators in Los Angeles-Long Beach are assessing the options contained in a study released in early March by Tioga/WCL Consulting. title: Blockchain success in shipping hinges on standardization
content: A Maersk Line container ship at the Port of Oakland. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. A current industry concern is how one makes sense of the barrage of blockchain announcements already this year and of the feeling that these may be the opening chess moves in a profound game that could reshape how the industry works in the coming years. On Jan. 16 Maersk Line and IBM announced the formation of a joint venture company to simplify visibility and documentation via blockchain. The announcement of an initial coin offering by the Global Shared Container Platform (GSCP) came on Feb. 28, aiming to create a global pool of containers, real-time tracking, and dwell time visibility. On March 14, a consortium of AB InBev, Accenture, APL, Kuehne + Nagel (K+N), and a European customs organization said it tested a blockchain solution to eliminate printed shipping documents. And on March 15, Hong Kong-based 300cubits said it successfully completed the first trial shipment in its TEU token smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain. There were likely others as well. This flurry of announcements, at a time when many people are still struggling to understand blockchain, raises more questions than it answers. Among them: If blockchain by its nature is supposed to be decentralized and neutral (like bitcoin, famously “owned by everyone and no one”), is the industry seeing the emergence of the antithesis — blockchains owned and controlled by a profit-making party intent on charging fees to use it? Will the blockchain ecosystem in logistics be made up of competing blockchains unable or unwilling to interact with each other? Alternatively, will the multiple emerging blockchains become interoperable, able to interact with each other in a compatible ecosystem? Or will one dominant blockchain emerge from the pack and, like Microsoft Windows, make its owners spectacularly rich in the process? “The way I see it, there are two ways this could evolve. The first way is one of these blockchain initiatives will gather a lot of momentum and become the standard for the industry that everyone must follow,” said Gordon Downes, CEO of the New York Shipping Exchange, or NYSHEX, which recently tested its container slot contract on the Hyperledger open source blockchain. “The alternative way might be that different blockchain initiatives become interoperable, meaning the use cases on the blockchain can be realized regardless of which underlying blockchain is being used.” Accepting that multiple blockchain initiatives are being created almost daily, a consensus view of sources contacted by JOC.com recently said they need to be interoperable for there to be any hope that major benefits would eventually accrue to the industry. “In my view, there is a strong need for the different blockchains emerging in the shipping industry to be interoperable. It would be detrimental for the shipping industry if the different factions and initiatives compete head-on trying to make their specific blockchain technology choice the de-facto standard for the industry,” said Peter Ludvigsen, CEO and founder of Blockshipping ApS, creator of the GSCP platform. “This would substantially delay benefits realization for the carriers and the customers and the industry as a whole.” “Siloed solutions will not work,” said Brian Laung Aoaeh, certified financial analyst, a partner with Particle Ventures in New York and founder of The New York Supply Chain Meetup. “If people go down the path of developing their own solutions, I think they have to ensure that those solutions can talk to one another, and maybe that is how it works.” That is why, he said, “My guess is that we’ll ultimately gravitate toward centralized blockchain applications and away from decentralized blockchain applications. The reason is simple; a centralized design is generally preferred when there’s a need for a high degree of consistency within the system or network.” Others agree. “This is not going to be a Betamax versus VHS type of outcome. You are going to have by necessity some kind of interoperability of standards and data, and not too far away from now,” said Fauad Shariff, co-founder and CEO of the non-vessel operator-focused startup CoLoadX. “Blockchain is looking more and more like infrastructure, so can you charge a toll for the use of your blockchain?” Shariff said. “It’s debatable when there is another one that does the same thing at the same speed, so it’s much easier to collaborate and then build apps and extensions off of that, and that is where we’re probably going to head.” Ludvigsen said one factor that should not be an obstacle to interoperability is trust. The core of blockchain technology is defined by encryption and agreed-upon standards that should overcome any trust issues. “The use of blockchain technology enables global container carriers who are fierce competitors and who do not trust each other to use a system where the trust is built into the system,” he said. According to Otto Schacht, executive vice president of sea logistics at K+N, the world’s largest ocean freight forwarder, “The still-open question is what such a model might look like, and to what extent it may change the roles of the different players in the market. Currently, the launch of the first prototypes across different industries is about to reveal the real world potentials and limitations of blockchains.” Contact Peter Tirschwell at peter.tirschwell@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @petertirschwell. © 2026 S&P Global. title: India sets stakeholder deadline for digital, central portal
content: The Optical Character Recognition gate technology used at the DP World Nhava Sheva Terminal is a first for Indian ports. Photo credit: DP World Subcontinent. As the container shipping industry deploys assets to research and develop the potential breakthrough technology of blockchain-based supply chains, India’s government this week set a firm April 2 deadline for stakeholders to transition to the port community system (PCS) after a recent review found that the use of digital applications critical to supply chain efficiency continues to lag expectations. Several years in planning, the central portal is designed to handle delivery orders, transport orders, gate open cut-off times, delivery gate schedules, gate-in bookings, and pre-gate schedules electronically, instead of in hard-copy form — an existing system that entails long delays and lacks shipment visibility. “On a review of the use of these functionalities in PCS by various stakeholders, it is seen that many stakeholders in the [PCS] are yet to use these features. In order to improve the flow of sea trade among the [PCS] and for the benefit of all stakeholders concerned, it is essential that all stakeholders across the maritime trade flow use these features,” the decree stated. India’s government specifically highlighted that those missing links in supply chain online services are causing long cargo dwell times and impacting the country’s ease-of-doing-business competitiveness. The widely circulated decree also said the PCS module has been upgraded to include all port locations for the clearance of import cargo under the direct port delivery program, a facility that was previously limited to Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT). In addition to major, public ports, the web-based single window mandate applies to privately operated, minor cargo terminals and third-party inland logistics players. The directive also said moving forward, senior shipping ministry officials, along with executives from the Indian Ports Association, that oversees the PCS rollout, will take stock of the progress on a monthly basis and initiate “further actions as appropriate.” Eliminating trade bottlenecks and reducing supply chain costs have been a major focus of the Modi administration, and those efforts have borne fruit: a 30-spot jump for India in the World Bank’s latest ease-of-doing-business report. Gate automation to speed truck turnarounds and radio-frequency identification technology-enabled tagging systems to improve cargo visibility are some of the other notable trade facilitation measures already in place at gateway ports. Shippers using terminals in the JNPT harbor have been the biggest beneficiaries of these initiatives. Further, the widely discussed blockchain technology is also slowly making its way through the Indian transportation industry. Mumbai-based logistics firm J. M. Baxi Group reached a memorandum of understanding with IBM to jointly pursue blockchain-enabled services for domestic logistics companies. “The two companies will collaborate on multiple projects by bringing the joint expertise in domain knowledge, techno-functional expertise and technology expertise to solve business problems affecting the exim [export-import] trade and logistics industry,” a release stated. Further, taking a cue from global technology-driven logistics providers such as Freightos and Flexport, and buoyed by New Delhi’s renewed digital push, an array of domestic, tech start-up companies have also sprung up in recent years. These firms cite price transparency as their core selling point versus the traditional freight forwarding community. Mumbai-based Shipwaves is one such online shipping services provider, and it says it has signed more than 1,000 shippers and enjoys special pricing arrangements with major carriers such as Maersk Line, Cosco Container Lines, CMA CGM, and Mediterranean Shipping Co. Officials at Shipwaves told JOC.com that the company currently has a presence in Mumbai, Mundra, Nagpur, Nashik, Mangalore, Chennai, and Vishakapatanam, and is looking to expand further. “Shipwaves achieves real-time freight visibility by cooperating with all the various entities involved and plugging their own systems with the aggregated data from different sources like various carriers, ports, truckers, or geolocation technology,” officials said. It is still too soon to tell how these internet marketplaces will fare in the long run, officials generally agree, but there is no denying that digitization will play a pivotal role in India’s freight industry as the emerging economy expands and develops. © 2026 S&P Global. title: ELD mandate spurs innovation in US truck tech
content: A truck travels on a US road. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. In a few short months, the electronic logging device (ELD) mandate for truck drivers has unveiled a host of inefficiencies in US supply chains. Transit times for shipments have grown longer, especially in lanes ranging from 450 to 550 miles, as drivers keep a tighter rein on their hours. That is spurring innovation aimed at improving time management within supply chains. With out-of-service enforcement of ELD violations set to begin April 1, companies are racing the clock to comply with the mandate, provide drivers with the means to cope with more precise enforcement of hours-of-service (HOS) rules, and reset the timing on their supply chains. These are only early ripples in a wave of ELD-inspired changes to transportation technology. Trucker Path and Convoy introduced new products Tuesday aimed at helping drivers better manage their time and loads in the ELD era. The products directly or indirectly help shippers struggling to match their freight and lanes with the networks and needs of for-hire trucking companies and drivers. They also aim to deliver more time to time-strapped truckers. Trucker Path launched an ELD of its own, a device with an app that tracks HOS and miles driven within a state. (This information is needed to calculate fuel tax payments.) The company plans to integrate the ELD app with its Trucker Path app, a marketplace of driver services with 600,000 active monthly users, as well as a its Truckloads load-matching app. For Trucker Path, founded in 2013, the ELD is a natural extension of its existing portfolio of services. “We’re a navigation app that’s used by about 30 percent of over-the-road drivers to find destinations, services, [and] parking,” said Sam Bokher, director of business operations. Its Truckloads marketplace, built on the same technology platform, was launched in 2016. “We’re launching the ELD as a separate app, but we’ll be integrating into the Trucker Path app,” Bokher said. “We’ll be able to show drivers how much time they have left and where there’s truck parking in the area. That’s going to help a lot of drivers.” Integrating the ELD and the Truckloads app will give Trucker Path “even more visibility into the market,” he said. Truck parking was scarce back when the US economy was growing more slowly. With US GDP expansion heading toward 3 percent or higher in 2018, locating a place to park a truck and take the required 10-hour, off-duty period each day is an even tougher task for drivers. Truckstops fill up quickly, and drivers may have no choice but to park illegally. With the ELD mandate heralding stricter enforcement of the 11-hour daily driving limit, more truck drivers reportedly are stopping earlier, ending their day well short of the 11-hour limit in order to ensure they have a space for the night. Integrating the ELD and parking information in the Trucker Path system could save drivers significant time now spent searching for parking. As the mandate, which took effect Dec. 18, begins to be fully enforced in April, truckers without ELDs will be issued out-of-service orders that will put them off the road for 10 hours. They will then be allowed to proceed to their next scheduled stop but will not be able to go beyond that point without installing an ELD. The effect could be stranded freight and drivers across the United States. “It’s going to be a little bit of a painful transition,” Bokher said. “This is showing us the HOS regulations are far from perfect. Maybe it’s a sign for the [Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration] to review some of their rules and make changes. The short-term impact will be painful, but the long-term positive is that it’s a step to digitize trucking and more visibility.” Convoy, founded in 2015, is one of several technology “platforms” focused on connecting shippers with small carriers and drivers, including Trucker Path, Uber Freight, and NEXT Trucking. Convoy is not rolling out an ELD, but it is launching services designed with the ELD era in mind, Kristen Forecki, vice president of carrier engagement and expansion, said Monday. On Tuesday, Convoy introduced services called Suggested Reloads, Request a Load, and Automated Detention, all aimed to help drivers find freight and move it faster. “These features came about from talking to carriers and drivers about the pressure they feel from ELDs,” Forecki said. “One driver told me it’s like living in an episode of ‘24,’ there’s that much pressure.” The Request a Load feature lets drivers or dispatchers enter when and where their trucks will be empty into the Convoy app ahead of time, along with where they want to go next. The app then alerts them to matching loads as they become available. Drivers and dispatchers can accept and confirm a job instantly, Forecki said, reducing the time their trucks driver empty. Suggested Reloads is a complement to that feature. Through it, Convoy suggests loads near drop-off locations that they can book. “We will automatically show you shipments that are possible backhauls for that load or take you on another tour,” Forecki said. “That minimizes the amount of time it takes to find a load, reduce the amount of time driving empty.” The feature with perhaps the biggest potential to help drivers and shippers is Automated Detention, which automatically calculates the time a truck has been at a facility, and if it has been detained for more than two hours, it allows the driver to request detention pay directly in the Convoy app. The app instantly confirms eligibility and processes payment, she said. “Drivers historically have had to fight with shippers or brokers to get that detention payment,” Forecki said. “We’ll pay the driver even if the shipper doesn’t even pay us.” The information on detention time also will help Convoy work with its 400 shippers to determine the cause of dockside delays and move drivers through unloading or loading more quickly, she said. “This will really make a difference in our partnerships with shippers,” said Forecki. “Using our data, we can help them learn how to improve performance at their facilities and reduce detention overall. We can get ahead of spikes at a facility that may increase driver wait times. We can rank them against their other facilities and other facilities in their area.” The location data obtained through the ELD are the key to cracking the detention problem, she believes. If that is so, it will be a boon to drivers, carriers, and shippers alike. Contact William B. Cassidy at bill.cassidy@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @wbcassidy_joc. © 2026 S&P Global. Its Truckloads marketplace, built on the same technology platform, was launched in 2016. “We’re launching the ELD as a separate app, but we’ll be integrating into the Trucker Path app,” Bokher said. “We’ll be able to show drivers how much time they have left and where there’s truck parking in the area. That’s going to help a lot of drivers.” Integrating the ELD and the Truckloads app will give Trucker Path “even more visibility into the market,” he said. Truck parking was scarce back when the US economy was growing more slowly. With US GDP expansion heading toward 3 percent or higher in 2018, locating a place to park a truck and take the required 10-hour, off-duty period each day is an even tougher task for drivers. Truckstops fill up quickly, and drivers may have no choice but to park illegally. With the ELD mandate heralding stricter enforcement of the 11-hour daily driving limit, more truck drivers reportedly are stopping earlier, ending their day well short of the 11-hour limit in order to ensure they have a space for the night. Integrating the ELD and parking information in the Trucker Path system could save drivers significant time now spent searching for parking. As the mandate, which took effect Dec. 18, begins to be fully enforced in April, truckers without ELDs will be issued out-of-service orders that will put them off the road for 10 hours. They will then be allowed to proceed to their next scheduled stop but will not be able to go beyond that point without installing an ELD. The effect could be stranded freight and drivers across the United States. “It’s going to be a little bit of a painful transition,” Bokher said. “This is showing us the HOS regulations are far from perfect. Maybe it’s a sign for the [Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration] to review some of their rules and make changes. The short-term impact will be painful, but the long-term positive is that it’s a step to digitize trucking and more visibility.” Convoy, founded in 2015, is one of several technology “platforms” focused on connecting shippers with small carriers and drivers, including Trucker Path, Uber Freight, and NEXT Trucking. Convoy is not rolling out an ELD, but it is launching services designed with the ELD era in mind, Kristen Forecki, vice president of carrier engagement and expansion, said Monday. On Tuesday, Convoy introduced services called Suggested Reloads, Request a Load, and Automated Detention, all aimed to help drivers find freight and move it faster. “These features came about from talking to carriers and drivers about the pressure they feel from ELDs,” Forecki said. “One driver told me it’s like living in an episode of ‘24,’ there’s that much pressure.” The Request a Load feature lets drivers or dispatchers enter when and where their trucks will be empty into the Convoy app ahead of time, along with where they want to go next. The app then alerts them to matching loads as they become available. Drivers and dispatchers can accept and confirm a job instantly, Forecki said, reducing the time their trucks driver empty. Suggested Reloads is a complement to that feature. Through it, Convoy suggests loads near drop-off locations that they can book. “We will automatically show you shipments that are possible backhauls for that load or take you on another tour,” Forecki said. “That minimizes the amount of time it takes to find a load, reduce the amount of time driving empty.” The feature with perhaps the biggest potential to help drivers and shippers is Automated Detention, which automatically calculates the time a truck has been at a facility, and if it has been detained for more than two hours, it allows the driver to request detention pay directly in the Convoy app. The app instantly confirms eligibility and processes payment, she said. “Drivers historically have had to fight with shippers or brokers to get that detention payment,” Forecki said. “We’ll pay the driver even if the shipper doesn’t even pay us.” The information on detention time also will help Convoy work with its 400 shippers to determine the cause of dockside delays and move drivers through unloading or loading more quickly, she said. “This will really make a difference in our partnerships with shippers,” said Forecki. “Using our data, we can help them learn how to improve performance at their facilities and reduce detention overall. We can get ahead of spikes at a facility that may increase driver wait times. We can rank them against their other facilities and other facilities in their area.” The location data obtained through the ELD are the key to cracking the detention problem, she believes. If that is so, it will be a boon to drivers, carriers, and shippers alike.

title: West Coast portals offer path to country-wide visibility
content: The Port of Los Angeles. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Technology is transforming virtually every sector of the transportation supply chain, but beneficial cargo owners (BCOs) are not achieving the end-to-end visibility and cargo velocity that technology promises because the proprietary nature of the industry prevents the sharing of shipment data throughout the supply chain. West Coast ports have taken the lead in breaking down the barriers to information sharing by establishing information portals that will allow all port users to access the shipment data they need in a secure environment. This development promises to accelerate productivity measures such as extended gate hours, trucker appointments, and container dray-offs already in place, by giving BCOs, truckers, and other port users advance information on shipments before vessels arrive at the ports. The increasing number of mega-ship calls, and the intensity of their import discharges, along with some shippers’ need for faster delivery, are pressuring transportation providers to speed cargo fluidity for BCOs and take new approaches to reduce congestion flare-ups. In the final report of a task force led by the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) and composed of industry stakeholders, the regulatory agency in December recommended a privately funded national industry portal. “If we can harmonize the behavior of the actors in our supply chain and stop working at cross purposes, it will boost American economic growth and competitiveness,” FMC Commissioner Rebecca Dye said in a press release. “Many supply chain inefficiencies result from poor information availability, inaccurate information, or untimely information. Without timely, critical information, supply chain actors are ‘flying blind,’” the report, a culmination of 18 months of study, said. Although linking supply chain partners through a single digital platform has been a West Coast development, these programs are scalable, and if they prove to be effective in improving cargo velocity, ports on the East and Gulf coasts can be expected to work with technology providers to establish information-sharing portals tailored to their needs. The Port of Los Angeles for more than a year has been piloting a port information portal through its partnership with General Electric (GE) Transportation. Some terminals in neighboring Long Beach are preparing to join the portal. Oakland has partnered with Advent Intermodal Solutions to develop a digital platform for port users to be rolled out this summer. The Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA) of Seattle and Tacoma intends to work with a technology provider to establish a portal and is expected to choose a partner this year. Technology providers have developed a number of productivity tools to increase cargo velocity throughout the supply chain, from inside the marine terminal to the terminal gate to distribution warehouses and intermodal railyards. The tools do not communicate with products developed for other industries, however. The “system of systems” GE Transportation is developing with Los Angeles allows all technology providers to plug into a single platform. “We want to partner with other technologies. One technology provider can’t do it all,” Jennifer Schopfer, vice president of transportation logistics, told the Harbor Transportation Club on March 6 in Long Beach. Sharing of shipment information does not come naturally to private-sector companies, so Los Angeles chose to become the facilitator for the port community. The largest US port also has the financial resources to pull it off. “It takes leadership,” Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, told the 18th Annual TPM Conference in Long Beach on March 7. “This is how you do it as a port complex. There is too much singular, siloed information. You need a system of systems.” Los Angeles approached GE Transportation, which had developed a single platform linking hundreds of GE plants around the world, to help the port develop a similar information-sharing platform for carriers, terminal operators, BCOs, truckers, cargo intermediaries, equipment providers, and railroads. The Los Angeles project is designed to eliminate the black holes that prevent port users from following the progress of shipments from origin to destination. GE Transportation and Los Angeles last year began small, with one terminal operator, two ocean carriers, and a handful of truckers, BCOs, and other port users, Schopfer said. Now that the pilot has proved information sharing in a secure environment is possible, the port portal is being expanded to all six container terminals in Los Angeles. Two of the six terminals in Long Beach are signing on as well. Oakland is partnering with Advent to roll out its digital collaboration shipping portal by the third quarter of this year. The portal will enable participants to get personalized cargo status updates, check ocean vessel schedules, pay freight-handling fees, make appointments to pick up containers, and perform a variety of other functions. A key goal of the Oakland portal, as with all port portals, is to provide users with advanced information so they can plan their asset and labor needs ahead of vessel arrival. BCOs will know with greater precision when their merchandise will be cleared for pick up, and drayage companies will know exactly when and where to dispatch drivers, said Eric Napralla, Oakland’s senior project administrator. The NWSA is exploring available technologies as it determines which portal regime to adopt, spokesperson Tara Mattina said. “A portal system that provides real-time visibility to the supply chain has been the vision of the NWSA’s Operations Service Center since it launched a couple of years ago,” she said. Because a good deal of preparatory work already has been completed, migrating portals to other ports should take place quicker than Los Angeles experienced as the first adopter, Schopfer noted. “This is designed to be modular, with 60 to 80 percent of the pieces being reusable by other ports,” she said. Port portals will be successful if they incorporate service enhancements already experienced by users of technologies in the shipping, trucking, and warehousing sectors, said Reade Kidd, president of E*Dray, a digital port services platform for drayage operations. Container terminals today are struggling to handle growing cargo surges from mega-ships on facilities that were established to handle vessels one-half to one-third the size, a development Kidd saw unfold when he was director of international logistics at The Home Depot. The marriage of technology and process improvements such as block stowage and container peel-offs is possible through the port portals, he said. Technology developed for one industry can become a force multiplier when it is linked to other technologies through the port portal. For example, the intermodal trucking software solution provided by Profit Tools was developed for the trucking industry, but the 5 to 20 percent improvement in efficiency it produces in the field helps drivers to get more daily turns, and helps to mitigate the driver shortage in the drayage industry, said Brian Widell, founder and CEO of intermodal equipment solutions provider Profit Tools. Similarly, a portal that incorporates block stowage of containers on vessels, peel-offs from the marine terminal, and drayage of the containers to off-dock sites relieves congestion in the port supply chain to the benefit of all port users, Kidd said. As port portals spread to gateways throughout North America, they will be tailored to meet the unique needs of individual ports, be it dealing with a driver shortage or increasing cargo velocity to mitigating terminal congestion, said James Swanston, founder and CEO of Voyage Control. “Every port has its challenges,” he said. “Every terminal has its challenges. This is about how to use technology to improve efficiency.” Contact Bill Mongelluzzo at bill.mongelluzzo@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @billmongelluzzo. © 2026 S&P Global. title: US Customs says ACE final phase launched without incident
content: The US Customs and Border Protection building in New York. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) bureau has implemented the final phase of its long-delayed Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) system largely without incident, and the first month of operation went as well as can be expected, the executive director of the agency that oversaw the launch said. The deployment of the final phase of the system, on Feb. 24, triggered the participation of about 150 users to call each of the five telephone conference support calls in the subsequent week, which were held to discuss and resolve issues and problems with the system, the agency said. Through this, the agency tracked and responded to 23 issues raised by users from the implementation, Deborah Augustin, executive director of the Trade Transformation Office, which oversees the program said, in an interview with JOC.com. She called that figure “pretty standard for an effort of this magnitude and complexity.” The ACE system — an electronic filing system — was designed with the intent of streamlining cross-border trade, replacing the antiquated Automated Commercial System and enabling shippers to easily transmit documents with government agencies, saving time and money. However, the project is more than three years behind schedule and more than $1 billion over budget, even weeks before its launch. “From our perspective, the system is working as it was designed to work,” Augustin said. “The deployment went really well, to me [it is] considered successful,” she said. “Anecdotally, we heard folks say on the trade side it went a lot better than expected.” Jonathan Gold, vice president of supply chain and customs policy for the National Retail Federation, said the fact that he has not heard much from his members about the implementation may be significant. “I haven’t heard a lot of reaction recently,” he said. “If there was something that was really going wrong I am sure I would have heard it.” Just before and just after the implementation, the system continued to draw scrutiny. A white paper by the National Customs Brokers and Forwarders Association of America (NCBFAA) on the ACE system released shortly before CBP implemented the final phase concluded that it was still a “work in progress” and that it is “still in need of a substantial infusion of common sense policy, solid programming, additional budget allocation and good government oversight.” Three weeks after the deployment, based on an audit largely conducted in the year before the Feb. 24 start, a report by the US Government Accountability Office said users have identified shortcomings such as “difficulty in transmitting messages and required information.” CBP plans to upgrade the system to deal with them, the report said, adding that the agency has “not yet established an approach for the management of ACE after the end of February 2018.” Augustin said her agency had responded to the NCBFAA’s concerns as much as they could. “In some cases, issues were resolved,” she said. “In some cases, some things that they were asking for would require a regulatory or policy program update so it’s not just a fix we can do at ACE.” Contact Hugh R. title: JNPT handled record volume last year, but competition intensified
content: Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust, India’s largest public port, handled 4.83 million TEU last fiscal year, which ended March 31, a gain of 7.4 percent compared with fiscal 2016-2017, according to an analysis of new port statistics. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) finished fiscal year 2017-2018 with record volume, but it will have to increase productivity more and deploy an enhanced shipper outreach effort to take full advantage of the 2.4-million-TEU capacity addition from PSA International’s new Bharat Mumbai Container Terminals (BMCT). JNPT, India’s largest public port, handled 4.83 million TEU last fiscal year, which ended March 31, a gain of 7.4 percent compared with fiscal 2016-2017, according to an analysis of new port statistics collected by JOC.com. Furthermore, that growth rate is a substantial achievement, given India’s very competitive market. The volume total was led by the APM Terminals-operated Gateway Terminals India, whose annual traffic surged 13 percent to 2.03 million TEU from 1.8 million TEU in the prior year. Port-owned Jawaharlal Nehru Container Terminal (JNCT) registered a 3.4 percent decline, to 1.48 million TEU from 1.53 million in 2016-2017; JNCT’s ship calls also fell to 438 from 473 in the previous year. Selected ocean carriers have reorganized their berthing window arrangements at JNPT to achieve economies of scale and higher productivity rates, following the opening of BMCT, and as part of that process JNCT lost the weekly Indamex Service in the India-North America trade to DP World’s Nhava Sheva (India) Gateway Terminal (NSIGT). Moreover, that setback is expected to place more volume pressure on JNCT in the months ahead. Further, DP World Nhava Sheva, which includes Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal (NSICT), had mixed results last year. NSIGT’s volume surged 48 percent to 659,400 TEU from 445,111 TEU a year ago, with the terminal benefiting from the Dubai-based company’s strategic operational realignment at JNPT to lessen the impact of royalty payments and tariff complications. However, NSICT registered a 12 percent drop to 641,122 TEU from 728,560 TEU, which means it handled only a modest amount of volume over the 600,000-TEU minimum, annual guarantee stipulated under a concession deal. New concessionaire BMCT, which opened full-fledged operations in early February, loaded and discharged 23,212 TEU in its first two months — a volume that would have been higher if it had enjoyed seamless, mixed-train handling with its peers. Further, although volume surges continue to cause intermittent truck backups, as evidenced in the past few weeks, traffic is undeniably brisk through all terminals in the harbor, aided by automated gate systems and newer measures to streamline traffic flows. In addition, government reforms like direct port delivery and direct port entry services have substantially decreased cargo dwell times at the port. Also, the use of a radio frequency identification (RFID) container tracking service is another factor that authorities believe has played a major role in meeting shippers' expectations regarding end-to-end supply chain visibility. The tagging and tracing procedure enables shippers to track goods in transit through the port to inland container depots, container freight stations, and to end-users, thus decreasing logistics costs while also improving predictability and optimizing cargo flow. New statistics released by RFID services provider DMICDC Logistics Data Services shows that there has been a substantial reduction in JNPT dwell times. APM Terminals Mumbai leads the list, with an average dwell time of 41 hours in February, down from 45.8 hours in January. Still, despite the aforementioned productivity improvements, JNPT faces a contested landscape characterized by intensifying competition. Private rival Mundra is working harder than ever to expand its hinterland reach and ocean carriers increasingly are undertaking multiple west coast port calls to maximize liftings. One example is that Mediterranean Shipping Co. last week announced a revamp of its India-Europe service network with regular, weekly sailings from JNPT, Mundra, and Hazira. © 2026 S&P Global. title: MOL Group aims to secure US truck capacity for Asian vendors
content: T.K. Konishi, chief executive representative, Americas, for Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, with Lidia Yan, co-founder of digital trucking marketplace NEXT Trucking. Photo credit: NEXT Trucking. Moving containerized freight inland from US ports is a daunting task this year for US-based importers, let alone smaller overseas exporters trying to break into US markets. To help those companies find US truck capacity, Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL Group) is partnering with a digital trucking marketplace, NEXT Trucking, which has a warehousing sister company, iDC Logistics. The goal of the partnership is to help smaller Asian enterprises co-load containers bound for the United States, and deconsolidate and transload them near the ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles via iDC and NEXT Trucking. Trucks sourced on the NEXT digital platform would then deliver the goods to distribution centers (DCs) or stores throughout the United States, the companies told JOC.com. “This is basically an end-to-end solution that can allow even small- and medium-sized vendors to ship products to the United States,” said Jeff Baumgardner, chief commercial officer at MOL Consolidation Services, a logistics subsidiary of Japan’s MOL Group. On the shipping company’s side, the partnership involves MOL Consolidation Services and MOL Logistics, he said. The logistics companies are part of MOL Group, which merged its MOL container carrier with Japan’s other two shipping lines, “K” Line and NYK, creating Ocean Network Express (ONE) in a joint venture April 1. “Things have changed here with the liner group joining ONE,” Baumgardner said. “The focus here is logistics. We’ve spent a lot of time creating the MOL brand, and the idea is to continue to grow MOL throughout the world, and especially here in the United States with the logistics group.” “With the MOL partnership, we’ll offer a one-stop solution from ocean to drayage to warehousing to trucking,” Lidia Yan, co-founder and CEO of NEXT Trucking said. It is a big step for the three-year-old digital trucking platform, which has focused on matching loads bound out of California with truckers looking for freight at locations and rates they prefer. “We allow truckers to dictate what loads they want; we let drivers tell us what routes they prefer.” Inland trucking, distribution woes getting worse The MOL Group-NEXT Trucking deal comes at a time when shipping lines, forwarders, and port marine terminals all are looking for ways to better handle the flow of containerized goods inland and get a grip on rising landside transportation costs. Maersk Line is trying to emulate global integrators such as UPS, FedEx, and DHL and become a one-stop shop for shippers. Cosco Shipping Holdings is aggressively expanding its landside reach, and marine terminal operators in North America are extending logistics services inland. As a non-vessel operating common carrier and freight forwarder, MOL Logistics and MOL Consolidation Services see opportunity to smooth the inland leg of a container journey using NEXT’s digital platform. “We’re facing the same difficulties as other shipping companies,” Baumgardner said. “Trucking shortages, chassis issues, infrastructure problems — and they’re going to continue to get difficult with larger volumes and mega-vessels coming in and customers requiring much tighter supply chains.” The over-the-road capacity crunch “is going to put pressure on all networks,” he said. MOL Group’s logistics and forwarding arm is unique to date in addressing the inland truck capacity issue through a partnership with a digital technology platform providing trucking services. NEXT Trucking is one of several such technology platforms or digital trucking marketplaces evolving quickly, including Uber Freight, Convoy, and Trucker Path, among others. NEXT, which got its start in 2015, was founded by Yan and co-founder Elton Chung to solve truck capacity problems for iDC Logistics, their logistics firm, founded in 2004. Los Angeles-based iDC specializes in international freight, offering drayage, warehousing, transloading, and transportation services. iDC handled $25 billion worth of cargo in 2017. “The old ways of shipping freight aren't working," Chung said at the time. "It's no wonder there aren't enough truckers to do the job.” Three years later, truckers are still hard to find, in part because there is so much more freight to haul. NEXT was designed as a “trucker-centric” platform in order to attract owner-operators and small carriers seeking freight, Yan said. “We established the company with very little capital,” she said. “In our second year we did $30 million in revenue. We’re looking for extra revenue this year.” NEXT lets truckers choose the loads, routes, and rates they want based on preferences they enter into the system, Yan said. NEXT handles payment. “We want to empower small- and medium-sized companies,” she said. Shippers, including large retailers importing goods from Asia, get better visibility from pickup to delivery and just as important, save time. “Shippers can see their loads in real time and retrieve proof of delivery documents the moment loads are delivered,” said Yan. Enterprise shippers can import shipment and delivery data directly into their transportation management systems. The agreement with MOL Group extends NEXT’s reach in the international supply chain. MOL Consolidation Services will help small- to medium-sized companies in China and other Asian countries that do not ship full containers of freight consolidate shipments with other vendors, co-load and move them to Southern California, and then transfer freight to iDC and NEXT. “MOL Consolidations Services is really a global freight forwarder,” Baumgardner said. “We’re working on consolidating shipments in China, shipping them to the United States by the best possible carrier, bringing them into iDC to be deconsolidated, and then sending them to the customer in the United States through NEXT trucking. It’s an end-to-end solution to ship products to the United States.” Just as US-bound containerized goods are co-loaded in Asia, trailers headed to the same DC in the United States could share shipments from several vendors, Yan said. “We deconsolidate and transload and consolidate directly into truckload, rather than LTL [less-than-truckload],” she said. “That’s going to decrease costs for vendors.” One of the major problems getting freight “off the coast” is scheduling truck pickups at the transload point, Baumgardner said. “This will allow the truckers to build their own schedule and keep moving. The current model isn’t that efficient. That’s been the nature of our industry, and it leads to an imbalance of equipment.” Today, “you can’t have these inefficiencies.” MOL Group’s core business is not co-loading. “The co-loaded box is separate from the true BCO [beneficial cargo owner or importer] model, though we do consolidate loads for our customers from vendors overseas,” Baumgardner said. But the MOL-NEXT partnership could be expanded. “This is a service we plan to offer to our current retail customers,” he said. “As we get growing in China, we’ll be able to build more boxes,” he said. “I don’t know what the future will hold, but I believe this kind of platform could grow to other areas besides the United States. China could use a trucking platform like this.” Contact William B. Cassidy at bill.cassidy@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @wbcassidy_joc. © 2026 S&P Global. All rights reserved. title: US shipper guide to new ELD surface market
content: US truck capacity may get worse before it gets better, as electronic logging device enforcement begins this month with anywhere from 10 to 25 percent of drivers not having the required device in their cabs. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The electronic logging device (ELD) mandate for truck drivers that took effect Dec. 18 has affected nearly every transportation mode and every industry that uses trucks, and even some that do not, lengthening transit times and tightening available capacity just as US shippers need more trucks and faster service to meet sharper delivery demands from their customers. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration mandate, required by Congress in the 2012 transportation spending act, forces commercial truck drivers to stop using paper logs to record daily and weekly record of duty status (RODS) reports and use electronic devices linked directly to engines instead. It is the biggest regulatory change for trucking since the 1980s, when deregulation and the introduction of the commercial drivers license reshaped the industry. Trucking costs kept climbing during the first quarter, typically the slowest quarter of the year for truck demand, with spot rates rising by double digits year over year and truckload and less-than-truckload contract rates creeping higher. Shippers are likely to see additional rate hikes and capacity constraints in coming months as the US economy continues to grow. Full enforcement of the mandate, delayed several months as part of a “phased” implementation of the rule, began April 1. State and federal officials now can place truckers out of service for not having an ELD. That means the driver, truck, and freight will be stopped for 10 hours. Afterwards, truckers may complete their delivery or proceed to their next stop, but they will be prohibited from operating beyond that point without installing an ELD. The violation will also adversely affect trucking company Compliance, Safety, and Accountability (CSA) scores. The implications for shippers, as well as their trucking and logistics partners, are serious. Full enforcement of the ELD mandate comes just as many US retailers and vendors enter their “spring peak season.” They are already planning for the bigger peak this autumn. Q: What percentage of truck drivers are compliant with the ELD mandate? One survey from CarriersList finds that 97 percent of fleets surveyed are in compliance with the mandate and over the last three weeks the rolling average is about 93 percent. Another survey from load board operator DAT finds that 81 percent as of mid-March had an ELD with another 9 to 10 percent claiming an exemption to the regulation. Ken Evans, CEO of ELD supplier Konexial, thinks the compliance rate is about 75 percent. That means one out of every four drivers could be placed out of service, if stopped. Evans bases his estimates on the number of units manufactured versus how many drivers operate interstate long-haul routes, rather than a driver survey. “Whenever the [crackdown] starts and carriers are actually getting $1,000-plus fines, taken out of service, and their CSA scores are hit, we’re anticipating a crushing tidal wave like the world has never seen in this industry,” he said. “The amount of manufacturing that’s happened so far is not going to be enough to deal with that wave.” Evans also said about half of the devices purchased since December have not even been activated yet and will likely only be activated when drivers hear about the first crackdown from law enforcement. A: Here are some types of drivers exempt from the regulation: There are also a number of temporary waivers, delays, or exemptions in certain subsets of the trucking industry, including agricultural haulers, short-term truck rentals, movie and television production drivers, and oilfield operations. Q: What is the likely impact on daily productivity? A: For carriers just beginning to use ELDs, Zipline Logistics found transit times on average rose from 1.05 transit days to 1.22 transit days afterwards on hauls between 450 and 550 miles, an increase of 16.2 percent. This equates to about four additional hours of transit time, on average, enough to turn a seven-hour lane into an 11-hour lane, pushing drivers to the limits of their daily legal driving time. It is enough to turn a same-day haul into a next-day delivery. “That’s a pretty big impact,” said Andrew Lynch, Zipline president. “The cost to run the truck hasn’t changed, so these guys are just losing time,” and that is pushing up freight costs, he said. The impact on the shorter lanes is greater than on longer runs. “On shipments between 750 and 1,000 miles, we saw a 10 percent increase in transit days,” which measure time from departure to arrival, he said. Q: How have spot market truck rates been impacted? A: Spot market truck rates rose 37 percent in January, 30 percent in February, and 25 percent in March on a year-over-year basis, according to DAT. “We know that rates are much higher than a year ago, but our survey shows drivers still perceive themselves as driving fewer miles and making less money, especially with an ELD. So there will still be pressure on rates and it will remain that way for awhile because the individual driver is losing productivity,” said DAT analyst Peggy Dorf. In the coming months, too, DAT senior industry analyst Mark Montague expects another “price shock” heading into the busy produce and manufacturing season between now and July 4. “Rates will probably remain 20 to 25 percent higher than a year ago between now and July 4. But I wouldn’t be surprised if it jumped back over 30 percent between now and then too,” he said. For the last week in March, DAT’s national spot rates were $2.53 per mile in flatbed, $2.40 for refrigerated, and $2.15 for dry van. Truckstop.com, another load board operator, pegged the national rates at $2.59 for flatbed, $2.49 for refrigerated, and $2.32 for dry van. The Trans-Logistics Group North American Truckload Freight Rate Index, which includes contract and spot prices from 14,700 lanes, jumped 17 to 25 percent in January. Q: What has the impact been on contract rates? A: On the contract side, DAT’s data show rates are 8.3 percent higher on an annualized basis compared with 2017, although in some cases there have been double-digit increases. Load-to-truck ratios are climbing sharply, particularly in the flatbed business. DAT reports the load-to-truck ratio set a new record of 101.5 loads for every one available truck in the week ending March 31. Flatbed loads rose 7 percent week over week while the number of posted trucks available dropped 8 percent. Although the ratios are not as pronounced in dry van (7.2 to 1) and refrigerated (10.4 to 1), they are also higher than a year ago. Truckstop.com’s Market Demand index is hovering at 60 and is expected to remain at these levels through April, according to the load board operator. On a year-over-year basis, the index is more than double the reading from 2017. “We are once again hitting record highs for the Market Demand Index, and we haven’t even gotten into [the second quarter] yet. Week 13 surpassed the 60 market — hitting 60.42 — and I can only expect rates will shortly follow suit,” said Noël Perry, chief economist with Truckstop.com. “We outlined a path forward for 2018 that would put us on the heels of hitting new record rates by the end of [the second quarter]. The updated chart shows that we are well surpassing that trajectory. We continue to be reminded that we are not in a ‘normal’ environment right now.” Q: How are US truckload carriers and third-party logistics providers addressing the capacity crunch? A: Some of the largest for-hire carriers are levying surcharges on some shippers on freight above and beyond the contracted allotment, treating the load essentially as a spot move. Schneider National, Covenant Transport, and Hub Group, among others, charged these fees to reposition trucks in the typically slow January and February months, a harbinger of potentially even more tight times ahead. “It’s going to be insane and if any one of my peers tells you any different, they’re kidding themselves,” said Dave Rusch, CEO of CRST International, a for-hire carrier handling dry-van, refrigerated, and flatbed freight, in a March conversation with JOC.com. However, Trinity Logistics chief operating officer Sarah Ruffcorn does not think there will be a dramatic change in conditions from Dec. 18 to March 31, other than rates going up even more. She said that ELDs, though, are making it more difficult to find drivers in its carrier network to take a load. “It makes it harder to find capacity when drivers load ‘hop’ to better paying freight. However, this is the market that we thrive in as a [third-party logistics provider],” Ruffcorn said. The lack of predictability of where the market is going could pose challenges to intermediaries working off annual contracts with shippers. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, for example, saw margins erode when purchased transportation costs rose in the latter half of the year because a majority of its business is conducted through annual contracts. Landstar System, in contrast, does a lot of spot market business, and so the company has already raised its 2018 guidance and announced truck revenue per load jumped 21 percent in the initial eight weeks of the year. Other logistics executives have said they are rebalancing their freight mix to include more spot business, thereby limiting the guesswork on how to offer an annual price to a shipper. Q: How are ocean carriers reacting to these rising costs? A: Since drayage rates are climbing at the same pace as the US domestic truckload environment, according to fleets, the ocean carriers are feeling the effects on their store-door contracts with shippers. CMA CGM, Mediterranean Shipping Company, and Hyundai Merchant Marine have or will soon institute $300 surcharges per container to beneficial cargo owners on door deliveries. CMA CGM and MSC have targeted these fees to certain markets while HMM will apply it nationwide but negotiate the exact amount on a case-by-case basis. Maersk Line increased its inland tariff on March 14, two days before the CMA CGM surcharge went into effect. Zim Integrated Shipping Services is taking a similar tactic to Maersk Line, adjusting the tariff structure on an ongoing basis. Cosco Shipping has done neither but plans to address the inland transportation costs in the ongoing contract negotiations. Privately, some trucking executives have commented that ocean carriers have undercut prices for years by booking cheap draymen willing to haul any containers. There are also draymen frustrated with the rail delays altogether and may transition into another mode of trucking, or refuse to do any hauls unless they are less than 100 air miles. “I would say 50 percent of the drivers or more are considering flipping to [over-the-road] to avoid the ramps. Owner-operators just get fed up and no longer want to do rail freight because of the time wasted at ramps. It’s a vicious circle,” said Susan Keldani, vice president of On Track Transportation in Illinois. Delays have been a problem for the truckers receiving and returning containers in railroad terminals in Chicago, Detroit, and Memphis, Tennessee, among other markets. Canadian National Railway, CSX Transportation, Union Pacific Railroad, and BNSF Railway have experienced prolonged delays since the beginning of the year. While conditions improved in March as the volumes dropped after the Lunar New Year, expect more stress on the rail networks this spring and summer. Q: What can shippers do to navigate through the ELD impact? A: If the true compliance rate is only 75 percent and not 91 percent, then the ability for a shipper to find a truck could get precarious in the coming weeks and months as the transportation community faces the stark new reality. “We will see a significant amount of carriers get shut down in April and when that happens it will create a tsunami effect that will make the last fourth quarter peak season look like we were on vacation,” warned Greg Ritter, chief customer officer with XPO Logistics, in a webinar hosted by NASSTRAC and TranzAct Technologies. “In my view, this market will last well into 2019 and even into 2020 before we see any significant changes.” Tracy Rosser, Wal-Mart’s senior vice president of transportation and supply chain, said there has been “shock in the system” since hurricanes Harvey, Irma, and Maria struck late last summer. However, he suggests shippers mitigate the shock by using better planning and forecasting. “There are a lot of suppliers that shut down at 3 p.m. and don’t ship on the weekends. Think about the capacity you can open up there. Create a drop-and-hook environment. Engage in strategic planning. There is not a lot of slack in the market right now, so unplanned volume can get pricey. Data can be your friend. Figure out where the waste is, find the root cause and work to solve those issues,” Rosser said. Those who do not use technology to maximize their supply chain speed should strongly consider doing so. “Customers are looking to maximize their value of a dollar as freight charges rise, so anything we can do, such as offer them our TMS [transportation management systems or] optimize their freight, are services that are a bigger part of the discussion in these types of markets,” Ruffcorn said. Dave Venberg, senior director of transportation and logistics with Ardent Mills, believes the best way to thrive in this market is to be proactive rather than reactive to the situation. “We want to build long-term relationships with our carriers. We want to be considered a strategic partner with the carriers we have in our portfolio, and the carriers we choose are strategic partners for us, not transaction in nature,” he said. “We’re comfortable with some transactional relationships but I don’t think that’s how you win in this environment.” The phrase “shippers of choice” has been frequently used in recent months, a way to survive the capacity crunch by standing out from other competitors during interactions with motor carriers. For example, use data to give carriers enough time to plan a haul rather than a last-minute request for capacity. Treat the drivers with respect and eliminate any unnecessary detention because drivers need to move to earn a living. A: On the contract side, DAT’s data show rates are 8.3 percent higher on an annualized basis compared with 2017, although in some cases there have been double-digit increases. Load-to-truck ratios are climbing sharply, particularly in the flatbed business. DAT reports the load-to-truck ratio set a new record of 101.5 loads for every one available truck in the week ending March 31. Flatbed loads rose 7 percent week over week while the number of posted trucks available dropped 8 percent. Although the ratios are not as pronounced in dry van (7.2 to 1) and refrigerated (10.4 to 1), they are also higher than a year ago. Truckstop.com’s Market Demand index is hovering at 60 and is expected to remain at these levels through April, according to the load board operator. On a year-over-year basis, the index is more than double the reading from 2017. “We are once again hitting record highs for the Market Demand Index, and we haven’t even gotten into [the second quarter] yet. Week 13 surpassed the 60 market — hitting 60.42 — and I can only expect rates will shortly follow suit,” said Noël Perry, chief economist with Truckstop.com. “We outlined a path forward for 2018 that would put us on the heels of hitting new record rates by the end of [the second quarter]. The updated chart shows that we are well surpassing that trajectory. We continue to be reminded that we are not in a ‘normal’ environment right now.” Q: How are US truckload carriers and third-party logistics providers addressing the capacity crunch? A: Some of the largest for-hire carriers are levying surcharges on some shippers on freight above and beyond the contracted allotment, treating the load essentially as a spot move. Schneider National, Covenant Transport, and Hub Group, among others, charged these fees to reposition trucks in the typically slow January and February months, a harbinger of potentially even more tight times ahead. “It’s going to be insane and if any one of my peers tells you any different, they’re kidding themselves,” said Dave Rusch, CEO of CRST International, a for-hire carrier handling dry-van, refrigerated, and flatbed freight, in a March conversation with JOC.com. However, Trinity Logistics chief operating officer Sarah Ruffcorn does not think there will be a dramatic change in conditions from Dec. 18 to March 31, other than rates going up even more. She said that ELDs, though, are making it more difficult to find drivers in its carrier network to take a load. “It makes it harder to find capacity when drivers load ‘hop’ to better paying freight. However, this is the market that we thrive in as a [third-party logistics provider],” Ruffcorn said. The lack of predictability of where the market is going could pose challenges to intermediaries working off annual contracts with shippers. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, for example, saw margins erode when purchased transportation costs rose in the latter half of the year because a majority of its business is conducted through annual contracts. Landstar System, in contrast, does a lot of spot market business, and so the company has already raised its 2018 guidance and announced truck revenue per load jumped 21 percent in the initial eight weeks of the year. Other logistics executives have said they are rebalancing their freight mix to include more spot business, thereby limiting the guesswork on how to offer an annual price to a shipper. Q: How are ocean carriers reacting to these rising costs? A: Since drayage rates are climbing at the same pace as the US domestic truckload environment, according to fleets, the ocean carriers are feeling the effects on their store-door contracts with shippers. CMA CGM, Mediterranean Shipping Company, and Hyundai Merchant Marine have or will soon institute $300 surcharges per container to beneficial cargo owners on door deliveries. CMA CGM and MSC have targeted these fees to certain markets while HMM will apply it nationwide but negotiate the exact amount on a case-by-case basis. Maersk Line increased its inland tariff on March 14, two days before the CMA CGM surcharge went into effect. Zim Integrated Shipping Services is taking a similar tactic to Maersk Line, adjusting the tariff structure on an ongoing basis. Cosco Shipping has done neither but plans to address the inland transportation costs in the ongoing contract negotiations. Privately, some trucking executives have commented that ocean carriers have undercut prices for years by booking cheap draymen willing to haul any containers. There are also draymen frustrated with the rail delays altogether and may transition into another mode of trucking, or refuse to do any hauls unless they are less than 100 air miles. “I would say 50 percent of the drivers or more are considering flipping to [over-the-road] to avoid the ramps. Owner-operators just get fed up and no longer want to do rail freight because of the time wasted at ramps. It’s a vicious circle,” said Susan Keldani, vice president of On Track Transportation in Illinois. Delays have been a problem for the truckers receiving and returning containers in railroad terminals in Chicago, Detroit, and Memphis, Tennessee, among other markets. Canadian National Railway, CSX Transportation, Union Pacific Railroad, and BNSF Railway have experienced prolonged delays since the beginning of the year. While conditions improved in March as the volumes dropped after the Lunar New Year, expect more stress on the rail networks this spring and summer. Q: What can shippers do to navigate through the ELD impact? A: If the true compliance rate is only 75 percent and not 91 percent, then the ability for a shipper to find a truck could get precarious in the coming weeks and months as the transportation community faces the stark new reality. “We will see a significant amount of carriers get shut down in April and when that happens it will create a tsunami effect that will make the last fourth quarter peak season look like we were on vacation,” warned Greg Ritter, chief customer officer with XPO Logistics, in a webinar hosted by NASSTRAC and TranzAct Technologies. “In my view, this market will last well into 2019 and even into 2020 before we see any significant changes.” Tracy Rosser, Wal-Mart’s senior vice president of transportation and supply chain, said there has been “shock in the system” since hurricanes Harvey, Irma, and Maria struck late last summer. However, he suggests shippers mitigate the shock by using better planning and forecasting. “There are a lot of suppliers that shut down at 3 p.m. and don’t ship on the weekends. Think about the capacity you can open up there. Create a drop-and-hook environment. Engage in strategic planning. There is not a lot of slack in the market right now, so unplanned volume can get pricey. Data can be your friend. Figure out where the waste is, find the root cause and work to solve those issues,” Rosser said. Those who do not use technology to maximize their supply chain speed should strongly consider doing so. “Customers are looking to maximize their value of a dollar as freight charges rise, so anything we can do, such as offer them our TMS [transportation management systems or] optimize their freight, are services that are a bigger part of the discussion in these types of markets,” Ruffcorn said. Dave Venberg, senior director of transportation and logistics with Ardent Mills, believes the best way to thrive in this market is to be proactive rather than reactive to the situation. “We want to build long-term relationships with our carriers. We want to be considered a strategic partner with the carriers we have in our portfolio, and the carriers we choose are strategic partners for us, not transaction in nature,” he said. “We’re comfortable with some transactional relationships but I don’t think that’s how you win in this environment.” The phrase “shippers of choice” has been frequently used in recent months, a way to survive the capacity crunch by standing out from other competitors during interactions with motor carriers. For example, use data to give carriers enough time to plan a haul rather than a last-minute request for capacity. Treat the drivers with respect and eliminate any unnecessary detention because drivers need to move to earn a living.

title: JNPT names four 3PLs for import direct port delivery program
content: Port data from JOC.com show that Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (above) handled nearly 40 percent of its laden imports during March via direct port delivery. Photo credit: Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust. Shippers using Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) have long been on the receiving end of trucker cartelization, arbitrary pricing, and lengthy wait times, but a new government-controlled transport solution, with a published tariff that is scheduled to start May 1 is capable of dramatically changing the game of inland logistics at India’s busiest container harbor. However, after a long bidding process, marred by legal complications, the public port has awarded contracts to four third-party logistics (3PL) companies for the movement of import cargo, cleared under its direct port delivery (DPD) program, on five select hinterland routes. “The rates of each route, along with transporter names, are to be published on the websites of JNPT terminals and customs’ website,” the port said in a presentation to the trade. JNPT estimates that the volume of DPD containers moved on these five routes will reach 600,000 TEU if the DPD percentage remains at 35 percent, and 1 million TEU if the DPD percentage increases to 60 percent. These projections are based on current data and trends. Dubbed an Uber-like, on-demand operation, the new, streamlined logistics solution will have digital capabilities and will involve well-defined standard operating procedures at each terminal to ensure efficiency. Under the DPD, importers are able to clear their cargo direct from the wharf within 48 hours of landing, instead of routing through an off-site container freight station. Buoyed by significant cost savings versus the traditional “CFS [container freight station] delivery” model, which customs officials put at about 30,000 rupees ($461) per TEU, shippers’ interest in the DPD clearance plan has increased rapidly lately, and the new transport arrangement stems from that increased interest. On the downside, the reform has also been dogged by controversy, with supply chain intermediaries such as marine terminals, shipping lines, and warehouse services providers showing some reluctance to follow guidelines set by customs regarding DPD handling rates and processes, given the high stakes tied to the CFS-based operation. On the upside, customs and port agencies, under persistent government pressure regarding dwell time reductions, quelled those stumbling blocks and increased the DPD handling at a steady pace. Reflecting that progress, a new JOC.com port data analysis shows JNPT handled nearly 40 percent of its laden imports during March via DPD, a target India’s government wanted the port to reach within the last fiscal year. By volume, DPD accounted for 55,794 TEU, out of 142,521 TEU import discharges at the port during the month. APM Terminals-operated Gateway Terminals India accounted for nearly half of that DPD volume, processing 26,929 TEU, out of 62,518 TEU of imports, or an impressive 43 percent share. March DPD numbers at the other three terminals were as follows: port-owned Jawaharlal Nehru Container Terminal, at 14,632 TEU, out of 38,494 TEU; DP World-operated Nhava Sheva (India) Gateway Terminal, at 10,268 TEU, out of 31,744 TEU; and DP World's flagship Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal, at 3,965 TEU, out of 9,765 TEU. For the fiscal year, which runs from April 2017 to March 2018, JNPT handled 545,365 TEU of DPD shipments, out of the total 1.7 million TEU laden imports, or a 32.4 percent share, according to the analysis. Amid the long-running spar between JNPT and its private terminal concessionaires, over uniform DPD handling rates, India’s government sees DPD as a crucial factor in decreasing cargo dwell times and by extension, alleviating port congestion. “In the last four years, JNPT’s biggest achievement has been solving the congestion problem, which was a perennial problem that the port faced since 2008. The path-breaking initiatives of [DPD] and direct port entry [for gate-in of exports] have started showing results helping in not only reducing transaction cost and time, but increasing the overall efficiency of the port,” JNPT acting chairman Neeraj Bansal said. Other DPD improvement efforts in the pipeline include round-the-clock clearance services at all terminals, establishment of a dedicated truck lane for speedy imports, and use of barges for en masse transport to the nearby Port of Mumbai for distribution of cargo to customers from that location. Another proposal calls for making DPD mandatory for all pre-approved importers, which authorities believe can boost DPD share at JNPT to 57 percent — another data point of progress toward reaching the long-term goal of 70 percent. © 2026 S&P Global.
