For Ardent Mills, having a centralized vantage point is key. “When we first started, we had several large carriers tell us they had portals in which customers could track shipments,” Venberg said. “For us, that would mean going to about 50 portals to track loads.” Having visibility into all Ardent Mills shipments from a central point “is the game changer for us.” That allows visibility data to be integrated with other systems and used in business intelligence and analytics to solve larger supply chain questions than simply, “Where’s my freight?” “From a shipper’s standpoint, this is a tough environment, with rates going up,” Venberg said. “I’m optimistic that shippers, by embracing this data, will actually lower their costs by working with their carrier base to drive efficiencies. Then you can be smart about pricing.” For example, Ardent Mills is using FourKites’ technology to track the amount of time drivers spend at its plants and customer facilities. “You can create a geofence around a plant and really understand how long it takes for a truck to penetrate and then leave that geofence,” he said. “We’re having great conversations with our customers around this,” said Venberg. “One plant may do a great job, and another take too long [to load or unload]. The shipper, carrier, and receiver all they need to work together to make sure the driver is utilized and is not sitting around.” That need has taken on new urgency in the electronic logging device (ELD) era. Since the ELD mandate took effect in the United States on Dec. 18, shippers say shipment transit times have lengthened, as drivers more carefully manage their time in order to not run out of daily work hours. Based on data from 40 shippers, Zipline Logistics found transit times on lanes of 700 to 1,000 miles increased 10 percent after the ELD deadline and 16 percent on lanes of 450 to 550 miles. Same-day shipments became next-day shipments, and two-day shipments three-day runs. That level of disruption has businesses scrambling to get a better view of where their shipments are and where they can source capacity. At the same time, vendors shipping goods to retailers with strict delivery requirements are suddenly having trouble meeting customer deadlines. Wal-Mart, which drove those retail deadlines when it rolled out its “on-time, in-full” delivery requirements last August, is now easing its standards to allow suppliers of certain products to deliver them a day early. (The retailer had penalized suppliers for late or early deliveries.) As of April 1, shippers sending truckloads to Wal-Mart have to deliver on the scheduled arrival date at least 85 percent of the time or face a penalty based on the value of the products shipped. That is a bump up from a 75 percent on-time requirement introduced last year. According to Arkansas Online, Wal-Mart decided to allow food, consumable, and health and wellness suppliers to make deliveries a day before the scheduled date. Wal-Mart told Arkansas Online the change gives suppliers who handle food and general merchandise more flexibility. “I think it’s good to see Wal-Mart open up and be more flexible there,” said Brian Belcher, co-founder and chief operating officer of LoadDocs, a technology company specializing in workflow management, digitizing paperwork handled by truck drivers in the shipping process. “This is clearly in regard to what they’re seeing happening with drivers and hours-of-service rules,” Belcher said. As ELD out-of-service orders pile up, he said, “there’s going to be havoc at some of these shipping sites. It’s not just about being paid for detention. It’s the hours.” And those hours cannot be managed effectively without better supply chain visibility. There are more ways to gain visibility than just tracking drivers and assets, Belcher suggests. For example, tracking documents throughout the shipping process, from order to receipt. “Ultimately, it’s about speeding up those documents,” Belcher said. “When the bill of lading is signed, it should be immediately available in the TMS [transportation management system] to bill. That visibility does not happen right now. Carriers are waiting for the driver to go to a truckstop, scan the BOL [bill of lading], and fax it back.” With smartphone, wireless networks, and onboard computing technology, there is no reason, Belcher said, to rely on the fax machine at a truckstop to get vital data about shipments. And at some point data on the location of goods will be bundled with other needed shipping data. If tracking a truck or shipment is “table stakes,” the competitive battle is shifting to business intelligence and predictive analytics, with an advantage to those who can provide a level of visibility that is broad and deep. Consider that the “context” for individual shipments. For example, XPO Logistics’ new digital marketplace, XPO Connect, is designed to provide shippers with visibility not just into individual movements but all shipments on XPO’s multimodal platform, from non-asset brokered truckloads to LTL and intermodal shipments. “We’re using proprietary data analytics to help our customers make informed decisions in all areas of the supply chain, including capacity management and workforce planning,” said Troy Cooper, chief operating officer. Optimizing capacity is an “integral service,” he said. Visibility is a prerequisite to such optimization, but it is also key to improved forecasting and advance planning, both steps to creating capacity and controlling transportation costs. “Having visibility to please the customer is one thing, but it can also give you a competitive advantage,” said Kuriyama’s Venchuk. “You can connect the dots, but you also want to be able to put a ‘what if’ scenario in there. Otherwise you’re rehashing what’s already happened.” Associate Editor Ari Ashe contributed to this story.

title: ELDs seen reshaping US truck shipping patterns
content: In the US trucking sector, smaller carriers are gravitating toward shorter-haul freight, Zipline Logistics has found. That could put more pressure on longer-haul capacity. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The US electronic logging device (ELD) mandate is redrawing trucking service maps, with smaller trucking firms shying away from even intermediate trip lengths that could leave them short of hours at the end of the day, a new carrier survey from Zipline Logistics finds. The trends identified in the survey could have a considerable impact on US shippers and the flow of freight between North American markets, both international and domestic moves. The survey supports reports that transit times are getting longer and daily driving hours shorter. Smaller carriers, the survey indicates, increasingly want short-haul freight, and they are leaving shipments of 450 miles or longer to larger fleets. That could put even more pressure on long-haul capacity, as the majority of active carriers in the United States have fewer than six trucks. The growing rift between short-haul and long-haul freight, large and small carriers, could affect site selection decisions in warehousing and distribution, exacerbating trends driving up rents in what industrial real estate developer Prologis calls “last-touch/last-mile” markets close to consumers. The trip tipping point is between 450 and 700 miles, Andrew Lynch, president of the Columbus, Ohio-based third-party logistics company, said. Among the 101 carriers that responded to the Zipline survey, those with fewer than 30 trucks said they are rejecting runs of that length. “Those runs are now two days for those guys, so they don’t want them,” Lynch said. “The smaller carrier will lose a day or a half day on that load, between staying within hours of service and getting the delivery done. To keep them in the fold, the rate has to go up dramatically.” Since Dec. 18, the ELD mandate has required most commercial truck drivers to use electronic devices to log on- and off-duty time, rather than paper logbooks. As a result, it is much tougher to falsify daily and weekly “records of duty status” to rack up additional hours and dollars. Truckers that in the past would have taken a five- or six-hour run, made a delivery, picked up a new load, and returned home are now bumping against the 11-hour daily driving limit. They are also stopping earlier to secure overnight parking, rather than risking a violation. An earlier Zipline survey that found truckload transit times increased 16 percent in lanes between 450 and 550 miles after the ELD mandate took effect Dec. 18. That amounts to an additional four hours, enough to make what had been a same-day trip a two-day trip. “Our company doesn’t do long-haul anymore because it’s more stressful for the drivers to be on duty 14 straight hours without the flexibility of going off duty when tired,” one carrier told Zipline. “[We] have had to be more aware of each driver’s hours. [It is] hard to accept long distance.” Larger carriers told Zipline they preferred longer lanes, especially in the 450- to 700-mile range and 1,001 to 2,000-mile range. Less than half, 41.8 percent, of the smaller carriers said they have had electronic logs for more than a year, compared with 73.9 percent of the larger carriers. Lynch expects to see larger trucking firms using a mix of linehaul and local drivers to get loads over the hours-of-service road bump that has come into clearer focus in the ELD era. Those carriers are switching trailers near destinations rather than running dock to dock, he said. “That’s how the largest fleets, who already have ELDs, were able to adjust,” he said. “Rather than being a fleet of trucks operating independently, they turned themselves into integrated networks. They’re dropping and swapping trailers at locations partway through a trip.” Larger carriers, for Zipline those with anywhere from 30 to a few hundred trucks, can take advantage of what network scale they have to get that load, he said. “Where a smaller carrier might charge $850, they’ll charge $750, which is still higher than the $650 they used to charge.” If they are using more than one driver and tractor to deliver a load, they will incur higher costs, however. That could contribute to the reduction in productivity carriers reported to Zipline, and higher rates, until networks are optimized and freight flows find the right lanes and levels. Shippers surprised by longer transit times have had to rethink their shipping choices since Dec. 18. “We didn’t expect as big of an impact on five- to six-hour runs,” said John Janson, global logistics director at SanMar, an Issaquah, Washington-based wholesale apparel distributor. “We would have expected it on longer hauls, but these are well within the legal limits and have always been acceptable. Now they’re getting turned down,” he told JOC.com. SanMar has looked for new carriers that need freight in the lanes most affected by the ELD mandate. “Shippers are wise to take a more holistic look at how logistics is used in their operations,” said Lynch. “Up until late 2017, almost every company on the consumer goods side looked at logistics as a cost center, a necessary evil, not as integral to relationships and decision making.” The new reality, he said, “is that everyone has to align here.” Major retailers “have to ask how do your delivery requirements lineup with production cycles and the realities of trucking now.” Ninety-five percent of the carriers surveyed said it is now tougher to make deliveries on time. At the same time, Lynch is not seeing plummeting on-time delivery numbers. It is harder “to find capacity that can assuredly meet delivery times,” he said. “There’s so much pressure to meet tight delivery windows. If you can’t meet those requirements, you’ll be bounced out.” Contact William B. Cassidy at bill.cassidy@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @wbcassidy_joc. © 2026 S&P Global. title: E-commerce drives double-digit warehouse rent hikes in top markets
content: The demand for “last mile/last touch” warehouses at major seaport cities and inland hubs has developers looking to costly infill locations close to consumers. (Above: An Amazon fulfillment center in the United States.) Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Rapid growth in e-commerce is stressing the supply of US warehouse space in major population centers and is driving double-digit rent growth at the consumer end of the supply chain, but e-commerce is also presenting truckers with new opportunities to participate in this booming segment of the supply chain. The demand for “last touch” warehouses at major seaport cities and inland hubs has developers looking to costly infill locations close to consumers. Chris Caton, senior vice president of research at industrial real estate developer Prologis, said rents at infill locations in urban core areas are experiencing “mid-teen rises,” while rent increases are “4 percent everywhere else.” Caton said industrial rents in urban core areas will continue to increase throughout 2018. With e-commerce consumers demanding next or same-day delivery, truckers are taking creative steps to ensure on-time delivery of containers to the last-touch warehouses. Harbor truckers are establishing satellite yards where they store containers overnight for delivery to the fulfillment centers as needed. “If they need it on Tuesday, they need it on Tuesday,” said Weston LaBar, CEO of the Harbor Trucking Association in Southern California. In that scenario, Monday is too early and Wednesday is too late. The satellite yards also address the driver shortage that is fueled by electronic logging device (ELD) requirements because truckers call on different drivers from the ports to the satellite yards, and from the yards to the e-commerce fulfillment centers. The Prologis report, “E-Commerce, the Service Imperative and Essential Location Strategies,” released Thursday states that e-commerce development now accounts for 20 percent of new leasing in the industrial sector, up from 5 percent less than a decade ago. In addition to the pure-play online retailers such as Amazon, brick-and-mortar retailers are experiencing double-digit e-commerce growth “which may now account for an impossible-to-ignore 25 percent of revenues,” the report stated. Given the demands of customers for rapid delivery, e-commerce retailers must locate fulfillment centers as close to consumers as possible. In large cities, that means warehouses must be located deep within the urban core, usually at older infill sites where land is scarce and costly. Those facilities, which could be teardowns or warehouses that need renovation, generate what is often called “last-mile” deliveries, but Prologis refers to them as last-touch because the distance to the end consumer is usually longer than one mile. The last-touch warehouses have extended the international supply chain. The traditional supply chain involves moving imported merchandise to a large import distribution center (DC), and from there to a regional DC close to major population centers where the containers are deconsolidated and the goods are shipped to stores. This has led to higher average rents per square foot, with rents in New Jersey up 11.7 percent year over year in the first quarter to $7.14 per square foot, while rents in Los Angeles are up 7.6 percent from last year to $9.84, and rents in the Inland Empire are up 9.6 percent to $6.84. Industrial real estate pricing data from JLL can be found on the JOC Shipping & Logistics Pricing Hub. The e-commerce model adds an extra layer of real estate and transportation costs to the supply chain, and it is forcing retailers to look at total network costs rather than the traditional model of focusing on individual silo costs, Caton said. “More and more, they are taking an end-to-end view of the supply chain,” he said. “They must manage total supply chain costs,” he said. Truckers are seizing upon this opportunity to participate in the e-commerce supply chain. Quik Pick Express in Southern California and in Oakland has opened satellite yards to store inbound containers overnight and then deliver them to the last-touch fulfillment centers the next day. George Boyle, president and CEO, said the overnight storage fee he charges is “a fraction” of the cost fulfillment centers would incur if they had to send trucks to the import DCs in the Inland Empire 50 miles from Los Angeles-Long Beach or to DCs in Northern California, or if they missed delivery deadlines and incurred costly fines. The satellite yards also help trucking companies to cope with the driver shortage that is present throughout the country, especially since the April 1 enforcement of the federal requirement for trucks to be equipped with ELDs. Boyle said one set of drivers will pull the containers from the ports to the satellite yards, and different drivers deliver the containers to the fulfillment centers, with each set of drivers better able to work within the hours-of-service limitations. Furthermore, most e-commerce companies could not retrieve the inbound containers at the ports and dray them directly to their last-touch facilities the day before they are needed. “The fulfillment guys don’t have warehouses built to store inventory,” Boyle said. On the other hand, since quality service and customer retention are key goals of e-commerce, the added supply chain costs are not daunting. The Prologis report notes that real estate accounts for about 5 percent of supply chain costs and less than 1 percent of total costs. The last-touch facilities in urban core areas do not resemble the 1-million-square-foot, highly automated import DCs in Southern California’s Inland Empire or Central and Western New Jersey and the Lehigh Valley. The infill warehouses can range from fewer than 20,000 square feet to more than 100,000 square feet and are generally not highly automated. Most inventory is moved quickly to consumers, Caton said, although he emphasized that this model is still evolving. The last touch facilities can handle 53-foot trailers inbound, while deliveries to consumers are carried by smaller trucks or vans. Online retailers are willing to pay the higher rents and labor costs for fulfillment centers in urban core locations because the primary goal is customer satisfaction, which in the e-commerce world means rapid, just-in-time delivery. Costs are managed in the e-commerce network because the final leg of the journey to dozens of consumers is much shorter than it would be if the individual shipments were made from distant regional distribution facilities. The greatest challenge for online retailers is the higher barrier to supply of real estate options that is inherent in the urban core areas, Prologis stated. “These major population centers have relatively few new land sites. Hence, occupancies are very high, and rents are rising quickly,” the report stated. Metropolitan Los Angeles is a prime example, with the industrial vacancy rate at 1 percent or less. title: Asia-Russia rail shippers gain shorter transits
content: Low freight train speed has been a longstanding, major problem in Russia, something that has hindered transport of Asia cargo through Russia and also Kazakhstan. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. China shippers transporting cargo to the European Union via Russia will be able to have their cargo delivered substantially faster on many routes, including sections of the Trans-Siberian Railway (Transsib), as a result of recent upgrades to Russia’s railway system, Russian officials announced this week. Cargo can now make the East Russia-Europe trip in about six to seven days, as opposed to 10 to 11 days previously, owing to railway improvments that enable higher speeds. As a result of recent rail system upgrades, container trains now average 75 kilometers per hour (about 47 miles per hour). Prior to 2017, speeds averaged 30 to 40 kilometers per hour. (Cargo by rail transport in China also averages about 30 to 40 kilometers per hour.) Low freight train speed has been a longstanding, major problem in Russia, something that has hindered transport of Asian cargo through Russia and also Kazakhstan. The higher speeds have also enabled officials to increase the number of daily trains on the Transsib, as well as their trip length: to 1,750 to 1,800 kilometers from 1,400 to 1,500 kilometers. Officials also increased the container railcar supply by renovating passenger railcars. According to Vladimir Kosoy, president of the Russian Center for Economic Infrastructure (and a Russian shipping analyst), passenger trains can be perfectly converted to container cargo transport after their refitment. Cargo is placed on pallets, existing containers, or in newly built containers. Transport companies also hope to attract more shippers to the Transsib as a result of the introduction of a stricter rail timetable. Also, high-speed rail services will be launched on the current Moscow-Kazan-Ekaterinburg rail route; the new service will connect central and eastern Russia. According to Russian railway monopoly RZD, the rail system improvements, so far, have not resulted in substantially higher tariffs on Transsib, which currently are $6,000 to 7,000 per TEU. This price is typically affordable for shippers and transport companies specializing in the delivery of high-priced cargo in containers, rail officials agree. The rail price, however, is significantly higher than China-to-Russia by ocean carrier transport, which costs about $1,200 to $2,000 per TEU, depending on the season. Currently, cargo delivery from Shanghai to St. Petersburg is about $1,500 per TEU. From Vladivostok seaport, a considerably longer route, the cost is higher: about $3,800 to $4,000 per TEU. The government of China’s initial plan called for the re-direction of up to 15 percent of its container cargo flows currently transported to the European Union by ocean carrier to be shifted to rail transport. However, the plan will likely be revised, as the use of the New Silk Road remains unprofitable for the majority of transport companies involved in transit on it. Meanwhile, Russia continues to subsidize transport, which has been a factor in rail’s volume growth, and all indications are that this policy will continue for the forseeable future. In the past two years, China-EU/China-Russia volume has increased about 60 percent to 420,000 TEU in 2017, according to Russian Minister of Transport Maxim Sokolov. The Russian government hopes additional railway upgrades will help China-EU and China-Russia traffic increase to 1 million TEU by 2020. The majority of this traffic will be on the Transsib, with an average daily run being 2,000 kilometers. Evenutually, Kosoy said, Russia hopes to increase the average train speed on Russian territory to 160 to 180 kilomters per hour. However, most analysts agree that speeds higher than 90 to 100 kilometers per hour probably will not be impossible, due to the high rate of rail utilization and lack of modernization. cleaned_content: Low freight train speed has been a longstanding, major problem in Russia, something that has hindered transport of Asia cargo through Russia and also Kazakhstan. com. China shippers transporting cargo to the European Union via Russia will be able to have their cargo delivered substantially faster on many routes, including sections of the Trans-Siberian Railway (Transsib), as a result of recent upgrades to Russia’s railway system, Russian officials announced this week. Cargo can now make the East Russia-Europe trip in about six to seven days, as opposed to 10 to 11 days previously, owing to railway improvments that enable higher speeds. As a result of recent rail system upgrades, container trains now average 75 kilometers per hour (about 47 miles per hour). Prior to 2017, speeds averaged 30 to 40 kilometers per hour. (Cargo by rail transport in China also averages about 30 to 40 kilometers per hour.) Low freight train speed has been a longstanding, major problem in Russia, something that has hindered transport of Asian cargo through Russia and also Kazakhstan. The higher speeds have also enabled officials to increase the number of daily trains on the Transsib, as well as their trip length: to 1,750 to 1,800 kilometers from 1,400 to 1,500 kilometers. Officials also increased the container railcar supply by renovating passenger railcars. According to Vladimir Kosoy, president of the Russian Center for Economic Infrastructure (and a Russian shipping analyst), passenger trains can be perfectly converted to container cargo transport after their refitment. Cargo is placed on pallets, existing containers, or in newly built containers. Transport companies also hope to attract more shippers to the Transsib as a result of the introduction of a stricter rail timetable. Also, high-speed rail services will be launched on the current Moscow-Kazan-Ekaterinburg rail route; the new service will connect central and eastern Russia. According to Russian railway monopoly RZD, the rail system improvements, so far, have not resulted in substantially higher tariffs on Transsib, which currently are $6,000 to 7,000 per TEU. This price is typically affordable for shippers and transport companies specializing in the delivery of high-priced cargo in containers, rail officials agree. The rail price, however, is significantly higher than China-to-Russia by ocean carrier transport, which costs about $1,200 to $2,000 per TEU, depending on the season. Currently, cargo delivery from Shanghai to St. Petersburg is about $1,500 per TEU. From Vladivostok seaport, a considerably longer route, the cost is higher: about $3,800 to $4,000 per TEU. The government of China’s initial plan called for the re-direction of up to 15 percent of its container cargo flows currently transported to the European Union by ocean carrier to be shifted to rail transport. However, the plan will likely be revised, as the use of the New Silk Road remains unprofitable for the majority of transport companies involved in transit on it. Meanwhile, Russia continues to subsidize transport, which has been a factor in rail’s volume growth, and all indications are that this policy will continue for the forseeable future. In the past two years, China-EU/China-Russia volume has increased about 60 percent to 420,000 TEU in 2017, according to Russian Minister of Transport Maxim Sokolov. The Russian government hopes additional railway upgrades will help China-EU and China-Russia traffic increase to 1 million TEU by 2020. The majority of this traffic will be on the Transsib, with an average daily run being 2,000 kilometers. Evenutually, Kosoy said, Russia hopes to increase the average train speed on Russian territory to 160 to 180 kilomters per hour. However, most analysts agree that speeds higher than 90 to 100 kilometers per hour probably will not be impossible, due to the high rate of rail utilization and lack of modernization.

title: Vehicle shippers need plan for myriad of risks
content: For original equipment manufacturers of vehicles, even minor dings and dents multiplied by thousands of units can result in big-dollar losses. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Manufacturers and shippers of autos and other vehicles have some of the most detailed contingency plans in the transportation industry for adjusting to weather events, port congestion, rail disruptions, and truck capacity issues. However, if shippers do not have a resilient supply chain that enables them to shift seamlessly to a plan B after an unexpected event, they could face millions of dollars in unexpected costs. “Have a plan in place, but also be resilient,” Scott Goodwin, vice president original equipment manufacturer (OEM) services at KHS Global, told the North America Finished Vehicle Logistics Conference March 13 in Huntington Beach, California. Vehicle shippers should have a well-tested plan that enables them to reboot their supply chains in response to redundant events such as port congestion during busy periods or rail service issues that often occur in the winter months in northern climates. However, it is the unexpected mega-event that can be a major disruptor. Vehicle shippers learned that lesson last year when Houston was slammed with a once-in-500-year hurricane. “Nature happens,” said Mark Boucher, director of vehicle logistics at Volkswagen Group of America. Like other OEMs, Volkswagen has prepared its supply chain to respond to hurricanes and flooding, “but when there is 34 feet of water where there shouldn’t be 34 feet of water, you’ve got a problem,” he said. In addition to continuous internal planning for the master recovery plan, OEMs should establish relationships with a variety of outside sources of information and transportation to plan for what is not known, Boucher said. The finished vehicle logistics industry must deal with costly disruptions on two fronts. Like all shippers, supply chain issues are paramount in their recovery plans. Vehicle shippers must have a plan to quickly recover from port congestion, labor disruptions in the transportation chain, rail disruptions such as have occurred this winter in Canada, and the northern tier of the United States, and truck capacity and driver shortage problems at seaports and inland hubs. Generally, OEMs everywhere have refined their logistics recovery plans through years of experience. However, given the high per-unit costs of autos and light trucks, and the fact that each OEM ships and stores hundreds of thousands of vehicles in conditions that expose them to severe weather occurrences such as hail storms, even minor dings and dents multiplied by thousands of units can result in big-dollar losses. Wade White, senior vice president of sales at VPS, said that due to climate change, severe weather events are increasing in intensity and frequency. “Specifically, hail is getting more severe,” he said. A hail event can set off a series of costly requirements including not only the repairs to the vehicles, but the logistics costs of transporting damaged vehicles back and forth to be repaired and the lost marketing dollars involving vehicles that are not on the dealer floors for sale when they should be, White said. Vehicle manufacturers and shippers in regions prone to hail storms can mitigate losses by building parking structures covered by solid roofs or less-costly nets, or by covering each vehicle to prevent damage. Those OEMs who have not taken such precautions should consider doing so as the frequency of hail storms increases, he said. Vehicle shippers in recent years have also experienced a variety of traditional supply chain disruptions such as the 2014-2015 West Coast port congestion problems during longshoreman contract negotiations, railcar shortages that result when railroads must run shorter trains during severe winter cold snaps, and the truck driver shortages. The driver shortage has gotten worse with the federal requirement for electronic logging devices (ELD). Truckers must now use the ELD to ensure they are driving within their hours-of-service limitations, and this is contributing to a driver shortage that was already developing in recent years because of an aging driver force. Railyards have become a bottleneck in the transportation supply chain, said Bob Farrell, executive director of the Automobile Carriers Conference of the American Trucking Associations. “This year we struggled” as railroads dealt with increasing volumes, he said. The rail problems reverberated throughout the supply chain, resulting in an artificial reduction in truck capacity. “When one part of the supply chain falls down, everything backs up,” he said. This problem, like others in transportation logistics, must be addressed through improved communication among all stakeholders, a tall order given that different sectors of the supply chain often resist sharing information with each other. “The information is so siloed. If change is desired, we must incentivize everyone to work together,” Farrell said. At present, the OEMs, vehicle inspection companies, and railroads have no incentive to share information. “What if we get OEMs together that use the same rail ramp and run a pilot to see what works best?” he said. Because the finished vehicle industry will never have a utopian supply chain in which vehicles arrive at ports on time and damage free, railroads run without disruption, and there is always sufficient truck capacity to handle every shipment, the only course of action is to develop a resilient supply chain, Boucher said. “The resilient supply chain works around the clock, sets up shop quickly, leverages valuable relationships, and gets back to work quickly after an interruption,” he said. title: Amid tight US truck capacity, tech pushes visibility boundaries
content: Shippers tired of ‘piecemealing’ visibility solutions together are pushing for faster development of end-to-end multimodal systems. ‘Visibility’ will be the foundation new services are built on to better manage supply chains and freight capacity. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Pummeled by rising freight transportation costs, US shippers are turning to technology not only to track freight in motion but to help them find available trucks or even create capacity when needed. The technology exists to build such solutions, but is it actually available today? “It is so challenging to find a platform that takes into account all parts of the supply chain,” Laura Venchuk, corporate logistics manager at Kuriyama of America, told JOC.com. “What happens at the ports, what happens at customs, at the dray, at LTL [less-than-truckload], there are so many [variables].” Her company, a Schaumburg, Illinois-based manufacturer of industrial hoses, has been looking for a system to track goods across modes, step by step, “and I question whether it can really be developed,” she said. “In the meantime, you have to make do. You’re stuck piecemealing.” Technologically, putting those pieces together is possible, though true, end-to-end solutions may not be available to every shipper, especially smaller ones. But companies, logistics and technology firms, are racing to solve the visibility problem. One of them, project44, just received $35 million to speed development of software linking global and surface freight networks. “A year ago there was still a lot of dissension about whether change was needed,” Tommy Barnes, president of project44, said. “Now I believe that most shippers and even more so, third-party companies, recognize the need to change to stay competitive or potentially die.” Founded in 2014, project44 set out to replace electronic data interchange with application programming interfaces (APIs) connecting transportation systems in the LTL market in real time. Expansion into volume LTL, truckload, and rail markets followed. The $35-million investment, which follows $10.5 million in Series A funding in 2016, will help project44 roll out its ocean and air-freight forwarding APIs “in the coming quarters,” Barnes said. “We’ve been focused on APIs that have the right quality attributes, not just points on the map.” In other words, project44 is looking at the connectivity and data flow needed to track containers and shipments as they clear ports, not just cross oceans. “In ocean shipping today, where do most of the delays occur? At the port. A lot of times we don’t focus enough on the port itself.” Along with GE Transportation, project44 is piloting an information portal at the Port of Los Angeles for carriers, terminal operators, beneficial cargo owners, truckers, cargo intermediaries, equipment providers, and railroads. The idea is to eliminate all the gaps in visibility at the port. “At GE, they use the word ‘stitching’ a lot,” Barnes said. Each step of the container’s multimodal journey “has to be stitched together to create visibility. You’re creating a single integration layer for all that activity.” And project44 will provide the APIs that hold that “layer” together. Building integrated platforms that connect modal silos will spur not just optimization of truck routes or trade lanes but supply chains. With larger vessels calling at ports and truck capacity tightening, there has never been a time that optimization, and visibility, were more needed. “We don’t know how to fix things unless we can see them,” Mark Carroll, director of product strategy at Descartes MacroPoint, another visibility technology supplier, told JOC.com. “It’s no longer a question of if people will deploy visibility but how people will deploy systems.” Descartes MacroPoint is developing a service based on its tracking technology that will help shippers not just follow freight but find capacity. “We are using some of our data now to begin matching up capacity for people as they continuously move trucks,” Carroll said. The capacity-matching product is in beta tests with several customers, he said, and should be ready to roll out late in the second quarter or early third quarter. “In the near term, we’re playing in the capacity-matching space, and beyond that we’ll be a complete visibility solution,” he said. Like project44 and competitor FourKites, Descartes MacroPoint offers a multimodal view of supply chains. “Our core focus is certainly trucking, but we do offer intermodal tracking through an aggregator and we are introducing steamship [container tracking] as well,” Carroll said. He also sees visibility as a prerequisite to further advances in technology that will not just make current shipping processes more efficient, but lead to changes in those processes. As supply chain technologies begin to merge, a broader level of supply chain visibility will emerge. “End-to-end tracking is the biggest thing people are focused on, but there are other cool things happening” with visibility, Carroll said. “Document tracking is part of that. There are some really good products coming out that will help manage payments” by expediting documents. Such advances will help shippers scale “visibility” into their supply chains, from the 30,000-foot-view of inventory in motion across continents and oceans to the ground level tactical perspective of a pallet in a tractor-trailer moving down the highway. title: XPO’s asset/non-asset strategy comes together
content: Some said it could not be done, but Bradley Jacobs is forging new shipper services by integrating assets and resources from across XPO Logistics’ diverse operating network. Photo credit: XPO Logistics. Since Bradley S. Jacobs began assembling XPO Logistics in 2011, investors, competitors, and other observers have questioned how, or whether, the non-asset and asset-based companies drawn into XPO’s orbit would fit together. On Tuesday, they got an answer when XPO launched an e-commerce distribution platform drawing on its trucking, last-mile/last-touch, and logistics units. XPO Direct is a “shared-space distribution model” for omnichannel and e-commerce retail customers. XPO warehouses and last-mile hubs will serve as “flexible stockholding sites,” XPO said in a statement Tuesday. The transportation link is provided by the company’s brokered and owned truck capacity, which includes the second-largest US less-than-truckload (LTL) carrier. “Retailers and e-tailers are looking for new ways to position goods more efficiently to shorten delivery transit times without adding overhead,” Jacobs said. XPO Direct shares “our technology, trucks, and workforce at over 100 sites, with hundreds of additional sites at the ready. In essence, we’re renting out our scale and disrupting traditional thinking.” In a sense, it is all about capacity. Retailers can use XPO’s space and assets as a cushion at a time when rapid growth in e-commerce is stressing the supply of US warehouse space in major population centers and is driving double-digit rent growth. Locations in urban core areas are experiencing “mid-teen rises” in rents, according to industrial real estate developer Prologis. XPO Direct is an alternative for consumer and retail customers to gain flexibility and scale,” Ashfaque Chowdhury, president of supply chain, Americas and Asia Pacific, said in an interview. “Many times they have demand they just don’t have infrastructure to meet. They just need the flexibility and scale we provide. This is a large-scale, shared-space supply chain solution.” But XPO is not just disrupting “traditional thinking” about what Jacobs called the “capital-intensive, regional distribution model.” Earlier this month, the company rolled out XPO Connect, a cloud-based, digital freight marketplace designed to give shippers access not just to XPO’s brokerage business but all of its transportation options through a single point. In March, the Greenwich, Connecticut-based company introduced WMx, a cloud-based, mobile warehouse platform that also cuts across XPO’s global business lines. And last week XPO announced an integration of its last-mile logistics service with Amazon Echo and Google Home. Now consumers can simply ask “Alexa” whether their last-mile delivery will arrive on time. For the investment community, this was supposed to be the year XPO returned to the acquisition trail — and it may yet. To date, however, more emphasis has been placed on leveraging XPO’s extensive asset and non-asset services in trucking, brokerage, forwarding, contract logistics, intermodal, and last-mile delivery to create new services for customers. Jacobs has been talking about blending resources in such a way for more than year. He told JOC.com XPO was building a service combining elements of its contract logistics, LTL, and last-mile delivery businesses in February 2017. “Why not design one engineered solution?” he said. “The larger e-commerce customers like having one invoice.” That solution sounds like a forerunner of XPO Direct. “XPO Direct uses our proprietary technology to link multiple sites with cross-network visibility,” said Chief Information Officer Mario Harik. Algorithms analyze customer data to identify behavior patterns, and XPO uses that data to predict when and where to place products and reflow goods to other sites, he said. Changes in consumer behavior are driving more shipments closer to that last-mile/last-touch facility where truckloads and pallets are broken down into packages. “There is a lot of change due to e-commerce growth and consumer expectations,” Chowdhury said. Those demands are changing so quickly, [retailers] are not always able to handle demand in the most efficient way.” Even the electronic logging device (ELD) mandate could factor into customer need for share-spaced warehousing. As the distances truck drivers are willing to drive in a day get shorter, transit times get longer, and distribution networks may be thrown out of whack. XPO’s transportation and shared real-estate assets could help shippers adjust to the ELD era. Contact William B. XPO’s transportation and shared real-estate assets could help shippers adjust to the ELD era.

title: ELDs not yet denting US truck detention
content: A survey of more than 600 US owner-operators and small carriers shows little change in detention practices at shipper docks, despite electronic logging and market pressures. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. If US shippers are trying to help speed truck drivers through their gates, owner-operators have not noticed yet. More than 77 percent of the independent truckers and small carriers surveyed by DAT Solutions said it still takes more than two hours to get shippers and co-signees to load or unload trucks, despite widespread talk about being a “shipper of choice.” About one-third of the 645 carriers surveyed by DAT in late February said one out of every five loads involved detention of more than two hours at a shipper or consignee dock. That is better than the 16 to 18 percent of carriers who cited detention every two or three out of five loads, but the response suggests shippers have a long way to go before practice matches intent. Unloading rates hardly were better. About 37 percent of the truckers surveyed said they were unloaded in two hours or less, but another 34 percent said unloading took between two to three hours, and another 15 percent said unloading took from three to four hours. As with loading, any time beyond two hours drivers are held up at the dock is considered detention time. When asked how many shippers or receivers prioritize loading and unloading based on a driver’s available hours of service, more than 80 percent of the truckers said “none.” Ten percent said “a few.” The results were slightly better when talking about brokers, with about 62 percent of carriers saying “none” and 22 percent “a few” were prioritizing drivers based on hours. DAT released its survey in mid-April, as full enforcement of the electronic logging mandate (ELD) mandate took effect. Driver detention will become an even more heated topic for truckers, shippers, brokers, and carriers as the use of electronic logs becomes prevalent. With ELDs, drivers and their employers will have a digital record of the hours spent at a shipper or receiver dock. Carriers are expected to use that hard evidence of detention to drive changes in shipper customers’ behavior. The US Department of Transportation’s (DOT) Office of the Inspector General (OIG) released a report Jan. 31 on the effects of driver detention on the US economy, the efficiency of the transportation system, motor carrier safety, and the livelihoods of truck drivers. The OIG concluded driver detention does affect highway safety, supporting some truck driver claims. “We estimated that a 15-minute increase in average dwell time — the total time spent by a truck at a facility — increases the average expected crash rate by 6.2 percent,” the OIG said. But gathering accurate data on detention and total dwell time at a shipper or receiver has been difficult, the report said, as until now there has been no mechanism to report or verify that data. “Accurate data on driver detention are not available because motor carriers and drivers do not collect data on the time spent actually loading and unloading and delays,” the OIG report said. Enter the ELD. Carriers now have that data, time stamped and stored electronically. The OIG estimated detention time may reduce annual earnings for truck drivers by $1,281 to $1,534 per year, although some of that loss may be offset by detention fees paid by shippers to carriers. The total cost of detention tops $1 billion, the DOT inspector general’s office said. In its survey, DAT also found most of the truckers already compliant with the ELD mandate. In total, 81 percent of the carriers already had ELDs installed, and another 10 percent said they were exempt from the mandate, either operating pre-2000-model-year trucks, or using another exemption authorized by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA). That means about 9 percent of the respondents at the time were openly violating the ELD mandate. About 57 percent of those carriers had purchased or tried to purchase an ELD, however. Some said they were still waiting for the device to arrive, some said their device “didn’t work,” and some were still struggling to learn how to use the ELD they had purchased. About 2 percent of the carriers surveyed said they were “waiting until I’m forced to use electronic logbooks.” With out-of-service enforcement of ELD violations in effect since April 1, they may not have long to wait. FMCSA data reveal a marked increase in truck driver violations associated with ELDs handed out in roadside inspections through March 30, 2018. In the first three months of 2018, inspectors issued 33,100 violations to truck drivers for operating a device “not registered with the FMCSA,” meaning not registered as an ELD. That includes nearly 15,000 violations issued between Feb. 24 and March 30, when the FMCSA’s online analysis and information database was last updated and released to the public. Contact William B. title: INTTRA to launch automated contract rate management pilot
content: Inna Kuznetsova, president and chief operating officer of INTTRA, said optimizing the management of rates was a key issue for shippers, carriers, and forwarders and the pilot would address this. (Above: The Port of Antwerp.) Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Electronic container shipping platform INTTRA is launching an automated contract rates management pilot program in the second half of the year to improve accuracy in the rate filing system and reduce admininstrative burden. Inna Kuznetsova, president and chief operating officer of INTTRA, said optimizing the management of rates was a key issue for shippers, carriers, and forwarders and the pilot would address this. While INTTRA was not ready to announce the organizations that would be participating in the pilot, the company said it had already completed a proof of concept using real rates and transactions. “The current system for managing rates often leads to errors as high as 30 to 45 percent with incorrect freight invoices due to how contract rate changes are managed and communicated,” INTTRA said in a statement following its hosting of a technology summit in Hamburg aimed at advancing the digital transformation of the ocean freight industry. The freight rate and contract management software market, where forwarders use tools to aggregate and systematize the procurement and disseminate rates, has been largely dominated by a handful of players, like CargoSphere Catapult, Freightgate, Info-X, and more recently Freightos. INTTRA has been a strategic partner to some of these vendors, including Catapult and CargoSphere (which was acquired in 2017 by the freight forwarding enterprise software provider WiseTech Global). Those partnerships essentially saw INTTRA sell those integrated rate management solutions to forwarders using the INTTRA platform. Rate management has become a critical area of operational differentiation for forwarders, in that it allows them to quickly and accurately access rates from carriers, and then layer margin on those rates. More recently, CargoSphere has introduced a new wrinkle by providing a conduit for direct, real-time rate feeds from carriers to freight forwarders. Automation is one part of a digitalization wave that is sweeping through the container transport and logistics industry. “It is clear, based on the feedback from our attendees, and the momentum in our business, that the industry has moved over the digitalization tipping point. This is the year of moving from innovation to action,” said INTTRA CEO John Fay.This movement was also highlighted by Kuehne + Nagel CEO Detlef Trefzger, who said during a first-quarter earnings call with analysts that he was seeing a different perception in the market, not only with customers but also with other partners, carriers, customs offices, and officials. “That will help to change and improve the technology placement in supply chain management,” he said in the earnings call transcribed by Seeking Alpha. “At the moment, I wouldn’t talk about acceleration, maybe six months too early, but the attention and the willingness to try to understand and to collaborate and to partner and to test, for example, blockchain shipments had significantly increased.“Today, we see more and more customers that have moved to our [KN FreightNet] platform, and we see more and more market players trying to achieve the same. So there is a higher willingness to move into that direction,” he said.But a key issue that remained as yet unresolved was data sharing, which Kuznetsova said was really a large group of issues requiring setting standards and ensuring data quality and security. However, the industry was continuing to make great strides in that direction.“Sharing data across partners is the foundation of innovation and improvement, and the foundation of improving customer service,” she said.At the Hamburg tech summit, Kuznetsova said supply chain visibility was a significant concern among shippers and forwarders that attended the event. In a survey of container shipping challenges, 43 percent ticked the visibility box.The lack of visibility is closely tied to a lack of data sharing across the supply chain. Kuznetsova told JOC.com that a container goes through as many as 20 different parties on its way from factory to door. “A supply chain is only as strong as its weakest link and we don't have the level of discipline provided and tracking by the different members in the field,” she said. “It is not a rare situation where you have quality tracking for a moment and then you have a gap in that tracking. To get visibility across the entire supply chain is a very important issue today, and it will be solved with digitalization.” Contact Greg Knowler at greg.knowler@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @greg_knowler. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Analysis: ELDs are US trucking's inflection point
content: The need to make dramatic changes is frequently anathema to providers and purchasers. It also flies in the face of the traditional transportation credo, “It’s not the way we’ve always done it.” Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Twenty years ago, in his book, Only the Paranoid Survive, Andrew S. Grove, as president and CEO of Intel Corporation, described Intel’s survival through the existential threats created by the drastic changes in its primary market. Grove framed the concept of strategic inflection points as “an event that changes the way we think and act.” Grove observed that “not only didn’t we realize that the rules had changed — what was worse, we didn’t know what rules we now had to abide by.” While strategic inflection points offer an opportunity to elevate performance to new heights, they can also signal imminent demise. The need to make dramatic changes is frequently anathema to providers and purchasers. It also flies in the face of the traditional transportation credo, “It’s not the way we’ve always done it.” In the past 40 years, the industry has experienced several inflection points. Since 1980, the US economy has become based on just-in-time trucking with an underlying reliable supply of trucking capacity and generally “reasonable” rates, both of which were expected to last forever. Hours of service (HOS) for trucking date back to 1938, when the former Interstate Commerce Commission first limited work hours. Over the decades, permitted time periods (and allowable work durations) have varied. In 2003, after extensive fatigue research, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) imposed a 34-hour restart. Modifications followed, and a final rule was published December 27, 2011; it went into effect 18 months later, on July 1, 2013. FMCSA published the electronic logging device (ELD) final rule on December 16, 2015, with compliance due by December 18, 2017. Strict enforcement was deferred until April 1, 2018. The interim period has been noteworthy for temporary exemptions and a phased-in enforcement. Grove observed that the need for transformation could arise with the introduction of a different regulatory environment. Change is unavoidable, but strategic points of inflection are not always obvious in real time. In the future, it’s likely that April 1, 2018 — the date ELD enforcement “went live” — will be enshrined as a red-letter day for our industry. Many trucking companies have been ELD-compliant for years, but there has been ongoing online chatter from the late-adopters. While truckers complain about ELDs, they are most distressed that HOS rules will now be strictly enforced. Routine enforcement will directly impact drivers who had previously been exceeding legal driving times with multiple log books. Figure #1 illustrates the “Driver Pay Algebra” that is at the heart of this industry about-face. -Previous: Prior to ELD enforcement, a driver could accrue 750 miles daily by running an additional four hours every day. - Legal: With new ELD enforcement, the number of miles driven — and resulting compensation — will both be reduced by 27 percent (300 to 220 and $300 to $220, respectively). -Necessary: To make the driver economically indifferent, (by retaining daily compensation at $300), the rate-per-mile must increase by 36 percent ($0.40 to $0.55). This algebra applies independently of the other issues adversely impacting driver availability: demographics, full-employment, and minimum wage laws. -Notional: Theoretically, the driver could remain economically indifferent (by retaining daily compensation at $300) by increasing driving speed by 36 percent, so that daily mileage remained at 750. This ignores the additional fuel cost and risk of accidents and speeding tickets — and the resulting increase in insurance premiums. (Recent anecdotal information indicates that there has been an increase in speeding citations since mandatory ELD enforcement went into effect.) Since December, the truckload market has reflected this algebra. Rates have increased for two reasons. -Rates must increase to make the driver whole for shorter (but legal) work days -Since the reduction in available miles driven reduces available capacity, the laws of supply and demand will also apply upward rate pressure. (In other words, fewer trucks available for the same volume will increase the price paid for every order.) Microeconomics would define this as “Cost-Push Inflation.” This arises when there is a decrease in the aggregate supply of goods or services. Microeconomics also maintains that one substitute good (or service) can replace another. The price of these services increases (or decreases) along with the price of the other. This impact is displayed in Figure #2. When the price of truck increases from P1 to P2, then the demanded quantity decreases from Q1 to Q2. It will also result in intermodal’s demand curve shifting to the right — denoting a higher price. As ELD enforcement reduces the supply of truckload capacity, the price of truckload and intermodal increases. Figure #3 outlines the changes; not only do drivers’ driving time and mileage lessen, but mandatory breaks and reset periods also increase. Because of the length of haul, a 34-hour reset will be required after each transcontinental run. If the currently suspended requirement that the reset include two periods from 1:00 a.m. to 5:00 a.m., the (minimum) 34-hour reset could significantly increase. Figure #4 tracks the cumulative time and distance of intermodal and truckload shipments between Bakersfield, California, and the 3,002-mile transit to Boston, Massachusetts. Intermodal transit was — and remains — 113 hours. Prior to ELD enforcement, single truckers were providing a faster — albeit illegal — transit time of 101 hours. In today’s world, that transit time has significantly increased to a range of 145 to 151 hours. Whereas the truck alternatives have rest periods of no activity, the intermodal product is almost continuously moving. Figure #5 illustrates this change on four long-haul markets. These corridors are significant lanes in the transportation of fresh produce. The pre-ELD transit times were widely understood to be the single-truck standard which intermodal needed to match — or against which intermodal had to discount. This “don’t ask, don’t tell” service standard survived for years because the truckload segment was predominantly (if not exclusively) served by owner-operators that lacked ELDs and ignored HOS compliance. The long-haul produce lanes are not one-offs. The 870-mile length of haul between New York and Chicago was frequently viewed as a one-day, “overnight” truck lane. Without actual teams performing this service, team-like service provided by single drivers will also disappear. Evidence suggests that the one thing more difficult to recruit — and retain — than a driver is two (team) drivers who will stay together.When capacity requirements are examined beyond individual one-way moves, the capacity crunch is shown to be even more severe. Figure #6 defines the round-trip impact of ELDs. The long-haul transit is significantly slower in both directions. Furthermore, the mandatory breaks and reset periods increase the overall roundtrip. Figure #7 summarizes the roundtrip capacity reduction. Prior to ELD enforcement, a single driver might achieve 35 annual transcontinental roundtrips; however, post-ELD implementation, the same driver is legally constrained to 21. This represents a 40 percent capacity reduction. This draconian shrink is not yet obvious. Rather, it is a “rolling” impact, which will become evident over the next several months, and will either hasten the exit of truck drivers from the market or accelerate rate increases already extant in the market — or both. Grove believed that major transformation requires fear, which can overcome complacency bred by years of success. His book’s title mandated paranoia — a suspicion that things are changing against shippers — as the spark to light the fire of change. The strategic inflection point is for truckload shippers. Grove realized that Intel had to abandon its core business, and redirect resources into microprocessors. Shippers will need to take a similar leap of faith by abandoning their reliance on truck and growing their intermodal capabilities. Opportunity for intermodal right now is significant and obvious. Intermodal, no longer a “truck plus-one wannabe” is faster and more capable of offering reliable capacity. The advantage is clear on trans-continental lanes, but it exists in shorter corridors as well. Some 35 to 40 years ago, shippers and manufacturers remade their industries under transportation deregulation. Some were first-movers. Others were late adopters. The residual refused to change — and went out of business. Today’s challenges are the industry's opportunities. They are equally enticing, and their solutions could prove to be similarly ground-breaking. Prior to ELD enforcement, a single driver might achieve 35 annual transcontinental roundtrips; however, post-ELD implementation, the same driver is legally constrained to 21. This represents a 40 percent capacity reduction. This draconian shrink is not yet obvious. Rather, it is a “rolling” impact, which will become evident over the next several months, and will either hasten the exit of truck drivers from the market or accelerate rate increases already extant in the market — or both. Grove believed that major transformation requires fear, which can overcome complacency bred by years of success. His book’s title mandated paranoia — a suspicion that things are changing against shippers — as the spark to light the fire of change. The strategic inflection point is for truckload shippers. Grove realized that Intel had to abandon its core business, and redirect resources into microprocessors. Shippers will need to take a similar leap of faith by abandoning their reliance on truck and growing their intermodal capabilities. Opportunity for intermodal right now is significant and obvious. Intermodal, no longer a “truck plus-one wannabe” is faster and more capable of offering reliable capacity. The advantage is clear on trans-continental lanes, but it exists in shorter corridors as well. Some 35 to 40 years ago, shippers and manufacturers remade their industries under transportation deregulation. Some were first-movers. Others were late adopters. The residual refused to change — and went out of business. Today’s challenges are the industry's opportunities. They are equally enticing, and their solutions could prove to be similarly ground-breaking. Theodore Prince is executive vice president and chief operating officer of Tiger Cool Express, and a JOC contributor as an intermodal analyst.

title: US shippers explore LTL, rail due to US truckload tightness
content: With US truckload capacity tight, shippers are investigating any alternative method possible to get their freight off the docks. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Shippers struggling to find available capacity in the US truckload market due to the growing US economy and the electronic logging device (ELD) mandate are turning to intermodal and less-than-truckload (LTL) as options to move freight. As one intermodal executive told JOC.com on the condition of anonymity, “if it’s a rectangle and it can hold freight, shippers will use it to get loads off their docks.” Finding any solution to move the freight is better than having it idle on the docks. Shippers have told JOC.com that rollover freight — loads not picked up on the scheduled day to ship — is rising. The freight might move the following day, but cargo that remains on the dock an extra day complicates shipping schedules and adds to costs. Exploring options other than one-way irregular route truckload can yield options to keep the goods moving. It is also becoming increasingly necessary because drivers who use ELDs are driving fewer miles per workday, and therefore unable to finish as many jobs in a week, month, or year. “Shippers are asking, ‘With truckload rates going up, can I go and squeeze some of this freight into the less-than-truckload side?’ For the LTL, it tends to mess up the flow, it’s usually oversized, and it’s not efficient,” XPO Logistics president Troy Cooper told JOC.com. “Think of it from the shippers perspective. ‘Truckload rates going up, where can I mitigate some of these cost outs?’ So you have to think of a mode shift.” LTL carriers typically make the most money when they can combine a high number of loads into one trailer. A common expression in the LTL world is that “you will cube out before you weigh out;” in other words, loads tend to be lighter so the carrier wants to maximize every inch of the trailer (length, width, and height) to generate the highest returns. E-commerce has only exacerbated this effect with smaller but more frequent shipments. The reverse is true in US truckload: loads tend to be heavier and the trailer will weigh out to the legal limit before the three-dimensions are maxed out. But Cooper says that even truckload freight can be good LTL freight if it is priced correctly. Old Dominion Freight Line also cited pricing as the primary method in controlling how much freight spills over from the truckload market. Adam Satterfield, Old Dominion’s chief financial officer, told Wall Street analysts on April 26 that they do not want to do a disservice to their long-term, core LTL shippers. “Most of those heavy weight shipments would come in through a spot quote type of basis, and whether that's phone calls or through our website, and basically we turn up the rates to try to make sure that our operations don't get overwhelmed with any heavy weighted transactional type shipments that may be more one-time in nature,” he said. “I think some of that is probably indicative of the [third-party logistics providers] that are able to maximize the relationships they had in earlier periods when truckload was a little bit weaker ... And now that that capacity is tightened up, they're moving heavier weighted shipments that should be in the LTL world back into our environment.” Intermodal has also become a popular alternative. The Intermodal Association of North America reported that first-quarter volume increased 7.2 percent on a year-over-year basis to 1.57 million units. Domestic business outpaced international growth. Domestic volumes grew 7.4 percent to 803,795 units, led by a 14.5 percent jump in trailer on flatcar traffic to 128,002. Flexibility for domestic US shippers is easier than for an international shipper that may move freight under a door delivery contract. Under such an arrangement, the shipper does not usually have the freedom to shift modes from truck to rail, or vice versa, because the ocean carrier is controlling the end-to-end supply chain. But for the domestic shipper, such a decision can be made quickly and unilaterally to resolve supply chain slowdowns. “For a few years, the intermodal sell was cost, cost, cost. Now we’re back to viewing intermodal as a capacity play. And this year, shippers are looking for alternate solutions within the transportation network,” said Shelli Austin, president of Intek Freight and Logistics. “We’re selling the lesser of two evils,” said Robert Rich, CEO of Roar Logistics. “I will tell a shipper, ‘I can get you an intermodal container tomorrow and it will take 10 days end-to-end to the West Coast or I can abide by our contract and it will take me 10 days to get you a truck and three days on the road.’ It’s like so-so pizza or Chinese food, it may not be the best, but it’s still good enough.” Dave Yeager, CEO of Hub Group, told Wall Street analysts on April 26 that the service problems in January and February have eased somewhat over the last six weeks, echoing the conversations between JOC.com, shippers, and intermodal marketing companies. Hub’s on-time performance sagged on the East Coast due to the service woes from its partner Norfolk Southern Railway. “On a positive note, since mid-March, we have experienced gradual on-time improvement with our western rail partner. We believe that service will continue to improve in the west for the remainder of the year,” he said. “In the east, service problems appear to have bottomed out and we believe that improvements will be seen in the last half of the year. We continue to effectively work with our clients to minimize the impact of these rail service issues by establishing longer transits as benchmarks and communicating and intervening when loads are delayed.” Shippers, while communicating their dissatisfaction to the Surface Transportation Board about concerns about deeper issues among the railroads, are nonetheless sticking with the alternative, due to the lack of better choices. Hub Group and Schneider National are also doubling down on their railroad investments despite the congestion in the winter, banking on the theory that volumes will continue to grow as the US truckload market tightens with ELD enforcement throughout the year. Hub Group will be increasing its container count 7 percent this year, or an additional 2,500 domestic boxes to a total of 37,000. “The reason that we — if you remember from our last call, we did up that by about 500 containers to have those containers, that capacity, available for our customers when they need it. With transits as they are and with the demand that we've had, we thought it's prudent to increase the order by 500.” said Terri Pizzuto, Hub’s chief financial officer. Schneider will also add new domestic containers this year beginning in the second quarter. Chief Operating Officer Mark Rourke said that the company could have fulfilled 6,000 orders in the first quarter if only it had the available boxes. Schneider currently has about 18,000 domestic containers, the third-largest, private-owned fleet behind J.B. Hunt Transport Services and Hub Group, respectively. By the end of this year, Schneider plans to increase the container count to nearly 22,000. “We have had, and continue to see, just a real strong appetite for over-the-road to intermodal conversion, really, and all geographies and virtually all segments of the customer vertical space,” Rourke said on an April 26 earnings call. “We haven't added a great deal of containers over the last several years and based upon our ability to perform at where we are, we think it's absolutely the right time to do that.” Contact Ari Ashe at ari.ashe@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @ariashe_joc. © 2026 S&P Global. title: US truck shippers adjust to new rate reality
content: Shippers were surprised by the severity of price increases demanded by US truckers in the first quarter. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. ORLANDO, Florida — Shocked by price increases and a drive to raise rates that one logistics executive called “ruthless,” shippers are racing to expand relationships with asset-based carriers, both those already in their routing guides and new partners that potentially can bring additional capacity to the table. “I couldn’t have been more wrong last fall,” said one executive at the NASSTRAC 2018 Shippers Conference here who, as recently as the fourth quarter, expected close relationships with motor carriers and steady freight volumes would forestall significant rate increases. Last autumn, shippers surveyed by NASSTRAC, JOC.com, Truckstop.com, and the Transportation Intermediaries Association expected truckload rates to rise, but most other rates to remain flat over the next 12 months. Most shippers expected rate hikes of 5 percent or less. Shippers at the NASSTRAC event confirmed they are seeing freight cost increases in the high single-digit to the low double-digit percentage range, with much tighter capacity in the US truckload sector, but also in less-than-truckload and other transportation sectors as well. Even the closest partnerships, shippers say, can’t completely insulate a company from a market wave propelled by faster economic growth, higher freight demand, and constrained levels of capacity, not just in surface transportation, but in air cargo and distribution real estate. Shippers are looking not just for more carriers with available capacity (and there are few idle trucks on US highways), but for more efficient ways of using existing capacity and even “creating capacity” by better managing carrier relations and shipping processes. Capacity is tight “across the board” and across modes, Chris Tudtud, a senior manager in global logistics and procurement at Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals, a multibillion dollar specialty pharmaceutical manufacturer, told fellow shippers during a presentation at the conference. Part of the issue is dynamically changing global demand for his company’s products, which can change spending priorities quickly and decisions about where capacity is needed quickly, he said. “We’re reacting to those things, but capacity is tight across the board,” he said. Trucking companies that warned US shippers of rate increases last autumn are following through, and are willing to walk away from customers that refuse to pay, several logistics executives said. The situation is being exacerbated by the electronic logging device (ELD) mandate, they said. “There’s so much drama with the ELD, we’re just trying to keep up with how things are going,” said Tudtud, whose company was named NASSTRAC Shipper of the Year for 2018, in recognition of its efforts to develop a supplier relationship management (SRM) program. Since December, stricter adherence to truck driver hours-of-service rules under the ELD mandate has shortened the distance many drivers travel in a day, lengthening transit times, and creatred a situation in which trucking assets and drivers are “displaced.” Not only is demand higher than supply, but that supply isn’t where shippers expect it to be. “Never before have we seen this broad a disconnect between capacity and demand,” said John Larkin, managing director for transportation and logistics at Stifel. The largest truckload fleets, Larkin pointed out, have been shrinking. They have also been directing capacity toward specialized services, such as dedicated trucking. Smaller truckload carriers, however, “actually have been increasing in size on average,” he said. “Part of that has to do with used truck values remaining depressed, so it’s very cheap to get into the business or to add to your fleet if you’re adding used trucks,” said Larkin. “The tax reform bill [passed in December] gives you full depreciation even if you buy a used truck.” QualifiedCarriers.com, a risk management firm for shippers, has tracked an explosion of small trucking companies in the United States. According to CEO Jeff Tucker, the number of carriers with one to six trucks rose 90 percent from March 2012 to a total of 179,769 companies as of March 2018. Smaller carriers provide “a buffer” for larger fleets, said Larkin. The “disconnect” between supply and demand is narrower on the small fleet side of the market, he said. “If it weren’t for the small fleets, we’d be in a much bigger hole than we are now. Rates would be going up even faster.” To truly get access to more capacity, and control costs, shippers may have to think like a tree, according to Tudtud — specifically, like the oak trees of New Orleans whose intertwined root structure helped them weather Hurricane Katrina in 2005. “It’s called biomimicry,” he said. He’s not going out on a limb. Biomimicry involves the design and production of structures modeled on biological entities and processes. Tudtud sees an analogy in SRM, which his company has used to forge closer relations with its freight transportation suppliers. “We’re managing relationships now, rather than managing transactions,” he said. SRM, in a sense, takes the “shipper of choice” concept to the next level, one of embedded relationships. And the goal isn’t necessarily cost savings, although those savings will come, he said. “In a true partnership, there are going to be times when we know we’re going to be paying a little bit higher than market rates, because our suppliers need that,” said Tudtud. “You have to be able to give and take.” At the moment, however, shippers are giving and hoping to receive.
