title: Penske, NFI to road test Freightliner electric trucks
content: Heavy-duty and medium-duty electric trucks (e-trucks) from the largest US truck maker will get a workout in applications such as drayage as a step toward full production. (Above: A Daimler e-truck.) Photo credit: Daimler Trucks. Penske Truck Leasing and logistics company NFI are giving the development of the electric truck (e-truck) a fresh jolt of power by partnering with Daimler Trucks North America subsidiary Freightliner. The companies will deploy 30 electric-powered medium-duty and heavy-duty trucks, starting this autumn, and participate in what DTNA calls the “co-creation” of a US electric fleet. It’s a step toward full production by 2021, the truck manufacturer said. The electrification of trucking, however, won’t be as easy as throwing a switch. First, the next generation of e-trucks must prove equal to the task of hauling freight. Second, the infrastructure needed to operate the trucks — especially a network of charging stations — must be built. There’s little question such a network eventually will be built, however long that may take. Shippers want electric vehicles (EVs) that will reduce transportation costs and help meet emissions reduction targets set by corporate sustainability programs. Carriers want relief from volatile diesel fuel costs and the rising cost of heavy-duty trucks as diesel emissions regulations get stricter. One as-yet unanswered question is whether electricity will eventually supplant fossil fuels in trucking or simply supplement diesel and other alternatives, such as natural gas. Starting later this year, NFI will use 10 eCascadias, electric versions of Freightliner’s heavy-duty Cascadia Class 8 tractor, to handle container drayage between the ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles and Southern California’s Inland Empire. Penske will put 10 eCascadias and 10 medium-duty eM2 106 electric tractors to use in a variety of applications with its customers. While startups Tesla and Nikola have garnered widespread media attention with electric and hybrid electric-hydrogen vehicles, Daimler and other original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) have been plugging away at design and development of commercial e-trucks, as demand grows for alternatives to diesel power. DTNA unveiled the eCascadia and eM2 106 trucks June 6. At the same time, the German manufacturer established an E-Mobility Group across its operations and brands in North America, Europe, and Japan. The E-Mobility Group will “define the strategy for electric components or complete [EVs], and develop a standardized, worldwide electric architecture” for those vehicles, the company said in a statement. In the United States, DTNA launched an Electric Vehicle Council Wednesday to prepare customers to evaluate and integrate EVs into their operations. Technical learnings from the Freightliner Electric Innovation Fleet and test fleet will be shared with customers, and the council will gather feedback as the OEM moves toward commercialization of e-trucks. Through its EV Council, DTNA will work with trucking operators to develop the needed charging infrastructure and provide service support. The truck maker plans to offer consulting services to assist with site selection for electric trucking operations, different trucking applications, available federal and state government incentives, infrastructure deployment, and route identification. "The DTNA approach to bring commercial [EVs] to market is holistic,” said Richard Howard, senior vice president of sales and marketing for Freightliner Trucks. (Freightliner is the largest truck maker in the United States, with 40 percent of Class 8 US market share in 2017, according to the company. DTNA sold 140,000 trucks in the United States last year, a 15 percent increase.) “With the Freightliner Electric Innovation Fleet, we will be working hands-on with Penske and NFI. As a separate part of a co-creation process we will also launch the EV Council that emphasizes shared learning before we begin series vehicle production," Howard said. Even so, e-trucks still have a long road ahead of them, despite a groundswell of interest from potential owners, said Paul Rosa, senior vice president of procurement and fleet planning at Penske Truck Leasing. “The infrastructure, that’s going to take several years to develop, no doubt,” he said. “Truckstops and other places will have to think about altering locations.” Penske’s partnership with DTNA is part of a learning process that will test how the trucks perform in various applications with customers in California and the Pacific Northwest. The truck lessor has been running and testing electrics for several years, primarily buses and light-duty trucks. “We have a baseline, and this is going to take things to another level,” said Rosa. The company has logged more than 100 million miles with EVs, said Sherry Sanger, senior vice president of marketing. Regulatory pressures in Europe and California, as well as fuel costs, are a factor behind the global surge of interest in EVs, she said. “We see strong interest coming out of the US West Coast,” Sanger said. “People are interested in reducing air and noise pollution. And when diesel costs go up, [EVs] become more interesting.” From 2009 through 2016, sales of plug-in cars and light vans, not heavy vehicles or hybrids, topped a cumulative 2 million units, according to the International Energy Agency. “If we can make [e-trucks] work from a total-cost-of-ownership standpoint, we’ll see the interest grow,” Sanger said. “That’s one of the major hurdles right now. The vehicles are extremely expensive. It’s important for us to understand the new technology and bring that expertise to our customers. It’s about learning and understanding, and not following the hype.” At NFI, the eCascadias will augment existing sustainability efforts, which include a test of electric yard horse units and exploring the viability of electric battery and hydrogen fuel cell heavy trucks. NFI also operates Near Zero compressed natural gas trucks fueled with renewable natural gas and has ordered zero-emissions trucks to be delivered next year. “Social responsibility is a core value at NFI, and our collaboration with DTNA exhibits our shared commitment to innovation and sustainability,” said CEO Sid Brown. “NFI strives to continually invest in new, innovative technology that can help improve the impact that NFI and its customers has on the environment. We look forward to further partnering and supporting the California ports and their efforts to improve sustainability and create a cleaner community.” Rosa expects electric commercial vehicles to prove themselves first in localized applications, such as drayage. “They are really going to play well in yard tractor situations, at ports, for pick up and distribution in the city, and delivery drivers going out and coming back to their home base,” he said. “Long-distance trucking is going to be last” as charging infrastructure expands. “Even regional trucking will be a big challenge, until we understand how the batteries perform,” he said. The Freightliner eCascadia, designed for local distribution and drayage, is powered by a 730-horsepower, 550-kilowatt hour battery with a range of up to 250 miles. The battery can be recharged to around 80 percent within 90 minutes to cover 200 miles, DTNA said. The eM2’s 325-kilowatt hour engine will deliver up to 480 horsepower, DTNA said. The range of the eM2 is around 230 miles, and an 80 percent recharge will take 60 minutes and add another 184 miles. (Daimler also offers the light-duty electric Mitsubishi FUSO eCanter in the United States.) Improvements in battery design are fueling electricity’s revival as a truck fuel, pushing interest in EVs to a height not seen since the 1920s, when electric delivery trucks and charging stations were a common sight in large US cities. Improvements in combustion engine design, including the invention of the electric starter, eventually pulled the plug on those e-trucks. A hundred years later, the electrics are lining up for revenge. “You’re going to see more advancements in battery technology over the next three years than we’ve seen in the last 10 years,” Rosa said. “The time is now. There are more players entering the space, not just in Europe and Asia but the US. There’s a huge groundswell in the whole space.” Contact William B. title: Maersk taps Kontainers for e-booking, tracking pilot
content: Maersk Line has enlisted Kontainers, a small software company based in the north of England, to develop something that could be transformative in its future relationship with shippers: a portal to make bookings and track in-transit shipments. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Container lines may have been late out of the gate when it comes to developing e-commerce portals for shippers to transact with them, but in the world of modern software architecture, it doesn’t take long to catch up. In 2017, Maersk Line enlisted Kontainers, a small software company based in the north of England, to develop something that could be transformative in its future relationship with shippers: a portal to make bookings and track in-transit shipments. On Sunday, the shipping line unveiled that this platform, ship.maerskline.com, was “powered by Kontainers.” The software company, founded in 2015, started operations as a digital freight forwarder but in 2017 pivoted to build white-labeled online customer interfaces for shipping lines and freight forwarders. The company said it now has four shipping brands among the top five liner carriers and top 10 forwarders as customers. Maersk uses my.maerskline.com as its primary platform to transact directly with customers. The company said in its latest earnings call in mid-May that 60.2 percent of its volume was booked through its e-commerce platform in the final four weeks of the first quarter, a number that’s rising rapidly. The liner carrier told JOC.com that ship.maerskline.com platform is being piloted in a limited number of trades, “mainly for contractual customers of Maersk Line using our services between China to parts of Africa, Latin America and the Mediterranean.” The carrier added that ship.maerskline.com doesn’t replace my.maerskline.com or other customer portals it currently operates. Graham Parker, co-founder and CEO of Kontainers, said the idea behind his company is to give companies a customer-facing platform that enables them to compete with some of the more progressive freight forwarders in the world, ones that have built user interfaces that feel like easy-to-use transactional websites. The tool being used by Maersk is called Kontainers Enterprise, designed for companies with heavy transactional volume and a need to highly customize their interfaces. “They’re in full control,” Parker told JOC.com. “If they want a pink button on Tuesday, they get a pink button on Tuesday.” Kontainers also said it would be releasing a new version of its software called Kontainers Edge Sept. 1, designed to target the forwarding middle market. That version would be stripped down and less customizable, but more in the budget range of forwarders that are unable to take on the cost of a full freight forwarding enterprise software implementation. Parker likened his vision for this to SquareSpace, a website development platform that allows businesses to quickly get their online presence off the ground. He said the customer interface Kontainers provides can be used in a standalone fashion for companies without a backbone system, or it can integrate with broader freight forwarding enterprise suites such as those offered by WiseTech Global, Descartes, and BluJay Solutions. Kontainers is hardly the only company looking to build software for small and mid-sized forwarders hoping to give their shipper customers a digital front door that resembles those of Flexport, iContainers, FreightHub, and other digitally focused forwarders. And many of those other upstarts are likewise focusing on creating efficiencies around the transaction with the shipper. “There’s a real gap,” Parker said. “If you’re a business and want a [customer relationship management system], you get your credit card out and you’ll get 100 in an hour. If you’re a freight forwarder, there’s not really a similar situation. The industry has finally passed the point of no return. Kuehne + Nagel and Maersk are all in. Even if a customer has a bad experience online, they’re not going back.” Parker understandably is buoyed by Maersk’s decision to go public with the builder of its e-commerce platform, seeing it as lending credibility to a company often lumped together with a huge swathe of other logistics technology startups. He said he sees his company’s technology as helping democratize the business for forwarders of any size, enabling them to compete digitally with the likes of well-funded digital forwarders, while giving them market reach through the web to compete with the world’s biggest forwarders and carriers. His target is to provide any carrier or forwarder in the world with the ability to have their own branded digital platform set up in weeks for roughly the price of one salesperson when it’s taken most companies years to build. “This is a new genre of freight software,” Parker said. “In an industry that is used to having middlemen, switching to a digital interface between you and your customers may seem like the obvious next step. However, for our customers this is often a step which causes some anxiety. The growth they experience on the platform is a combination of their promotion and pricing principles, supported by a platform that just makes shipping very easy for everyone.” Kontainers’ platform is designed to use application programming interfaces (APIs) as a way to connect systems when available. Maersk told JOC.com that an API connection with Kontainers is available but is not currently used for the connection to ship.maerskline.com. “While this is an option we are exploring in the future, it’s not currently available today,” a carrier spokesperson said. Broader use of APIs would be a significant change for an industry that has leaned heavily on systems communicating via electronic data interchange (EDI), or via more manual means, to convey critical booking, shipping instructions, and container status events. Critically, EDI message sets do not cover rates, so that has been an avenue for software providers to push broader use of APIs. A range of experts at freight forwarders and software providers have said some liner carriers are as amenable as ever to using APIs. In Kontainers’ case, the company said it has built a hub of 50 APIs for forwarders and carriers to use in their electronic platforms. But a key hurdle could well be shippers themselves, as most have built their supply chains on EDI and are reticent to rip up the connections they’ve built with suppliers and transportation and logistics vendors to move to APIs. That step in the evolution of API usage doesn’t, however, preclude carriers and forwarders from using APIs to better present pricing and service options to shippers via a web interface. Parker called dynamic pricing a “holy grail” in the liner shipping industry. Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. © 2026 S&P Global. title: Pace of trace and track adoption centers on who pays
content: As the technical hurdles standing in the way of such advances are resolved, the focus turns to whether ocean carriers, shippers, or logistics companies are willing to accept the technology and pay for it. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. As the cost shrinks for sensor-based cargo tracking systems, the technology is still several years away from being routinely affordable to shippers and ocean carriers. But the speed and scale of adoption may hinge on one question: who pays? To some providers, shippers should foot the bill. Other providers sell the technology to carriers. And behind each scenario, the question looms of how ready shipper or carrier executives are to embrace the cultural change, added expense, and operational reorganization and scrutiny that will come with increased visibility along the supply chain. Sensor technology to track a single container at present costs from about $100 to about $150, and needs to come down to about $30 to be widely accepted, said Don Miller, vice president of global sales and marketing for Denmark-based Globe Tracker ApS. Miller — whose estimate is higher than those of some other providers, who put the current cost of low-end units in the low double digits — told the JOC Canada Trade Conference on June 20 that bringing the cost down to a price point that the industry widely accepts will require the production of large volumes of sensors to reap economies of scale. Yet that is no sure thing, given that “the ocean carrier part of the business is very conservative, and as such changing mindsets is a very difficult thing,” he said. While larger carriers such as Maersk Line, CMA CGM, and Mediterranean Shipping Co. have taken steps to embrace the technology, it won’t be commonly used until smaller ocean carriers follow suit, said Miller, whose business model involves the carrier paying for tracking technology. “We have MSC, who see on one hand [that] sharing the data is an open opportunity,” he said. “They seem happy to do so. It’s not the case across the board. Obviously, the pressure is on within the top five to provide similar services … People are looking at it. But it’s a slow moving train.” Maersk last week signaled that it is keen to advance in the market with an investment in a US-based startup called SensorTransport. The company offers inexpensive, disposable tracking devices meant to be affixed directly to goods (at the package or pallet level) and designed to monitor motion, humidity, temperature, light, magnetism, and sound. The data generated by the sensors are viewable by a mobile app. France-based ocean carrier CMA CGM said last week that it has made the Traxens Technology platform available to all customers, and MSC also is working with the technology provider. Traxens, a French startup that makes container sensors, has developed an associated data platform to give shippers information about the container’s location, outside temperature, impacts, movement, and vibration. Data collected by the permanently installed sensors, called TRAXENS-BOX S+, are relayed to a radio network that the company developed to cope with the obstacles of the physical shipping environment. For instance, the radio network is designed to reach boxes deep in the holds of the world’s largest containerships. The sensors can also detect when a container door has been opened, and will soon be able to detect the temperature and humidity levels inside the container, CMA CGM said. The potential benefit to logistics providers and their customers is broad, ranging from tracking and using the data to more accurately predicting the arrival of cargo at different points in the supply chain, to smaller examples. Miller said a GPS and geo-fence system designed to alert a shipper when a trucker arrived with cargo would give “proof of delivery within five minutes” of the cargo’s arrival. Insurance claims would be a lot easier if a sensor told the shipper exactly when a box was damaged, and so under whose responsibility it was at the time, he said. Peter Yost — senior director of strategic alliances at Four Kites, which provides sensor-based tracking systems for road, rail, and sea — cited the benefits for the operator of a 200-door warehouse if the trucking company or shipper could predict (for example, to within an hour) when the cargo scheduled for each door would arrive. “How much more efficiently could you schedule your resources?” he said. Yet as the technical hurdles standing in the way of such advances are resolved, the focus turns to whether ocean carriers, shippers, or logistics companies are willing to accept the technology and pay for it. Carriers, and other supply chain participants need to be ready for the added scrutiny on their performance that visibility brings, said Yost. “Once you have very reliable data, once you have GPS that is indisputable in its quality, accuracy, and timeliness, you can do things like shine a light on the performance of yourself and your carriers,” said Yost, whose company charges the shipper for tracking services. That raises a variety of “operational issues that impact on how this all works,“ Miller said. He recalled a scenario in which a shipper wanted to install sensors on containers, but the ocean carrier balked, concerned at what the customer would see. “I’m like, OK, this is your biggest customer why won’t you do it?” said Miller, and the carrier replied, “Because in this lane we always transship to Panama and it sits three or four days in Panama. And I don’t need them down my throat because it's waiting in Panama for the next shipment.” Najim Shaikh, vice president, commercial import, for MSC, said the carrier linked up with Traxen due to the clear benefit the technology could bring to the carrier. “We have no interest in having containers sit around for no reason,” he said, adding that tracking will help the company improve efficiency through analytics and help to “better understand our bottlenecks.” But at the end of the day, the carrier is merely offering the service through a third party, and the shipper will decide whether it is worth using, he said. “There is a cost element,” he said. “The question is, is it needed? Is someone willing to pay that amount for a container … And that’s really a question for our customers. How important is that data?” That question takes on added importance given the operational changes necessary to ensure that the user is able to respond to the insights provided by the track and trace data. As the cost shrinks for sensor-based cargo tracking systems, the technology is still several years away from being routinely affordable to shippers and ocean carriers. But the speed and scale of adoption may hinge on one question: who pays? To some providers, shippers should foot the bill. Other providers sell the technology to carriers. And behind each scenario, the question looms of how ready shipper or carrier executives are to embrace the cultural change, added expense, and operational reorganization and scrutiny that will come with increased visibility along the supply chain. Sensor technology to track a single container at present costs from about $100 to about $150, and needs to come down to about $30 to be widely accepted, said Don Miller, vice president of global sales and marketing for Denmark-based Globe Tracker ApS. Miller — whose estimate is higher than those of some other providers, who put the current cost of low-end units in the low double digits — told the JOC Canada Trade Conference on June 20 that bringing the cost down to a price point that the industry widely accepts will require the production of large volumes of sensors to reap economies of scale. Yet that is no sure thing, given that “the ocean carrier part of the business is very conservative, and as such changing mindsets is a very difficult thing,” he said. While larger carriers such as Maersk Line, CMA CGM, and Mediterranean Shipping Co. have taken steps to embrace the technology, it won’t be commonly used until smaller ocean carriers follow suit, said Miller, whose business model involves the carrier paying for tracking technology. “We have MSC, who see on one hand [that] sharing the data is an open opportunity,” he said. “They seem happy to do so. The data generated by the sensors are viewable by a mobile app. France-based ocean carrier CMA CGM said last week that it has made the Traxens Technology platform available to all customers, and MSC also is working with the technology provider. Traxens, a French startup that makes container sensors, has developed an associated data platform to give shippers information about the container’s location, outside temperature, impacts, movement, and vibration. Data collected by the permanently installed sensors, called TRAXENS-BOX S+, are relayed to a radio network that the company developed to cope with the obstacles of the physical shipping environment. For instance, the radio network is designed to reach boxes deep in the holds of the world’s largest containerships. The sensors can also detect when a container door has been opened, and will soon be able to detect the temperature and humidity levels inside the container, CMA CGM said. title: With cost cuts, container lines must create value to escape cycle
content: Like the US airline industry earlier, the global container shipping industry has reached a point where cost cutting and mergers will yield little if any additional value. This is the view of a longtime carrier executive, who argues creating value for customers will characterize the current era, with customer service the first visible change area. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Having spent the last decade cutting costs to a degree that often disadvantages customers, container carriers have reached a point where they can’t slash costs more; even mergers will yield little if any additional value. Thus, carriers have no choice but to begin looking at ways of escaping the vicious cycle of commoditization and finding ways to create value for customers. This is the view of longtime Hapag-Lloyd executive Wolfgang Freese, the Maritime Hall of Fame inductee who retired this spring as president of the carrier’s North America region. “The carriers’ ‘race to scale’ over the past 10 years, where we tried to drive down costs, and we have passed along those cost reductions to customers, has now run its course,” he told JOC.com. “The past was all about reducing unit costs, which overrode all other considerations including service quality. What was not seen, because there was no money available to spend, was investments in improving service quality including improvements in customer service. “The priorities have to change and will change,” he said. “I believe that the future will be about providing more reliability, consistent and more differentiated.” After a historic wave of consolidation over the past two years that took out several major brands, a new emboldened carrier industry will emerge. It stands to reason that something fundamental must change in an industry vital to global trade that generates more than $200 billion a year in revenue, yet achieved an average return on invested capital of just 2.6 percent from 1995 to 2016, according to a recent report on the future of container shipping by consultant McKinsey and cargo insurer TT Club. The report outlined four scenarios possible by 2043: the industry gets disrupted by new players able to effectively leverage digital; the industry leverages digitization to reinvent itself; a third wave of globalization in the developed world creates a new source of growth; and finally a “peak container” phenomenon occurs where global trade enters a long-term period of decline due to near-shoring, 3D printing, geopolitical tensions, and trade wars that lead to further consolidation among carriers. Fundamental change taking the industry in any of those directions has yet to occur — the recent imposition of emergency bunker surcharges shows how little by way of partnership exists between carriers and customers — but that is not to say change isn’t coming. Maersk’s attempted reinvention of its business as an integrated carrier in the ocean container space, the CMA CGM purchase of a stake in CEVA Logistics, and other moves suggest carriers are looking beyond their current business models. Freese believes customer service will be where major change will first start to be visible. “Something new is coming. The focus going forward will increasingly be [transitioning] from cost-cutting measures toward creating value for customers, in terms of how carriers can share in the value that is created. Carrier service will improve, as will schedule reliability, and customer service levels.” Perhaps hinting at where Hapag-Lloyd may be headed, Freese sees carriers able to do a much better job at what should be the simple task of setting clear customer expectations and delivering against them. “Carriers currently effectively sell on a ‘best effort’ promise, without being transparent or clear about service levels that customers can expect. When you promise the blue of the sky, customers could rightfully expect as much as possible because of lack of clarity having created expectation levels that carriers were never able to meet,” he said. In his view, “Cargo owners want more reliability on on-time delivery, more consistency, and they need clarity about what they are getting and what they are paying for. For example, a customer buys a certain service and asks for fast transit times and on-time delivery on intermodal. The carrier says, ‘Yes, we meet the requirements,’ [then] they go into the details, looking at port considerations and the current trucker challenge. “You need to be much more precise. You should tell the customer that different ports have different dwell times. It gets down to the details; by going into the details, you don’t disappoint your customer because you have discussed it in detail. It has not created an expectation level that you can never fulfill.” One school of thought is that carriers will have to demonstrate they can create value for customers as a first step to eventually being compensated for the value they create. That is a key point, suggesting that carriers will have to invest significantly in business reinvention on the premise that they can finally — after decades — break the cycle of arm’s length, price-based relationships. “The carriers are investing in ships, terminals, and technology so that they can deliver more integrated services. When this happens, the discussions with [beneficial cargo owners] will move from price to value,” said Bob Sappio, former longtime APL executive who is now CEO of SeaCube Container Leasing. title: How will cell phone data share rethink affect freight visibility?
content: Cell phone service providers may soon pull the plug on a key data pipeline underpinning domestic visibility software, but most companies have switched to other location systems. Shippers need to ensure that their providers aren’t overly exposed to this cell phone triangulation data. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. US-based cell phone service providers are reconsidering how they share their data with third-party companies, potentially hampering freight transportation visibility solutions and drawing shippers’ attention to how such providers accrue data. In mid-June, news outlets reported that three of the largest US mobile phone carriers — Verizon Wireless, AT&T, and T-Mobile — are deciding whether to provide network location data to a wide range of companies, including two that act as conduits to a range of freight visibility solutions providers. Most of the visibility solutions providers, or other software companies whose products rely on location data, have either publicly downplayed the significance of the move, or told JOC.com they don’t rely much or at all on such data. Shippers using such tools would do well to query their service providers about those companies’ reliance on third-party location data, and plan accordingly if they do. Freight visibility providers use a number of means to gain insight into the location of in-transit cargo. Cell phone location has been a key one in the past eight years, but other methods have grown in popularity more recently. Those include the use of data from electronic logging devices (ELDs) in trucks, the prevalence of apps downloaded by drivers, and the emergence of physical sensors that track cargo at the truck, pallet, or even item level. This has powered a rapid evolution in freight tracking technology that increasingly has shifted control over the location data from the carrier to the shipper. In terms of access to cell location data, the issue boils down to whether the three large US cell phone service providers will change the manner in which they share data with third-party companies, or stop providing data at all to the companies, which include California-based LocationSmart and Zumigo. That decision is not likely to come before November, sources told JOC.com. “The LocationSmart tech is a fallback,” said Jim Heide, vice president of administration at visibility provider 10-4 Systems. “Our primary source is either the carrier’s ELD or from their TMS [transportation management system], which is sourced by an ELD or a GPS system they have in the cab. That tends to be richer, more reliable, and more cost-effective than paying the cell providers for location.” Heide said that 10-4 also has a mobile app if they’re unable to get ELD or GPS data via a direct integration with the carrier or telematics provider. 10-4 has a direct line to major telematics provider PeopleNet, as both companies are owned by Trimble. “If the driver’s unwilling or unable to use our app, then we turn to LocationSmart,” Heide said, pegging the percentage of the data gathered via triangulation at less than 1 percent. LocationSmart — which told JOC.com it works with about two dozen companies in the cargo transportation market — said initial coverage of its role in the flow of data from cell phone carrier to visibility providers and freight brokers wrongly characterized the company as a data aggregator. “We’re not an aggregator,” said LocationSmart CEO Mario Proietti. “It’s more a request/response situation. “We only pass through data. Someone requests it, and we pass it through.” In an FAQ, the company said it has incorrectly been characterized as a company that allows marketers to track the location of cellphone users, without the consent of the users. “That description is wrong,” the company said. “LocationSmart does not provide location information about anyone without their consent.” LocationSmart has been supplying visibility providers with cell location data since 2010, but only of late have they fought the perception that they are collecting more data than they ought to be, Proietti said. Part of that is growing concerns over data privacy, which is becoming a larger factor in business decisions inside and outside the logistics industry. But Proietti emphasized that LocationSmart only has insight into the location of a cell phone based on a driver opting in, and that its insight ends when the driver opts out. That opt-in generally happens when a driver is prompted to do so at the start of a load, and ends when the driver delivers the load. At the heart of the issue is the evolving way visibility providers are gathering data. Providers are relying much less on cell phone data for a couple reasons. Many told JOC.com the data are less granular and somewhat less reliable than data acquired by other means. ELDs, for instance, track the exact location of vehicles, while driver apps are intended to run in the background on drivers’ phones. (Many are designed to create load-matching platforms between truckers and shippers.) Proietti doesn’t quibble with the notion that cell phone location data are less precise than, for instance, the GPS data collected via an app. The nature of cell phone network data means that LocationSmart is tapping into a triangulated location between cell service towers, not the exact, to-the-inch location of the phone. Visibility providers also said that the cell phone triangulation data tend to be more costly than gathering data via ELDs or through an app, through it’s less expensive than a network of physical sensors. App networks aren’t necessarily costly to develop from a software perspective, but they are hard to build from a network density perspective. But then, every shipper doesn’t need such granularity, particularly the bulk of multi-day truckload shipments. “To know where the phone is within a few hundred meters is quite good for long haul,” Proietti said. He added that cell phone providers have the ability to provide more granularity in their data — for instance, to help emergency assistance requested through 911 calls — but that the data provided for cargo tracking is less precise. LocationSmart’s biggest source of revenue is providing data for roadside assistance services. (Freight visibility data account for about 20 percent of its revenue, the company said). More prickly than the granularity issue are the data privacy considerations of using such data. “Many shippers and third-party logistics providers we know have expressed concerns about service disruptions that could impact their supply chain visibility,” FourKites CEO Mathew Elenjickal wrote in a June 20 blog post. “FourKites will not be impacted by any disruptions. Unlike older systems that rely on cell phone triangulation as the predominant method for tracking freight, less than 5 percent of our location tracking is derived from cellular data.” He wrote that FourKites uses a network of 5 million GPS and ELD telematics devices. Another visibility provider, project44, told JOC.com it doesn’t expect any potential changes by major wireless providers to interrupt its full truckload tracking services, as the company uses application programming interfaces (APIs) to connect directly to carriers and telematics devices. “The largest portion of our tracking information comes from a direct API connection with transportation carriers or by connecting telematics devices into our network,” the company said. “For smaller carriers that do not leverage advanced technology solutions, such as APIs or telematics devices, we look to leverage cell phone triangulation with the appropriate legal consent of the driver. For this very small percentage of our network, we do not expect service interruptions from wireless providers for the remainder of the calendar year, with the exception of Sprint [which earlier announced it would stop providing data to third-party companies].” Ziad Ismail, chief product officer at the load-matching platform Convoy, told JOC.com that his company doesn’t work with LocationSmart and Zumigo. “We explicitly ask for permission on the Convoy app from drivers before we use their location,” he said. “We look at location as a way to improve the experience for drivers. We also look at location as a way to improve the experience and service-quality for our shippers.” Trucker Tools, an app-based platform for drivers that also provides load matching, said it obtains GPS location data directly through its mobile application on the smart phones of drivers. The app integrates with the smart phone’s GPS software to capture location data, which is then transmitted over Trucker Tools’ network, and displayed in the company’s load tracking and carrier management applications. Descartes, which owns MacroPoint, another prominent visibility provider that championed the use of cell phone triangulation data, did not respond to a request for comment for this story. As shippers weigh the primary manner in which their visibility providers collect data, one source told JOC.com he expected the third-party data well to eventually run dry, especially as it relates to non-critical services like freight. Revenue from this segment of the business is not lucrative enough for cell phone carriers to take the risk of running afoul of data privacy regulations, or public backlash, the source said. We also look at location as a way to improve the experience and service-quality for our shippers.” Trucker Tools, an app-based platform for drivers that also provides load matching, said it obtains GPS location data directly through its mobile application on the smart phones of drivers. The app integrates with the smart phone’s GPS software to capture location data, which is then transmitted over Trucker Tools’ network, and displayed in the company’s load tracking and carrier management applications. Descartes, which owns MacroPoint, another prominent visibility provider that championed the use of cell phone triangulation data, did not respond to a request for comment for this story. As shippers weigh the primary manner in which their visibility providers collect data, one source told JOC.com he expected the third-party data well to eventually run dry, especially as it relates to non-critical services like freight. Revenue from this segment of the business is not lucrative enough for cell phone carriers to take the risk of running afoul of data privacy regulations, or public backlash, the source said. title: Bank's push of cross-border trade blockchain complicates single platform aim
content: Global trade-oriented blockchain solutions are moving from pilot to purported commercial viability in Asia and Europe, as shippers evaluate whether blockchain is something in which they should invest in the short term and which project to back. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The advancement of European- and Japanese-based blockchain consortiums reflects the financial industry’s growing interest in harnessing cross-border trade efficiencies, but also points to the potential complications of multiple offerings muddying the adoption of a common platform. The Japanese systems integration company NTT Data this week said it has enlisted a consortium of 14 companies to commercialize a trade-related blockchain platform it has been building since 2016. And this week, a European blockchain consortium of nine banks said it conducted its first cross-border commercial transactions, with 10 unnamed companies completing blockchain-executed trades via four banks. For shippers, the platforms represent one of the more potentially tangible applications of blockchain to be presented publicly in that it involves a wide cross-section of parties related to international trade. The parties involved in the consortium include several household names in the global maritime and freight forwarding business, notably “K” Line, MOL, and NYK Line, and Nippon Express. But the consortium also includes a range of Japanese banks, insurance conglomerates, and trading companies. Among the trading companies are Marubeni, a major player in cereal and paper pulp trading, Sojitz, which is involved in commercial aircraft sales, oil and gas commissions, and chemicals production, and Toyota Tsusho, the trading arm of the Toyota Group. The aim of the NTT Data platform is similar to those of other such proposals: to rid global trade of manual data entry and provide a database in which only legitimate processes and transactions are allowed. For example, Maersk and IBM have developed a joint venture company to build blockchain to facilitate global trade transactions. And Slync is a company building a plug-and-play blockchain for companies to use for track and trace, cold chain monitoring, and regulatory compliance. “International trade procedures involve various cross-national organizations, and documents are still sent in paper form or as faxes, e-mails, PDFs, or Excel files, and operators visually check them and then manually enter the data into that company’s system,” NTT Data said in a summary of the platform it sent to JOC.com. “No matter what kind of business it is or how big the company might be, such a process is repeatedly conducted every day all over the world, and the workload is enormous. Moreover, because visual and manual checks are being conducted, it is very difficult to avoid human error.” More specifically, the platform is designed to connect trade stakeholders, including importers, exporters, banks, insurance companies, carriers, and forwarders, and digitalize trade documents. NTT Data said it has plans to apply blockchain to two core areas of trade: letters of credit and cargo insurance. It has tested applications in both areas and sees the consortium’s participation as the vehicle to take those projects from pilot to commercialization. The company announced in June 2017 a “smart insurance” pilot, which it said reduced the shipper’s data-input workload by about 85 percent and the insurer’s workload by about 83 percent compared with conventional web-based systems for issuing insurance. That pilot was developed with Tokio Marine & Nichido Fire Insurance, a member of the consortium. “In international trade transactions, the time lag between delivery and payment can create risks, especially if the companies are far apart geographically and if the cargo shipment takes time,” Tetsunosuke Shinya, manager at Tokio Marine & Nichido Fire Insurance, said in a statement describing the problem facing shippers and insurers. “To avoid such risks, there is the universal business practice of utilizing letters of credit issued by banks, but this procedure is a little complicated and can take some time.” In December, NTT Data said it had also established an application programming interface (API) with Singapore’s National Trade Platform. The test case for the API involved Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group’s (MUFG) banking entity, the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, another consortium member. The API between NTT Data and the Singapore platform is intended to show that cross-border trade flows can be managed via blockchain. “It will see MUFG and NTT DATA collaborating to address and provide digital solutions to technical challenges prevalent in international trade, where differing trade regulations and documentation standards predominate,” the company said in a statement. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is attempting to link that trading platform to those in other countries, such as Hong Kong, and is developing blockchain-based inter-bank payment solutions. Meanwhile, another blockchain-related trade platform to note is we.trade, a consortium of nine European banks (including Deutsche Bank, HSBC, Rabobank, Banco Santander, Société Générale, and KBC) attempting to build a cross-border platform to underpin trade transactions between buyers and sellers. It uses Hyperledger Fabric, an open-sourced blockchain project that enables permissioned blockchains to help those buyers and sellers manage, track, and secure trade transactions. A permissioned blockchain is one where a party (or parties) gives permission to other parties to either add or access data (or both). More specifically, we.trade is trying to enable, among other things, buyers to more efficiently and securely identify unknown counterparties (i.e., foreign suppliers), set up event-based automated payment, and track and trace with more than 400 couriers. The Dublin, Ireland-based entity we.trade platform is currently available in 11 European countries. Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. title: UPS order shows CNG-powered rigs still trucking in electric age
content: Electric trucks have been grabbing headlines lately, as startups and established truck makers develop and test battery-powered models, but don’t discount compressed natural gas (CNG) as an alternative fuel. UPS last month invested $130 million to buy more than 700 new CNG-powered trucks and related technology, building on $190 million in CNG investments in the previous two years. That dwarfs the company’s order in January for 125 Tesla all-electric Semis. Those trucks, still in development, are expected to be delivered in 2019. “The buzz is all about electric. But unfortunately, we only have 300 electric vehicles [EVs] in our entire fleet,” Scott Phillippi, UPS senior director of maintenance and engineering, international operations, said in an interview. The CNG-powered truck “is what we hope electric evolves into,” Phillippi said. “It’s a viable option through the truck OEMs [original equipment manfacturers], you don’t need a boutique solution.” A fueling infrastructure is in place, and while CNG is not as ubiquitous as diesel, the fuel is available where needed. “CNG may not be the perfect solution, but let’s not let perfect be an enemy of good,” he said. This isn’t an “either one power-source or the other” situation, Phillippi stressed. “There’s so many different applications of technology, and in some cases, hybrid solutions.” In addition to the Tesla order, UPS is working with manufacturer Workhorse to develop an electric package car. “Electric is part of the equation, but right now it’s a combination for sure,” he said. The CNG investment helps UPS get closer to its goal of having one in four vehicles purchased be either an alternative fuel or advanced technology vehicle by 2020. By 2025, UPS hopes alternative fuels will represent 40 percent of total ground fuel, up from 21.8 percent a year ago. In 2017, UPS CNG vehicles racked up 1.8 million miles a day, or 8 million miles a week. Several factors are propelling UPS and other transportation operators toward alternative fuels, fuel economy and efficiency being just one. But UPS’s global customers are serious about corporate targets to reduce their carbon footprint and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Increased urban traffic also is leading to more local air quality regulation, as in Southern California. In Dublin, Ireland, UPS last year introduced an “eco package hub” distribution center from which deliveries are made either by foot or by bike — a throwback to UPS’s origins in 1907, when company founders James E. Casey and Claude Ryan made deliveries by bicycle. The largest global transportation provider, UPS tested electric-assist trailers and bikes in London too. UPS has more than 9,000 alternative fuel vehicles in its “rolling laboratory,” out of a fleet of more than 100,000 vehicles. They include electric and hybrid EVs, hydraulic hybrids, ethanol and propane vehicles, as well as CNG and liquefied natural gas trucks. “We don’t have any hydrogen vehicles in our fleet, but we want to be experienced in all areas,” Phillippi said. All of these vehicles, he pointed out, have strengths and weaknesses, and some may be better suited for specific regions or applications than others. In Europe, Phillippi said, there’s not as much interest in CNG as in the United States. “They’re more concerned about carbon footprint than [GHG] or NOx [nitrogen oxide] emissions,” he said. CNG, of course, is a carbon-based fuel. UPS is purchasing 400 Class 8 CNG tractors from Freightliner and Kenworth and 330 terminal trucks from TICO. The company also will build five new CNG fuel stations, and deploy the vehicles on routes connected to those stations. “Natural gas has a real important place in our fleet,” Phillippi said. “With CNG, you can add renewable natural gas by capturing methane [emissions] that would have gone into the atmosphere and burning it for fuel.” Most important, CNG technology is well established, with a nationwide fueling footprint. UPS has been working with the fuel since the 1980s, and has seen several generations of technical improvements. “There’s been a lot of lessons learned along the way,” Phillippi said. “We started out thinking there wasn’t going to be enough capacity for energy on board with CNG.” The ability to carry more CNG fuel onboard in stacked fuel tanks as vehicle design evolved was “probably our biggest leap forward,” Phillippi said. “Now we can do what a diesel [vehicle] can do from a [mileage] range standpoint, and that’s important. We used to talk about reliability with the fleet. We can now say the CNG fleet is performing as well if not better than the diesel fleet.” One factor driving interest in alternative fuels among truckers is the increasing cost of diesel emissions control technology. “With CNG, we’re trading diesel aftertreatment systems for spark plugs. That’s been a good trade for us,” Phillippi said. Diesel isn’t going away anytime soon as a major fuel, but the use of alternatives such as natural gas and electricity is sure to expand. There’s no doubt EVs will play a bigger and bigger role as the infrastructure needed to power them expands and their reliability increases. “We think electrification is getting really close to starting to make sense financially,” Phillippi said. “When you want to put 100 vehicles in a facility, you have to think about how to deploy a vehicle that uses that much energy.” “We’d like to see electric business cases drive this forward,” he said. “We need to quantify the value [EVs] bring to a business. My expectation is that electric will take the same role internal combustion engines did in the 1930s and 1940s, but we make decisions based on bottom-line impact, based on economics.” And currently, the economics for UPS favor CNG. title: JOC Blockchain Explainer: Demystifying the buzz for the shipping industry
content: Many experts argue that blockchain technology is tailor-made for container shipping’s international logistics work. But blockchain faces numerous hurdles — the biggest of which may be cultural. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Blockchain promises to help transform container shipping, but there’s plenty to resolve as this technology gains traction. The industry is not only split on whether blockchain is hype or real, but it’s also unclear about how the technology works and what it can do. Blockchain may be an overhyped promise for now, but it’s not an empty one. The architecture of the technology seems to marry perfectly with the structures of the modern supply chain. And, just as importantly, it has the vague hope of allowing the shipping and logistics industry to potentially leapfrog technologically. But there is a long way to go from here to there. In an attempt to clarify what blockchain is, how it works, what it can do, and the hurdles to adoption, JOC’s Blockchain Explainer will be updated as the industry learns more and sees pilots and proof of concepts put into action. At its most basic level, blockchain is a database, but it is a different kind of database than most in transportation and logistics are accustomed to. Think of it as the ability for multiple parties to absolutely rely on the accuracy of a single transaction or action. Now imagine a string of transactions and actions that build on each other cryptographically. For instance, blockchain could be set up to establish the chain of custody in a container shipment. Such a scenario would see ownership of the freight transferred digitally once a set of conditions has been met (such as delivery from origin port to destination port) with a specific action (such as confirmation that the container has been unloaded from the vessel) triggering the change of ownership and payment between parties. The underlying structure of blockchain, in theory, would confirm the veracity of the information being entered, the data that trigger those actions. If any data were incorrect, it would be identifiable by other entities participating in the blockchain. Chris Kirchner, CEO at the blockchain in supply chain software startup Slync, described it as a “collaborative system of record that provides a single source of truth among partners with immutability to protect against data manipulation.” To Kirchner, the key points of blockchain are immutability (meaning it cannot be changed) and the way its collaborative nature “reduces disputes and allows companies to hold their vendors accountable in real time versus requiring an audit to do so.” To many, even those in software, the benefits of blockchain technology remain elusive. It’s somewhat derisively referred to as a “solution in search of a problem,” while advocates portray it as the most transformational technology since the internet. In theory, anyone can use blockchain because, in theory, any application can be blockchain-enabled. Not to be obtuse, but the parties who would use it and the applications they would use it for are limited only by the imagination (and some other practical constraints, described in more detail below). From a technical perspective, blockchain is not considered a highly complicated technology. The differentiating feature is the type of encryption used in blockchain. The bigger challenges are finding specific uses where it provides value and return on investment, where it is not too disruptive to existing processes, and where multiple parties might agree to standards in which they are comfortable with the commercial and legal implications of blockchain-enabled transaction. Blockchain is not a piece of software so much as it is a way to build software, or to reconfigure an existing piece of software. As mentioned above, the key distinguishing feature of blockchain technology is the way it is encrypted. With that in mind, it’s theoretically possible to build blockchain around any existing process, system, or problem. This has been a problem early on in the adoption of blockchain in that it has become such a buzzword that it is likely being suggested for too many problems (many of which blockchain technology is not required to solve). “A blockchain is not a piece of software,” Fauad Shariff, founder of the freight forwarding software startup CoLoadX, wrote in a May blog post. “There is no controlling authority or a ‘blockchain world headquarters.’ There is no government, financial system, or outside entity that can interfere with a given blockchain unless it is already a party to its transactions. The blockchain’s decentralized structure [if you can call it that] closely mirrors the reality of logistics.” Here’s where things get fun. There have been numerous pilot projects conducted by a range of logistics (and logistics adjacent) parties over the past two years to test the efficacy of blockchain in a commercial trade or logistics setting. It’s hard to know exactly how successful these individual pilots have been given that most have been conducted in private, and generally with a limited scope. But they have universally touted the benefits of blockchain around the following metrics: elimination of middlemen; reduction of paperwork associated with data entry; the ability to link parties needing to share data on a common platform; increasing the trust associated with geographically dispersed trading partners; the ability to establish the provenance of a good or raw material from its origin; and the capability to trigger supply chain processes (including payment) in real time. The cynical answer is that blockchain is hot because the tech world needs a buzzword around which to build hype, and blockchaiin fulfills that role nicely. The more nuanced answer is that there are people — builders of blockchain solutions and potential users — who see a vision of what this technology can become in a few years and are eager to get the logistics industry (and many others) started down that path. And they see a pent up desire in logistics for a technology that would enable a quantum leap versus an incremental step change in efficiency, given that the industry has long operated inefficiently. Advocates also note that blockchain appears to be tailor-made for a multi-party environment such as international logistics. This is really impossible to answer at present because the technology is so early in its adoption curve that one would need a crystal ball to say with any authority how widespread the use of blockchain will become. It seems reasonably safe to say that blockchain will make an impact in logistics, but it also seems reasonably safe to say that it will not completely transform logistics in the way that many advocates have proposed. As noted above, there have been a plethora of blockchain pilots undertaken across the liner shipping, global trade, government regulatory, trade finance, insurance, and visibility realms. The most prominent is Maersk and IBM’s joint venture to create blockchain to support global trade. The two companies had previously participated in a pilot meant to demonstrate how much physical paperwork is associated with a single container shipment and how blockchain could digitize the production and collection of those documents. In March, Accenture, the shipping line APL, the freight forwarder Kuehne + Nagel, the beverage manufacturer InBev, and a European customs organization tested a blockchain solution on 12 shipments to eliminate paper or digital submission of documents associated with the cargo moves. And a handful of blockchain startups, such as Hong Kong-based 300Cubits, Denmark-based Blockshipping, and Slovenia-based CargoX have set out to show how blockchain and associated cryptocurrencies might transform core shipping processes, such as booking, container tracking, and bill of lading creation. And these are just the ones that have been publicly acknowledged. Nearly every software provider of any significance is dabbling in the technology. All of them are testing whether there is a commercially viable application to pursue. Simplifying and digitizing logistics documents When it comes to the possible implementation of blockchain in international logistics, the most straightforward idea is to provide a single, cloud-based repository of documents (or more simply the data behind the documents, as physical documents in a pure blockchain environment would disappear) to which appropriate parties involved in a shipment can interact. This repository would work on a permissioned basis, meaning some parties (most likely the beneficial cargo owner [BCO]) would have access to all information, while some parties (a supplier, a carrier, a third-party logistics provider [3PL], or a governmental agency) might only have access to the data relevant to them. In this scenario, the BCO would likely have access to all the information because the blockchain would pertain to its cargo, its vendors, and its data submission requirements. This use of blockchain is not all that revolutionary — it’s essentially what software-as-a-service shipment management software providers have been trying to do for more than a decade, to provide the so-called “single version of the truth.” What blockchain would do is more tightly govern where inaccuracies occur, who was responsible for them, and when. This is a relatively mundane use case for blockchain, but it’s a pain point in logistics nonetheless. “Data can be altered before being shared with partners in the current environment,” said Kirchner. “I’ve been surprised to find how commonplace this is in discussions with customers.” One of the more common use cases for blockchain in the supply chain so far has centered on the idea of product traceability, the idea that a shipper or its end consumers can have visibility to a product from cradle to grave. This could have branding benefits (such as in organic produce or fair trade goods), or it could help narrow down the origins of a public safety threat, such as a foodborne illness or counterfeit pharmaceuticals. This is a use case that extends beyond logistics and global trade into product sourcing and quality management. Perhaps the most compelling theoretical use case for blockchain is tied to payments in supply chains, whether from importer to suppliers, or from shipper to transportation and logistics providers. These payment processes are unwieldy, can be costly, and often rely on a third party (a bank) to underwrite a transaction, especially with an unknown party. The theory is that the trust engendered by blockchain would enable, for instance, an importer to more seamlessly and quickly pay an unknown supplier in a far flung region with which it has no history doing business. That transaction today would be underpinned by a bank’s letter of credit, so that the supplier would use that the order to tap into the credit to produce the order and then be reimbursed by the importer. Exciting as this is, lots of questions remain around this use case, including whether the supplier is sophisticated enough (and willing) to participate in blockchain application, and whether the data it enters are verifiable even if entered on blockchain. The theory here is that many small-size and mid-size companies rely on a model where they ship someone goods and get paid in 60 or more days, which translates to a lot of capital being tied up. Another interesting idea is using blockchain to more closely tether regulatory processes to physical logistics processes. To be clear, there is a subset of logistics technology called global trade management (GTM) software providers that address this issue today, largely through cloud-based software where shippers can undertake trade compliance and logistics processes in a coordinated manner. Blockchain might amp up that coordination one day by providing a single database where everything from the purchase order to the bill of lading to the customs entry all reside on a single ledger. The possibilities of attaching other relevant documentation would only make this approach more appealing. Even the most sophisticated users of GTM software still struggle to manage everything in one place, viewable by all. This is the blockchain-in-supply-chain advocate’s favorite use case. A smart contract is one where some event or action triggers a resulting event. For example, a smart contract could be set up so that when a drayage driver sends a text to a BCO confirming pickup of a container at a marine terminal, the BCO automatically pays an ocean carrier. To be clear, a smart contract does not need to be blockchained, but the theory is that a blockchain-enabled smart contract would provide a level of trust in the transaction that would make such actions indisputable, dependent on the development of standards that all relevant parties are willing to buy into. “Look for processes that are slow, costly, and error-prone,” said John Whelan, blockchain lab director with Santander Bank. “That’s where blockchain makes sense.” Many people have been justifiably confused about the difference between blockchain and cryptocurrencies and how they interrelate and interact. In short, bitcoin is an example of blockchain, but not vice versa, and bitcoin is one of many cryptocurrencies available globally (estimates suggest there are at least 1,500 globally, and growing rapidly). Some of these cryptocurrencies have defined uses, meaning they are designed to be used within a specific system or industry. Others are meant to be a more general store of value. “Crypto has helped us question the nature of money,” said Whelan. “Money is a faith-based concept. The dollar is just paper or numbers on a screen. It has value because we agree it has value. Money as a unit of account is helpful. A well-managed fiat money is also a store of value — my mortgage will be [the] same this year as next year. “Bitcoin is a store of value and a unit of exchange, but it’s not legal tender and not a unit of account. Bitcoin is similar to gold — you don’t price things in bitcoin [you price them in dollars and figure out how much that is in bitcoin].” So bitcoin is a “general store of value” currency, but a handful of others have been floated in the shipping and logistics industry as a way to induce a particular commercial behavior, generally around inefficient or counterproductive processes. Some of these cryptocurrencies are optional to use, while others must be used within the confines of a certain blockchain-backed platform. "Public blockchains truly only work with an incentive mechanism in place, and to get all players to be honest in the system it requires that there be both incentive for acting fairly and punishment for dishonesty,” said John Monarch, CEO of ShipChain, which is building blockchain and associated cryptocurrency to improve domestic freight visibility. CargoX, which is building blockchain to drive broader use of digital bills of lading, doesn’t require users to transact in its associated cryptocurrency, but does offer benefits for those that do. “CargoX will support all traditional banking payment options,” the company said in its FAQ. “We will, however, promote service payments with our own CXO tokens. For users that use or hold our CXO tokens, there will be additional features in the system available at a lower price or even for free.” 300Cubits is another example of a token tied to a specific logistics process — in this case, to compel liner carriers and shippers to honor container bookings. Blockshipping, meanwhile, is trying to use tokens to entice ocean shipping stakeholders to take part in a global container registry to enable more efficient use of the assets. It’s also important to note that cryptocurrencies are a way for companies to raise capital to build their company, an alternative to the more traditional mechanism of seed and venture capital funding rounds. As with almost any technology advertised as transformative in logistics, the first natural hurdle is resistance to change. But beyond the industry’s chronic fear of the unknown, there are other practical constraints more directly related to structure of blockchain. For instance, blockchain is presently a costly technology to implement. It is essentially a tightly encrypted, distributed ledger of actions, and that encryption is typically costly and resource-intensive. More than that, though, is the cost of building the distributed nodes that make blockchain work. Matt Tillman, CEO of the logistics software provider Haven, described these costs as exponentially more expensive than just the internal costs of building, since a company on blockchain is essentially expecting everyone it does business with to also be on that blockchain. If any aren’t, they’d be excluded from the scope of whatever efficiencies are gained by being on that blockchain. “Where this gets expensive is first in writing the smart contracts that run on the blockchain, second in getting other companies to participate in your scheme, and third in paying for the computing power to execute the smart contracts,” said Brian Glick, CEO of the supply chain connectivity provider Chain.io. Glick said, as a frame of reference, one of his company’s projects took 16 times the amount of development resources to build it on the blockchain as it would have taken to build it using technology it already had. On the second point, he noted that “to do collaboration on the blockchain, other companies have to subscribe to your vision and implement your protocol.” As for computing power, “to run a simple transaction on the blockchain means it has to execute on all [or most of the computers] participating in the network. This means that each ‘smart contract’ costs orders of magnitude more to execute than we're used to. I can't estimate how much it would cost us to write a single database record in our network because it's so small. Something like millionths of a cent. On the blockchain, the same transaction might cost 70 cents. Smart people are working on bringing this down, but they have a very long way to go.” Those costs will likely scare potential adopters away, until the price to build and maintain comes down, or unless there is a use case in which those costs are more than offset by the return on investment. And that, in turn, will depend on adoption by a large enough group of independent entities to create critical mass. “There are limitations around the technology, like latency, and the amount of energy it takes to verify a transaction, but because it’s about the technology, that will eventually go away,” said Ken Lyon, managing director of the consultancy Virtual Partners. Indeed, if the only thing preventing blockchain from being adopted were cost, the excitement around it might be more universal. But there are other nagging issues. Like the lack of a neutral body to set protocols that everyone would not only agree to, but adopt. The ability for key industry players to agree to common standards is a challenge in and of itself. Since blockchain’s development is often put in the context of the internet, that can be used as a basis for comparison when it comes to protocol. Today, everyone uses the TCP/IP protocol for internet access, but they don’t think much about using that protocol because it’s an accepted and established common platform. In order for blockchain to be widely used in shipping and logistics, there will need to be a similar protocol that everyone agrees to use. And it would likely need to be much more detailed, down to a contract-level of detail given that transactions are triggered via blockchains. Failing that, there will need to be a group of technology companies that essentially act as middleware, or a hub, to homogenize different blockchain protocols to make it simpler for end users. In the software industry, this is called an abstraction layer. And beyond that, it’s yet to be seen how governments might regulate blockchains — or more pertinently, how different governments might regulate transnational logistics blockchains differently. Perhaps there might emerge a single global regulatory entity, but there remains the question of what that regulating agency might be, given the international nature of global trade and logistics. “The player that controls the platform can control the data, and the industry is not comfortable to put data into a common platform [and that] is going to continue to hold the process back until we have regulations in place around how to treat that data,” said Mike DeAngelis, senior vice president, global carrier strategy and digitalization, at the freight forwarding enterprise software provider WiseTech Global. “Blockchain needs to be a non-proprietary and neutral platform.” Another major issue, especially when it comes to BCOs, is whether blockchain is just cool or whether it actually solves problems. BCOs, to this point, seem skeptical. “Blockchain is a technology that 90 percent of us do not understand, and as a shipper, we are concerned that we will not have a choice and will be pushed into something controlled by someone else,” said Ved Prakash, director of Gemini Corp., a trader of recyclable raw materials. Charles Thompson, chief information officer at the Port of Houston, said he’s cautiously optimistic about blockchain but emphasizes it won’t take hold in logistics unless a single platform comes into being. “It is not about the technology, it is about the business need and the problem we’re trying to solve,” he said. “I can’t plug into eight blockchains.” Then there are blockchain skeptics who doubt the technology’s usefulness in its entirety. “I would assert that there is no single person in existence who had a problem they wanted to solve, discovered that an available blockchain solution was the best way to solve it, and therefore became a blockchain enthusiast,” Kai Stinchcombe, CEO of True Link Financial, and founder of multiple software companies, wrote in an April blog post. “Blockchain systems do not magically make the data in them accurate or the people entering the data trustworthy, they merely enable you to audit whether it has been tampered with. A person who sprayed pesticides on a mango can still enter onto a blockchain system that the mangoes were organic.” Most people who describe blockchain as driving transparency mean that in creating a common, decentralized ledger, it is impossible to hide data. That is often brought up in the context of what blockchain means to freight forwarders, or freight brokers, companies that struggle with the perception that market opacity benefits them. Indeed, it has been posited that blockchain tying together, for example, a shipper, its suppliers, and its transportation providers would be able to disintermediate the work of a forwarder through a common ledger (outside of some hard-to-replicate work that a forwarder might do at origin). Realistically, this is too broad an application of blockchain technology in the current setting. And forwarders are undertaking their own blockchain pilots to understand what the technology means to them. Probably not. Most people don’t understand how the internet works, but are utterly and irrevocably reliant on the internet from a business and personal perspective. Many blockchain advocates advance the belief that blockchain will only truly take hold when people stop using the word blockchain, and instead refer to the user-facing applications enabled by blockchain. An analogy to consider: people washing their hands don’t think about the water treatment plant that cleaned the water, nor the pipes that brought the water to the bathroom. They tend to focus on whether the faucet works, whether the water pressure is strong enough, and whether the water temperature is comfortable. As Whelan put it, “You don’t need to understand how the cryptography works, but you do need to understand the implications.” Yes and no. Remember, at its core, blockchain is a distributed ledger. There has long been software that attempts to do something similar, mainly network-oriented software that’s accessible via a web portal. These days, those systems are more commonly referred to as cloud-based software. Users with permission can view and/or contribute to a database within those types of portals. It’s also unclear how easy it will be for laggards to catch up to, or indeed leapfrog over, early versions of logistics-oriented blockchain solutions. There is an expectation that blockchain technology will become cheaper over time. There is also a push to make it as easy to implement as possible. With that in mind, one of the more recent concepts to emerge is the idea of a blockchain hub (or in tech terms, an abstraction layer) where companies could plug into and reap the benefits of a templated blockchain solution without the steep development curve. In fact, some of the newer thinking around blockchain is that only some elements of a database need to be blockchained. In other words, it would create a similarly fragmented world of private systems and its constituent parties as exists today. “The basic concept of blockchain is great, in terms of creating an open platform for everyone to share and do things like smart contracts, but the challenge is when large organizations build their own blockchain solutions that are effectively private, they are actually going against the entire premise of what a blockchain is about,” said James Swanston, CEO of the technology provider Voyage Control.
