title: IBM-Maersk blockchain effort builds with nearly 100 users
content: Maersk and IBM have fleshed out their designs for an industrywide blockchain solution — an open-source platform called TradeLens. There are a host of other blockchain initiatives in development, but as one stakeholder noted, they joined the Maersk-IBM venture based on Maersk’s history of innovation and IBM’s technological prowess, which gives the platform a “high probability of success.” Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Maersk and IBM on Thursday closed the loop on an ambitious attempt they started in January to bring scalable blockchain solutions to liner shipping and global trade. The two companies unveiled a new entity called TradeLens that has already enlisted more than 90 parties ranging from shippers to terminal operators that touch 234 global gateways to participate on the platform. Notably, that number includes a cadre of shippers — including Torre Blanca/Camposol and Umit Bisiklet — and another container line, Pacific International Lines (PIL). The TradeLens brand emerges at an interesting time for blockchain in logistics. There are a host of other initiatives in development — most relevantly, one being developed by APL, Accenture, Kuehne + Nagel, and multinational brewer AB Inbev — but there has also been some rationalization of late about blockchain’s true potential in logistics. In other words, are blockchains required to underpin the variety of problems they are being pegged to answer? That dilemma is particularly acute for shippers making decisions about what broader technology investments they need to make. A blockchain is a distributed ledger encrypted in such a way as to make it virtually impossible to alter data entered into it. Blockchain advocates believe the technology matches perfectly with the disparate and data-hungry nature of global supply chains. For the Maersk/IBM venture in particular, there were also public and private concerns about the neutrality of the solution. Those concerns were amplified by the reach Maersk has with its sister companies Damco and APM Terminals. Maersk told JOC.com in an interview Tuesday that it and IBM focused on two areas over the past six months to ease concerns about the neutrality of the solution: open-source architecture, and the inclusion of a cross-section of industry participants. Among those 90 parties already on the platform are a handful of global terminal operators and port authorities, including PSA International, International Container Terminal Services Inc., Patrick Terminals, Modern Terminals in Hong Kong, port of Halifax, port of Rotterdam, port of Bilbao, PortConnect, PortBase, and terminal operators Holt Logistics at the Port of Philadelphia. Logistics providers Agility, CEVA Logistics (in which Maersk rival CMA CGM owns a 25 percent stake), Kotahi, PLH Trucking Company, Ancotrans, and WorldWide Alliance as well as customs authorities in the Netherlands, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Australia, and Peru have also signed on. Participants will be able to use the blockchain solution to track arrival times of vessels and container “gate-in,” and to produce documents such as customs releases, commercial invoices, and bills of lading. More broadly, the platform is designed to allow parties to “interact more efficiently through real-time access to shipping data and shipping documents, including [Internet of Things] and sensor data ranging from temperature control to container weight,” Maersk said in a statement. “We’re intent on getting as many ecosystem members participating in this as possible,” Mike White, TradeLens leader for Maersk, said in the interview with JOC.com. “We’re excited about the breadth as well as the volume of participants. We’ve studied other initiatives in development and we haven’t seen any solutions that encompass the entire scope of what we’re trying to achieve.” To assuage skepticism about neutrality of the solution, Maersk and IBM said they have made TradeLens’ application programming interfaces open and available for developer access. “This is not a solution for Maersk and IBM alone,” White said. “There’s the ability for other network members to put applications on top. Both IBM and Maersk are committed to open architecture. The solution is the architecture and the network and you only get value when you get broad adoption.” Peter Levesque, CEO of Modern Terminals, told JOC.com that Modern signed onto TradeLens based on the belief that Maersk’s history of innovation and IBM’s technological prowess gives the platform a “high probability of success.” “We fully expect there will be many competitors to create a standard in the industry,” he said. “We take our data and provide it to numerous platforms. In the future, it could be the same thing, except we’re providing it on much better platforms. Whether it’s just TradeLens or TradeLens and other platforms, from the Modern Terminals perspective, we’ll just populate those platforms with what we’re requested to do, whether it’s one or whether it’s 12. “Seems to me we have a tremendous opportunity to make a major change in the industry. Because of the opportunity, it makes sense to go with players that will make this happen as fast as possible and get to a standard.” From the terminal operator’s perspective, the ability to create a single repository of data that can be authenticated more securely is a big advancement. “There’s never been a shortage of documentation and data,” Levesque said. “TradeLens will be able to put all of that into one place. To have all these pieces in one spot that’s secure, from the port perspective, is very valuable. Container movement on/off vessels, gate in, ship arrivals. All this stuff we have, to be able to convey that to participants will have tremendous value. Customers benefit from that — we become more efficient. Systems where you’re able to view a bill of lading or a purchase order or a certificate of origin — being able to view it is one thing, knowing the authenticity of it is another thing. It’s been an issue we’ve grappled with for many years. Who even did the documentation?” In terms of adoption of the blockchain in the broader world of logistics, Levesque said it is likely that uptake will be more rapid on the origin side of supply chains, areas where there is generally less clarity around parties and the data they contribute. “Any operators, whether 3PLs [third-party logistics providers] or a terminal operator sitting at the origin point of manufacuating and seeing the complexity of documentation at origin side, sees the value of something like TradeLens,” he said. “There’s a difference between having to generate all those documents versus being on the receiving end. If you lower your supply chain costs by 20 to 30 percent, you’ll see heavy incentive at origin to make it happen.” On the destination side, border agencies and customs authorities will likely see the initial value first, “because they have certainty about what’s in the pipeline. It could be someday that customs require this, maybe it’s not an option. You won’t be able to send into a country unless you’re on a blockchain.” Maersk and IBM adapted their go-to-market strategy for TradeLens after consulting with interested parties over the past 12 months, White said. He called the relationship between the two a collaborative agreement rather than a joint venture, another signal to the industry that TradeLens is not designed to be a bespoke solution for the Danish line and its sister companies Damco and APM Terminals. Levesque, for instance, said the platform might help it to better manage berth planning, operating windows, and communication with customers related to physical cargo handoffs and documentation. “CEVA sees a unique opportunity in TradeLens, joining forces with IBM, Maersk and other actors from our industry to promote global standards around an open and neutral solution, delivering on the promise of blockchain,” Christophe Cachat, CIO of CEVA Logistics, said in a statement. White, meanwhile, said Maersk and IBM are actively seeking other shipping lines aside from PIL to join the platform, and they are in “serious engagement with a number of other carriers.” The partners are also driving broader adoption from 3PLs and beneficial cargo owners (BCOs). “As the network increases, so does the richness of the data,” he said. Liner shipping analyst Lars Jensen, CEO of SeaIntelligence Consulting, said in a LinkedIn post Thursday that while the number of parties participating is impressive, it is notable that only one carrier has agreed to be publicly associated with the platform. “Does this mean that TradeLens might falter due to lack of carrier buy-in?,” he wrote. “If one was to be a pessimist, it can be argued that Maersk and IBM have now [spent] more than half a year to get stakeholders onboard, and apart from PIL they have not yet succeeded in doing so on the carrier side. On the other hand, one might also argue that other carriers might not necessarily need to jump into bed directly with TradeLens.” Jensen noted that TradeLens is working with openshipping.org to develop alignment on standards, which might provide a smoother path to industry adoption. "Multiple blockchain trials are in progress in the industry, and it is beginning to look less likely that all will coalesce around one specific solution/product,” Jensen wrote. “Rather we might see a landscape of varying solutions, but all centered around the adoption of new standards.” Those standards might, however, prove elusive, since other attempts to standardize processes in liner shipping — everything from bill of lading format to invoicing — have fallen flat. There’s also the argument that traditional standards run counter to the optimal use of blockchain. Aside from the ability to produce shipping documents, TradeLens is also trialling a trade document module called ClearWay that is intended to enable importers/exporters, customs brokers, and customs and other government agencies to collaborate on the production and submission of those documents. “When we talk about global supply chains, customs and government agencies are often omitted from carrier-customer relationships,” White said. “They have the same problems, ever increasing levels of trade.” The ability to link freight and trade compliance documents in a single decentralized database may well set TradeLens apart from a number of other blockchain initiatives, which tend to be focused on one element or the other. For instance, the APL consortium is initially building a blockchain solution for electronic bills of lading, as is the independent startup CargoX. The startup Slync is building a flexible smart contract-based platform to manage everything from trade document creation to product provenance. Those startups, of course, haven’t set off with the brand recognition that Maersk and IBM have. That could be seen as a positive though, as some shipping lines and BCOs have called for the emergence of neutral, flexible platforms not affiliated with a carrier. White said Maersk understands the blockchain solution needs to be transparent and benefit parties that are using it or are compelled to do so by other supply chain partners. “We need to understand it from the participant’s perspective,” White said. “We won’t have captive vendors — they need to have value from this. We lose our right to validity if this doesn’t provide them value.” The TradeLens solution is available today through the platform’s Early Adopter Program. TradeLens is expected to be fully commercially available by the end of this year, the companies said. Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. title: Skepticism of Maersk-IBM’s TradeLens hit bigger blockchain questions
content: A LinkedIn discussion served as a microcosm for how shippers and the broader logistics industry are wrestling with a few key questions regarding blockchain. Are blockchain’s proponents inordinately and/or prematurely boosting the new technology — including its appropriateness and efficiency-enhancing capabilities? Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Last week’s launch of Maersk’s and IBM’s blockchain platform, called TradeLens, was met by encouragement but also skepticism of its benefits to shippers, broader claims of productivity, and who’s verifying the latter. The discussion is a microcosm for how shippers and the broader logistics industry is wrestling with a few key questions regarding blockchain: its cost, its imminent applicability, which parties will provide solutions, and whether there is value in being an early adopter. The introduction of TradeLens, first hinted at by Maersk and IBM in January when they said they were working together to build a commercially viable blockchain platform for global trade, has brought some of those concerns into sharper relief. The platform purports to be the conduit for disparate trading partners to conduct core global shipping and trade processes, using blockchain technology to ensure the veracity, security, and timeliness of data submissions and movements between parties. Maersk said in a briefing last week with JOC.com that it sees massive potential for shippers from the solution in terms of creating a single, immutable repository for shipping and trade documentation. The carrier also said it would enable shippers to get shipment milestones and documents provided to the platform “in structured and unstructured form,” said Mike White, TradeLens leader for Maersk. But it’s not the only game in town. There are dozens of global trade-related blockchain initiatives, including some backed by rivals of Maersk, and the hype has created a bubble of uncertainty about whether shippers need to invest in the technology, and when. There have also been questions about the scalability of blockchain platforms developed by single liner carriers — not just Maersk’s, but also ones being built by APL and CargoSmart, long linked to OOCL. Both Maersk and APL have said they are seeking to drive adoption of their solutions by other carriers. Blockchain, at its most basic level, is a highly encrypted database that advocates believe matches well with the structure of global supply chains. These proponents see blockchain as the platform for data to be shared and, in the future, they envision blockchain allowing new, more efficient shipping processes to germinate. But skepticism among shippers remains, crystallized by Andrew Nutting, former director of international logistics at Bob’s Discount Furniture, who started a thread on LinkedIn Friday questioning a report that claimed the solution could reduce “shipping times” by 40 percent. “For argument, let us say the typical transit from [Shanghai] to [Los Angeles] via ocean is 14 days,” Nutting wrote. “Is it the case IBM is saying they will cut this to eight days? This is my biggest criticism of [blockchain] technology, the over-exaggerated claims. Shipping times get cut nearly in half, by having a distributed ledger of data?” While the reports probably meant to refer to either a potential reduction in end-to-end shipment time, or more likely, such a reduction in the human resources needed to manage a shipment, the thread seemed to underscore the extent to which shippers are exposed to inaccurate information or inflated expectations surrounding blockchain’s role in logistics. “When blockchain moves from competing platforms to a global standard adopted across your supply chain ecosystem, it should reduce transaction administration and traceability effort by even more than 40 percent,” wrote Colin Taylor, founder and principal at Cleaca Consulting and a veteran of Maersk Data and IBM. “But shipping times of international cargo? ... no. Blockchain attracts false kudos for shipment visibility, which is confused with traceability.” Part of the issue may be that blockchain is so early in its maturation, and there are so few tangible examples of commercialized products in logistics, that single-use cases get extrapolated into broader potential too easily. “I'm very confident that what IBM and Maersk is doing will provide long term benefit, but when I see ‘one example’ at the beginning of any stat, it is likely the author capturing an outlier as a best case scenario,” said Brian Glick, founder and CEO of logistics technology provider Chain.io. “Even a 10 percent to 20 percent impact on time in transit due to reduced port delays across a large swath of shipments would be awesome. I think the tech can accomplish that.” “It is a pretty big stretch to go from ‘one example’ to ‘average,’” he wrote. “I understand the principle of how [blockchain] will speed transactions in theory, but in most cases, shipments are pre-cleared prior to arrival and departure. Meaning, prior to any availability of departure or delivery documents have already been submitted and confirmed. In practical application, if your shipment is already cleared five days prior to the first available date of delivery, how do [you] increase the speed from there? On the first day it is available, the documents have cleared. I am struggling to see how that transaction is made faster by any measure by blockchain.” "We believe that all players across the supply chain stand to benefit from the digitization of trade, with the exact benefits depending on the individual participant, needs and nature of business. At this point we do not have statistics or figures on general impact for the various ecosystem across the supply chain to share," said TradeLens Spokesperson Janina von Spalding, noting that the company provided examples of how TradeLens saved participants time and cost during its pilot phase. James Stewart, a global account executive with Crane Worldwide Logistics and veteran of Geodis and CargoSmart, concurring, said shipment documentation is not what is slowing down supply chains. “Blockchain in shipping has a lot of hype around it at the moment, and just because IBM and Maersk think it’s interesting doesn’t mean the market needs, nor can it afford, whatever solution they come up with,” he wrote. “The paperwork and payment are the last things slowing down cargo flows, but don’t tell that to the venture capital flooding the space.” Aside from TradeLens, a consortium of APL, Accenture, Kuehne + Nagel, and AB InBev is working to create a container shipment documentation blockchain solution, while startups are also aiming to digitize the primarily paper- and email-based documents related to trade. Glick intimated that while most blockchain vendors are overreaching in applying blockchain to processes where it’s not required, there is some value to the exposure the technology is receiving. “I feel like most of the benefits don't ‘need’ blockchain, but it seems like an incredible motivator for companies to share data the way they should have been all along,” he wrote. The thread also delved into how application programming interface (API) connectivity, not blockchain, is what is driving value in terms of linking trading partners, carriers, and logistics companies in a real-time manner. “I have often said blockchain will work, and it is secure,” Nutting said. “Some of the characteristics being [ascribed] to blockchain technology are not actually part of the blockchain. For instance, when you talk about real-time visibility, a blockchain solution will do that, but not because of the blockchain but rather the API functionality tied to the blockchain. The blockchain is not the mechanism driving the real-time visibility, it is the benefactor of the API integration.” APIs are a method of system-to-system communication that are gaining traction in shipping and logistics as a more real-time way to shuttle data back and forth. However, beneficial cargo owners, particularly large ones, are still reliant on the frameworks they’ve created through electronic data interchange (EDI), particularly the structure inherent in those networks. The issue, though, is that EDI and blockchain are not well-suited to each other. Blockchain platforms, as Nutting noted, rely on data fed to and from them by APIs. “Blockchain in logistics seems to be more code for ‘hey, let's stop using a fax and courier for our docs’ than actual blockchain,” wrote Caro Krissman, chairman and founder of the freight forwarding software provider INLT. “The real answer here is APIs connecting all the niche and disparate players that make up the supply chain, or some type of [communication] uniformity.” Meanwhile, another strain of chatter around the TradeLens announcement centered on the idea that the venture is making blockchain more tangible in the eyes of the shipping community. That line of thinking was summarized neatly by Fauad Shariff, co-founder and CEO of the forwarding software provider CoLoadX, who wrote, “To a large extent IBM and Maersk are forced to remind us that their blockchain platform is real. It’s obviously still too early to be operational, but let’s not trouble ourselves with those details.” The TradeLens platform has nearly 100 parties formally attached to it, the companies said last week, and expect the solution to be commercially operational by the end of the year. “I think the hype is starting to fade,” he wrote. “An interesting take in another conversation I was involved [in] focused around a lack of education/understanding. My position has been: I think people ‘get it’ but a fair number have said they are not interested. In everything I have seen, blockchain in supply chain will work to some extent. It will provide some ancillary benefits, but not to the full extent being reported, and not without adding some additional challenges. I believe the industry is quietly and politely saying they are not interested or at least not currently interested. Blockchain is the overly persistent salesperson.” Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric. title: Tentative ILA-USMX master contract bans full terminal automation
content: For shippers, agreement approval would remove the uncertainty hanging over the Gulf and East coast ports as the Sept. 30 expiration of the contract approaches. The ban on fully automated terminals, however, could also quash shipper hopes that some of the East and Gulf coasts’ more expensive ports might harness automation and technology to cut costs and improve efficiency. (Above: The Port of New York and New Jersey.) Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. A tentative, six-year master contract between the International Longshoremen’s Association (ILA) and United States Maritime Alliance (USMX) would prohibit fully automated terminal operations for six years at East and Gulf ports covered by the contract, according to a summary of the deal posted on the union’s website. The agreement, reached by the ILA and USMX on June 6, also addresses the challenges of the mega-ship era, according to the 14-minute video featuring a presentation of the contract by ILA executive vice president Dennis A. Daggett. The contract gives terminals greater flexibility in managing union workers — allowing a reduced mandatory work period — in situations in which a vessel fails to arrive on schedule. The video provides the first details of the contract, which, if approved by rank-and-file ILA members, would ensure labor peace on both coasts until at least 2024, and parallels a labor deal for US West Coast ports lasting until 2022. For shippers, approval of the agreement would remove the uncertainty hanging over the Gulf and East coast ports as the Sept. 30 expiration of the contract approaches. The union has yet to ratify the agreement, and declined to comment on it beyond the video. The ban on fully automated terminals, however, could also quash shipper hopes that some of the East and Gulf coasts’ more expensive ports — among them the Port of New York and New Jersey — might harness automation and technology to cut costs and improve efficiency. The contract also gives union members a $1 an hour base pay increase in four years out of six, increases by $104 million the worker share of container royalties generated, and sets aside money for a defined contribution retirement plan, according to the video. USMX declined to comment on the contract or the video, which appears to be aimed at union members who have the right to vote to ratify the contract. But one USMX official, who asked not to be identified, called the video a “clear and unambiguous representation of the [proposed] agreement.” The ILA-USMX master contract covers wages, medical benefits, carrier-paid container royalties, and other coastwide issues. Bargaining on supplementary local and regional contracts, which cover work rules, pensions, and other port-specific issues, are conducted separately. Union leaders say they want the union’s locales to reach an agreement on local issues before voting on the master agreement. But although the ILA and the Port of New York and New Jersey reached an agreement in early July, not all of the locales met a July 10 deadline by which ILA president Harold Daggett had hoped to get all the local contracts wrapped up, and some are still negotiating. In the video, Dennis, Harold’s son, said he believes the deal is “the best ILA contract ever negotiated” adding that it represents a “giant step forward” for the union. Indeed, the contract goes far deeper into the union-employer relationship than did the West Coast contract extension, which was reached after the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) and the Pacific Maritime Association agreed to limit the negotiations to two basic items, wages and pensions and length of contract. The extension, which lasts until July 2022, does not address hot-buttonissues such as ILWU jurisdiction or automation. West Coast labor disruptions, including a 10-day lockout in 2002 and months of delays during contract negotiations from 2014 to 2015, triggered a shift in cargo volumes away from the West Coast and towards East and Gulf coast ports, which hope to retain the market share they gained. Since 2010, the West Coast’s market share of loaded cargo has dropped from 50.45 percent, to 44.9 percent in 2017, according to PIERS, a sister product of JOC.com. The East Coast share of all loaded containers rose from 41.7 to 46 percent between 2010 and 2017, the PIERS figures show. The Gulf Coast share of all loaded container increased from 6.9 percent to 8.5 percent from 2010 to 2017, according to PIERS. Among the passel of issues addressed in the East Coast and Gulf Coast contract, automation was the most sensitive. Harold Daggett last year listed union opposition to fully automated terminals as the ILA’s top contract issue. And talks broke down in December over what constituted an automated terminal and what is a semi-automated terminal, which the union accepts. The current contract, which runs from 2012 to September 2018, handles the issue by creating a New Technology and Automation Committee of ILA and USMX representatives to evaluate the impact of new technology initiatives, to minimize job losses from them, and provide assistance to any workers displaced by new technology. The committee must agree in order for a new automation projects go through. If no agreement is reached, a second panel will consider the issue, and if no agreement is reached there, the issue will go to binding arbitration. That system is not part of the proposed 2018-2024 contract. Instead, it “emphatically states that no fully automated terminals and no fully automated equipment will be implemented during the life of the contract,” Dennis Daggett says in the video. Fully automated, he says, is defined as “machinery or equipment that is devoid of human interaction.” Whether that results in a complete ban on fully automated terminals may not be clear until it is put to the test, however. Even at TraPac terminal in Los Angeles and Middle Harbor Terminal in Long Beach, which are seen as fully automated and considered to be the most automated in the United States, human involvement is needed for the ship-to-shore cranes and the automated stacking cranes in the yard. And so the terminals are arguably not “devoid of human interaction.” Daggett adds in the video that “management and the ILA agree that no semi-automated equipment, and no technology automation, will be implemented until both parties agree to workforce protections and staffing levels.” At present, Global Container Terminals Bayonne terminal in New York-New Jersey and Virginia International Gateway in Norfolk have some level of automated processes. “Without a doubt the tentative agreement is unique because it’s the only collective bargaining agreement to date, that imposes definite limits on automation while incorporating a workforce protection program for the implementation of new technology,” Daggett says in the video. In addition, Daggett said, the union “has had to recognize that with larger ships coming online, and resulting additional restrictions, the carriers need flexibility when vessels do not arrive as scheduled.” As a result, the proposed master contract requires that each port or district implement a “setback/cancellation policy at waterfront facilities within two hours of the vessel start time.” That would allow terminals to reduce existing contract rules that often require workers to be paid for eight hours if they come to work, regardless of how long they are needed for. title: Center’s projects test sharing of European port data
content: The Hamburg Vessel Coordination Center is launching collaborative projects to help determine if it is meaningful to continue bilateral information exchanges or to replace it with a central data hub to support improved terminal asset utilization and liner route and network planning. (Above: Rotterdam port.) Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. The day is approaching when a central data hub to exchange port call information between Europe’s ports in real time could be set up in an improved traffic planning system — not dissimilar to that currently in place for the Europe’s aviation sector. The Hamburg Vessel Coordination Center (HVCC), which coordinates vessel traffic visiting terminals at the port of Hamburg, is launching new collaborative projects that will help determine if it is meaningful to continue with bilateral exchanges of information around port calls or to replace it with a central data hub to support improved terminal asset utilization and liner route and network planning. “We see this as a more efficient and logical way of doing things that would deliver much more transparency and predictability in the European port call environment and all of the benefits that come with that,” HVCC managing director Gerald Hirt told JOC.com. HVCC rolled out a first-of-its-kind collaborative, data exchange initiative with the port of Rotterdam earlier this year. The initiative involves the exchange of data related to planned and actual arrival and departure times for ships coming from or heading to Hamburg and Rotterdam. HVCC has since been approached by several other European ports seeking information about the initiative. “The direct exchange of data between Hamburg and Rotterdam is the logical first step towards building a network of ports all over Europe,” said Hirt. “This is particularly true when it comes to increasing ability to react to delays and provide both shipping companies and terminals with improved and reliable support for the arrival and dispatching of ships.” Immediately available data means faster reaction and improved coordination to respond to ad-hoc schedule changes. This leads to better allocation of terminal resources and liner route and network planning. Bunker fuel costs can also be reduced and there are environmental benefits as ships can travel slower. An HVCC calculation found that if an 18,000-TEU ship can be informed directly before departure from Rotterdam heading towards Hamburg that it can travel at only 14 knots — instead of an originally planned 18 knots — to reach its destination terminal on schedule, bunker consumption would drop by around 22 tonnes (24.3 tons). This is equivalent to a 66-tonne reduction in carbon dioxide emissions. The direct digital interface replaces the standard cumbersome information exchange by e-mail, phone, and in some cases even fax. HVCC’s Nautical Terminal Collaboration department takes care of traffic planning for large-sized vessels and in 2017 coordinated about 3,000 vessels and distributed 2,250 inbound and outbound traffic plans. Collaborative data sharing for traffic management is a relatively well-developed concept in the airline sector. In Europe, the Airport Collaborative Decision Making (A-CDM) system is overseen by Eurocontrol, an intergovernmental organization focused on creating a ‘Single European Sky’ to address challenges facing European aviation, including capacity and performance. A-CDM focuses on aircraft turnaround and pre-departure sequencing processes. It is now fully implemented in 28 European airports, including the major gateways of Amsterdam; Frankfurt; London (Gatwick and Heathrow); Paris Charles de Gaulle, and a host of smaller airports. On the surface, there seem to be clear parallels with container shipping in terms of the potential benefits of collaborative data-sharing and the variety of inefficiencies it can help to resolve. The benefits of A-CDM for airports, for instance, include improved use of stands/gates, fewer late stand changes, more stable traffic flows, and reduced taxi times. Collaborative data sharing results in shorter runway lines and less congestion on aprons and taxiways. Airlines benefit from better awareness of the status and location of aircraft, more accurate aircraft arrival times, and improved departure sequence information. Fuel burn is also reduced with economic and environmental benefits. The inefficiencies A-CDM addresses are reflective of those plaguing container shipping networks: non-optimized turnaround performance; poor punctuality; lack of transparency in overall airport plans; poor network data that can result in high regulation at facilities; and poor interface between stakeholders with lack of access to real-time systems showing turnaround and delay status. The key challenges in implementing A-CDM in the European airline sector may also hold valuable lessons for container shipping. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), the most challenging aspect in airline sector implementation is the cultural change required among stakeholders. “The human element of A-CDM and the impact it can have on an organization and its employees, should not be underestimated; this is by far the most challenging aspect of an implementation,” the IATA said. The day is approaching when a central data hub to exchange port call information between Europe’s ports in real time could be set up in an improved traffic planning system — not dissimilar to that currently in place for the Europe’s aviation sector. The Hamburg Vessel Coordination Center (HVCC), which coordinates vessel traffic visiting terminals at the port of Hamburg, is launching new collaborative projects that will help determine if it is meaningful to continue with bilateral exchanges of information around port calls or to replace it with a central data hub to support improved terminal asset utilization and liner route and network planning. “We see this as a more efficient and logical way of doing things that would deliver much more transparency and predictability in the European port call environment and all of the benefits that come with that,” HVCC managing director Gerald Hirt told JOC.com. HVCC rolled out a first-of-its-kind collaborative, data exchange initiative with the port of Rotterdam earlier this year. The initiative involves the exchange of data related to planned and actual arrival and departure times for ships coming from or heading to Hamburg and Rotterdam. HVCC has since been approached by several other European ports seeking information about the initiative. “The direct exchange of data between Hamburg and Rotterdam is the logical first step towards building a network of ports all over Europe,” said Hirt. “This is particularly true when it comes to increasing ability to react to delays and provide both shipping companies and terminals with improved and reliable support for the arrival and dispatching of ships.” Immediately available data means faster reaction and improved coordination to respond to ad-hoc schedule changes. title: Damco posts strong revenue growth on volume, new customers
content: The unit, which comprises Damco, Maersk’s freight forwarding operation, and the inland activities of APM Terminals, its global container terminal unit, increased revenue by 6.7 percent to $1.5 billion in the second quarter. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Maersk’s recently established logistics and services unit posted higher profits and revenue in the second quarter driven by increased volumes in its supply chain management and land haulage operations and “significant new customer wins.” The unit, which comprises Damco, Maersk’s freight forwarding operation, and the inland activities of APM Terminals, its global container terminal unit, increased revenue by 6.7 percent to $1.5 billion from $1.4 billion a year earlier. Further, gross profit rose 4.9 percent to $278 million versus $265 million last time. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) slumped, however, by 38 percent to $28 million from $46 million, due to higher IT costs including continued investments in new digital solutions and lower returns in inland services. Ocean forwarding revenue declined by 13 percent to $148 million from $170 million in the second quarter of 2017, mainly due to a 6.8 percent drop in volume to 156,000 TEU from 168,000 TEU. Margins increased 2.7 percent to $180 per TEU, due to the “continuous de-selection of low margin business.” However, this was offset by the lower volume, which reduced gross profit by 4.3 percent to $28 million. Air freight forwarding revenue dipped 2.6 percent to $147 million from $151 million, due to a 12 percent drop on traffic to 44,000 tonnes (48,501 tons) from 50,000 tonnes, reflecting the axing of low margin business and “significant” exposure to China, Maersk said. Inland haulage revenue rose 11 percent to $648 million, driven by a 4.2 percent increase in traffic to 953,000 FEU. Gross profit rose to $16 million from $10 million, boosted by higher volume in Africa and India that were partly offset by higher fuel costs and increased trucking rates in North America, due to a shortage of capacity. The company said it achieved significant customer wins during the quarter, including a large Europe-based fashion company and its first large online retail customer in China. Supply chain management revenue jumped 14 percent year-on-year to $194 million driven by volume growth of 8.9 percent that boosted gross profit by 19 percent to $83 million. Damco also signed a 10-year lease of a six-building logistics campus in the Los Angeles industry area during the quarter to meet growing customer demand for last-mile logistics space in the local market. title: US port portals enter new markets with new features
content: The concept of a single electronic platform for port users is gaining momentum with truckers, beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), and other port users, with GE Transportation’s Port Optimizer at the Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Long Beach achieving breakthroughs as a pacesetter. (Above: the Port of Los Angeles.) Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. GE Transportation and Advent Intermodal Solutions are adding new features to their port portal products and expanding their services to new ports as the concept of a single electronic platform for port users gains momentum with truckers, beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), and other port users. Building upon the lessons learned from last year’s pilot project at the APM Terminal in Los Angeles, GE Transportation introduced last week its Port Optimizer software to neighboring Long Beach, adding features such as match-backs and geo-fencing to improve fluidity in the inland supply chain. Advent, which offers intermodal solutions in New York-New Jersey, Los Angeles-Long Beach, Oakland, the Northwest Seaport Alliance of Seattle-Tacoma, and Port Everglades, Florida, is making its products — including trucker appointments, fee payments, drayage truck registry, dashboard metrics, and cargo key performance indicators — available to additional users throughout its network. Port portals connect shipping lines, marine terminals, truckers, railroads, and equipment providers in a particular gateway through a single platform. Each segment of the supply chain is served by dozens of technology providers whose products improve efficiency within their particular space. However, BCOs, truckers, and other vendors must navigate through numerous websites to get the specific information they seek. The port portal allows access through a single platform. “It involves fewer clicks to the different systems,” said Jennifer Schopfer, vice president and general manager of transport logistics at GE Transportation. Since launching a pilot project last year at the Port of Los Angeles, GE Transportation has concentrated most of its efforts in Southern California. Proving the effectiveness of a community portal in the largest US port complex, which will handle about 16 million TEU this year, could provide a template for other ports looking to use technology to improve cargo fluidity. “Moving goods more efficiently through this important gateway is the key to accommodating future cargo growth. The data collected during this pilot of some of our busiest terminals could help to accomplish this,” said Lou Anne Bynum president of the Long Beach Harbor Commission. Long Beach and Los Angeles, like most major gateways, are contending with increasingly complex supply chains caused by realignment of carrier vessel-sharing alliances, degraded vessel schedule integrity, weather events and congested terminals in Asia and Europe, and rail service issues. GE Transportation and the Port of Los Angeles last year launched the port portal at APM Terminals. Initial users were Maersk Line and Mediterranean Shipping Co., as well as a handful of truckers and BCOs. Regular users now vary over time between 30 and 60, and with the latest expansion efforts “by the end of the year we want to have several hundreds,” Schopfer said. Users of the Port Optimizer software provide data that is shared by others in the supply chain to gain improved shipment visibility from the origin in another country, to the US marine terminal, and on to the importer’s warehouse. Although much of this information is already accessible through individual technology providers via their websites, Port Optimizer seeks to become the single platform for access. The latest rollout connects GeoStamp and MatchBack Systems to Port Optimizer. GeoStamp has been used by truckers in Southern California for the past two years to gain real-time visibility to truck queues at terminal gates and congestion-causing delays within the terminals. MatchBack Systems facilitates street turns, allowing importers and exporters to exchange containers while avoiding the delays involved in returning equipment to busy marine terminals. The Port Optimizer does not replace the use of existing technologies throughout the supply chain, but instead enhances their effectiveness by eliminating the need to move from website to website to access those tools, in effect becoming a system of systems. “We want to integrate with different technology providers to improve the user experience,” Schopfer said. Advent has expanded its eModal appointments in Long Beach to all three terminals operated by SSA Marine, said Allen Thomas, chief strategy officer at Advent. The product also allows truckers the ability to pay all SSA fees via eModal. Making appointments and paying fees upon arrival at the terminal can take 10 minutes to 30 minutes. “By transferring to eModal, the trucker is allowed immediate entry instead of waiting for the EDI message,” Thomas said. The port portal concept is built upon sharing advance notice of cargo arrival so BCOs, truckers, and service providers can marshall the labor and equipment they will need when the vessel arrives in port. The importance of accessing advance notice of cargo arrival 10 days to 14 days in advance is especially important today, given the poor on-time arrival performance of ocean carriers in the major east-west trade lanes, which has been as low as 35 percent this year. Port congestion is also a problem as container discharges from mega-ships with capacities of 10,000-TEU and greater can overwhelm a marine terminal’s yard. Ships of that size now call regularly at ports on both coasts. The complexity of port logistics is also impacted by spot chassis shortages and rail service issues, and these conditions call for a platform that allows BCOs and truckers real-time visibility to shipment information and port conditions each day. Marine terminal operators in Los Angeles-Long Beach this year have encountered delays in train arrivals and departures, especially those terminals served by the Union Pacific, which has acknowledged crew and rail car shortages. Port Optimizer allows BCOs and terminal operators to access notifications of train arrivals to build intermodal trains more efficiently. “We’re working with the railroads and the lines to facilitate more data sharing for both sides,” Schopfer said. After more than a year of testing the pilot at a single terminal in Los Angeles, GE Transportation has now expanded Port Optimizer to all six terminals in Los Angeles and to three of the six terminals in Long Beach: Long Beach Container Terminal, Total Terminals International, and International Transportation Service. GE Transportation is adding new features at a rate of about once each month. Advent is expanding its service offerings up the West Coast and in New York-New Jersey and Port Everglades, Florida. Advent has expanded its eModal Trucker Check module from Seattle to four terminals in Tacoma, and has expanded its Oakland community portal project to include dashboard metrics and cargo KPIs, as well as integrated turn times for all gates. Advent has also expanded its eModal portal for customers in Port Everglades. Advent serves all of the terminals in New York-New Jersey, and continues to upgrade the service offerings through TIPS, the Terminal Information Portal System, Thomas said. With US containerized imports projected to increase more than 5 percent to 6 percent over last year’s record performance, ports must turn increasingly to technology and process improvements to handle the growing cargo volumes that are stressing the international supply chain. With land dedicated to port expansion at a premium or non-existent in many gateways, ports must increase the density of their operations, and technology is seen as the most efficient way to move growing container volumes on the existing footprint. Supply chain optimization through the use of technology and process improvements was a focus of the Federal Maritime Commission under Mario Cordero, who is now executive director of the Port of Long Beach. The Port Optimizer is expected to play an important role in this effort in Southern California. “We are always searching for new means toward improving operational efficiencies in the supply chain as it moves through this port complex. We look forward to observing Port Optimizer in action,” Cordero said. The ultimate goal of Port Optimizer and Advent is to incorporate predictive analytics into their platforms. Schopfer said the industry has yet to develop true predictive analytics software, but allowing all members of the supply chain to gain visibility to shipments from the foreign port of exit to the US terminal and on to the import warehouse is a step in that direction. title: Analysis: Digital bill of lading holds manifold benefits
content: E-commerce, led by Amazon, and couriers UPS, FedEx, and the US Postal Service are years ahead of shipping, including trucking logistics, with regard to digital bill of lading. A shift is long overdue and would offer multiple benefits. Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Shippers across all industries and in all parts of the country are feeling the impact of increased transportation costs. There are many reasons for the imbalance in demand and supply that is driving up the cost. However, it seems everyone — including shippers, carriers, and analysts — wants to blame the cost increases on the driver shortage. It is easy to associate this pain to an external factor out of one’s control. While there are many areas shippers and carriers can control that impact the cost of transportation service, this commentary focuses on the extensive use of paper bill of lading (BOL) used to tender less-than-truckload (LTL) shipments. The practice of using the paper bill of lading dates back to the period prior to deregulation of the industry. In the 1970s, shippers used typewriters to generate business documents and then mailed them via the first-class mail service provided by the US Post Office to be received by the recipient in three to five days. In contrast, shippers now generate written documents via computers or mobile phones, transmitting them via the internet, with recipients getting them within seconds. This transformation from paper to digital media has not been lost on the transportation industry. The parcel carriers have gained huge traction with shippers transmitting parcel details in advance of the pickup. The parcel details include origin and destination address (commercial or residential), parcel weight, special services, and much more. With new emphasis on dimensional charges, shippers may provide parcel dimensions as well. So, why have the parcel carriers put such emphasis on getting parcel details in an electronic format prior to the pickup? There are many operational advantages, including that it ensures the pickup vehicle has adequate capacity for the expected number of parcels, it avoids billing errors, it prevents misrouting, and it helps carriers achieve higher cube load factor in the intercity linehaul network. The operational needs to get shipment details in advance are even greater for the LTL industry because of the diversity of shipments handled — rolls of carpet, overhead garage doors, vehicle transmissions, auto body parts, pallets of boxes, and farm implements, etc. Despite greater value in getting shipment data in electronic format and in advance, the LTL carriers have not pushed for elimination of the paper bill of lading. On the contrary, many LTL sales representatives still sign up new customers by handing them a stack of paper BOLs to use their service. In addition, while shippers are demanding real-time visibility from the carriers on the delivery status of every load, they refuse to do their part of converting from paper to digital BOL. No wonder, after 20 years of seeking shipper cooperation to convert paper BOL to electronic, the LTL industry still handles about 75 percent of shipments tendered using paper. In contrast, UPS and FedEx handle less than 5 percent of parcels that are tendered using paper air bill. This contrast can only be fathomed when the percentages are converted into absolute numbers. For benchmark, the parcel industry handles more than 47 million parcels on an average day. With 95 percent of parcels tendered via electronic manifest, the shippers are using digital media to tender more than 44 million parcels per day. With the LTL industry handling 640,000 shipments per day, the LTL shippers tender 40 million shipments in a whole year via electronic method. This full-year figure for LTL shipments is less than a one-day figure for the parcel carriers. With many shippers using LTL and parcel services, it is logical that most shippers can easily convert from paper to digital media for tendering LTL shipments. The benefit of the electronic bill of lading has far-reaching impact on helping the carriers control the cost of LTL service. The pickup operation still utilizes just the floor area of the trailer, which results in use of longer trailers and thereby about 50 percent cubic capacity utilization of pickup trailers. In contrast, parcel carriers utilize more than 80 percent of the cubic capacity of the package vans in the pickup operation. For the linehaul, with huge variation in the shape and size of shipments, LTL carriers have a greater need than parcel carriers to gain the physical attributes of shipments in advance to achieve better cube utilization of the intercity linehaul trailers. While ignoring the needs of LTL carriers to convert paper to electronic media, the same shippers are sending notices to their suppliers requiring them to sign up for ACH payment to avoid the cost of mailing hardcopy checks. This requirement is primarily to eliminate the administrative cost and postage of mailing a check. The shippers fail to realize that the cost of handling paper BOL is many times more than the cost of mailing a check. Yet, the same shippers fail to comply with LTL carriers’ request to use the electronic manifest and to provide advance transmission of shipment details. No doubt, the parcel carriers have had greater success in this regard partly due to the top three carriers controlling 90 percent of the market. In contrast, the fragmented LTL industry created opportunity for shippers to leverage one carrier against the other to resist dropping the use of paper BOL. With tight capacity in LTL and truckload segments, now is the perfect time for LTL carriers to target reduction of paper BOL from 75 percent to below 50 percent by 2019. Satish Jindel is president of SJ Consulting Group, a consulting firm focused on the transportation sector with offices in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and Jaipur, India. The parcel details include origin and destination address (commercial or residential), parcel weight, special services, and much more. With new emphasis on dimensional charges, shippers may provide parcel dimensions as well. So, why have the parcel carriers put such emphasis on getting parcel details in an electronic format prior to the pickup? There are many operational advantages, including that it ensures the pickup vehicle has adequate capacity for the expected number of parcels, it avoids billing errors, it prevents misrouting, and it helps carriers achieve higher cube load factor in the intercity linehaul network. The operational needs to get shipment details in advance are even greater for the LTL industry because of the diversity of shipments handled — rolls of carpet, overhead garage doors, vehicle transmissions, auto body parts, pallets of boxes, and farm implements, etc. Despite greater value in getting shipment data in electronic format and in advance, the LTL carriers have not pushed for elimination of the paper bill of lading. On the contrary, many LTL sales representatives still sign up new customers by handing them a stack of paper BOLs to use their service. In addition, while shippers are demanding real-time visibility from the carriers on the delivery status of every load, they refuse to do their part of converting from paper to digital BOL. No wonder, after 20 years of seeking shipper cooperation to convert paper BOL to electronic, the LTL industry still handles about 75 percent of shipments tendered using paper. In contrast, UPS and FedEx handle less than 5 percent of parcels that are tendered using paper air bill. This contrast can only be fathomed when the percentages are converted into absolute numbers. For benchmark, the parcel industry handles more than 47 million parcels on an average day. With 95 percent of parcels tendered via electronic manifest, the shippers are using digital media to tender more than 44 million parcels per day. With the LTL industry handling 640,000 shipments per day, the LTL shippers tender 40 million shipments in a whole year via electronic method. This full-year figure for LTL shipments is less than a one-day figure for the parcel carriers. With many shippers using LTL and parcel services, it is logical that most shippers can easily convert from paper to digital media for tendering LTL shipments. The benefit of the electronic bill of lading has far-reaching impact on helping the carriers control the cost of LTL service. The pickup operation still utilizes just the floor area of the trailer, which results in use of longer trailers and thereby about 50 percent cubic capacity utilization of pickup trailers. In contrast, parcel carriers utilize more than 80 percent of the cubic capacity of the package vans in the pickup operation. For the linehaul, with huge variation in the shape and size of shipments, LTL carriers have a greater need than parcel carriers to gain the physical attributes of shipments in advance to achieve better cube utilization of the intercity linehaul trailers. While ignoring the needs of LTL carriers to convert paper to electronic media, the same shippers are sending notices to their suppliers requiring them to sign up for ACH payment to avoid the cost of mailing hardcopy checks. This requirement is primarily to eliminate the administrative cost and postage of mailing a check. The shippers fail to realize that the cost of handling paper BOL is many times more than the cost of mailing a check. Yet, the same shippers fail to comply with LTL carriers’ request to use the electronic manifest and to provide advance transmission of shipment details. No doubt, the parcel carriers have had greater success in this regard partly due to the top three carriers controlling 90 percent of the market. In contrast, the fragmented LTL industry created opportunity for shippers to leverage one carrier against the other to resist dropping the use of paper BOL. With tight capacity in LTL and truckload segments, now is the perfect time for LTL carriers to target reduction of paper BOL from 75 percent to below 50 percent by 2019. Satish Jindel is president of SJ Consulting Group, a consulting firm focused on the transportation sector with offices in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and Jaipur, India. title: Penske joins global effort to charge e-trucks
content: The discussion of electric vehicles, like electricity, is everywhere. But without standardized charging stations and network, e-truck functions will be limited, and that’s why Penske this week joined a worldwide industry alliance focused on developing a universal charging standard for commercial vehicles. Photo credit: Penske. Electric trucks such as the Tesla Semi, with its aerodynamic, futuristic design, draw attention. What doesn’t get as much attention, however, are the charging systems that will power them. Without the required “wires and plugs,” however, shipper dreams of using cheaper, abundant, zero-emissions electricity to power commercial trucks will remain just dreams. “The charging piece has been left out of the conversation, but from our perspective, it was one of the first things we thought about,” said Bill Combs, director of connected fleet at Penske Truck Leasing. “There are several OEMs [original equipment manufacturers] working on this technology, and if they all have unique charging systems, we’re going to have a real problem.” That “we” includes shippers who increasingly see electric vehicles (EVs) as a means of meeting carbon-reduction goals set by corporate sustainability plans, and trucking operators who would like to plug into the grid rather than top off their tanks with increasingly expensive diesel. For-hire trucking companies and shipper-run private fleets don’t have just one make, model, and model year vehicle. “The idea of multiple charging standards and different plugs and adaptors for different kinds of heavy- and medium-duty trucks is pretty overwhelming.” Combs said. But that’s what Penske and other truck lessors and operators could face if they don’t act now. Penske Truck Leasing this week joined the Charging Interface Initiative (CharIN), a worldwide industry alliance focused on promoting the combined charging system (CCS) developed by members of CharIN as the global standard for charging all types of EVs. CharIN’s CCS standard is supported by the Society of Automotive Engineers. Penske’s role will be to help promote EV charging standards for commercial vehicles in North America by participating in CharIN’s High Power Charging for Commercial Vehicles Task Force. Penske is the first fleet operator to join the task force, said Oleg Logvinov, spokesperson for CharIN in North America and president and CEO of IoTecha. There’s a lot for Penske and partners, such as IoTecha — which is focused on integrating EV charging systems with the electric grid — to do. There’s a great difference between charging an electric car in a residential garage overnight and charging a medium- or heavy-duty truck. When it comes to commercial vehicles, charging systems require higher voltages and amperages. “The idea is that if the small and large players get together and agree on where this should go, what kind of plug is needed, what voltage levels, what communications standards between the charger and truck, it will make things a lot easier,” said Combs. “It’s not a third-party establishing a standard, but the industry getting together to see what the best standard should be.” Electric cars, he said, can “trickle charge” overnight. But energy requirements for cars and trucks are quite different. “The passenger cars are used less than 10 percent of the day, while trucks are going to be used a large percentage of the day,” and may have to be fully recharged, Combs said. “To charge a truck faster, you need higher voltage and more amperage.” Magnify that problem by 100 trucks charging at one facility overnight, and perhaps hundreds of facilities across a major metropolitan area charging trucks, and electric utilities will face a major challenge. “There’s an important relationship between manufacturers of charging systems and trucks and the utilities to ensure there’s enough electricity for these fleets of trucks,” he said. “There’s electricity everywhere, but how do you get the right amount of electricity to those trucks that they need to run on any given day,” said Combs. The solution may call for more charging stations in unusual places, not just truck terminals. “A lot of trucks end up at loading docks, and if you install chargers there, you could have opportunity charging throughout the day.” The future shape of the commercial EV charging network really depends on the future use of commercial EVs. They are most likely to first succeed in localized or short-haul applications just as store delivery, pickup and delivery, and drayage. Penske will begin testing electric trucks built by Daimler Truck North America’s Freightliner division in such applications this autumn. The truck lessor has already logged more than 100 million miles with EVs, according to Sherry Sanger, senior vice president of marketing. Regulatory pressures in Europe and California, as well as volatile fuel costs, are a factor behind the global surge of interests in EVs, she said. Interest in EVs has reached heights not seen since the 1920s, when electric delivery trucks and charging stations were a common sight in large US cities. Improvements in combustion engine design, including the invention of the electric starter, eventually pulled the plug on those e-trucks. A hundred years later, electric trucks appear to be in line for a revival. Contact William B. Cassidy at bill.cassidy@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @willbcassidy. title: JNPT officials expect gate automation to boost productivity
content: Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust. Photo credit: Nhava Sheva Container Operators' Welfare Association. Authorities at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) — which handles the majority of India’s container trade — are hopeful that truck turn times and overall productivity rates will improve substantially with the Sept. 1 scheduled completion of the final phase of gate automation upgrades at the port. State-owned Jawaharlal Nehru Port Container Terminal (JNPCT) will transition to a more-advanced electronic, radio frequency identification technology gate operating procedure, joining its privately operated peers that have taken the lead on digitization at the public harbor. With the above in mind, JNPT has distributed a “standard operating procedure” to various stakeholders — such as shipper trade groups and logistics providers, along with steps to be followed for inter-terminal truck movement. “The stakeholders will ensure that all the tractor trailers coming to the JNPCT have drivers and tractor trailers registered before coming. The registration has to be through E-Form 13 portal, for which access will be given to authorized parties,” the port advisory stated. The Form 13 documentation has been a cumbersome, manual process with extensive paperwork, which typically creates long delays/congestion at port gates. To get around those issues, authorities implemented the inter-terminal transfer method in February 2015, by which truckers are able to drop off laden export containers at one terminal and pick up import units from any of the other neighboring facilities. This program — somewhat akin to mixed-train handling — is essentially intended to eliminate unnecessary multiple gate transactions and, in turn, enhance gate productivity. That single entry-exit process accounts for a considerable portion of port volume/activity, with July numbers pegged at 15,765 truck trips and 20,701 gate transactions, according to new data released by the port. In addition, JNPT argues that the program offers substantial cost savings, due to reduction in fuel consumption and related operational/logistics advantages. JNPCT’s peers APM Terminals-operated Gateway Terminals India and DP World Nhava Sheva, which includes Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal and Nhava Sheva (India) Gateway Terminal, have already decreased truck turn times considerably with paperless gate operations. New concessionaire PSA International-operated Bharat Mumbai Container Terminals is also equipped with automated gates. With all terminal gates operating digitally at full speed, officials expected productivity and cost benefits to continue to show improved results — results that are critical in India’s hyper-competitive trade market. Further, although there is no denying that JNPT has made great strides in reducing operational inefficiencies via a slew of ease-of-doing-business measures and digitization, intermittent gate closings — as a result of volume surges and inherent landside infrastructure bottlenecks — remain a concern for exporters/importers who use the port. In addition, local transport authorities have imposed temporary restrictions on truck movement in/around JNPT to facilitate major road improvement projects under way. This ad-hoc step will also likely cause truck buildups at the port, where the bulk of freight — estimated at roughly 85 percent — is handled by road. JNPCT reportedly operates 11 truck gates — five for exports, four for imports, and two for empty movement — and has a 1.35 million-TEU annual capacity. title: Carriers embrace direct rate feeds to meet shipper transparency demands
content: Both freight intermediaries and ocean carriers are under pressure to avoid sitting on obsolete rate data, pressure that’s been placed on them by the rise of transparent freight pricing models. (Above: Maersk Eureka at the Port of Oakland.) Photo credit: Shutterstock.com. Maersk Line’s joining of Hapag-Lloyd in tapping CargoSphere to provide direct rate feeds to its freight forwarder and non-vessel-operating common carrier (NVOCC) customers illustrates building pressure on both container lines to provide dynamic pricing and on intermediaries to quote to shippers more quickly. The world’s largest container line will begin using CargoSphere’s system to disseminate its rates in a real-time, automated fashion. That provides forwarders and NVOCCs with the opportunity to get to those customer rates that are essentially dynamic and more accurate. The world’s largest container line will begin using CargoSphere’s system to disseminate its rates in a real-time, automated fashion. That provides forwarders and NVOCCs with the opportunity to get to those customer rates that are essentially dynamic and more accurate. This is particularly pertinent to shippers that don't have the volume or leverage to negotiate long-term rates and capacity commitments with ocean carriers. Both freight intermediaries and liner carriers are under pressure to avoid sitting on obsolete rate data, pressure that’s been placed on them by the rise of transparent freight pricing models, like marketplaces and digital forwarders. Established forwarders and NVOCCs have essentially had to work around the issue that ocean carriers don't provide them direct rate feeds by either taking hours or days to respond to rate requests or hoping that carrier rates don’t change significantly and wipe away their margins. CargoSphere, which was acquired in 2017 by the enterprise forwarding software provider WiseTech Global, gives forwarders and NVOCCs tools to manage and share contract rates. In March, the company set up a similar feed with Hapag-Lloyd, enabling the German container line to share rates directly with its customers. The concept of the direct feed is to get away from the use of static rate sheets, which may contain obsolete rates by the time a forwarder or NVOCC receives a rate request from a shipper. CargoSphere managing director Neil Barni, who founded the company in 1999, spent more than a decade pushing to get carriers to provide his company such direct feeds. He finally succeeded in 2016, when he got United Arab Shipping Company to provide its customer SEKO Logistics with a direct rate feed. UASC was eventually acquired by Hapag-Lloyd. “Digital ocean rate distribution removes many of the manual processes that have acted as a drag on rates management for many years,” Barni said in a statement. “Having Maersk Line go live on the CargoSphere platform is a big signal of its intent to transform its own key processes and the industry solutions it brings to market.” The concept of the direct feed is to get away from the use of static rate sheets, which may contain obsolete rates by the time a forwarder or NVOCC receives a rate request from a shipper. Forwarders generally oversee the movement of goods on behalf of BCOs, while NVOCCs act as the carrier to BCOs, contracting for capacity with carriers and then selling that capacity to shippers. Often a company is a forwarder and an NVOCC. The direct feed is critical to the ability of forwarders and NVOCCs to compete for shipper business as it solves a pain point that they often face — the lag in time to get shippers a quote, or the inaccuracy of a quote (since the rate may have changed from the time it was uploaded to the forwarder’s or NVOCC’s system to the time that intermediary provides a quote to its customer). This has profit margin implications for those forwarders and NVOCCs, who are already battling against a persistently low-rate ocean freight environment. If a rate changes by, say, $100 per FEU from the time the carrier sends its rates by spreadsheet to a forwarder and those rates are uploaded by the forwarder to the time the forwarder quotes a price to the shipper, that could wipe away a sizable portion of its margin. The freight rate management software market as a whole has been gaining steam — witness WiseTech’s purchase of CargoSphere — as forwarders and NVOCCs realize the critical role such systems play in allowing them to respond to rising shipper expectations. Among the other major providers of such systems are Catapult, Info-X Software, and Freightgate. INTTRA, which partners with many of the providers in the market, also signaled in May its intent to build such a system. Online rate marketplace providers and digital forwarders — who put a premium on making price discovery a key feature of their service offering — have upped the ante by promising shippers instant quotes. Barni has argued that freight forwarders don’t benefit from such open price discovery and thus need a more private platform from which to quote to customers that they are trying to form long-term relationships with. In many ways, freight rate and contract management software is designed to be a bulwark against the more transparent pricing environment championed by a new breed of freight forwarding startups. More broadly, however, Maersk’s and Hapag-Lloyd’s willingness to provide a direct rate feed to its customers is a signal that carriers are also ready to convey dynamic pricing data downstream, whereas they have traditionally more closely guarded such information (or provided it by a less electronically structured means). CargoSphere previously set out to get around the lack of the direct data feeds from carriers by providing its electronic Smart Upload and Diagnostics Solution (eSUDS), which helped it map flat files (like carrier rate PDFs) and turn that data into electronic rates in its rate sharing network. Under the system, a carrier creates a file of new or exported rates that is sent to CargoShere, where the eSUDS system detects the new carrier rate file and initiates the diagnostics process, the company said. The eSUDS system reads the carrier file, converts carrier codes and data structures into standards set by the company’s Rate Mesh, and places them in the cloud for direct distribution to the customer. The company said the direct feed will go through eSUDS, but it clearly allows for a more efficient way to convey rates from carrier to shipper via the intermediary. CargoSphere said the feed also complements Maersk’s existing online quoting solutions. Contact Eric Johnson at eric.johnson@ihsmarkit.com and follow him on Twitter: @LogTechEric.
